items.t: Oilbirds and some swiftlets use echoes to fly through caves and trees at night.
items.d: This echolocation is simpler than a bat's or a dolphin's, but it helps them steer.

items.t: Sounds at or below 70 dBA are unlikely to harm hearing, even over a long time.
items.d: Normal conversation is about 60 to 70 dBA, inside this safer range.

items.t: The Doppler effect is a pitch change when the sound source and the listener move relative to each other.
items.d: The source can keep the same note. Motion changes the pitch that you hear.

items.t: Count the seconds between lightning and thunder. Divide by 3 to estimate kilometres.
items.d: Count 6 gives an estimate of 2 kilometres (6 divided by 3), or 1.2 miles (6 divided by 5).

items.t: A passing siren sounds higher while it approaches, then lower as it moves away.
items.d: The siren keeps the same note. The Doppler effect changes the pitch you hear.

items.t: A sonic boom is made when waves from a faster-than-sound plane pile into one shock.
items.d: The waves stack together until they become one sharp shock that you hear as a boom.

items.t: A whip's crack is a tiny sonic boom. The tip moves faster than sound.
items.d: The faster-than-sound tip creates a small shock wave that we hear as a crack.

items.t: Folds in the outer ear help you tell if a sound is in front, behind, above, or below.
items.d: Those folds change the sound a little, and your brain turns that into a direction.

items.t: Your voice starts with two small folds in your throat that open and close very fast, letting out puffs of air.
items.d: Those puffs of air make sound waves that travel out of your mouth.

items.t: When you whisper, your vocal folds do not vibrate. The rushing air makes a noisy hiss instead.
items.d: Try humming, then whispering. Put your fingers on your throat to feel the difference.

items.t: Your muscles cannot shake your vocal folds directly. They vibrate far too fast for muscles to keep up.
items.d: The air flowing past the folds makes them vibrate, not a muscle twitch.

items.t: Your mouth and throat boost some sound frequencies more than others. These boosts are called formants.
items.d: Changing your mouth shape changes the sound, even when your pitch stays the same.

items.t: Vowels like 'ee' and 'ah' sound different mainly because of the first two formants made by your mouth shape.
items.d: Say 'ee' then 'ah' slowly and feel your tongue and lips move.

items.t: How high or low a voice sounds depends on the length, size and tension of the vocal folds.
items.d: These features affect how fast the folds vibrate.

items.t: Vocal folds vibrate about 125 times a second in a grown man, 210 in a grown woman and over 300 in children.
items.d: That means a child's vocal folds can vibrate more than 300 times in one second.

items.t: Children have higher voices because their vocal folds are much shorter than those of adults.
items.d: Shorter vocal folds can vibrate faster, which makes a higher sound.

items.t: Vocal folds are about 6 to 8 mm long at birth. By the teen years they are about 8 to 16 mm.
items.d: As the folds grow longer, the voice usually gets lower.

items.t: Harmonics are tones whose frequencies are whole-number multiples of the lowest tone, called the fundamental.
items.d: If the lowest tone vibrates 100 times a second, the next ones are 200, 300 and 400.

items.t: The second harmonic sounds exactly one octave higher than the fundamental.
items.d: An octave is the jump between two notes with the same name, like one C to the next C.

items.t: An instrument's tone colour, called timbre, mostly depends on how strong each of its harmonics is.
items.d: That is why a flute and a trumpet sound different even on the very same note.

items.t: A clarinet has weaker even-numbered harmonics than a saxophone, so they sound different.
items.d: A saxophone's tube is cone-shaped.

items.t: Your brain can hear a note's pitch even if its lowest harmonic is missing. This is the missing fundamental.
items.d: Your brain fills in the pitch from the other harmonics.

items.t: A piano makes sound when a key makes a felt-covered hammer hit a string.
items.d: The hammer bounces back right away so the string can ring freely.

items.t: Piano string vibrations pass through a bridge to a big wooden soundboard, which makes them louder.
items.d: The soundboard pushes on lots of air, like a big wooden loudspeaker.

items.t: Most piano notes have three strings struck together. The lowest bass notes have only one or two.
items.d: Thick, heavy bass strings are strong enough to make a loud sound alone.

items.t: When you let go of a piano key, a damper presses on the string and stops the sound.
items.d: The right pedal lifts all the dampers so notes keep ringing.

items.t: A modern piano has 88 black and white keys.
items.d: That is 52 white keys and 36 black keys.

items.t: A guitar string is stretched between two fixed points. When it vibrates, it makes sound.
items.d: Plucking a string moves it back and forth many times each second.

items.t: On an acoustic guitar the hollow wooden body makes the quiet string sound much louder.
items.d: Without the body, a plucked string would be very quiet.

items.t: Pressing a guitar string against a fret makes the string shorter, so the note sounds higher.
items.d: A shorter vibrating string usually vibrates faster, which makes a higher note.

items.t: An electric guitar's pickups turn string vibrations into electric signals. An amplifier makes them louder.
items.d: The solid body does not need to be hollow, because the amplifier does the loud part.

items.t: A bass guitar is usually tuned E, A, D, G, an octave below the bottom four strings of a six-string guitar.
items.d: Longer, thicker strings make lower sounds.

items.t: A violinist draws a bow across a string. The string vibrates and makes a long, steady sound.
items.d: Bowing can keep the note going.

items.t: Bow hair is rubbed with rosin so it grips. Friction between hair and string makes the string vibrate.
items.d: Without rosin, the bow would slide over the string and stay quiet.

items.t: The four violin strings are tuned a perfect fifth apart: G, D, A and E.
items.d: Going from one string to the next goes up by the same musical step.

items.t: A violin's bridge carries the strings' vibrations into the hollow wooden body.
items.d: Inside, a small wooden soundpost helps shape how the body vibrates.

items.t: A flute makes sound when a stream of air across a hole makes the air inside the tube vibrate.
items.d: You can try this by blowing gently across the top of an empty bottle.

items.t: Opening and closing a flute's finger holes changes the length of its vibrating air. That changes the note.
items.d: A shorter air column gives a higher note.

items.t: Recorders and tin whistles are called fipple flutes. A duct sends air onto a sharp edge.
items.d: The duct does the job that a flute player's lips do.

items.t: Blowing harder on a flute can make it jump to a higher harmonic. This is called overblowing.
items.d: The same tube can play higher notes without changing its length.

items.t: Flutes with hand-bored holes from the Stone Age are among the oldest known musical instruments.
items.d: People were making music with tubes and holes long before cities existed.

items.t: A whistle makes a nearly pure tone, a clean note with very few extra harmonics.
items.d: A whistle's sound comes from a stream of air hitting a sharp edge.

items.t: A drum is a stretched skin, called a drumhead, over a shell. Hitting the skin makes it vibrate and make sound.
items.d: The drumhead affects how a drum sounds more than any other part.

items.t: Tightening a drumhead makes the drum's pitch higher.
items.d: A tight skin springs back faster, so it vibrates faster.

items.t: A drum with a larger shell diameter usually has a lower pitch.
items.d: A big bass drum booms low, while a small drum often sounds higher.

items.t: The wooden or metal shell of a drum vibrates with the skin and can make the sound louder.
items.d: A drum without a shell would sound much thinner and quieter.

items.t: A snare drum has wires stretched across one or both heads. They buzz when the drum is hit.
items.d: That buzz gives a snare drum its crisp, rattling sound.

items.t: Timpani are big orchestra drums. A foot pedal lets players quickly change them to exact notes.
items.d: Pressing the pedal tightens the skin, which raises the pitch.

items.t: Symphony orchestras usually tune to the note A at 440 vibrations per second.
items.d: Players tune their instruments to this shared reference.

items.t: Equal temperament, common in Western music, splits an octave into twelve equal musical steps.
items.d: Each step changes frequency by the same ratio.

items.t: Two almost-matching notes make a wobbling sound called beats. The beats slow down as the notes get closer.
items.d: Tuners listen for the beats to stop. Then the notes match.

items.t: A tuning fork is a U-shaped bar of springy metal, usually steel, with two prongs.
items.d: When you hit it, the prongs move back and forth and make a clear sound.

items.t: A tuning fork makes a very pure tone, mostly at just one frequency.
items.d: That is why musicians use one as a clean reference note.

items.t: A tuning fork's pitch depends on the length and mass of its prongs.
items.d: Longer prongs vibrate slower, so they make a lower note.

items.t: A brass player's buzzing lips make the air inside the instrument's tube vibrate.
items.d: The tube makes the buzz louder and shapes it into a musical note.

items.t: Pressing a trumpet valve sends air through extra tubing. The tube gets longer and the note gets lower.
items.d: A longer tube means a lower note, just like a longer organ pipe.

items.t: Each organ pipe plays only one pitch, so a pipe organ needs a lot of pipes.
items.d: Longer pipes sound lower, and shorter pipes sound higher.

items.t: An organ can hold a note as long as the key is pressed, because air keeps flowing through the pipes.
items.d: A piano note fades away, but an organ note can last as long as you hold it.

items.t: Clarinets and saxophones use one reed. Oboes use two reeds that vibrate against each other.
items.d: Most reeds are cut from a tall, tough cane plant.

items.t: Every bar of a xylophone is tuned to a note of a musical scale.
items.d: Shorter bars sound higher and longer bars sound lower.

items.t: A loudspeaker has a coil that moves back and forth when an electric signal flows through it.
items.d: A permanent magnet makes the strong magnetic field the coil moves in.

items.t: A speaker's light cone is attached to the coil. As the coil moves, the cone pushes air and makes sound waves.
items.d: If you touch a loud speaker lightly, you can feel the cone shaking.

items.t: A woofer plays low sounds and a tweeter plays high ones. A crossover sends each sound to the right one.
items.d: Big drivers handle low sounds well. Small drivers handle high sounds well.

items.t: Headphones began because telephone operators needed their hands free.
items.d: Early headsets let them take calls and work at the same time.

items.t: Active noise-cancelling headphones can reduce outside noise by 20 decibels or more.
items.d: They play a sound wave that cancels some of the noise.

items.t: American physicist Wallace Sabine did the first modern scientific study of how sound behaves in rooms.
items.d: He used what he learned to help design Symphony Hall in Boston.

items.t: Sound bouncing around a room makes standing waves and natural resonances.
items.d: Singing in a small bathroom can make some notes sound extra loud.

items.t: Diffusers scatter sound in many directions, which can make a room sound better.
items.d: Concert halls often have bumpy walls for this reason.

items.t: Reverberation time is how long a sound takes to fade by 60 decibels.
items.d: A big stone church has a long reverberation time. A carpeted bedroom has a short one.

items.t: Rooms for speech need a short reverberation time so words stay clear.
items.d: Too much echo mixes the words together, so they are hard to understand.

items.t: Sound reflections less than about 50 milliseconds apart blend into reverberation, not echoes.
items.d: A true echo needs a longer gap, like shouting at a far-away wall.

items.t: White sunlight is a mix of all the rainbow colours.
items.d: Sunlight looks white, but those colours are mixed together.

items.t: Air scatters blue light more strongly than most other colours.
items.d: That scattered blue light makes the daytime sky look blue.

items.t: Blue light has shorter waves than red light.
items.d: The shorter blue waves scatter more easily in air.

items.t: The sky often looks pale blue or white near the horizon.
items.d: Light from the horizon crosses more air, mixing more scattered colours.

items.t: Sunsets look red and yellow because much of the blue light scatters away.
items.d: Sunlight crosses more air when the Sun is low.

items.t: Tiny particles of dust in the air can make a sunset look even redder.
items.d: The particles scatter some of the blue light away.

items.t: Mars has an orange or reddish daytime sky.
items.d: The sky looks that way because of fine dust in the thin air.

items.t: A sunset on Mars can look blue-gray around the Sun.
items.d: That is very different from the red sunsets often seen on Earth.

items.t: Violet scatters more than blue, yet our sky usually looks blue.
items.d: Our eyes are less sensitive to violet, and sunlight contains less of it.

items.t: Human eyes see wavelengths from about 380 to 700 nanometres.
items.d: Visible light is only a narrow part of the full spectrum.

items.t: Violet has the shortest waves in visible light, while red has the longest.
items.d: Each rainbow colour has its own band of wavelengths.

items.t: A prism separates white light because each colour bends differently.
items.d: The separated colours form a rainbow-like band.

items.t: Isaac Newton used a prism to study how visible light bends.
items.d: He found that different colours bend at slightly different angles.

items.t: Hotter glowing objects shine with bluer light than cooler ones.
items.d: The cooler star Betelgeuse looks redder than the hotter star Rigel.

items.t: Cone cells in your eyes help you detect visible light and colour.
items.d: They act like tiny receivers tuned to visible wavelengths.

items.t: The three primary colours of light are red, green and blue.
items.d: Mixing these lights in different amounts makes many colours.

items.t: Red light mixed with green light looks yellow.
items.d: Light mixing follows different rules from paint mixing.

items.t: Red, green and blue light mixed together can look white.
items.d: Screens blend these three colours to make white areas.

items.t: Many screen pixels contain tiny red, green and blue parts.
items.d: From the couch, the three parts blend into one colour.

items.t: A magnifying lens can reveal the red, green and blue parts of a screen pixel.
items.d: Without magnification, your eyes usually blend them together.

items.t: Light and paint follow different colour-mixing rules.
items.d: Light adds colours, while paint and ink remove parts of the light.

items.t: Colour printers use cyan, magenta and yellow as primary inks.
items.d: They combine these inks to print many other colours.

items.t: Cyan ink absorbs red light, magenta absorbs green, and yellow absorbs blue.
items.d: The light that is not absorbed reaches your eyes.

items.t: Printers add black ink to sharpen pictures and use less coloured ink.
items.d: Cyan, magenta, yellow and black are called CMYK.

items.t: Primary colours depend on what you are mixing.
items.d: Light uses red, green and blue. Printing uses cyan, magenta and yellow.

items.t: No real set of paints or lights can make every possible colour.
items.d: Each colour-mixing system has a limited range.

items.t: Humans usually have three kinds of colour-sensing cone cells.
items.d: The three cone types respond to short, medium and long wavelengths.

items.t: Rod cells help you see in very dim light but do little for colour vision.
items.d: Colours become harder to tell apart when a room is very dark.

items.t: Dogs have two kinds of cone cells, while humans usually have three.
items.d: Dogs can tell blue, green and yellow apart, but not orange from red.

items.t: Many birds can see ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see.
items.d: Some birds have four kinds of cone cells.

items.t: Bees can see ultraviolet light but are not sensitive to red.
items.d: Their colour vision covers a different range from ours.

items.t: A human eye can tell apart about 10 million colours.
items.d: Your three cone types work together to create this rich colour vision.

items.t: Pink and magenta are not single colours in the visible spectrum.
items.d: They appear when your visual system combines different wavelengths.

items.t: Ultraviolet and infrared sit just beyond the light humans can see.
items.d: Bees see ultraviolet, and some snakes can sense infrared heat.

items.t: Screens make magenta by mixing equal amounts of red and blue light.
items.d: Turn off the green part of a white RGB pixel to leave magenta.

items.t: A green picture can leave a magenta afterimage when you look away.
items.d: Magenta and green are complementary colours.

items.t: An afterimage can remain briefly after the original picture is gone.
items.d: Activity in the retina continues for a short time.

items.t: Red-green colour blindness makes red and green hard to tell apart.
items.d: It is the most common kind of colour vision difference.

items.t: A rarer colour vision difference makes blue and yellow hard to separate.
items.d: Different colour vision differences affect different colours.

items.t: Colour blindness usually runs in families, and most people with it are born with it.
items.d: It changes how some colours are told apart.

items.t: A pixel is the smallest controllable part of a digital picture.
items.d: The word pixel comes from picture element.

items.t: One megapixel means one million pixels.
items.d: A 2 megapixel image contains 2 million pixels.

items.t: Most digital cameras place red, green and blue filters over their light sensors.
items.d: The coloured filters cover a grid of tiny light sensors.

items.t: Many camera sensors use twice as many green filters as red or blue ones.
items.d: This helps match the strong sensitivity of human vision to green.

items.t: Liquid crystals in an LCD do not make their own light.
items.d: An LCD needs a backlight behind its liquid crystal layer.

items.t: The ocean looks blue partly because water absorbs more red light.
items.d: More blue light is left for our eyes to see.

items.t: Particles and sediment can make ocean water look green or other colours.
items.d: Light bouncing from the particles changes the colour we see.

items.t: Each eye has a blind spot with no light-detecting cells.
items.d: It is where the optic nerve leaves the retina.

items.t: You rarely notice your blind spot because your brain fills in the missing view.
items.d: It uses nearby details and information from your other eye.

items.t: A concave mirror curves inward and brings light rays together.
items.d: Its curved surface collects light and brings it to a focus.

items.t: A convex mirror curves outward and spreads light apart.
items.d: It reflects light outward, so the rays do not meet at a real focus.

items.t: The focal point of a convex mirror sits behind the mirror.
items.d: No real light meets there. The rays only seem to come from that point.

items.t: Many passenger-side car mirrors are convex.
items.d: The curve shows a wider view of the road than a flat mirror.

items.t: A concave shaving mirror can make your face look bigger.
items.d: Concave mirrors are used in shaving and makeup mirrors to magnify a face.

items.t: Torches and car headlamps use a concave mirror to make a beam.
items.d: The mirror gathers light from a small bulb and sends it out together.

items.t: A magnifying glass is a convex lens, usually set in a frame with a handle.
items.d: It bends light so small print or a tiny insect looks much bigger.

items.t: A magnifying glass can gather sunlight into one hot spot.
items.d: Its convex lens concentrates sunlight into a small area.

items.t: Refraction means a wave bends as it enters a different material.
items.d: Light bends this way when it passes from air into water or glass.

items.t: A pencil in a glass of water looks bent at the surface.
items.d: Refraction bends the light, so the underwater part looks out of line.

items.t: Water has a refractive index of about 1.33. Air is about 1.
items.d: This difference helps explain why light bends when it enters water from air.

items.t: Lenses and prisms steer light by refraction.
items.d: Both can change the direction in which a light ray travels.

items.t: Apollo 11, 14, and 15 astronauts left retroreflectors on the Moon.
items.d: Shine light at one, and it bounces that light straight back to you.

items.t: A simple periscope has two mirrors, each tilted at 45 degrees.
items.d: The mirrors are parallel, with one at each end of a tube.

items.t: Early glasses used convex lenses to help farsighted people.
items.d: Farsightedness is also called hyperopia.

items.t: Concave lenses for short-sighted eyes first appeared in the mid-1400s.
items.d: Short-sightedness is also called myopia.

items.t: The first eyeglasses were made in northern Italy in the late 1200s.
items.d: People there began wearing lenses to help them see more clearly.

items.t: A kaleidoscope has two or more mirrors tilted at an angle.
items.d: Repeated reflections of loose pieces make a symmetrical pattern.

items.t: David Brewster, a Scottish inventor, coined the word kaleidoscope.
items.d: The name was published in a patent granted on 10 July 1817.

items.t: A camera obscura projects a picture that is upside down.
items.d: The picture is also flipped left to right.

items.t: Making a pinhole smaller gives a sharper picture, but a dimmer one.
items.d: Less light gets through a tiny hole, so the image looks darker.

items.t: Adding a lens lets a camera obscura stay bright and in focus.
items.d: The lens can focus light from a wider hole than a tiny pinhole can.

items.t: Binoculars are two matching refracting telescopes side by side.
items.d: You look through both at once, with one telescope for each eye.

items.t: Binoculars marked 8x42 magnify 8 times and have 42 mm objective lenses.
items.d: The first number is the power. The second is each front lens's diameter in millimetres.

items.t: Using both eyes with binoculars helps your brain judge depth.
items.d: Each eye gets a slightly different picture, and the brain compares them.

items.t: A Fresnel lens is split into rings, so it needs much less glass.
items.d: It can be much thinner than an ordinary lens that bends light the same way.

items.t: Augustin-Jean Fresnel reinvented a ring-section lens for lighthouses.
items.d: The first Fresnel lighthouse lens was lit at Cordouan on 25 July 1823.

items.t: Percy Shaw named the cat's eye road stud after a cat's shining eyes.
items.d: He patented it in 1934 and began making the studs in Halifax in 1935.

items.t: A corner cube reflector sends light straight back to its source.
items.d: Three flat faces meet at right angles and bounce the ray back.

items.t: Clear or white bicycle reflectors bounce back the most light.
items.d: They return the biggest share of the light that hits them.

items.t: Light stays inside an optical fibre by total internal reflection.
items.d: The beam keeps bouncing along the core instead of leaking out.

items.t: An optical fibre's core is wrapped in cladding with a lower refractive index.
items.d: That difference helps keep light inside the core.

items.t: Optical fibres carry phone and internet signals.
items.d: The signals can travel along thin threads of glass.

items.t: Light signals in a glass fibre travel at about 200,000 kilometres per second.
items.d: In one second, that signal can cover about 200,000 kilometres.

items.t: A telescope's front lens bends parallel rays to one focal point.
items.d: Light from a far star arrives almost parallel, then meets at that point.

items.t: A reflecting telescope gathers light with a curved primary mirror.
items.d: That curved mirror is the main part, in place of a big glass lens.

items.t: Simple lenses can add color fringes. Curved mirrors do not.
items.d: The color blur is called chromatic aberration.

items.t: Isaac Newton built the first practical reflecting telescope in 1668.
items.d: His curved mirror collected light instead of a large glass lens.

items.t: Very large glass lenses sag under their own weight.
items.d: Lens telescopes stay about 1 metre wide. The largest mirrors exceed 10 metres.

items.t: Early metal telescope mirrors reflected only about two-thirds of the light.
items.d: They also tarnished easily, so the shiny surface grew dull.

items.t: Hubble's main mirror was ground to the wrong shape, so images looked blurry.
items.d: In 1993, servicing mission STS-61 corrected the telescope's optics.

items.t: In 1611, Kepler designed a telescope with a convex lens where you look.
items.d: The design showed the scene upside down.

items.t: The Webb telescope's main mirror is 6.5 metres wide.
items.d: It is made of 18 hexagonal pieces that join into one big mirror.

items.t: Webb's mirror has a gold coating that reflects infrared light well.
items.d: The coating helps direct infrared light into the telescope's instruments.

items.t: The James Webb Space Telescope launched on 25 December 2021.
items.d: An Ariane 5 rocket carried it into space that day.

items.t: An optical microscope bends visible light with lenses.
items.d: The light passes through a thin sample and the view looks much bigger.

items.t: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek magnified objects about 300 times with one lens.
items.d: On 9 October 1676, he reported tiny living things seen in his microscope.

items.t: In 1931, Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll built the first electron microscope test model.
items.d: It makes a picture with a beam of electrons instead of light.

items.t: Galileo built a telescope in 1609 and used it to study the sky.
items.d: A convex lens at the front and a concave lens at the eye formed the view.

items.t: Light is one small slice of a huge wave family called the electromagnetic spectrum.
items.d: Your eyes can only see the visible slice. Radio, X-rays and more are all around, hidden from sight.

items.t: The electromagnetic spectrum runs from very long radio waves to very short gamma rays.
items.d: Radio waves are the longest in the family, and gamma rays are the shortest.

items.t: Tuning a radio and sending a text both use electromagnetic waves.
items.d: Your phone and a radio talk to the world through waves you cannot see.

items.t: The Sun sends out energy across the whole electromagnetic spectrum.
items.d: Sunlight is only the part we can see. The rest is invisible.

items.t: In 1932, Karl Jansky showed that stars and other things in space give off radio waves.
items.d: So space is not silent. Telescopes can listen to it with radio dishes.

items.t: Radio telescope dishes can be full of tiny holes, because long radio waves pass over the holes.
items.d: The holes make the dish lighter, but it still catches the waves.

items.t: Microwave ovens heat food by making water and fat molecules in it spin.
items.d: That spinning makes the food warm, like rubbing your hands together.

items.t: Some microwaves can travel through clouds, dust, smoke, snow and rain.
items.d: This is why satellites can use them to peek at Earth in bad weather.

items.t: A satellite can measure sea height by timing how long a microwave pulse takes to bounce back.
items.d: Longer trip means the sea is farther below the satellite.

items.t: The cosmic microwave background is faint microwave energy that fills the whole universe.
items.d: It was found by accident in 1965 and is a clue to how the universe began.

items.t: You cannot see infrared light, but you can feel it as heat.
items.d: Hold your hand near a warm lamp and you feel infrared.

items.t: Infrared light passes through thick clouds of space dust better than visible light does.
items.d: That lets infrared telescopes see things hidden from normal telescopes.

items.t: X-rays have tiny wavelengths, only about 0.03 to 3 nanometres long.
items.d: A nanometre is a billionth of a metre, far smaller than a speck of dust.

items.t: Bones show up on X-ray pictures because dense bone soaks up more X-rays than skin does.
items.d: That is why bones look bright in an X-ray picture.

items.t: X-ray telescopes use mirrors set at very shallow angles to focus X-rays.
items.d: The rays skim the mirror like a stone skipping on water.

items.t: UV rays can reach you on cloudy and cool days, not just hot sunny ones.
items.d: Sun protection is a good idea even when the sky is gray.

items.t: A shadow shorter than you are means the sun's UV rays are stronger.
items.d: Check your shadow on a sunny day to see.

items.t: Most TV remotes send tiny pulses of infrared light that your eyes cannot see.
items.d: A digital camera can often show the flashing light from a remote.

items.t: Wi-Fi lets nearby devices share data using radio waves.
items.d: Most Wi-Fi uses radio bands of about 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz.

items.t: The metal mesh in a microwave door keeps microwaves inside but lets you see in.
items.d: The tiny holes are too small for the waves, but light slips through.

items.t: All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in empty space.
items.d: That is about 300,000 km per second.

items.t: A mirage is a real optical effect, not a trick of the mind.
items.d: A camera can photograph a mirage.

items.t: On a hot, sunny day, a road may seem to have puddles that are not there.
items.d: Bent light creates the watery-looking image.

items.t: A 22-degree halo is a large ring around the Sun or Moon.
items.d: Tiny ice crystals in the air make the ring.

items.t: Halos form when light passes through tiny ice crystals high in the air.
items.d: These crystals are often inside thin cirrus clouds.

items.t: Ice crystals can bend and bounce light like tiny prisms and mirrors.
items.d: This helps create bright halos in the sky.

items.t: Ice crystals can split light into rainbow-like colours.
items.d: The splitting of light into colours is called dispersion.

items.t: A light pillar is a vertical column of light near the Sun.
items.d: It may appear around sunrise or sunset.

items.t: Auroras begin with charged particles from the Sun.
items.d: The particles collide with atoms in Earth's atmosphere.

items.t: Auroras can shine in green, red and purple.
items.d: Different gases and conditions produce different colours.

items.t: Auroras glow when collisions excite oxygen and nitrogen in the air.
items.d: The excited gases release colourful light.

items.t: Auroras can form shapes like curtains, rays and spirals.
items.d: Their glowing patterns can shift across the sky.

items.t: Bioluminescence is light made and released by a living thing.
items.d: Some ocean animals make their own glow.

items.t: Bioluminescence comes from a chemical reaction inside a living thing.
items.d: A substance called luciferin reacts with an enzyme.

items.t: Some squid glow to match light coming from above.
items.d: This can hide their shadow from animals looking up from below.

items.t: Under ultraviolet light, many substances glow with visible colours.
items.d: This effect is called fluorescence.

items.t: Highlighter ink is often fluorescent.
items.d: Many highlighters contain a glowing chemical called pyranine.

items.t: Many calcite minerals glow under ultraviolet light.
items.d: This glow is fluorescence.

items.t: Fluorescent light usually has less energy than the light the material absorbed.
items.d: It also usually has a longer wavelength.

items.t: Flying squirrels can glow pink under ultraviolet light.
items.d: This surprising fluorescence was noticed by chance in 2019.

items.t: Glow-in-the-dark toys, stickers and paints use phosphorescence.
items.d: They keep shining after the room becomes dark.

items.t: Glow sticks shine by chemiluminescence, not phosphorescence.
items.d: Their light comes from a chemical reaction.

items.t: In a laser, one passing photon can trigger the release of an identical photon.
items.d: This process is called stimulated emission.

items.t: Dennis Gabor invented holography in 1948.
items.d: He was trying to improve images from an electron microscope.

items.t: TV remote controls use infrared LEDs to send signals.
items.d: Infrared light cannot be seen by human eyes.

items.t: Blue LEDs made practical white LED lights possible.
items.d: Their invention was honoured by the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.

items.t: Stars twinkle because their light passes through moving layers of air.
items.d: The turbulent atmosphere bends the starlight in changing ways.

items.t: Absolute zero is the coldest temperature. It is 0 kelvin, or -273.15 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That equals about -460 degrees Fahrenheit. Nothing can be colder.

items.t: Scientists can get very close to absolute zero, but they cannot quite reach it.
items.d: Each try gets closer. There is always a tiny bit left to go.

items.t: Even at absolute zero, tiny particles still keep a little energy.
items.d: A tiny minimum energy stays, even when the temperature cannot go lower.

items.t: Liquid helium does not turn solid at normal pressure, even near absolute zero.
items.d: Almost everything else would be frozen solid. Helium can stay a liquid.

items.t: Near absolute zero, some matter becomes superconducting or superfluid.
items.d: These unusual states appear only under extremely cold conditions.

items.t: The kelvin temperature scale is named after William Thomson, Lord Kelvin.
items.d: Say 300 kelvins, not 300 degrees kelvin. Degree is not part of the name.

items.t: Below freezing, the dew point is called the frost point.
items.d: Frost appears when water vapor turns straight into ice, skipping the liquid.

items.t: One kelvin is the same size step as one degree Celsius.
items.d: If something warms by 10 degrees Celsius, it also warms by 10 kelvins.

items.t: The Celsius scale is named after Anders Celsius, a Swedish astronomer.
items.d: He proposed a first version of this temperature scale in 1742.

items.t: Anders Celsius first marked 0 for boiling water and 100 for freezing.
items.d: Later the numbers were flipped. Now freezing is 0 and boiling is 100.

items.t: Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100, at 1 atmosphere.
items.d: One atmosphere is about the air pressure you feel at sea level.

items.t: To change Celsius to Fahrenheit, multiply by 9/5, then add 32.
items.d: At 100 degrees: 100 times 9/5 is 180, and 180 plus 32 is 212.

items.t: The dew point is the temperature where air becomes full of water vapor.
items.d: Cool the air to the dew point and drops of water begin to form.

items.t: On the Fahrenheit scale, water freezes at 32 degrees.
items.d: That is the same cold mark as 0 degrees Celsius.

items.t: At standard sea-level pressure, water boils at 212 degrees Fahrenheit.
items.d: That is the same temperature as 100 degrees Celsius.

items.t: To change Fahrenheit to Celsius, subtract 32, then multiply by 5/9.
items.d: 212 minus 32 is 180. 180 times 5/9 is 100 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Celsius and Fahrenheit match at -40 degrees. Both scales say -40.
items.d: Check: -40 minus 32 is -72, and -72 times 5/9 is -40.

items.t: When water evaporates, it takes heat from the air and the air cools.
items.d: Sweat cools your skin the same way. Drying water carries heat off.

items.t: Evaporative cooling works best where the air is dry.
items.d: Low humidity lets more water evaporate, making the cooling stronger.

items.t: Liquid nitrogen boils at about 77 kelvins.
items.d: That is about -196 degrees Celsius, far colder than a home freezer.

items.t: A heat pump moves heat from place to place instead of making heat.
items.d: Moving heat can warm a home with less energy than burning gas.

items.t: A heat pump can deliver about 4 units of heat for 1 unit of electricity.
items.d: The extra heat is moved in from outside, so the electricity is not the only heat.

items.t: A heat pump can work like a refrigerator running in reverse.
items.d: A fridge pulls heat out. Run the idea backward and heat is pushed in.

items.t: A refrigerator stays cold by moving heat out of the inside.
items.d: The warmth ends up in the room. Coils give that heat to the room air.

items.t: Inside a fridge, a liquid turns into gas and soaks up heat from the air.
items.d: That heat leaves the food area, which is why the inside stays cold.

items.t: Before electric fridges, icehouses and iceboxes kept food cool.
items.d: They gave people cool storage for most of the year.

items.t: Most materials get longer, wider, and larger when they get hotter.
items.d: Heating usually increases a material's length, area, and volume.

items.t: Railways and bridges need gaps so they can grow on hot days.
items.d: The gaps help prevent a sun kink, when rails bend out of shape in the sun.

items.t: A bimetal thermometer bends because its two metals expand differently.
items.d: The side that grows more bends the strip, and the bend tells the temperature.

items.t: Liquids usually grow in volume more than solids do when heated.
items.d: Water near freezing is an exception. It can shrink as it warms toward 4 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Expansion joints let buildings and bridges grow and shrink safely.
items.d: They absorb changes caused by temperature and help structures avoid cracks.

items.t: Greenhouse gases cause most of the greenhouse effect around Earth.
items.d: Carbon dioxide and water vapor take in heat rays and hold them awhile.

items.t: With no greenhouse effect, Earth's average temperature would be about -18 degrees Celsius.
items.d: Water vapor and carbon dioxide keep the real surface much warmer than that.

items.t: Condensation is a gas changing into a liquid.
items.d: Morning dew on the grass is water that condensed overnight.

items.t: At home, condensation forms when warm moist air meets a cool surface.
items.d: That is why the bathroom mirror fogs up during a hot shower.

items.t: High in the mountains, water boils at a lower temperature.
items.d: Air pressure is lower there, so water reaches its boiling point at a lower temperature.

items.t: A liquid boils when its vapor pushes as hard as the air around it.
items.d: For water at normal pressure, that balance is at 100 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Higher pressure raises the boiling point, up to a limit called the critical point.
items.d: A pressure cooker uses this. Extra pressure makes the water boil hotter.

items.t: Supercooling cools a liquid below its freezing point without freezing it.
items.d: With no seed crystal to start the ice, the liquid can stay liquid.

items.t: Very pure water can be supercooled to about -48 degrees Celsius before it freezes.
items.d: It freezes when ice crystals finally start all through the water.

items.t: Stratus and cumulus clouds often contain drops of supercooled water.
items.d: The drops are colder than freezing, yet they are still liquid.

items.t: Latent heat is energy absorbed or released during a change of state at constant temperature.
items.d: Melting ice at 0 degrees takes in a lot of heat, but it stays at 0 while melting.

items.t: It takes 2257 kilojoules to turn 1 kilogram of boiling water into steam.
items.d: That huge heat of vaporization is why a kettle boils for a while before the water is gone.

items.t: Water's triple point is 0.01 degrees Celsius, or 273.16 kelvins.
items.d: At that point, ice, liquid water, and water vapor can exist together.

items.t: Because ice floats, ocean water can stay liquid beneath a surface layer of ice.
items.d: If ice sank, oceans could freeze from the bottom up.

items.t: Liquid water is densest at about 4 degrees Celsius.
items.d: Above 4 degrees, cooling makes it shrink. Below about 4 degrees, cooling makes it expand.

items.t: To warm 1 kilogram of water by 1 degree Celsius takes 4184 joules.
items.d: That is its specific heat near 20 degrees Celsius. Oceans warm and cool slowly.

items.t: Energy is never used up. It only changes from one form to another.
items.d: When you eat lunch and then run, food energy turns into motion and heat.

items.t: In an isolated system, the total amount of energy always stays the same.
items.d: Energy can change form inside it, but the total does not change.

items.t: A machine that gives out energy with nothing put in can never exist.
items.d: Such a perpetual-motion machine would break the law of energy conservation.

items.t: Mathematician Emmy Noether showed energy conservation comes from physics rules staying the same over time.
items.d: The rules of physics work the same today as they did yesterday.

items.t: A German doctor, Julius Robert von Mayer, stated the modern idea of energy conservation in 1842.
items.d: Big ideas in physics can come from people with other jobs, like doctors.

items.t: The watt is named after James Watt, the Scottish inventor who improved the steam engine in 1776.
items.d: A watt measures power, how fast energy is used.

items.t: One watt means one joule of energy is used every second.
items.d: A 60 W bulb uses 60 joules of energy every second.

items.t: A laser pointer gives out about 5 milliwatts of light power.
items.d: That is only 0.005 watts, a tiny amount of power.

items.t: A small electric heater can use about 1 kilowatt of power.
items.d: 1 kilowatt is 1,000 watts, the same as ten 100 W bulbs.

items.t: A 100 W bulb left on for one hour uses 0.1 kilowatt-hour of energy.
items.d: Ten hours of that bulb would use 1 kilowatt-hour.

items.t: One kilowatt-hour is 3,600,000 joules of energy.
items.d: 1,000 watts for 3,600 seconds (one hour) is 1,000 x 3,600 = 3,600,000.

items.t: A 100 kg person climbing a 3 m ladder in 5 seconds works at roughly 600 watts.
items.d: Climbing the same ladder faster takes more power.

items.t: One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves something one metre in its direction.
items.d: A newton is about the weight of a small apple.

items.t: An adult needs about 1,600 to 3,000 food Calories of energy every day.
items.d: Food is fuel for your body. Very active people need more.

items.t: In a power station, a turbo generator turns energy from pressurized steam into electricity.
items.d: Moving steam spins the turbine, and the spinning makes electricity.

items.t: Einstein showed that mass and energy are related.
items.d: One kilogram of mass has an energy equivalent of about 90 million billion joules.

items.t: A swinging pendulum with no friction keeps swapping energy between stored and moving forms.
items.d: At the top of the swing it is stored. At the bottom it moves fastest.

items.t: Most roller coaster trains are pulled up a lift hill by a chain or cable, then let go.
items.d: The train starts its fast ride from the highest point.

items.t: On a roller coaster, energy stored by climbing the lift hill turns into motion on the way down.
items.d: Higher at the start means more energy to use for the whole ride.

items.t: Each hill on a coaster is usually lower than the one before it.
items.d: Friction and air drag turn some mechanical energy into heat, so the train cannot climb as high.

items.t: A roller coaster usually stops on a brake run, where motion energy becomes heat.
items.d: Brakes can get warm, like your hands when you rub them together.

items.t: Some roller coasters skip the lift hill and use a flywheel or linear motor to launch.
items.d: The launch system gives the train its starting speed.

items.t: Ordinary roller coaster trains have no engine. Gravity does the work after the first lift.
items.d: The chain does the climbing work, then gravity pulls the train around.

items.t: The ancestors of roller coasters were ice slides called Russian Mountains, from the 1600s.
items.d: People slid down tall ice hills in what is now Saint Petersburg, Russia.

items.t: An early track-based roller coaster, Thompson's Switchback Railway, opened at Coney Island in 1884.
items.d: It was a long way from today's tall, fast coasters.

items.t: An old-style filament bulb turns less than 5% of its energy into visible light. The rest is heat.
items.d: That is why old-style bulbs become hot.

items.t: Old-style filament bulbs usually last only 1,000 to 2,000 hours.
items.d: Left on all the time, that is only about 6 to 12 weeks.

items.t: White LED bulbs can last an estimated 35,000 to 50,000 hours.
items.d: Used 3 hours a day, 35,000 hours is more than 30 years.

items.t: Edison's successful lamp test on 22 October 1879 lasted 13.5 hours.
items.d: It was an early test of Edison's lamp design.

items.t: Alessandro Volta built the first electrochemical battery, the voltaic pile, in 1800.
items.d: Batteries have been storing energy for more than 200 years.

items.t: Inventor Joseph Swan's house, Underhill, was the first in the world lit by a lightbulb.
items.d: Electric light was once so new that one house made history.

items.t: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics honoured the inventors of the blue LED.
items.d: Blue LEDs made bright white LED lights possible.

items.t: In an LED, electrons give up energy as tiny packets of light called photons.
items.d: The light comes from inside a tiny piece of semiconductor.

items.t: An electric motor turns electrical energy into motion.
items.d: Fans, washing machines and electric cars all use motors.

items.t: Elastic energy is stored when something is squashed, stretched or bent.
items.d: A stretched rubber band or a squashed spring is storing energy.

items.t: When a stretched or squashed object springs back, its stored energy can become motion and sound.
items.d: Release a stretched rubber band and it springs back with a twang.

items.t: An ideal spring stores four times more energy when you stretch it twice as far.
items.d: Stretch it 2 cm and then 4 cm, and the 4 cm stretch stores 4 times as much.

items.t: A regenerative brake uses an electric motor as a generator to catch energy that might become heat.
items.d: The slowing train or car helps make electricity.

items.t: Energy caught by regenerative braking can be stored in a battery, capacitors or a spinning flywheel.
items.d: The saved energy can help the vehicle speed up again.

items.t: On the Kiruna to Narvik line, downhill trains make more electricity than the railway uses.
items.d: Their regenerative brakes act like generators.

items.t: The joule, a unit of energy, is named after English physicist James Prescott Joule.
items.d: He lived from 1818 to 1889.

items.t: One joule is about the energy needed to lift an apple one metre.
items.d: Lifting it just one metre, about up to your chest, takes about one joule.

items.t: One calorie equals about 4.184 joules.
items.d: So 10 calories is about 41.84 joules.

items.t: Food labels in most countries give energy in kilojoules.
items.d: One kilojoule is 1,000 joules.

items.t: For small swings in one place, a pendulum's swing time depends on its length, not its mass.
items.d: A short pendulum swings faster than a long one.

items.t: Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656, a big step toward accurate clocks.
items.d: Older clocks could be wrong by 15 minutes a day. His was off by about 15 seconds a day.

items.t: A clock pendulum needs a small push each swing to replace the energy lost to friction.
items.d: Without the little pushes, the pendulum would slowly stop.

items.t: A generator turns motion energy into electrical energy.
items.d: Wind, water or steam can spin a generator.

items.t: Hydropower uses moving water as fuel, but the water is not used up.
items.d: After passing through the plant, the water returns to the water cycle.

items.t: Moving water can push turbine blades and make them turn.
items.d: It works a bit like wind spinning a pinwheel.

items.t: A spinning water turbine drives a generator, which makes electricity.
items.d: The turbine provides motion, and the generator changes that motion into electricity.

items.t: More flowing water can help a hydropower plant make more electricity.
items.d: Water falling from a greater height can also provide more power.

items.t: Rain and snow help refill the water supplies used for hydropower.
items.d: This happens through Earth's repeating water cycle.

items.t: Flowing water has kinetic energy, which means energy of motion.
items.d: Hydropower plants capture some of this moving energy.

items.t: Hydropower was one of the first energy sources used to make electricity.
items.d: People learned to use moving water for electrical power long ago.

items.t: A penstock is a large pipe that carries water toward a hydro turbine.
items.d: The rushing water leaves the pipe and pushes the turbine blades.

items.t: Pumped-storage plants pump water uphill to store energy.
items.d: They release the water to make electricity when more power is needed.

items.t: Most U.S. hydropower plants use a dam and reservoir to hold water.
items.d: The stored water can later flow through equipment that makes electricity.

items.t: Geothermal energy is heat found inside Earth.
items.d: Geo means Earth, and thermal relates to heat.

items.t: Geothermal energy is renewable because Earth keeps producing heat.
items.d: Its power source is heat from inside our planet.

items.t: Some of Earth's inner heat comes from radioactive particles slowly breaking down.
items.d: This natural process releases heat deep inside the planet.

items.t: Rocks and water usually get hotter as you travel deeper into Earth.
items.d: Geothermal systems can use this underground heat.

items.t: People use geothermal heat for hot-spring bathing and for electricity.
items.d: The same kind of underground heat can serve different purposes.

items.t: Geothermal power plants can run day and night in any weather.
items.d: Their heat source is underground, so sunshine and wind are not required.

items.t: Geothermal heat has made electricity in the United States for over 60 years.
items.d: Power plants have used Earth's inner heat for many decades.

items.t: Steam turbines make most of the world's electricity.
items.d: Steam spins a turbine that helps drive a generator.

items.t: Many power plants burn fuel in a boiler to make hot water and steam.
items.d: The steam then spins a turbine.

items.t: A combustion gas turbine works somewhat like a jet engine.
items.d: It burns a gas or liquid fuel to produce power.

items.t: Nuclear power plants use fuel rods to produce steam.
items.d: The steam spins turbines used to make electricity.

items.t: Diesel-engine generators can use several kinds of fuel.
items.d: Petroleum diesel is one fuel they can use, but it is not the only one.

items.t: Nuclear fission splits atoms and releases energy.
items.d: A nuclear power plant uses the released energy as a source of heat.

items.t: Most nuclear power plants use uranium atoms as fuel.
items.d: Energy is released when uranium atoms split through fission.

items.t: Nuclear plants use a kind of uranium called U-235 as fuel.
items.d: U-235 atoms can split and release energy.

items.t: A nuclear reactor carefully controls its fission reaction.
items.d: The reaction is controlled to produce the amount of heat the plant needs.

items.t: A huge amount of energy holds the particles in an atom's nucleus together.
items.d: Nuclear energy comes from this tiny central part of an atom.

items.t: Coal is a black or brownish-black rock rich in carbon.
items.d: Its stored chemical energy can be released as heat when coal burns.

items.t: Coal stores energy from plants that lived hundreds of millions of years ago.
items.d: Many of those ancient plants grew in swampy forests.

items.t: Anthracite coal is about 86 to 97 percent carbon.
items.d: It generally has the highest heating value of the coal ranks.

items.t: Lignite is a moist, crumbly kind of coal with a low heating value.
items.d: Its high moisture helps explain why it provides less heat.

items.t: Natural gas formed from buried remains changed by heat and pressure.
items.d: The remains came from ancient plants and animals.

items.t: Methane is the largest part of natural gas.
items.d: Natural gas can contain other substances too, but methane is its main component.

items.t: One methane molecule has one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms.
items.d: Its chemical formula is CH4.

items.t: Natural gas has no color, smell, or taste on its own.
items.d: Its familiar smell does not come from the gas itself.

items.t: Gas companies add a smelly chemical called mercaptan to natural gas.
items.d: The added odor makes leaking gas easier to notice.

items.t: Mercaptan gives natural gas a smell often compared to rotten eggs.
items.d: The smelly chemical added to the gas is harmless.

items.t: Crude oil is a fossil fuel formed from the remains of plants and animals.
items.d: It is a mixture of substances called hydrocarbons.

items.t: The living things that became crude oil lived in ancient seas.
items.d: They lived millions of years ago, even before dinosaurs existed.

items.t: Heat and pressure changed buried remains into crude oil.
items.d: Crude oil is also called petroleum.

items.t: The word petroleum means rock oil, or oil from Earth.
items.d: Petroleum is another name for crude oil.

items.t: An oil refinery separates crude oil into useful products.
items.d: Some of those products are fuels.

items.t: Wind begins because the Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly.
items.d: Uneven heating makes air move from place to place.

items.t: Windmills can use wind energy to pump water.
items.d: Water-pumping windmills were once used all over the United States.

items.t: A daytime sea breeze forms when cool air moves from water toward warmer land.
items.d: Warm air over the land rises, and cooler air rushes in to replace it.

items.t: At night, a coastal breeze can reverse because land cools faster than water.
items.d: The different cooling speeds change how the nearby air moves.

items.t: Wind turbine blades collect the kinetic energy of moving air.
items.d: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.

items.t: Wind creates lift as it flows over turbine blades, making them turn.
items.d: The effect is similar to lift on an airplane wing.

items.t: If one bulb burns out in an old series string of Christmas lights, the whole string goes dark.
items.d: The bulbs share one loop. Break one bulb and the current has nowhere to go.

items.t: In a parallel circuit, each bulb has its own branch. One bad bulb does not stop the rest.
items.d: House lamps are wired this way. One lamp can be off while others stay lit.

items.t: In a series circuit, the same current flows through every part.
items.d: There is only one path, so the same flow passes each part in turn.

items.t: In a series circuit, the parts share the battery voltage. The shares add up.
items.d: Each part uses some of the push. Together they use the whole battery.

items.t: In a parallel circuit, every branch gets the same voltage.
items.d: Each branch connects across the battery, so each one gets the full push.

items.t: In a parallel circuit, the branch currents add up to the battery's total.
items.d: If two branches use 1 amp each, the battery supplies 2 amps.

items.t: Four matching bulbs in series on a 12-volt battery get only 3 volts each.
items.d: The share is small, so those bulbs may glow dimly or not at all.

items.t: Four bulbs in parallel on a 12-volt battery each get the full 12 volts.
items.d: Each bulb gets the full voltage, so they all glow.

items.t: Georg Ohm published his results about current and voltage in 1827.
items.d: He was a German physicist studying how a push drives current in a wire.

items.t: Ohm's law is V = I x R. Voltage equals current times resistance.
items.d: If 2 amps flow through 3 ohms, the voltage is 2 x 3 = 6 volts.

items.t: A resistor is a small part with two legs that adds resistance.
items.d: Current has to push through it, so less current flows for the same voltage.

items.t: People use resistors to reduce the current in a circuit.
items.d: A resistor next to an LED keeps the current from growing too large.

items.t: Resistance is measured in ohms, named after Georg Ohm.
items.d: The symbol for the ohm looks like a horseshoe: Ω.

items.t: Resistors in series add up. Two 10-ohm resistors make 20 ohms.
items.d: Current must pass through one, then the other, so both resistances count.

items.t: The electric power a resistor takes in turns into heat.
items.d: That is why a working resistor can feel warm. Too much heat can damage it.

items.t: Copper conducts electricity very well, so it is widely used for wires.
items.d: Silver conducts a little better, but it costs too much for most wiring.

items.t: In a metal wire, the moving charges are tiny particles called electrons.
items.d: Electrons are far too small to see, but a huge number of them can flow together.

items.t: An insulator is the opposite of a conductor. It resists the flow of charge.
items.d: The plastic coat on a wire is an insulator. The copper inside does the conducting.

items.t: A fuse holds a thin metal strip that melts when too much current flows.
items.d: The melted strip opens the circuit and stops the extra current.

items.t: A fuse protects a circuit by breaking itself. Then you must replace it.
items.d: Once the strip melts, you put in a new fuse so the circuit can work again.

items.t: The first LEDs, made in 1962, gave off infrared light people cannot see.
items.d: Infrared is a kind of light just beyond red, outside what eyes can see.

items.t: An LED lights only when current flows through it in the right direction.
items.d: Flip the LED around and it stays dark. It is a one-way path for current.

items.t: LEDs make more light from the same electricity than old bulbs that get hot.
items.d: More of that electricity becomes light you can see.

items.t: Most TV remotes send invisible infrared light to the TV.
items.d: You cannot see the beam, but a sensor in the TV can.

items.t: An infrared remote needs a clear view of the TV.
items.d: Stand in the way, or hide the sensor, and the signal cannot get through.

items.t: In 1955, Eugene Polley made a wireless remote that shone a light beam at the TV.
items.d: The beam hit one of four light sensors to control the set.

items.t: An early light-beam TV remote could be fooled by sunlight or a lamp.
items.d: Its sensor could not tell the remote's light apart from other light.

items.t: A photoresistor senses light. More light makes its resistance drop.
items.d: Bright light lets more current through. Darkness holds the current back.

items.t: Some streetlights use photoresistors to turn on by themselves at night.
items.d: As daylight fades, the sensor changes, and the lamp can switch on.

items.t: A thermistor is a resistor that changes a lot when temperature changes.
items.d: Warm it or cool it, and the current it allows will change too.

items.t: An NTC thermistor has lower resistance when it gets hotter.
items.d: Heat lets more current flow through an NTC thermistor.

items.t: A PTC thermistor has higher resistance when it gets hotter.
items.d: Heat holds current back more in a PTC thermistor.

items.t: Thermistors can work as temperature sensors.
items.d: The circuit reads the resistance and turns that into a temperature.

items.t: A circuit breaker is a safety switch that opens when current is too high.
items.d: It protects wires from a current bigger than they are meant to carry.

items.t: A circuit breaker can be reset and used again. A blown fuse cannot.
items.d: After it trips, you can switch it back on once things are safe.

items.t: A breaker allows a brief small surge, like a motor starting, but trips on a big one.
items.d: A fridge motor may draw extra current for a moment. A real overload is much bigger.

items.t: Alessandro Volta built the first battery, the voltaic pile, in 1800.
items.d: His pile was the first battery that made current from a chemical reaction.

items.t: Volta's pile was a stack of copper and zinc discs with salty paper between them.
items.d: The paper was soaked in brine, which is salty water.

items.t: A battery is made of one or more cells that make electricity.
items.d: A small flashlight cell is one cell. Bigger batteries join cells together.

items.t: The minus end of a battery is where electrons come out.
items.d: They leave the minus end, travel around the circuit, and return at the plus end.

items.t: A rechargeable battery can be used up and charged again, many times.
items.d: A charger pushes current back in, so the battery is ready to work again.

items.t: Electric current is measured in amperes, named after Andre-Marie Ampere.
items.d: An ammeter is the tool that measures how much current is flowing.

items.t: In direct current, charge flows one way. In alternating current, it keeps reversing.
items.d: Direct current is called DC. Alternating current is called AC.

items.t: Voltage is the push between two points. People also call it electric pressure.
items.d: Like a pump pushing water around pipes, voltage pushes charge around a circuit.

items.t: The volt is named for the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta.
items.d: A voltmeter measures the voltage, the push, between two points.

items.t: A switch is closed when its contacts touch, and open when they are apart.
items.d: Closed means on, because current can flow. Open means off. The simplest switch is only on or off.

items.t: A push-button switch springs back when you let go.
items.d: A doorbell works like that. You press it, it clicks on, then it springs off.

items.t: A capacitor stores energy by collecting charge on two surfaces close together.
items.d: The earliest capacitors were glass jars of water, called Leyden jars.

items.t: A capacitor can block steady direct current but let alternating current pass.
items.d: A steady flow charges it up and then stops. A flipping flow keeps moving.

items.t: A transistor can act as a switch that electricity turns on or off.
items.d: A tiny signal can control a much bigger one. The first working transistor was made in 1947.

items.t: Static electricity is an imbalance of electric charge on or inside a material.
items.d: Rub a balloon on your hair and the charge makes it stick to the wall.

items.t: When two materials touch, electrons can move from one material to the other.
items.d: That moving charge is what makes things feel zappy afterwards.

items.t: Rubbing materials together is the main cause of the static electricity we notice every day.
items.d: Sliding down a plastic slide can leave your hair standing up.

items.t: Static charge can make your hair stand up.
items.d: Each hair gets the same kind of charge, and like charges push each other apart.

items.t: A balloon rubbed on hair picks up extra electrons, so it becomes negatively charged.
items.d: That charge lets the balloon stick to a wall for a while.

items.t: Foam packing peanuts can cling to a cat's fur because of static electricity.
items.d: Charged things attract light, uncharged things nearby.

items.t: A static spark happens when built-up charge suddenly escapes. This is an electrostatic discharge.
items.d: You may feel a tiny snap after walking on a carpet and touching a door handle.

items.t: A lightning bolt is like an ordinary static spark, only much bigger.
items.d: Both are charge jumping across a gap to even things out.

items.t: Dry air lets static charge build up more easily than damp air.
items.d: That is why you get more zaps in dry winter weather.

items.t: Static charge stays on an object until it can flow away as a current or discharge.
items.d: Touching a metal doorknob gives it a path, so you feel the little zap.

items.t: The word electron comes from elektron, the Greek word for amber.
items.d: People noticed that rubbing amber could give it an electric charge.

items.t: In 1600, William Gilbert found that glass, wax and sulphur also make static when rubbed, not just amber.
items.d: So static is not special to amber. Many materials do it.

items.t: Charles Du Fay found two kinds of electric charge.
items.d: He named them after glass and resin.

items.t: A triboelectric series lists materials by the charge they tend to gain when rubbed.
items.d: Johan Wilcke made one in 1757.

items.t: A photocopier uses static electricity to put toner powder in the right places on paper.
items.d: This process is called xerography.

items.t: Inside a copier, a drum is given an even coat of static charge first.
items.d: A thin wire gives the drum its charge before copying starts.

items.t: Early copier drums used selenium, which holds charge in the dark but loses it when light hits it.
items.d: So bright parts of a page can wipe the charge away.

items.t: A copier shines light from your page onto the drum, leaving a hidden pattern of charge.
items.d: This invisible pattern is called a latent image.

items.t: Copier toner is a fine powder that gets a static charge by rubbing against tiny carrier particles.
items.d: It is the same rubbing trick as a balloon on hair.

items.t: Charged toner sticks to the parts of the drum with the opposite charge, which makes the picture show up.
items.d: Static attraction is doing the drawing.

items.t: A copier moves toner from the drum onto paper using pressure and static attraction.
items.d: The powder jumps from the drum to the page.

items.t: Lightning heats the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is several times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

items.t: Thunder is the sound of air that was heated so fast by lightning that it made a shock wave.
items.d: The air shoves outward very quickly, and we hear a boom.

items.t: The main current surge in a lightning bolt can move at up to one third the speed of light.
items.d: Light moves about 300,000 km each second.

items.t: Lightning strikes somewhere on Earth about 44 times every second.
items.d: That adds up to nearly 1.4 billion flashes every year.

items.t: The most common kind of lightning stays inside the clouds.
items.d: Many flashes never reach the ground at all.

items.t: Airplanes are hit by lightning fairly often, but strikes are generally not dangerous to them.
items.d: So a flash near a plane is rarely a problem.

items.t: A lightning rod is a metal rod on a building that helps protect it from lightning.
items.d: It gives lightning an easy path to follow.

items.t: Most lightning rods are made of copper or a mix of metals that contains copper.
items.d: Copper carries electricity very well.

items.t: Benjamin Franklin came up with the lightning rod in 1749.
items.d: He wanted to protect buildings from lightning.

items.t: A lightning rod must be connected to the ground to work.
items.d: The wire leads the electricity into the earth.

items.t: On a flat roof, lightning rods are usually placed around the edge.
items.d: Several rods spread around the roof protect the whole building.

items.t: Sharp points start electric discharges more easily because the electric field is stronger at the tip.
items.d: This is why lightning rods have pointed tops.

items.t: St. Elmo's fire is a blue or violet glow that can appear on tall pointed things like ship masts in storms.
items.d: The air itself glows as electricity leaks from the point.

items.t: A Van de Graaff generator uses a moving belt to pile up charge on a hollow metal dome.
items.d: It is often used in science museums.

items.t: If you touch a Van de Graaff generator, your hair stands out because each hair has the same charge.
items.d: Like charges push apart, so the hairs spread out.

items.t: A small tabletop Van de Graaff generator can make about 100,000 volts.
items.d: That is high voltage, but it carries only a tiny current.

items.t: Large Van de Graaff generators in open air can reach about 5 million volts.
items.d: Robert Van de Graaff invented the machine in 1929.

items.t: A Leyden jar is a glass jar with metal foil on the inside and outside. It can store electric charge.
items.d: It was an early way to hold static electricity.

items.t: The Leyden jar was the first way to store electric charge in large quantities.
items.d: Ewald von Kleist and Pieter van Musschenbroek discovered it independently in the 1740s.

items.t: Benjamin Franklin concluded that a Leyden jar stores its charge in the glass, not the water.
items.d: Before that, many people thought the water inside held it.

items.t: Electric eels are not true eels. They are more closely related to knifefish and catfish.
items.d: They just look a bit like eels.

items.t: An electric eel stacks about 6,000 special cells in a row, like batteries, to make a strong shock.
items.d: The cells add their small voltages together.

items.t: An electric eel can give shocks of up to about 860 volts to stun its food.
items.d: Its electric organs are made from changed muscle cells.

items.t: Electric eels have poor eyesight, so they sense their surroundings with electric signals.
items.d: This sense is called electrolocation.

items.t: Electric eels get most of their oxygen by gulping air at the water's surface.
items.d: Even though they live in water, they must come up to breathe.

items.t: A platypus has almost 40,000 electric sensors on its bill to find food.
items.d: They are arranged in stripes along the bill.

items.t: Sharks are the most electrically sensitive animals known.
items.d: They can sense the faint electric fields given off by other animals.

items.t: Messages travelling along your nerves are tiny electrical signals.
items.d: One whole signal takes only a few thousandths of a second.

items.t: Magnetism comes from moving electric charges.
items.d: Moving charges create magnetic effects around them.

items.t: Each spinning electron acts like a tiny magnet.
items.d: Electrons are tiny parts of atoms.

items.t: Iron, cobalt, and nickel can be strongly magnetic.
items.d: Many of their electrons act like tiny magnets pointing the same way.

items.t: Moving molten metal in Earth's outer core helps make its magnetic field.
items.d: The moving metal creates electric currents deep inside Earth.

items.t: Earth's magnetic poles are not at its geographic poles.
items.d: Magnetic north and the North Pole are in different places.

items.t: Cooling rocks can save a record of Earth's magnetic field.
items.d: Scientists study these rocks to learn where magnetic poles used to be.

items.t: Earth's magnetic poles have switched places hundreds of times.
items.d: This has happened since Earth formed.

items.t: A compass needle lines up with Earth's magnetic field.
items.d: This helps travelers find directions.

items.t: Electric current through a coil of wire creates a magnetic field.
items.d: This is the basic idea behind an electromagnet.

items.t: An electromagnet's field vanishes when its current is switched off.
items.d: Unlike a permanent magnet, it can be turned on and off.

items.t: The Sun sends a stream of charged particles called the solar wind.
items.d: This stream flows outward through the solar system.

items.t: Earth's magnetosphere shields us from harmful charged particles in space.
items.d: It acts like a giant magnetic shield around our planet.

items.t: Solar particles can make glowing auroras near Earth's poles.
items.d: Earth's magnetic field guides the particles toward polar regions.

items.t: During magnetic storms, energy follows Earth's field lines into the upper atmosphere.
items.d: That energy can create bright auroras.

items.t: Huge aurora displays need the Sun's and Earth's magnetic fields to line up just right.
items.d: That special alignment does not happen all the time.

items.t: A burst of material from the Sun can supercharge Earth's magnetosphere.
items.d: Such a burst is called a coronal mass ejection.

items.t: MRI scanners use strong magnets to line up protons in the body.
items.d: Protons are tiny particles found inside atoms.

items.t: An MRI uses radio waves to knock lined-up protons out of place.
items.d: Sensors detect energy as the protons line up again.

items.t: Body tissues respond at different speeds inside an MRI scanner.
items.d: These differences help doctors tell one type of tissue from another.

items.t: Maglev trains float above their tracks using magnets.
items.d: They move without rolling on ordinary train wheels.

items.t: Some maglev trains are pulled upward toward a steel rail.
items.d: A feedback system keeps a steady gap between the train and track.

items.t: Some maglev systems create electric currents in the track.
items.d: The resulting magnetic attraction and repulsion lift the train.

items.t: In 1820, Hans Christian Orsted showed that electric current makes a magnetic field.
items.d: A nearby current moved a compass needle.

items.t: William Sturgeon invented an electromagnet in 1824.
items.d: His magnet weighed about 200 grams and could lift about 4 kilograms.

items.t: Joseph Henry made powerful electromagnets using many layers of insulated wire.
items.d: One of his magnets could support 936 kilograms.

items.t: An iron core can make a coil's magnetic field thousands of times stronger.
items.d: The core is placed inside the wire coil.

items.t: More current makes an electromagnet stronger.
items.d: Changing the current lets people adjust the magnet's strength.

items.t: Giant electromagnets can lift heavy pieces of scrap iron and steel.
items.d: Switching off the current lets the metal go.

items.t: Electromagnets work inside motors, generators, speakers, and maglev trains.
items.d: Electricity and magnetism help each of these machines work.

items.t: Navigation compasses appeared in China by 1088.
items.d: Shen Kuo described them during the Song dynasty.

items.t: Early compass makers magnetized iron needles with lodestone.
items.d: Makers struck the needles with a lodestone.

items.t: True north and magnetic north are usually different directions.
items.d: The angle between them is called magnetic declination.

items.t: A gyrocompass uses a fast-spinning wheel to find true north.
items.d: Iron in a ship's hull does not disturb it.

items.t: A compass stops showing one clear direction very close to a magnetic pole.
items.d: The needle may begin to drift instead.

items.t: Near Earth's magnetic poles, a compass needle tilts up or down.
items.d: This tilt is called magnetic inclination.

items.t: A map line where a compass points exactly toward true north is called an agonic line.
items.d: Along that line, magnetic declination is zero.

items.t: A motor turns when a magnetic field pushes on a wire carrying current.
items.d: The push makes the motor's rotor spin.

items.t: A commutator flips a motor's current every half turn.
items.d: This keeps the motor spinning in the same direction.

items.t: Michael Faraday built the first electromagnetic generator in 1831.
items.d: It was called the Faraday disk.

items.t: Power station generators can be spun by steam, gas, or moving water.
items.d: Turbines provide the turning motion.

items.t: Moving a magnet and a wire circuit past each other can produce voltage.
items.d: This effect, called induction, is the idea behind generators.

items.t: A transformer passes energy between two coils using a magnetic field.
items.d: The two circuits do not need a metal wire connecting them.

items.t: A transformer needs changing current to work.
items.d: Changing current creates the changing magnetic field it uses.

items.t: Transformers raise voltage to reduce heating losses in power lines.
items.d: This helps electricity travel far from power stations to homes.

items.t: A speaker uses a magnet and an electric coil to move its cone.
items.d: The moving cone pushes air and makes sound waves.

items.t: A moving-coil speaker works like a microphone in reverse.
items.d: A speaker makes sound from a signal, while a microphone makes a signal from sound.

items.t: Some bacteria contain chains of tiny magnetic crystals.
items.d: The crystals, called magnetosomes, act like a compass needle.

items.t: Green aurora light comes from oxygen at lower altitudes.
items.d: Oxygen at the highest aurora altitudes can glow red.

items.t: Nitrogen molecules can give auroras blue and purple colors.
items.d: Different gases and heights help paint an aurora's colors.

items.t: A truss is a frame of bars. Each bar is pushed or pulled only at its two ends.
items.d: The force along each bar either stretches it or squeezes it.

items.t: Trusses use triangles because a triangle keeps its shape if its sides stay the same length.
items.d: This makes triangles useful for building stiff truss frames.

items.t: Every bar in a truss is either stretched or squeezed.
items.d: Stretching is called tension. Squeezing is called compression.

items.t: In many bridge trusses, top bars are squeezed and bottom bars are stretched.
items.d: The top is pressed together. The bottom is pulled tight, like a rope holding the ends in.

items.t: In a Pratt truss, upright bars are squeezed and slanting bars are stretched.
items.d: The uprights take the push. The diagonals take the pull.

items.t: The simplest 3D truss is a tetrahedron, a pyramid of four triangles.
items.d: Join four triangle faces with bars. If the bars stay the same length, the shape will not wobble.

items.t: The keystone is the top block of an arch. It locks the other blocks in place.
items.d: Look at a stone doorway or an old bridge. The center block at the top locks the curve.

items.t: A stone arch is made of wedge-shaped blocks called voussoirs.
items.d: Each block is wider at the outer end, so the pieces jam together under the load.

items.t: In a true arch, the blocks are squeezed hard against each other.
items.d: That squeeze is compression. It lets stone carry a heavy load across a gap.

items.t: An arch pushes outward at both ends, so it needs heavy supports there.
items.d: Those end supports are abutments. A thick wall or rocky bank can keep the arch from spreading.

items.t: With the same amount of material, an arch can span farther than a flat beam.
items.d: A flat lintel must fight bending. An arch sends the weight out to the supports.

items.t: Robert Hooke wrote that a hanging flexible line, turned over, gives the shape of an arch.
items.d: He described this idea in 1676. The hanging shape becomes an arch shape when it is flipped.

items.t: On a suspension bridge, cables are stretched and the towers are squeezed.
items.d: The road hangs from the cables. The cables pull on the towers and push them downward.

items.t: Each main cable of the Golden Gate Bridge is about 91 centimetres across.
items.d: That is about as wide as a doorway. A cable that thick helps hold up the long roadway.

items.t: The Brooklyn Bridge was the first suspension bridge with steel wire cables.
items.d: Steel wire is very strong when it is pulled, which is the job of a bridge cable.

items.t: A geodesic dome is the top of a ball, built from a frame of triangles.
items.d: Straight bars form the triangles, and together they make a strong curved roof.

items.t: Buckminster Fuller did not invent geodesic domes, but he designed many and patented them.
items.d: He patented his designs in the United States. Other builders had made triangle domes first.

items.t: On a bike, the pedals turn the cranks and start the parts that drive the wheel.
items.d: Your feet push the pedals around in a circle, and the cranks spin with them.

items.t: Most bicycles use a chain to carry power to the rear wheel.
items.d: The chain loops around gears at the pedals and gears at the back wheel.
