items.d: This is how plants get minerals from the soil.

items.t: Water can pull table salt apart by loosening the hold between sodium and chloride.
items.d: The salt seems to disappear when you stir it in.

items.t: Hard water has a lot of dissolved calcium and magnesium in it.
items.d: These minerals come from soil and rock the water passed through.

items.t: In hard water, calcium reacts with soap to make a sticky scum.
items.d: You may see a ring of scum around a bathtub.

items.t: You need more soap to get clean when the water is hard.
items.d: Some of the soap is used up reacting with the minerals.

items.t: Heating hard water can leave a chalky solid called scale, made of calcium carbonate.
items.d: Look inside an old kettle for a white crust.

items.t: Scale can build up inside pipes and slow the water down.
items.d: The pipe gets narrower, like a clogged straw.

items.t: Hard water is not considered a health danger. It can still be a nuisance.
items.d: It can make soap work poorly and leave scale in pipes.

items.t: Hard water forms when water seeps through limestone, chalk or gypsum.
items.d: The rock dissolves a tiny bit into the water.

items.t: Shake soap in water. If there is hardly any foam, the water may be hard.
items.d: In hard water, soap makes a white solid instead of lather.

items.t: Boiling can remove some hardness, because calcium carbonate separates out of the water.
items.d: That separated solid is the chalky crust in a kettle.

items.t: Ion-exchange water softeners swap calcium ions for sodium or potassium ions.
items.d: The swap stops scale from forming.

items.t: A sand filter removes solid bits from water, but it does not remove dissolved salt.
items.d: Dissolved salt passes through a sand filter.

items.t: Distillation boils water to steam and then cools it back to liquid, giving very pure water.
items.d: The minerals stay behind in the pot.

items.t: Sublimation happens when a solid changes straight into a gas.
items.d: The solid skips the liquid state.

items.t: Deposition happens when a gas changes straight into a solid.
items.d: It is the opposite of sublimation.

items.t: Dry ice turns straight from a solid into a gas at room temperature.
items.d: This change is called sublimation.

items.t: Gently heated iodine gives off purple fumes as it sublimes.
items.d: The solid iodine changes into a gas.

items.t: Snow and ice can slowly turn into vapour without melting first.
items.d: This can happen even when the air is too cold for melting.

items.t: Freeze-drying removes ice from frozen food by sublimation.
items.d: Low pressure helps the ice change straight into vapour.

items.t: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide.
items.d: At normal air pressure, it becomes gas at about -78.5 C.

items.t: Dry ice does not melt into a puddle at normal air pressure.
items.d: Carbon dioxide cannot be a liquid at that pressure.

items.t: The thick fog around dry ice in water is made of tiny water droplets.
items.d: The carbon dioxide gas itself is invisible.

items.t: Dry ice is often used to keep food cold.
items.d: It is colder than ordinary water ice.

items.t: Very pure water can remain liquid down to about -48 C.
items.d: It freezes when ice crystals finally begin to form.

items.t: Supercooling needs very pure water.
items.d: Tiny specks can give ice crystals a place to start growing.

items.t: Clouds can contain supercooled water droplets.
items.d: These droplets are liquid even below water's normal freezing point.

items.t: Plasma is often called the fourth state of matter.
items.d: The first three are solid, liquid, and gas.

items.t: More than 99% of the visible matter in the universe is plasma.
items.d: Stars contain enormous amounts of plasma.

items.t: Water boils at about 93.4 C at an altitude of 1,905 metres.
items.d: Lower air pressure lowers its boiling point.

items.t: Water boils at about 71 C on the summit of Mount Everest.
items.d: The air pressure there is much lower than at sea level.

items.t: Boiling creates vapour bubbles throughout a liquid.
items.d: Evaporation happens only at the liquid's surface.

items.t: Water's triple point is 273.16 K at about 611 pascals of pressure.
items.d: At that exact condition, ice, liquid water, and water vapour can coexist.

items.t: Water drops can skitter across a very hot pan instead of vanishing at once.
items.d: A cushion of steam supports them. This is the Leidenfrost effect.

items.t: Condensation is the change from a gas into a liquid.
items.d: It is the reverse of vaporization.

items.t: Frost forms when water vapour becomes ice on a freezing surface.
items.d: The water usually skips the liquid state.

items.t: Liquid nitrogen boils at about -196 C.
items.d: It boils at once when it touches much warmer objects.

items.t: Density tells how much mass fits in a certain volume.
items.d: Divide the mass by the volume. Pack more mass into the same space and the density rises.

items.t: Liquid water's density is about 1 gram per cubic centimetre.
items.d: That is about 1000 kilograms per cubic metre. One litre of water has a mass of about 1 kilogram.

items.t: Fresh water is at its densest at about 4 degrees Celsius.
items.d: A kilogram of fresh water takes up the least room at about that temperature.

items.t: If a material is less dense than water, it floats in water.
items.d: Its mass is less than the same volume of water, so the water can hold it up.

items.t: Gold is more than 19 times as dense as water.
items.d: Gold's density is about 19,320 kilograms per cubic metre. A little piece feels heavy.

items.t: At sea level, air's density is only about 1.2 kilograms per cubic metre.
items.d: Liquid water is about 1000 kilograms per cubic metre, so air is far lighter.

items.t: Mercury is about 13.5 times as dense as water.
items.d: Its density is about 13,546 kilograms per cubic metre, so even a small jar is heavy.

items.t: Sea water is denser than pure water because of dissolved salt.
items.d: The salt adds mass. A full cup of ocean water weighs more than a full cup of fresh water.

items.t: Above 4 degrees Celsius, water gets less dense as it warms.
items.d: The particles spread out a little. The same mass of warm water takes up more space.

items.t: At 0 degrees Celsius, ice's density is about 0.917 grams per cubic centimetre.
items.d: Liquid water is about 1.00 grams per cubic centimetre, so ice has less mass for its size.

items.t: Water grows about 9 percent in volume when it freezes.
items.d: Ice needs more room than the water did. Pipes full of water can crack as the ice forms.

items.t: Particles in a solid are packed tightly and stay in place.
items.d: They only vibrate. They do not slide past each other the way liquid particles do.

items.t: A solid keeps its own shape and its own volume.
items.d: A rock keeps the same shape in a bucket or sitting on the ground.

items.t: Particles in a liquid stay close, but they can slide past each other.
items.d: That sliding is why a liquid pours and can change its shape.

items.t: A liquid takes its container's shape and is very hard to squash.
items.d: The volume stays about the same. Water poured into a glass matches that glass.

items.t: Particles in a gas are far apart and move about freely.
items.d: A bike pump squeezes air into a smaller space because the particles have big gaps.

items.t: A gas spreads until it fills all of its container.
items.d: Air spreads through a room and fills the space from floor to ceiling.

items.t: A gas can be pictured as particles in nonstop random motion.
items.d: This idea is the kinetic theory. Particles zip around, bump, and bounce away.

items.t: Gas pressure is made by particles hitting the walls and bouncing off.
items.d: In a balloon, tiny particles hit the rubber all the time and push it outward.

items.t: A gas is hotter when its particles have more motion energy.
items.d: Temperature goes up with the average motion energy. Faster particles mean a hotter gas.

items.t: A gas is mostly empty space between tiny particles.
items.d: Added together, the particles' own volume is almost nothing next to the container.

items.t: In 1827, Robert Brown saw pollen grains jiggling nonstop in water.
items.d: Under a microscope, the tiny grains kept moving in a jittery, random way.

items.t: In 1905, Albert Einstein explained why tiny grains jiggle in water.
items.d: Water molecules bump the grains. Uneven bumps keep them jiggling.

items.t: The jiggling of tiny grains helped prove that atoms are real.
items.d: Invisible water particles keep hitting the grains, so the grains never sit still.

items.t: Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to flowing.
items.d: A thick milkshake resists flow more than plain milk. That resistance is viscosity.

items.t: At 20 degrees Celsius, honey is thousands of times more viscous than water.
items.d: Honey's viscosity is about 2,000 to 10,000 millipascal-seconds, so it drips very slowly.

items.t: Most liquids flow more easily after they are warmed.
items.d: Warm honey slides off a spoon faster than cold honey. Heat lowers its viscosity.

items.t: Gases grow more viscous when heated, unlike most liquids.
items.d: A hotter gas resists flow a little more. A hotter liquid usually resists flow less.

items.t: In 1927, a teacher began an experiment to show that pitch flows.
items.d: Thomas Parnell set it up at the University of Queensland so students could watch pitch move.

items.t: Pitch is roughly 230 billion times more viscous than water.
items.d: Water flows easily. Pitch is so thick that its slow flow is hard to see.

items.t: In the pitch drop experiment, drops fall about once each decade.
items.d: The first drop fell in December 1938. The eighth drop fell on 28 November 2000.

items.t: Diffusion is particles spreading from crowded places to emptier ones.
items.d: Movement is random. More particles leave a crowded spot than return, so things even out.

items.t: A drop of dye in still water slowly spreads through the glass.
items.d: No stirring is needed. Dye particles wander out from the drop into the clear water.

items.t: Diffusion gets faster as the temperature rises.
items.d: Warmer particles move faster, helping diffusion happen more quickly.

items.t: Oobleck is a mixture of cornflour and water.
items.d: Cornflour is also called cornstarch. Stirred into water, it makes oobleck.

items.t: The harder you hit oobleck, the thicker it acts.
items.d: Push slowly and your finger sinks in. Hit it fast and the surface feels almost solid.

items.t: Ketchup pours more easily once you shake it.
items.d: The shaking makes ketchup runnier, so it comes out of the bottle more easily.

items.t: Toothpaste needs a push before it will flow.
items.d: Until you squeeze the tube, it keeps its shape and does not run off the brush.

items.t: When heated, particles move more and most materials expand.
items.d: Particles vibrate more and usually leave slightly bigger gaps between them.

items.t: Bridges and railway tracks use expansion joints so they can expand and shrink.
items.d: The joints make room for changes caused by hot and cold weather.

items.t: A fluid pushes up with a force equal to the weight of fluid an object pushes aside.
items.d: This is Archimedes' principle. A heavy boat floats when it pushes aside enough water.

items.t: An iron lump sinks, but the same iron can float if shaped like a bowl.
items.d: The bowl pushes aside much more water. The bigger upward push can hold the iron up.

items.t: A ship floats by pushing aside water equal to its own weight.
items.d: Airships are designed the same way in air. Submarines are designed this way in water.

items.t: Water pushes up, so a submerged object feels lighter.
items.d: A 10-newton rock that pushes aside 3 newtons of water seems to weigh 7 newtons.

items.t: Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe.
items.d: Its gas has about 7 percent of air's density. It makes up about 75 percent of ordinary matter by mass.

items.t: A hot air balloon goes up because the air inside is less dense.
items.d: A burner heats the air inside. That warm air is lighter than the air outside.

items.t: Lava lamp wax rises when warm and sinks when cool.
items.d: Heat makes the wax less dense, so blobs rise. Cooling makes it denser, so it sinks.

items.t: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at standard temperature and pressure.
items.d: Mercury is also commonly called quicksilver.

items.t: A separation process splits a mixture into two or more different products.
items.d: Salty water can be split into fresh water and salt.

items.t: Separation methods use differences in the properties of things in a mixture.
items.d: Sand is bigger than salt grains, so a sieve can tell them apart.

items.t: Distillation separates substances by heating and cooling them.
items.d: Heat turns a liquid to vapour. Cooling turns it back into liquid.

items.t: Aluminium metal is made from bauxite ore by using electricity to separate it out.
items.d: This method is called electrolysis.

items.t: Crude oil is a mixture. Gasoline and other products made from it are mixtures too.
items.d: Refineries have to separate each product from the raw oil.

items.t: Often one separation is not enough. Several steps are linked one after another.
items.d: Each step takes out something different until the final products are ready.

items.t: Chromatography separates dissolved substances because they travel through a material at different speeds.
items.d: Fast travellers end up far from the start. Slow ones stay close.

items.t: Flocculation uses a chemical to make tiny bits clump together so they can be taken out of a liquid.
items.d: The clumps are bigger, so they are easier to separate.

items.t: Distillation is used for mixtures of liquids that have different boiling points.
items.d: The liquid with the lower boiling point turns to vapour first.

items.t: Aristotle noticed long ago that when salt water turns to vapour, it becomes fresh water.
items.d: That is the idea behind distilling seawater.

items.t: People have used distilled water for more than 1,800 years.
items.d: Alexander of Aphrodisias described the process around 200 CE.

items.t: Pot stills are still used today to make some drinks, like whisky.
items.d: Pot stills have been used for a very long time.

items.t: Distillation can turn seawater into drinking water. This is called desalination.
items.d: Boiling leaves the salt behind, and cooled vapour becomes fresh water.

items.t: Distillation uses a lot of energy because it relies on boiling and cooling.
items.d: Roughly a quarter of all industrial energy goes into it.

items.t: A botanist named Mikhail Tsvet developed chromatography between 1901 and 1905.
items.d: He worked in universities in Kazan and Warsaw.

items.t: Tsvet used chromatography to separate plant colours, including chlorophyll.
items.d: Chlorophyll is the green stuff that helps plants make food.

items.t: The word chromatography comes from Greek words meaning color and to write.
items.d: It is like writing with colours.

items.t: In paper chromatography, you put a small dot of sample on special paper.
items.d: The liquid creeps up the paper and carries the dot's parts with it.

items.t: Martin and Synge won the 1952 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their chromatography work.
items.d: Their work led to paper chromatography and gas chromatography.

items.t: A cream separator in a dairy is a centrifuge.
items.d: It spins milk fast so the cream separates from the rest.

items.t: Medium-sized centrifuges are found inside washing machines.
items.d: The fast spin flings water out of your clothes.

items.t: A coffee filter separates the liquid coffee from the grounds.
items.d: The liquid passes through the paper. The grounds stay behind.

items.t: Melitta Bentz invented the first paper coffee filter you could buy, in 1908.
items.d: She wanted to remove the bitter taste caused by over-brewing.

items.t: Your kidneys filter your blood and remove waste such as urea.
items.d: They also take back many useful substances your body needs.

items.t: A colander is a bowl-shaped sieve used in cooking to strain food.
items.d: Pasta stays in the colander while the water runs out.

items.t: Sieving is a simple way to separate bits of different sizes.
items.d: Small grains fall through the holes. Big ones stay on top.

items.t: Decanting separates two liquids that do not mix, like oil and water.
items.d: In a jar of salad dressing, the oil floats on the water.

items.t: Winnowing separates chaff from grain.
items.d: Chaff is the light, dry outer covering of the grain.

items.t: A solute dissolves. A solvent does the dissolving.
items.d: In salt water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent.

items.t: A saturated solution cannot dissolve any more solute.
items.d: Any extra solute stays undissolved.

items.t: Most solid and liquid solutes dissolve more at higher temperatures.
items.d: Warm liquid can often dissolve more of a solid than cold liquid can.

items.t: Table salt dissolves easily in water.
items.d: Water is highly polar, which helps it dissolve sodium chloride.

items.t: Chemists often say, "Like dissolves like."
items.d: A substance tends to dissolve best in a liquid that is chemically similar to it.

items.t: Stirring can make a substance dissolve faster.
items.d: How fast it dissolves depends on how well you mix it.

items.t: Water can help separate salt from sand.
items.d: The salt dissolves in water, while the sand stays behind.

items.t: Tiny particles in a colloid scatter light. This is called the Tyndall effect.
items.d: It can make a beam look cloudy or glowing.

items.t: Milk contains tiny globules of fat spread through water.
items.d: The particles are fat droplets, not single fat molecules.

items.t: Fog, clouds, and mist are colloids of tiny water droplets in air.
items.d: This kind of colloid is called a liquid aerosol.

items.t: Milk, mayonnaise, and hand cream are emulsions.
items.d: An emulsion has droplets of one liquid spread through another liquid.

items.t: Agar, gelatin, and jelly are examples of gels.
items.d: A gel is a type of colloid.

items.t: Colloid particles are about 1 nanometre to 1 micrometre across.
items.d: They are too small to see one by one with your eyes.

items.t: Every colloid has tiny bits and something for those bits to float in.
items.d: Scientists call these the dispersed phase and continuous phase.

items.t: If colloid particles are denser than the liquid, they can slowly sink.
items.d: This sinking is called sedimentation.

items.t: The Tyndall effect is named after physicist John Tyndall.
items.d: He studied this scattering of light during the 1800s.

items.t: Blue light scatters much more strongly than red light in the Tyndall effect.
items.d: That is why scattered light from some mixtures looks bluish.

items.t: A light beam can help tell a solution from a colloid.
items.d: A colloid shows the Tyndall effect, but a true solution does not.

items.t: An emulsion is a mix of liquids that normally do not mix.
items.d: Oil and water can form an emulsion when one becomes tiny droplets in the other.

items.t: An emulsifier helps an emulsion stay mixed.
items.d: It lowers the tension where oil and water meet.

items.t: Egg yolk contains lecithin, an emulsifier used in mayonnaise.
items.d: It helps oil and water blend together instead of separating.

items.t: Milk is a natural emulsion of fat in water.
items.d: Milk also contains other substances, including proteins.

items.t: A simple oil-and-vinegar dressing is an unstable emulsion.
items.d: It separates because it has no emulsifier to hold it together.

items.t: Particles in a suspension settle if the mixture is left still.
items.d: The mixture can look different after it has rested.

items.t: Muddy water is a suspension.
items.d: Particles of soil, clay, or silt are held in the water.

items.t: Suspension particles are usually larger than 1 micrometre.
items.d: They are larger than the particles found in colloids.

items.t: A flour-and-water suspension can scatter a beam of light.
items.d: This scattering is the Tyndall effect.

items.t: A foam is made of gas bubbles trapped in a liquid or solid.
items.d: The bubbles form a structure filled with tiny cells.

items.t: A bath sponge is an open-cell foam.
items.d: Its holes connect, so water can flow through and push air out.

items.t: Bread rises because yeast makes tiny gas bubbles.
items.d: Those bubbles become the holes you see inside the bread.

items.t: Gels are mostly liquid, yet they can behave like solids.
items.d: A linked network inside holds the liquid in place.

items.t: Some hydrogels contain more than 90 percent water.
items.d: A network in the gel keeps all that water held in place.

items.t: Removing liquid from a gel without shrinking it can make an aerogel.
items.d: Aerogel is a very light material filled with tiny pores.

items.t: Many gels become runny when stirred and set again while resting.
items.d: This change is called thixotropy.

items.t: Rock candy grows from a supersaturated sugar solution.
items.d: A seed crystal gives the dissolved sugar a place to start forming crystals.

items.t: A tiny seed crystal can make a supersaturated solution start crystallizing.
items.d: This process is called seeding.

items.t: A supersaturated solution holds more dissolved solute than it normally would.
items.d: It is in an unstable state that scientists call metastable.

items.t: Fizzy drinks contain carbon dioxide dissolved under pressure.
items.d: Opening the container lowers the pressure, so gas escapes as bubbles.

items.t: Henry's law links gas pressure to how much gas dissolves in a liquid.
items.d: At equilibrium, greater gas pressure means more of that gas dissolves.

items.t: Tiny particles in water jiggle because water molecules keep bumping them.
items.d: This constant jiggling is called Brownian motion.

items.t: Oobleck is a suspension of starch in water that behaves in an unusual way.
items.d: It seems to get thicker when you push on it harder.

items.t: Ketchup flows more easily after it is shaken or squeezed.
items.d: It is shear-thinning, meaning force makes it less thick and easier to pour.

items.t: An atom has a nucleus in the center, with electrons around it.
items.d: The nucleus holds protons and, in most atoms, neutrons too.

items.t: Protons are positive. Neutrons have no charge at all.
items.d: Protons and neutrons are the pieces that build the nucleus.

items.t: More than 99.9 percent of an atom's mass sits in the nucleus.
items.d: Electrons are real, but they weigh almost nothing beside that center.

items.t: A typical atom is about 100 picometers across.
items.d: That width is about one ten-millionth of a millimeter.

items.t: The first electron shell can hold only two electrons.
items.d: It is the smallest shell. Any further electron must start a new one.

items.t: Graphite is flat sheets of carbon atoms bonded inside each sheet.
items.d: Some electrons can move through the sheets, so graphite conducts electricity.

items.t: Each shell farther out can hold more electrons than the one inside.
items.d: At most: shell 1 holds 2, shell 2 holds 8, shell 3 holds 18, shell 4 holds 32.

items.t: Sodium is where the third shell, called M, starts to fill.
items.d: Sodium is element 11. Electron 11 is the first one in the M shell.

items.t: Valence electrons are the electrons in an atom's outer shell.
items.d: Sodium's one outer electron is easily lost when it forms a positive ion.

items.t: Sodium has one outer electron, and it loses that electron easily.
items.d: The atom becomes a positive ion. That easy loss makes sodium very reactive.

items.t: Atoms with a full outer shell tend not to react.
items.d: A full outer shell tends to make an atom chemically unreactive.

items.t: Helium has only two electrons, but its shell is already full.
items.d: Its full shell makes helium chemically very unreactive.

items.t: Halogens like fluorine and chlorine are the most reactive nonmetals.
items.d: Fluorine and chlorine are examples of halogens.

items.t: Copper, aluminum, silver, and gold conduct electricity well.
items.d: These four metals are examples of good electrical conductors.

items.t: Many main-group atoms tend to bond until they have eight outer electrons.
items.d: This tendency is called the octet rule.

items.t: In salt, sodium gives one electron to chlorine.
items.d: Sodium becomes a plus ion and chlorine a minus ion, lined up in a crystal.

items.t: Hydrogen needs only two electrons to fill its shell.
items.d: That is the duet rule. One extra electron gives hydrogen a helium-like shell.

items.t: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared by two atoms.
items.d: Sharing lets each atom count the pair toward a full outer shell.

items.t: Hydrogen gas is two atoms sharing two electrons.
items.d: We write it H2: two hydrogen atoms joined by one covalent bond.

items.t: If atoms share electrons unequally, the bond is polar.
items.d: In HCl, chlorine pulls the shared electrons closer than hydrogen does.

items.t: Oxygen gas is often drawn as two oxygen atoms joined by a double bond.
items.d: It is shown as O=O, with two shared pairs between the atoms.

items.t: An ionic bond is the pull between a plus ion and a minus ion.
items.d: Opposite charges attract. That pull holds ionic solids like salt together.

items.t: Most ionic compounds are crystals of repeating ions.
items.d: Table salt is one. Sodium and chloride ions keep a tidy pattern.

items.t: Melted or dissolved ionic compounds can conduct electricity.
items.d: Solid salt usually cannot. Its ions are locked and cannot move to carry charge.

items.t: Diamond is a network of carbon atoms joined by covalent bonds.
items.d: Strong covalent bonds throughout the network make diamond very hard.

items.t: In rock salt, six chloride ions surround each sodium ion.
items.d: Rock salt is the crystal of sodium chloride, the same stuff as table salt.

items.t: A simple model shows positive metal ions in a sea of moving electrons.
items.d: Attraction between the ions and conduction electrons makes the metallic bond.

items.t: Layers of metal atoms can slide, so metals bend and stretch.
items.d: You can hammer metal flat or pull it into wire, and it holds together.

items.t: Metals conduct electricity because electrons can move through them.
items.d: The moving electrons are the electric current in a metal wire.

items.t: Free electrons also carry most of the heat inside a metal.
items.d: That is why a metal spoon warms up fast in a hot drink.

items.t: Pure gold is very soft, so gold jewelry usually uses alloys.
items.d: Gold alloys are preferred for jewelry because pure gold is very soft.

items.t: Tungsten has a higher melting point than any other metal.
items.d: It stays solid at heat that would melt iron, gold, and every other metal.

items.t: An ion is an atom or molecule that carries an electric charge.
items.d: The charge shows up when the count of electrons and protons does not match.

items.t: A cation is a positive ion. It has fewer electrons than protons.
items.d: Lose one negative electron, and the ion's charge is plus one.

items.t: An anion is a negative ion. It has more electrons than protons.
items.d: Gain one electron, and the ion's charge becomes minus one.

items.t: A gecko can cling to a wall using thousands of tiny hairs.
items.d: The hairs make many weak van der Waals forces that add up to a firm grip.

items.t: A compound contains atoms of at least two different elements.
items.d: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. A single element is not one.

items.t: A pure element is not a compound, even when its atoms are bonded.
items.d: Oxygen gas is O2, two oxygen atoms bonded. It is still just an element.

items.t: Fluorine pulls on shared electrons harder than any other element.
items.d: Linus Pauling's 1932 scale gives fluorine 3.98, the highest score.

items.t: Hydrogen bonds are usually weaker than covalent or ionic bonds.
items.d: They are still stronger than van der Waals forces, which are very gentle.

items.t: A chemical formula shows the proportions of atoms in a compound.
items.d: Water is H2O. The small 2 means two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom.

items.t: Each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen.
items.d: The three atoms are held together by covalent bonds.

items.t: In water, the bend at oxygen is an angle of about 104.5 degrees.
items.d: The two hydrogen atoms are not in a straight line. Water is bent.

items.t: Water is a polar molecule.
items.d: Its oxygen end is partly negative, and its hydrogen ends are partly positive.

items.t: One water molecule can make at most four hydrogen bonds.
items.d: Four is the largest number of hydrogen bonds one water molecule can join.

items.t: Water has unusually high surface tension because of hydrogen bonding.
items.d: That pull keeps drops round. Some insects can even stand on water.

items.t: Trees can move water upward more than 100 meters.
items.d: Cohesion from hydrogen bonding and adhesion help the water rise.

items.t: Water boils at a high temperature for such a tiny molecule.
items.d: Extra heat is needed to separate molecules linked by hydrogen bonds.

items.t: Hydrogen bonds help hold the two strands of DNA together.
items.d: Paired bases on the two strands tug each other and keep the helix shape.

items.t: A chemical reaction turns one set of substances into a different set of substances.
items.d: Baking a cake turns batter into something new.

items.t: The starting substances in a chemical reaction are called reactants.
items.d: Wood and oxygen are the reactants when a campfire burns.

items.t: The new substances made in a chemical reaction are called products.
items.d: Burning wood makes new products like ash and gases.

items.t: Products usually look and behave differently from the reactants that made them.
items.d: Shiny iron and air make flaky orange rust.

items.t: In a reaction, the atoms are not lost or created. They just get rearranged.
items.d: The same atoms go in as come out, in new groups.

items.t: Balancing an equation means putting numbers in front so both sides have the same atoms.
items.d: CH4 + 2O2 makes CO2 + 2H2O, with 4 H and 4 O on each side.

items.t: Splitting water with electricity makes hydrogen gas and oxygen gas.
items.d: This is called electrolysis.

items.t: In a closed system, the total mass stays the same before and after a reaction.
items.d: If you burn a candle in a sealed jar, the jar weighs the same.

items.t: Lavoisier's experiments showed that the old phlogiston idea was wrong.
items.d: He weighed everything very carefully.

items.t: Most enzymes are protein catalysts that work inside living things.
items.d: Your body has many of them.

items.t: Tiny catalyst particles have more surface area than one big lump of the same mass.
items.d: More surface means more places for a reaction to happen.

items.t: Many enzyme names are the substrate's name plus the ending -ase.
items.d: Lactose gives lactase. Protein gives protease.

items.t: Digestive enzymes break big food molecules into small ones your body can use.
items.d: Amylases work on starch and proteases work on protein.

items.t: In a physical change, a substance changes form but is still the same substance.
items.d: Melting ice makes liquid water, which is still water.

items.t: Many physical changes can be undone with physical methods.
items.d: Boil away salty water and you get the salt back.

items.t: In a chemical change, the composition changes and new substances form.
items.d: Rust is not iron anymore.

items.t: Mass conservation is often summed up as: nothing is lost, nothing is created, everything is transformed.
items.d: Matter changes form, but its total mass stays the same in a closed system.

items.t: Lavoisier showed that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, not a single element.
items.d: People had thought water was an element for over 2,000 years.

items.t: Soot is solid carbon that can form when a flame has too much fuel for the air it gets.
items.d: A smoky candle flame can leave soot on a spoon.

items.t: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen while water is present.
items.d: A bike left in the rain can get rusty.

items.t: Decomposition splits one substance into two or more simpler ones.
items.d: It is the opposite of combining substances.

items.t: Heating calcium carbonate makes calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
items.d: Chalk and limestone are mostly calcium carbonate.

items.t: The Maillard reaction between amino acids and certain sugars browns food and creates flavors.
items.d: It helps give toast and roasted meat their flavors.

items.t: Activation energy is the smallest energy boost needed to start a chemical reaction.
items.d: It is like the first push needed to get a ball rolling uphill.

items.t: Activation energy is measured in kilojoules per mole.
items.d: A mole is a very large, fixed number of tiny particles.

items.t: Svante Arrhenius introduced the term activation energy in 1889.
items.d: Arrhenius was a Swedish scientist who studied reaction speeds.

items.t: The highest point on a reaction energy graph is called the transition state.
items.d: After particles reach this peak, they can continue toward the products.

items.t: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.
items.d: The same catalyst can often help again and again.

items.t: Activation energy does not decide if a reaction is favored.
items.d: It tells us about the starting barrier, not whether the whole change is favored.

items.t: An exothermic reaction sends energy into its surroundings.
items.d: The released energy often warms nearby matter.

items.t: An exothermic reaction can give off heat, light, electricity, or sound.
items.d: Heat is the most common form released.

items.t: An exothermic process gets warmer if its heat cannot escape.
items.d: Energy stays inside the system, so its temperature rises.

items.t: An exothermic reaction releases more energy than it needs to get started.
items.d: It still may need an opening energy push called activation energy.

items.t: When a vapor condenses into a liquid, it releases heat.
items.d: Condensation is an exothermic physical change.

items.t: An endothermic process takes in heat from its surroundings.
items.d: The energy moves from the surroundings into the changing material.

items.t: Endothermic reactions usually make their surroundings colder.
items.d: They cool nearby matter by absorbing some of its heat.

items.t: The word endothermic has a Greek part, endon, meaning within.
items.d: The word describes heat moving into a system.

items.t: Melting ice is endothermic.
items.d: Ice absorbs heat from its surroundings as it changes into liquid water.

items.t: Some instant cold packs cool down as ammonium nitrate dissolves in water.
items.d: Dissolving it absorbs heat, so the pack feels cold.

items.t: Air-activated hand warmers contain iron powder and several other materials.
items.d: They may also contain cellulose, activated carbon, and vermiculite.

items.t: Some hand warmers make heat as iron reacts with oxygen in the air.
items.d: This slow rusting reaction is exothermic.

items.t: Salt helps the iron in an air-activated hand warmer rust faster.
items.d: Faster rusting makes the warmer release heat more quickly.

items.t: Flexing the metal disk in a reusable hand warmer starts its heat release.
items.d: A small metal disk inside the warmer starts the heat when bent.

items.t: Sodium acetate trihydrate is sometimes nicknamed hot ice.
items.d: It can form ice-like crystals while giving off heat.

items.t: Sodium acetate can cool to room temperature without forming crystals.
items.d: This unusual liquid is called a supersaturated solution.

items.t: Sodium acetate releases heat when it forms crystals.
items.d: Its crystallization is an exothermic process.

items.t: Boiling can dissolve a sodium acetate heat pack's crystals and reset the pack.
items.d: Slow cooling then prepares it for its next use.

items.t: A reaction can go faster when its reactants are more concentrated.
items.d: More particles in the same space means more frequent collisions.

items.t: Heating a reaction gives more particles enough energy to react.
items.d: A larger share of their collisions can cross the activation barrier.

items.t: A powdered solid can react faster than one large piece of the same mass.
items.d: Crushing the solid creates more total surface area.

items.t: A catalyst offers a reaction a route with a lower energy barrier.
items.d: More particle collisions can take this easier route, so the reaction speeds up.

items.t: Higher pressure can make reactions between gases go faster.
items.d: Squeezing gas particles closer together makes collisions more frequent.

items.t: Pressure has only a weak effect on most reactions in liquids and solids.
items.d: Squeezing liquids or solids does not speed most reactions very much.

items.t: Collision theory helps scientists predict how fast reactions will happen.
items.d: It looks at how often particles collide and whether collisions can react.

items.t: Not every collision between particles causes a reaction.
items.d: A useful collision must have at least the activation energy.

items.t: Max Trautz proposed collision theory in 1916.
items.d: William Lewis independently proposed it in 1918.

items.t: Collision theory works better for simple molecules than for complex ones.
items.d: It gets less reliable as the molecules get more complicated.

items.t: Svante Arrhenius proposed his reaction-rate equation in 1889.
items.d: He was working with Wilhelm Ostwald in Leipzig.

items.t: A reaction's speed can change sharply when its temperature changes.
items.d: The Arrhenius equation describes this temperature effect.

items.t: For typical reactions, a 10°C rise can make them about 2 to 3 times as fast.
items.d: The exact change depends on the reaction.

items.t: Catalysts change reaction speed, but not how far a reaction can go.
items.d: They help a reaction reach its final balance sooner.

items.t: Enzymes are protein-based catalysts in living things.
items.d: They help the chemical reactions that keep cells working.

items.t: Enzymes can speed some reactions by millions of times.
items.d: They work by lowering the reaction's activation energy.

items.t: An enzyme may work faster as it warms, but too much heat makes it slow down.
items.d: High heat can unfold the enzyme and change its useful shape.

items.t: A refrigerator slows food spoilage, but it does not stop it forever.
items.d: Cool conditions slow many changes caused by microbes and chemistry.

items.t: About 3 to 5°C is a good refrigerator temperature for perishable food.
items.d: Cold storage helps food stay usable longer.

items.t: Iron needs both water and oxygen to rust.
items.d: Keeping either one away can slow the rusting reaction.

items.t: Iron usually rusts faster in salt water than in fresh water.
items.d: Salt helps the oxidation reaction happen more quickly.

items.t: The pH scale goes from 0 to 14. A pH of 7 is neutral.
items.d: Neutral means the liquid is not an acid or a base.

items.t: Below 7 is acidic. Above 7 is basic, or alkaline.
items.d: On this water scale, basic and alkaline both mean above 7.

items.t: On the pH scale, each whole step is a change of ten times.
items.d: A drop of one number means ten times more acid.

items.t: Danish scientist S. P. L. Sorensen introduced pH in 1909.
items.d: His scale lets us compare how acidic water is.

items.t: Only liquids that contain water have a pH.
items.d: Vegetable oil and pure alcohol do not have a pH.

items.t: Normal rain is a little acidic, with a pH of about 5.6.
items.d: A little carbon dioxide from the air dissolves in each raindrop.

items.t: Water from an old coal mine can have a pH of 2.
items.d: Five steps below 7, so 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 = 100,000 times more acidic.

items.t: A pH meter measures pH. Litmus paper gives only a rough idea.
items.d: The meter uses a probe. The paper only changes color.

items.t: Very basic water can taste bitter. Very acidic water can corrode metal.
items.d: Corrode means the acid slowly wears the metal away.

items.t: Acids taste sour.
items.d: Lemons and vinegar taste sour because they contain acids.

items.t: Bacteria on your teeth turn sugar into acid.
items.d: That acid can slowly wear away the hard enamel on a tooth.

items.t: Vinegar is a weak mix of acetic acid and water.
items.d: The sour taste on a salad comes from that acid.

items.t: Oranges and lemons contain citric acid.
items.d: Other citrus fruits have it too. It makes them taste sour.

items.t: Your stomach uses hydrochloric acid to help digest food.
items.d: The acid switches on enzymes that break food into smaller bits.

items.t: Vitamin C is an acid. Its science name is ascorbic acid.
items.d: Your body needs this vitamin to stay healthy.

items.t: Some ants make formic acid to protect themselves.
items.d: It is one of their tools for staying safe.

items.t: A car battery contains sulfuric acid.
items.d: Many cars use this acid inside their batteries.

items.t: Fizzy drinks get carbonic acid from dissolved carbon dioxide.
items.d: That gas is what makes the bubbles when you open the bottle.

items.t: Bases dissolved in water feel slippery.
items.d: Wet soap feels slippery, and soap is a weak base.

items.t: Soap is a weak base made from fats and a strong base.
items.d: The strong base turns the fat into soap that can wash you.

items.t: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
items.d: Every alkali is a base. A base that does not dissolve is not an alkali.

items.t: An acid and a base can react to make salt and water.
items.d: We call this reaction neutralization.

items.t: Milk of magnesia is a base that can calm an upset stomach.
items.d: Its magnesium hydroxide neutralizes extra acid in the stomach.

items.t: Baking soda is a weak base that helps cakes rise.
items.d: Bakers mix a little into batter before it goes in the oven.

items.t: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2.2.
items.d: That low number means lemon juice is very acidic.

items.t: Vinegar has a pH of about 2 to 3.
items.d: It is sour and much more acidic than milk or pure water.

items.t: Human blood is slightly alkaline, with a pH of about 7.4.
items.d: That is just a little above 7, the neutral point.

items.t: Seawater is slightly alkaline, about pH 7.5 to 8.4.
items.d: The ocean is a weak base, a bit above pure water.

items.t: Bleach has a very high pH of about 12.5.
items.d: That is very basic. Do not taste it or get it on your skin.

items.t: Cow's milk is close to neutral, about pH 6.5 to 6.8.
items.d: It is only a little acidic, very near the middle of the scale.

items.t: Pure water at 25 degrees Celsius has a neutral pH of 7.
items.d: At that temperature, pure water is neither acidic nor basic.

items.t: Stomach acid has a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5.
items.d: It is among the most acidic liquids in the human body.

items.t: Red cabbage has a dye you can use as a pH test.
items.d: The colored water from the cabbage changes with pH.

items.t: In acid, red cabbage dye turns red or pink. Neutral dye looks purple.
items.d: A splash of lemon juice can move the color toward red.

items.t: In a base, red cabbage dye can turn blue, green, or yellow.
items.d: These colors show the liquid is alkaline, above pH 7.

items.t: Cooked red cabbage usually turns blue. Vinegar can keep it red.
items.d: Vinegar is acidic, and acid holds the dye on the red side.

items.t: Anthocyanins are plant dyes that dissolve in water.
items.d: Their color can be red, pink, purple, blue, or nearly black, depending on pH.

items.t: Blueberries and black rice are rich in dyes called anthocyanins.
items.d: Raspberries and black carrots are full of the same colorful dyes.

items.t: Hydrochloric acid plus sodium hydroxide makes table salt and water.
items.d: Table salt is sodium chloride. Only do this in a lab, never at home.

items.t: Gardeners add lime to soil that is too acidic for plants.
items.d: Lime or limestone makes the soil less acidic so plants can grow better.

items.t: An antacid neutralizes extra acid in the stomach.
items.d: People take one for heartburn, indigestion, or an upset stomach.

items.t: Soap molecules form tiny balls, called micelles, that trap oily dirt.
items.d: Water can rinse those balls away, which is how soap helps you get clean.

items.t: Litmus dye comes from lichens.
items.d: People put the dye on paper to test acids and bases.

items.t: Blue litmus paper turns red in acid. Red litmus paper turns blue in a base.
items.d: A quick color change shows which kind of liquid you have.

items.t: Some hydrangeas are usually blue in acidic soil and pink or red in alkaline soil.
items.d: The same kind of plant can change flower color when the soil pH changes.

items.t: Your stomach makes thick mucus to protect itself from its acid.
items.d: The mucus is a thick barrier between the acid and the stomach wall.

items.t: Vinegar is used to pickle vegetables and other foods.
items.d: The acetic acid gives pickles their sour taste.

items.t: When baking soda meets an acid, it releases carbon dioxide gas.
items.d: The gas makes bubbles that lift cake batter and bread dough.

items.t: Baking powder is about 30% baking soda, plus acidic ingredients.
items.d: Add water and the acid meets the soda, so bubbles of gas appear.

items.t: Most fires need three things: heat, fuel and oxygen. This is called the fire triangle.
items.d: Take away just one, and the fire goes out.

items.t: A glass put over a small candle flame makes it go out.
items.d: The glass cuts off the air, so the flame runs out of oxygen.

items.t: Fire is the fast reaction of a fuel with oxygen. It gives off heat and light.
items.d: Chemists call this reaction combustion.

items.t: On the space station, a candle flame is round and blue, with no soot.
items.d: It looks very different from the yellow flame on Earth.

items.t: What really burns in a candle is wax vapour, not the solid wax.
items.d: The heat turns melted wax into a gas first.

items.t: When a hydrocarbon fuel burns completely, it makes carbon dioxide and water.
items.d: Candle wax and natural gas are hydrocarbons.

items.t: Wet fuel will not burn until heat dries it out first.
items.d: Damp wood is hard to light for this reason.

items.t: Rust is a mixture of iron oxides made when iron reacts with oxygen.
items.d: The reddish coating is made of new substances, not just dirty iron.

items.t: Water is the main helper that speeds up rusting.
items.d: Iron left somewhere damp usually rusts faster than iron kept dry.

items.t: Salt makes iron rust faster.
items.d: Seawater speeds up rusting because it contains dissolved salt.

items.t: Iron rusts very little in pure water alone or dry oxygen alone.
items.d: Rusting usually needs both water and oxygen working together.

items.t: Rust takes up more space than the iron that formed it.
items.d: The growing rust can push outward from the metal surface.

items.t: Rust is brittle and crumbly, unlike strong iron.
items.d: As iron turns to rust, the metal can lose strength.

items.t: Rust can range from red-orange to reddish-brown.
items.d: Its exact colour depends on the rust compounds and conditions.

items.t: Rust does not make a protective skin over iron.
items.d: Rust can crumble away and leave more iron open to air and water.

items.t: Stainless steel resists rust with a chromium oxide layer.
items.d: The layer shields the steel underneath from its surroundings.

items.t: The Statue of Liberty is green because its copper formed a natural patina.
items.d: That green comes from a natural coating on the copper.

items.t: The green coating on copper and bronze is sometimes called verdigris.
items.d: Verdigris is a kind of patina that forms on the surface.

items.t: A patina is a thin layer that can form on copper, brass or bronze.
items.d: It develops on the metal's outer surface over time.

items.t: Some patinas protect the metal underneath from more corrosion.
items.d: A thin surface layer can act like a shield against weather.

items.t: Copper patina forms slowly as copper reacts with carbon dioxide and water.
items.d: Both substances are found naturally in the air around us.

items.t: Copper develops patina faster near a damp coast than in a dry inland place.
items.d: Moist sea air helps the surface reactions happen faster.

items.t: Patinas can be yellow, blue, green, white, red or black.
items.d: Different materials and conditions produce different surface colours.

items.t: A wok's dark patina is made from cooking oils.
items.d: The oils are bonded into a coating on the wok's surface.

items.t: Silver needs hydrogen sulfide in the air to tarnish.
items.d: Without that gas, silver does not tarnish.

items.t: Tarnish stays near a metal's surface and can limit its own growth.
items.d: Rust is different and does not stop itself in the same way.

items.t: Tarnish is usually a metal oxide made by oxidation.
items.d: Oxidation changes the metal's surface into a new compound.

items.t: Outdoor tarnish can protect the metal below and become a chemical patina.
items.d: Not every changed metal surface needs to be removed.

items.t: Some people like the tarnish called toning on coins.
items.d: It can look pleasing, and it may add to a coin's value.

items.t: Galvanising protects steel or iron with a coating of zinc.
items.d: The zinc helps stop oxygen and water from rusting the iron.

items.t: Hot-dip galvanising coats metal by dipping it into molten zinc.
items.d: The zinc cools into a protective layer around the part.

items.t: On galvanised steel, zinc corrodes instead of the iron.
items.d: Zinc is called a sacrificial metal because it protects another metal.

items.t: Zinc can protect iron even where a galvanised coating has small gaps.
items.d: The nearby zinc reacts first, helping spare the exposed iron.

items.t: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it reacts with air first.
items.d: This useful reaction helps protect iron from rust.

items.t: Galvanised steel can last for many decades when it is cared for.
items.d: Its zinc coating gives the steel long-lasting rust protection.

items.t: Galvanising is named after Italian scientist Luigi Galvani.
items.d: His surname became part of the name for this protective process.

items.t: Stanislas Sorel of Paris patented a galvanising process in 1837.
items.d: His method used zinc to protect iron from rusting.

items.t: Anodising uses electricity to thicken a metal's natural oxide layer.
items.d: The thicker layer can improve the metal's surface.

items.t: Pure aluminium in air grows an oxide skin 2 to 3 nanometres thick.
items.d: A nanometre is one billionth of a metre.

items.t: During anodising, the aluminium object acts as the anode.
items.d: An anode is one of the electrodes in the electrical process.

items.t: Anodised coatings have tiny pores that can soak up dye.
items.d: The pores are sealed afterward so the colour stays in place.

items.t: Anodised aluminium has a harder surface than plain aluminium.
items.d: The thickened oxide layer helps the surface resist wear.

items.t: Anodised aluminium is used on phones, music players and multi-tools.
items.d: Its tough surface can also be coloured with dye.

items.t: Some anodised colours come from light waves interacting in a thin film.
items.d: These colours can appear without any dye.

items.t: Stainless steel needs at least 10.5% chromium to resist rust.
items.d: Chromium helps form the steel's protective surface film.

items.t: Stainless steel forms its chromium oxide film by itself when it meets air.
items.d: The protective film is far too thin to see.

items.t: The protective film on stainless steel can repair itself after a scratch.
items.d: Chromium at the surface reacts again and rebuilds the film.

items.t: Stainless steel's protective film blocks oxygen from reaching the steel below.
items.d: Keeping oxygen away slows further oxidation.

items.t: Rust on plain steel is porous and fragile.
items.d: Its iron oxide layer has tiny holes and breaks easily.

items.t: Salt can cause tiny pits in stainless steel.
items.d: Stainless steel resists rust well, but it is not protected from everything.

items.t: Corrosion changes refined metal into a more stable substance such as an oxide.
items.d: Rusting is one familiar kind of corrosion.

items.t: Passivation happens when an ultrathin protective film forms on a material.
items.d: This film can slow further reactions at the surface.

items.t: Protective films on aluminium and stainless steel are under 10 nanometres thick.
items.d: Such a tiny film can still make a big difference to corrosion.

items.t: Natural gold nuggets do not corrode, even over geological time.
items.d: Geological time means a very, very long part of Earth's history.

items.t: When two metals touch in a wet place, the more active metal corrodes faster.
items.d: Engineers choose metal pairs carefully when water may reach them.

items.t: In 1912, French chemist Louis Camille Maillard described a browning reaction.
items.d: We call it the Maillard reaction. It is why many cooked foods turn brown.

items.t: Maillard browning is fastest at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
items.d: A hot oven can reach that heat. Bread crust and fried onions brown there.

items.t: The golden-brown crust of bread is mostly made by the Maillard reaction.
items.d: The outside of the loaf gets the hottest, so it browns more than the soft inside.

items.t: Maillard browning creates the special flavour of browned food.
items.d: That is the toasty taste in fried onions, roasted nuts, and dark toast.

items.t: The Maillard reaction needs amino acids. Caramelising only heats certain sugars.
items.d: Amino acids come from proteins in meat and bread. Plain sugar does not have them.

items.t: Maillard reactions can make hundreds of different flavour chemicals.
items.d: This mix helps browned foods have rich, complex flavours.

items.t: Caramelising browns sugar and gives a nutty, buttery taste and a brown colour.
items.d: Cooks use it for caramel sauce and for a browned custard top.

items.t: When table sugar caramelises, it first splits into fructose and glucose.
items.d: Table sugar is called sucrose. Fructose and glucose are simpler sugars.

items.t: Heating sugar releases diacetyl, a chemical with a strong buttery taste.
items.d: That buttery chemical is part of why hot caramel smells so rich.

items.t: Brown sugar caramelises faster than white sugar because it still has molasses.
items.d: Molasses is a dark syrup left in brown sugar. It speeds up the browning.

items.t: Baking powder is a mix of a base, an acid, and a drying agent.
items.d: The drying agent is a desiccant. It helps keep the powder dry in the tin.

items.t: Double-acting baking powder works twice: once when cold, and again when hot.
items.d: The first step happens in the cold batter. The second happens in the hot oven.

items.t: Baking powder loses its power over time if it gets damp or hot.
items.d: Keep the tin closed and dry, or it may not make cakes and muffins rise.

items.t: Baking soda is also called bicarbonate of soda. Its formula is NaHCO3.
items.d: Na stands for sodium, H for hydrogen, C for carbon, and O3 for three oxygens.

items.t: Baking soda reacts with acids and releases bubbles of carbon dioxide gas.
items.d: A splash of vinegar sets it fizzing. Those bubbles help batter rise and turn light.

items.t: Baking soda is mainly used in baking to make dough and batter rise.
items.d: Bakers call this leavening. Gas bubbles push the mixture up as it cooks.

items.t: Mayonnaise is a mix of oil, egg yolk, and an acid such as vinegar or lemon juice.
items.d: This kind of mix is called an emulsion. The oil stays spread through the sauce.

items.t: Lecithin and proteins in egg yolk keep mayonnaise from splitting apart.
items.d: Lecithin is a natural helper in the yolk. The proteins help it hold the sauce.

items.t: A little mustard helps mayonnaise stay mixed, and it adds flavour too.
items.d: Mustard gives the emulsion extra hold, so the sauce is less likely to split.

items.t: Gelatin is made by breaking down collagen, a protein from animals.
items.d: Cooks use this protein to set desserts that wobble when you poke them.

items.t: Gelatin melts below human body temperature, so jelly can melt in your mouth.
items.d: A jelly sweet may feel firm in your hand, then soften as your mouth warms it.

items.t: Gelatin can soak up about 5 to 10 times its own weight in water.
items.d: It can trap lots of water when it forms a soft gel, like jelly.

items.t: Dry gelatin is brittle. When it gets wet, it becomes rubbery.
items.d: A dry sheet can snap in your fingers. After a soak, it bends instead.

items.t: Gelatin is see-through, colourless, and has almost no flavour of its own.
items.d: That is why jelly takes the colour and taste of the juice mixed into it.

items.t: Cutting an onion lets out a tear-making liquid that easily turns to gas.
items.d: You meet it at the chopping board, when the onion pieces are freshly cut.

items.t: When onion cells break, enzymes called alliinases start chemical changes.
items.d: These enzymes act on special sulfur-containing chemicals inside the onion.

items.t: Onion gas makes eyes water and sting when it reaches them.
items.d: Cooks know this feeling well. It is just the gas meeting your eyes.

items.t: Ethylene is a gas that plants make. It tells fruit when to ripen.
items.d: It is a plant hormone, which means a chemical message sent as a gas.

items.t: Some fruits, such as apples, keep ripening after they are picked.
items.d: These fruits are called climacteric. They keep changing off the plant.

items.t: As fruit ripens, green chlorophyll breaks down and other colours show.
items.d: Chlorophyll makes fruit look green. When it fades, other pigments become easier to see.

items.t: Fruit gets softer as its pectin changes into a form that dissolves in water.
items.d: The old pectin does not dissolve. The new kind does, so the fruit feels soft.

items.t: Bananas are usually picked green, then ripened after they have been shipped.
items.d: They are ripened on purpose once the journey is over.

items.t: Iodine can show how much starch remains in a fruit as it ripens.
items.d: In some fruits, much of the starch changes into sugar during ripening.

items.t: Drying is one of the oldest ways to keep food from going bad.
items.d: People have dried food since ancient times. Raisins are dried grapes.

items.t: Salt keeps food by pulling water out, so microbes struggle to grow.
items.d: This pull is called osmosis. Microbes are tiny living things that need water.

items.t: Lots of sugar helps jam last because it pulls water out of microbes.
items.d: Without enough available water, microbes struggle to grow. This is called plasmolysis.

items.t: A fridge keeps food fresh by slowing microbes and slowing enzymes.
items.d: Enzymes are nature's tiny helpers. Cold slows them down, but does not stop them.

items.t: Canning was invented by Nicolas Appert, a French maker of sweets.
items.d: His idea lets people keep fruit, vegetables, and soups for a long time.

items.t: Pectin makes jam and marmalade set into a soft jelly.
items.d: Without enough pectin, the fruit mixture would stay runny instead of setting.

items.t: Pectin is a carbohydrate found in the cell walls of plants.
items.d: It helps hold plant cells together, a bit like soft scaffolding in the fruit.

items.t: An emulsion is a mix of two or more liquids that normally will not mix.
items.d: Oil and water are the usual pair. Salad dressing is an emulsion you can see.

items.t: An emulsifier helps oil and water stay mixed.
items.d: It lowers the pull where oil and water meet, helping tiny droplets stay spread out.

items.t: A plain oil-and-vinegar dressing splits quickly unless you keep shaking it.
items.d: It is an unstable emulsion. Left alone, the oil soon floats above the vinegar.

items.t: Butter is an emulsion of tiny water drops spread through butterfat.
items.d: The water is scattered inside the fat, which is why butter is not watery.

items.t: Whipping egg whites for meringue unfolds their proteins and makes a foam.
items.d: Unfolding is called denaturing. The proteins then hold tiny bubbles of air.

items.t: A sourdough starter holds wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria together.
items.d: They live side by side in a bubbly mix of flour and water.

items.t: Sourdough tastes sour because fermentation makes lactic acid.
items.d: The bacteria in the starter make that acid. You taste it as a pleasant tang.

items.t: Carbon dioxide from yeast creates the little air pockets in bread.
items.d: Ethanol vapour forms too. Together these gases puff the dough full of holes.

items.t: Kneading helps a flour protein called glutenin form long, thin strands.
items.d: Those strands are like tiny chains. They make dough strong and stretchy.

items.t: A polymer forms when many small molecules, called monomers, join into a long chain.
items.d: Think of paper clips linked into a long chain. Each clip is a monomer.

items.t: The word polymer comes from two Greek words: polus, meaning many, and meros, meaning part.
items.d: So a polymer is a molecule with many parts.

items.t: Silk, wool, natural rubber, cellulose, DNA and proteins are all natural polymers.
items.d: Polymers are not only plastic. Nature makes lots of them.

items.t: Polyethylene is the most commonly produced plastic in the world.
items.d: It is used in products such as milk jugs and plastic bags.

items.t: Milk jugs use strong, straight-chain HDPE. Plastic bags use bendy, branched LDPE.
items.d: The same building block gives different plastics when the chains are shaped differently.

items.t: Ethylene, the building block of polyethylene, is also a gas that plants make to help fruit ripen.
items.d: Farmers can use it to ripen fruit like bananas.

items.t: A recycling number on a product does not mean your local area can recycle it.
items.d: Check with your local recycling service about what they accept.

items.t: To make nylon fibres, melted nylon is pushed through tiny holes, then stretched so the chains line up.
items.d: Lining up the chains makes the thread stronger.

items.t: Most natural rubber comes from the milky latex of the Para rubber tree. Workers cut the bark to collect it.
items.d: Cutting the bark this way is called tapping.

items.t: Natural rubber is a polymer called cis-1,4-polyisoprene.
items.d: It is a long chain made of many small isoprene units.

items.t: The Olmec people of ancient Mexico made rubber balls for a ballgame.
items.d: The Maya and Aztecs used rubber too.

items.t: The word vulcanization comes from Vulcan, the Roman god of fire.
items.d: Heat is needed to make rubber and sulfur link up.

items.t: Polypropylene is so light that ropes made of it float on water.
items.d: It also bends many times without breaking, like flip-top bottle lids.

items.t: Foam polystyrene is about 95 to 98 percent air.
items.d: That much trapped air makes the foam very light.

items.t: PTFE has only carbon and fluorine atoms. It is very slippery and unreactive.
items.d: That is why it is used to coat non-stick pans.

items.t: A drop of iodine solution turns dark blue when it touches starch.
items.d: Try it on a slice of potato.

items.t: Bioluminescence is light made by a living thing through a chemical reaction.
items.d: Fireflies and many sea animals can make this living light.

items.t: A light-making substance called luciferin reacts with an enzyme to make living light.
items.d: An enzyme helps the chemical reaction happen.

items.t: Bioluminescence evolved separately at least 94 times in different animal groups.
items.d: Nature discovered chemical light again and again.

items.t: Fireflies use flashes of chemically made light to attract mates.
items.d: The glow comes from a chemical reaction in the firefly.

items.t: About three quarters of major deep-sea animal groups studied in the eastern Pacific can make light.
items.d: Chemical light is common in the dark ocean depths.

items.t: Most light made by sea animals is blue or green.
items.d: Blue and green are the usual colors of this living light.

items.t: Some deep-sea dragonfishes can make red light.
items.d: This unusual glow comes from chemistry inside the fish.

items.t: A firefly's light reaction needs magnesium and ATP, a molecule cells use for energy.
items.d: It also needs luciferin and an enzyme called luciferase.

items.t: Hemoglobin is an iron-containing protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
items.d: It picks up oxygen and helps move it around the body.

items.t: Most mammal hemoglobin is built from four protein parts called subunits.
items.d: The four parts work together as one oxygen carrier.

items.t: Each heme group in hemoglobin holds an iron atom and can grab one oxygen molecule.
items.d: The iron is the spot where oxygen attaches.

items.t: One hemoglobin molecule can carry up to four oxygen molecules.
items.d: Each of its four heme groups can hold one oxygen molecule.

items.t: About 96 percent of a mammal red blood cell's dry weight is hemoglobin.
items.d: Red blood cells are packed with this oxygen-carrying protein.

items.t: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light but reflects green light.
items.d: The reflected green light is why many plants look green.

items.t: Photosynthesis uses light to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen.
items.d: Plants store some captured light energy in sugar.

items.t: In plants and algae, photosynthesis happens inside cell parts called chloroplasts.
items.d: Chloroplasts contain the machinery that captures light energy.

items.t: Plants, algae, and cyanobacteria release oxygen during photosynthesis.
items.d: Light-powered chemistry adds oxygen to their surroundings.

items.t: Green plants get electrons used in photosynthesis from water.
items.d: Water supplies tiny charged particles for the reactions.

items.t: Photosynthesis has two stages. One needs light, and the other does not need it directly.
items.d: The two stages work together to capture energy and build sugars.

items.t: Plants build sugars through a series of reactions called the Calvin cycle.
items.d: This cycle uses materials prepared by the light-powered stage.

items.t: In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz showed that plants need light, not only soil and water.
items.d: His work helped reveal the chemistry of photosynthesis.

items.t: Female silkworm moths release a chemical called bombykol to attract mates.
items.d: Bombykol is a pheromone, a chemical message between animals.

items.t: Ants mark paths with scent chemicals called pheromones.
items.d: Other ants can follow the chemical trail.

items.t: Ant trail pheromones evaporate quickly, so ants must keep renewing them.
items.d: A trail fades unless more ants add fresh scent chemicals.

items.t: A pronghorn's alarm scent has been compared to the smell of buttered popcorn.
items.d: Animals can use scent chemicals to send warning signals.

items.t: Male bumblebees mark paths with pheromones and patrol them to find mates.
items.d: Their scent marks make a chemical route outside the nest.

items.t: The word pheromone was created in 1959 by Peter Karlson and Martin Lüscher.
items.d: It names chemicals used for messages between members of one species.

items.t: Amylase in saliva starts breaking down starch while food is in your mouth.
items.d: It cuts cooked starch into smaller carbohydrate chains.

items.t: Pepsin is the main protein-digesting enzyme in the stomach.
items.d: It helps cut large protein molecules into smaller pieces.

items.t: Cells in the stomach lining release gastric lipase, an enzyme that digests fat.
items.d: This enzyme can work in the stomach's acidic conditions.

items.t: Protease enzymes split proteins into small peptides and amino acids.
items.d: Enzymes act like chemical scissors for large food molecules.

items.t: Pancreatic lipase breaks triglyceride fats into fatty acids and a monoglyceride.
items.d: Breaking fats into smaller parts helps the body absorb them.

items.t: Lactase splits the milk sugar lactose into glucose and galactose.
items.d: One sugar molecule becomes two simpler sugars.

items.t: The pancreas makes both hormones and digestive enzymes.
items.d: It works as two kinds of gland in one organ.

items.t: Most enzyme digestion happens in the first part of the small intestine.
items.d: This section is called the duodenum.

items.t: Anthocyanin pigments can look red, pink, purple, blue, or black.
items.d: Their color can change with the acidity around them.

items.t: Anthocyanins look red or pink in acidic solutions.
items.d: The same pigment can show another color when acidity changes.

items.t: Blueberries, raspberries, and black rice are rich in anthocyanin pigments.
items.d: These natural chemicals help give the foods their strong colors.

items.t: Red cabbage extract can act as a natural acid-base indicator.
items.d: Its color changes as a liquid's pH changes.

items.t: Carotenoids are yellow, orange, and red pigments made by plants and algae.
items.d: These natural chemicals add bright colors to living things.

items.t: Carotenoids help color pumpkins, carrots, corn, and tomatoes.
items.d: Different foods contain different amounts and kinds of these pigments.

items.t: The body can turn some carotenoids, including beta-carotene, into vitamin A.
items.d: A colorful plant pigment can become a useful nutrient.

items.t: Flamingos get their orange feather color from carotenoids in their food.
items.d: Pigment molecules from their diet become part of their coloring.

items.t: Carotenoids are the main autumn leaf pigment in about 15 to 30 percent of tree species.
items.d: These pigments can make autumn leaves look yellow or orange.

items.t: Capsaicin is the main active chemical that makes chili peppers taste hot.
items.d: The burning feeling is a nerve response, not a rise in temperature.

items.t: Capsaicin binds to a receptor called TRPV1 on pain-sensing nerves in mammals.
items.d: This receptor sends the signal that feels like spicy heat.

items.t: Birds do not feel capsaicin's burn because their TRPV1 channel does not respond to it.
items.d: A chili pepper can feel hot to a person but not to a bird.

items.t: Milk can soothe capsaicin's burning feeling because it contains casein proteins.
items.d: Casein helps with the oily capsaicin left in the mouth.

items.t: The Scoville scale measures how spicy chili peppers are.
items.d: More capsaicin usually means a higher place on the scale.

items.t: People made soap-like materials in ancient Babylon about 4,800 years ago.
items.d: That was around 2800 BC, long before soap came in bars and bottles.

items.t: A clay tablet from about 2500 BC wrote down a soap-like recipe.
items.d: It described how to make a soap-like substance.

items.t: Soap is made when fats or oils react with a strong base.
items.d: This reaction is called saponification, the key step in making soap.

items.t: Making soap turns fats into salts of fatty acids. Those salts are soap.
items.d: The fat splits, and the new fatty salts are the part that cleans.

items.t: Glycerin from soapmaking is sometimes left in the bar to soften it.
items.d: Glycerin is a bonus ingredient made while the soap itself forms.

items.t: In water, soap molecules bunch into tiny balls called micelles.
items.d: Those balls let soapy water grab grease and rinse it off your hands.

items.t: Soap can break apart the outer layer of some germs.
items.d: When that thin covering falls apart, those germs do not survive.

items.t: In hard water, soap does not lather well and can leave soap scum.
items.d: Instead of fluffy bubbles, you may see a cloudy film on the sink.

items.t: Sodium hydroxide makes firm soap. Potassium soap is softer or liquid.
items.d: A solid bar and a liquid hand soap can come from different bases.

items.t: Sand or pumice mixed into soap makes a rough scouring soap.
items.d: The grit helps rub off stuck dirt while the soap lifts grease.

items.t: A surfactant has a water-loving head and a tail that avoids water.
items.d: The head sits in the water. The tail grabs onto oil and grease.

items.t: Surfactants lower the surface tension of water.
items.d: Water spreads out and wets a dirty plate instead of beading up.

items.t: Surfactants can work as emulsifiers, letting oil and water mix.
items.d: The oil breaks into tiny drops that hang in the water.

items.t: Surfactants can make foam and help dirt let go of a surface.
items.d: They help loosen dirt so it can be washed away.

items.t: In a micelle, surfactant tails point in and the heads face the water.
items.d: Oil collects in that oily center, away from the water outside.

items.t: Surfactants are used in dish soap, shampoo, and shower gel.
items.d: They help water pick up oil so you can rinse the mess away.

items.t: Your lungs make a natural surfactant that helps you breathe.
items.d: It is made in your body and is not the same as bottle soap.

items.t: Bile salts from your liver are surfactants that help you digest fat.
items.d: They help fatty food mix with the watery juices in your gut.

items.t: Ancient Egyptians made tooth powder as far back as about 5000 BC.
items.d: That is about 7,000 years ago, long before toothpaste tubes.

items.t: Early Egyptian tooth powder used pumice, burnt eggshell, and myrrh.
items.d: Pumice is a gritty rock that could scrub teeth.

items.t: Toothpaste has tiny abrasives that help scrub plaque off teeth.
items.d: Those rough bits polish teeth while you brush.

items.t: Gentle abrasion is the main way toothpaste rubs stains off teeth.
items.d: Tiny grains buff the stain, like very soft sandpaper.

items.t: Fluoride is the most popular toothpaste ingredient for stopping cavities.
items.d: Check the tube. Many pastes list fluoride as the cavity fighter.

items.t: Fluoride was first added to toothpaste in the 1890s.
items.d: Older tooth cleaners mostly scrubbed. Fluoride added cavity protection.

items.t: A foaming agent in toothpaste helps spread it around your mouth.
items.d: The foam carries the paste so it reaches more of your teeth.

items.t: SPF 15 means only 1/15 of the sunburn rays reach your skin.
items.d: The sunscreen blocks the other 14/15 of those burning rays.

items.t: Titanium dioxide can help protect skin from the sun.
items.d: It can give good protection, but it does not cover the whole UVA range.

items.t: Some sunscreen ingredients absorb UV rays and give off the energy as heat.
items.d: The absorbed energy is changed into heat.

items.t: Broad spectrum means sunscreen protects you from both UVA and UVB.
items.d: UVA and UVB are two types of harmful ultraviolet rays.

items.t: A water-resistant sunscreen label may say it works for 40 minutes in water.
items.d: After that long in the water, put more sunscreen on.

items.t: Sunscreen needs to be put on again because it only lasts so long on your skin.
items.d: Do it sooner if you swim or sweat, because the layer wears off.

items.t: The word shampoo came into English from a Hindi word.
items.d: It meant to knead or massage the head and hair.

items.t: Shampoo washes away sebum, the natural oil that builds up in hair.
items.d: A little sebum is normal. Extra sebum is what makes hair look oily.

items.t: Early shampoo in Indonesia was made from rice husk and straw.
items.d: The rice husk and straw were called merang.

items.t: The first synthetic shampoo used human-made surfactants instead of soap.
items.d: Synthetic means people made the surfactant, not only soap from fats.

items.t: Neanderthals made tar from birch bark.
items.d: They heated the bark to turn it into tar.

items.t: Stone Age people in South Africa made stronger glue with red ochre.
items.d: They mixed the red earth into plant gum, and the glue got tougher.

items.t: Some natural glues are made from plant starch.
items.d: Flour can make a simple starch paste. Milk protein can make glue too.

items.t: Some glue sticks with only a light press, like on a sticky note.
items.d: A small push is enough to make the sticky note hold.

items.t: A hot glue gun melts a solid glue stick so the liquid glue can flow out.
items.d: The glue flows out hot and liquid, then turns solid and holds.

items.t: Do not mix vinegar with hydrogen peroxide.
items.d: The mixture can be dangerous.

items.t: Bleach reacts with colored substances and turns them colorless.
items.d: That is why a stain on a white shirt can fade in the wash.

items.t: Sodium hypochlorite is the most common household bleach.
items.d: It is used both to fade stains and to disinfect hard surfaces.

items.t: Chlorine-free peroxide bleach is called oxygen bleach or color-safe bleach.
items.d: People choose it when they do not want chlorine bleach on colors.

items.t: Never mix bleach with vinegar, ammonia, or other cleaners.
items.d: The mix can make harmful gas, and it does not disinfect better.

items.t: Washing hands with soap and water removes germs best in most cases.
items.d: Soap loosens the germs, and running water carries them off.

items.t: When you wash, scrub your hands with soap for at least 20 seconds.
items.d: Keep rubbing the whole time so the soap can lift dirt and germs.

items.t: Warm or cold running water both work for washing hands.
items.d: You do not need hot water. Soap and a good scrub do the real work.

items.t: If you have no soap, a sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol can help.
items.d: Soap and water are still the better choice whenever you can use them.

items.t: Keep cleaners in their own bottles so the label stays with them.
items.d: A label tells you what is inside and how to use it safely.

items.t: Lithium burns with a deep red flame when chemists test it.
items.d: Chemists use flame colours to tell elements apart.

items.t: Sodium makes a bright golden-yellow flame.
items.d: Salt contains sodium, so a pinch of it can turn a flame yellow.

items.t: Barium salts burn with a light apple-green flame.
items.d: Each metal gives its own colour, like a fingerprint made of light.

items.t: Potassium burns with a soft lilac flame.
items.d: Lilac is a pale purple.

items.t: Strontium salts give red fireworks.
items.d: Different metal salts in each star make different colours in the sky.

items.t: When you bend a glow stick, a glass vial inside breaks and two liquids mix to start the glow.
items.d: That is why you hear a little snap.

items.t: A warm glow stick glows brighter but for a shorter time. A cold one is dimmer but lasts longer.
items.d: Heat speeds up the reaction, and cold slows it down.

items.t: A glow stick cannot be switched off, and it can only be used once.
items.d: The reaction inside keeps going until the chemicals are used up.

items.t: Photochromic lenses darken in sunlight but not under ordinary lamps indoors.
items.d: Sunlight has plenty of UV light, and indoor lamps have very little.

items.t: Tyrian purple dye was made from a liquid taken from sea snails.
items.d: It was used in ancient times for the colour of fine cloth.

items.t: In 1908, about twelve thousand sea snails gave no more than 1.4 grams of pure purple dye.
items.d: That is about the weight of one paper clip.

items.t: People in ancient times made purple dye as early as about 1200 BC.
items.d: The Phoenicians were known for making it.

items.t: In 1856, 18-year-old William Perkin found the first widely known man-made dye, called mauveine.
items.d: He found it by accident.

items.t: The name ultramarine comes from Latin words meaning beyond the sea.
items.d: The stone was brought to Europe from far away.

items.t: Mood rings contain liquid crystals that change colour with temperature.
