items.d: We see a star 100 light-years away as it looked 100 years ago.

items.t: Stars twinkle because moving air bends their light.
items.d: Earth's atmosphere makes the light shift slightly from moment to moment.

items.t: Planets usually twinkle less than stars.
items.d: Their tiny disks of light are steadier when seen through moving air.

items.t: A star's color gives a clue to its surface temperature.
items.d: Blue stars are hotter than red stars.

items.t: A star can look bright because it is powerful, close, or both.
items.d: Distance changes how bright a star appears from Earth.

items.t: Nearly every star you can see without a telescope is in our Milky Way galaxy.
items.d: Other galaxies are much farther away and usually look like faint patches.

items.t: A constellation is a named area of the sky with a star pattern.
items.d: Its stars may be very different distances from Earth.

items.t: Astronomers divide the whole sky into 88 official constellations.
items.d: Together, they work like a map of the sky.

items.t: The Northern and Southern Hemispheres see different parts of the sky.
items.d: Some constellations never rise above the horizon in the other hemisphere.

items.t: Different constellations are easy to see in different seasons.
items.d: Earth faces different directions at night as it travels around the Sun.

items.t: From some places on Earth, a circumpolar constellation never sets below the horizon.
items.d: It seems to circle a sky pole during the night.

items.t: Polaris appears close to the north sky pole.
items.d: In the Northern Hemisphere, it can help observers find north.

items.t: Polaris is not the brightest star in the night sky.
items.d: Sirius appears brighter from Earth.

items.t: The Big Dipper is an asterism, not an official constellation.
items.d: Its seven bright stars are part of Ursa Major.

items.t: The ecliptic is the Sun's yearly path across our sky.
items.d: The Moon and planets also appear close to this path.

items.t: The zodiac constellations lie along the ecliptic.
items.d: The Sun appears to pass in front of them during the year.

items.t: Moon phases repeat about every 29.5 days.
items.d: This is the time from one new Moon to the next.

items.t: At new Moon, the Moon appears close to the Sun in our sky.
items.d: Its sunlit half faces mostly away from Earth.

items.t: At full Moon, Earth is roughly between the Sun and Moon.
items.d: The side facing Earth appears fully lit.

items.t: At a quarter Moon, half of the Moon's visible face looks lit.
items.d: The name describes how far the Moon is through its monthly cycle.

items.t: A waxing Moon shows more of its lit side each night.
items.d: It changes from new Moon toward full Moon.

items.t: A waning Moon shows less of its lit side each night.
items.d: It changes from full Moon toward new Moon.

items.t: People around the world see the same Moon phase at the same moment.
items.d: The phase may look tilted differently from different places.

items.t: Earthshine can faintly light the dark part of a crescent Moon.
items.d: Sunlight reflects from Earth to the Moon and back to us.

items.t: A lunar eclipse happens when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow.
items.d: Earth blocks some sunlight that would normally reach the Moon.

items.t: A lunar eclipse can happen only at full Moon.
items.d: That is when the Moon can pass behind Earth compared with the Sun.

items.t: Eclipses do not happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted.
items.d: The Moon usually passes above or below the needed line.

items.t: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day on average.
items.d: Its motion around Earth changes where it appears against the stars.

items.t: A full Moon rises near sunset and sets near sunrise.
items.d: It appears roughly opposite the Sun in the sky.

items.t: The Moon looks about half a degree wide in the sky.
items.d: Your little finger at arm's length can cover it easily.

items.t: The Moon illusion makes a low Moon look larger than a high Moon.
items.d: Its actual size in the sky changes very little during one night.

items.t: The bright side of the Moon always points toward the Sun.
items.d: Even when the Sun is below the horizon, this can reveal its direction.

items.t: The Sun's faint outer atmosphere is called the corona.
items.d: It becomes visible around the blocked Sun during a total solar eclipse.

items.t: Stars make energy by squeezing hydrogen together to make helium.
items.d: This process is called nuclear fusion.

items.t: A stable star balances two effects.
items.d: Gravity pulls inward while hot gas and radiation push outward.

items.t: Stars begin inside cold clouds of gas and dust.
items.d: Gravity can pull parts of a cloud together into dense clumps.

items.t: A protostar is a young, warming clump that may become a star.
items.d: It becomes a star when fusion begins in its center.

items.t: Stars spend most of their lives in the main sequence stage.
items.d: During this stage, they fuse hydrogen into helium.

items.t: A star's mass strongly affects how its life unfolds.
items.d: Mass changes its temperature, brightness and lifetime.

items.t: Massive stars use their fuel faster than smaller stars.
items.d: Although they have more fuel, they usually have shorter lives.

items.t: A red giant is a star whose outer layers have greatly expanded.
items.d: Its surface cools as the star grows larger.

items.t: A Sun-like star can leave behind a white dwarf.
items.d: A white dwarf is the hot, dense core left after outer gas drifts away.

items.t: A white dwarf can hold about a star's mass in an Earth-sized sphere.
items.d: Its matter is packed extremely tightly.

items.t: Some massive stars finish with a brilliant explosion called a supernova.
items.d: The blast can scatter newly made elements into space.

items.t: A neutron star is the crushed core left by some supernovas.
items.d: It packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere about the size of a city.

items.t: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star that sends out beams.
items.d: The beams can appear as regular pulses when they sweep past Earth.

items.t: A black hole has a boundary called an event horizon.
items.d: Past this boundary, not even light can escape.

items.t: Black holes do not pull in everything around them like vacuum cleaners.
items.d: Far away, their gravity acts like the gravity of any object with the same mass.

items.t: A binary star system contains two stars orbiting each other.
items.d: Many stars are members of pairs or larger groups.

items.t: In an eclipsing binary, one star regularly passes in front of the other.
items.d: The system's combined light dims in a repeating pattern.

items.t: A variable star changes in brightness over time.
items.d: It may swell, shrink, pulse, or be partly blocked by a companion.

items.t: An open cluster is a loose group of stars born from one cloud.
items.d: Open clusters are often found in a galaxy's disk.

items.t: A globular cluster is a crowded, round group of old stars.
items.d: Some contain hundreds of thousands of stars.

items.t: A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space.
items.d: Some nebulae form stars, while others contain material shed by stars.

items.t: An emission nebula glows because nearby hot stars energize its gas.
items.d: The Orion Nebula is a well-known example.

items.t: A reflection nebula shines by scattering nearby starlight.
items.d: Its gas and dust do not make their own visible light.

items.t: A dark nebula blocks light from stars behind it.
items.d: It can look like a dark shape against a bright background.

items.t: Stars formed much of the carbon and oxygen found in the universe.
items.d: Stellar processes build elements from lighter particles.

items.t: A star's spectrum can reveal which elements are in its atmosphere.
items.d: Each element leaves a special pattern of lines in the light.

items.t: A brown dwarf is not massive enough for steady hydrogen fusion.
items.d: It is more massive than a planet but less massive than a true star.

items.t: A spiral galaxy has a flat disk, a central bulge and winding arms.
items.d: Its arms often contain gas, dust and young stars.

items.t: An elliptical galaxy looks round or oval.
items.d: It usually has less cool gas and dust than a spiral galaxy.

items.t: An irregular galaxy has no simple spiral or oval shape.
items.d: Gravity from nearby galaxies can help distort its form.

items.t: The Milky Way belongs to a group of galaxies called the Local Group.
items.d: The group includes the Andromeda Galaxy and dozens of smaller galaxies.

items.t: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away.
items.d: Under a dark sky, it can be seen without a telescope as a faint smudge.

items.t: The center of the Milky Way lies toward the constellation Sagittarius.
items.d: Thick dust clouds hide much of it from visible-light telescopes.

items.t: Infrared and radio waves can pass through some space dust.
items.d: They help astronomers study regions hidden from visible light.

items.t: A supermassive black hole sits at the center of the Milky Way.
items.d: It is called Sagittarius A* and has about four million Suns of mass.

items.t: Galaxies gather into groups and clusters because of gravity.
items.d: Clusters can contain hundreds or thousands of galaxies.

items.t: The universe is expanding.
items.d: On very large scales, the space between distant galaxy groups grows.

items.t: Light from many distant galaxies is shifted toward redder wavelengths.
items.d: This redshift helps show that the universe is expanding.

items.t: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old.
items.d: Astronomers estimate this using expansion and ancient light.

items.t: The cosmic microwave background is faint light from the early universe.
items.d: It now reaches us mostly as microwaves from every direction.

items.t: A quasar is a brilliant center of a distant galaxy.
items.d: Gas falling toward a supermassive black hole releases enormous energy.

items.t: An asteroid is a rocky or metallic object that orbits the Sun.
items.d: Asteroids are much smaller than planets.

items.t: Most known asteroids orbit in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.
items.d: Jupiter's gravity helped stop them from joining into one planet.

items.t: Asteroids in the main belt are usually far apart.
items.d: A spacecraft can cross the belt without weaving through crowded rocks.

items.t: A comet has a nucleus made of ice, dust and rock.
items.d: Its frozen materials warm as the comet approaches the Sun.

items.t: A comet can grow a glowing cloud and tails near the Sun.
items.d: The cloud around its nucleus is called a coma.

items.t: A comet's tails point mostly away from the Sun.
items.d: Sunlight and the solar wind push material outward.

items.t: A comet may have a curved dust tail and a straighter ion tail.
items.d: The two tails respond differently to sunlight and the solar wind.

items.t: Many comets travel around the Sun on long, stretched orbits.
items.d: Some return after a few years, while others take centuries.

items.t: A meteoroid is a small natural rock or metal object in space.
items.d: Many are fragments of asteroids or comets.

items.t: A meteor is the streak of light made by a meteoroid entering our atmosphere.
items.d: Air heats the object and the gas around it until they glow.

items.t: A meteorite is a piece of space rock that reaches the ground.
items.d: It is what remains after passing through the atmosphere.

items.t: Meteor showers often happen when Earth crosses a comet's dusty trail.
items.d: Many tiny particles enter the atmosphere during the same nights each year.

items.t: Meteors in a shower seem to spread from one point in the sky.
items.d: This is a perspective effect, like parallel tracks seeming to meet far away.

items.t: A refracting telescope gathers and focuses light with lenses.
items.d: Its main lens sits at the front of the telescope tube.

items.t: A reflecting telescope gathers and focuses light with mirrors.
items.d: Many large research telescopes use curved mirrors.

items.t: A telescope's aperture is the width of its main lens or mirror.
items.d: A wider aperture collects more light and reveals fainter objects.

items.t: A larger telescope can separate finer details than a smaller one.
items.d: This ability is called resolution.

items.t: Radio telescopes detect radio waves from space.
items.d: They can use large dishes or groups of antennas working together.

items.t: Space telescopes observe above Earth's atmosphere.
items.d: They avoid clouds and the atmosphere's blurring of starlight.

items.t: Adaptive optics helps ground telescopes correct atmospheric blur.
items.d: A mirror changes shape rapidly to sharpen the view.

items.t: Binoculars can reveal more night-sky objects than unaided eyes.
items.d: They gather extra light and show a wide area of sky.

items.t: Eyes need time to adjust to darkness.
items.d: After about 20 to 30 minutes, faint stars can become easier to see.

items.t: Every star starts inside a cloud of dust and gas.
items.d: Clumps in that cloud can grow into many new stars.

items.t: Gas clumps in a star cloud gather more material, then spin and heat up.
items.d: As they pull in more gas, they spin faster and grow hotter.

items.t: A baby star begins when its core hits about 15 million degrees Celsius.
items.d: That heat starts nuclear fusion, the power source that makes the star glow.

items.t: Inside a star, protons squash together to make helium.
items.d: This joining is called fusion, and it releases the energy that makes the star shine.

items.t: A small star can shine steadily for billions of years.
items.d: It uses fuel slowly, so its light can stay steady for a very long time.

items.t: When a small star runs low on fuel, it swells into a red giant.
items.d: It can grow wide enough to reach planets that orbit close by.

items.t: A red giant can blow its outer layers off into space.
items.d: That glowing cloud is a planetary nebula, and no planets are involved.

items.t: A white dwarf is about Earth-sized, but extremely heavy.
items.d: One teaspoon of its material would weigh more than a pickup truck.

items.t: The biggest stars use up their fuel in only a few million years.
items.d: For a star, a few million years is a very short time.

items.t: When a giant star runs out of fuel, its core collapses inward.
items.d: The collapse sets off a supernova, an enormous explosion in space.

items.t: Supernova blasts and planetary nebulae scatter elements into space.
items.d: Those elements later end up in new stars, new planets, and things on Earth.

items.t: A neutron star is only about the size of a city.
items.d: Small as a city, it still packs in a huge amount of mass.

items.t: One teaspoon of neutron-star material would weigh as much as a mountain.
items.d: Picture a whole mountain squeezed down to the size of a spoon.

items.t: Stars form in cold, dense clouds called molecular clouds.
items.d: Clumps in these clouds collapse under gravity and heat up.

items.t: A protostar is a baby star still forming from falling gas.
items.d: Its early heat comes from that falling gas, not from joining atoms together.

items.t: The main sequence is the longest part of a star's life.
items.d: During it, the star joins hydrogen atoms together to make helium.

items.t: A star like the Sun stays in its calm main-sequence stage for about 10 billion years.
items.d: That is about 10,000,000,000 years of steady shining.

items.t: A white dwarf is a hot, Earth-sized leftover that cools for billions of years.
items.d: It fades slowly, losing a little heat over that huge stretch of time.

items.t: For a huge star, iron in the core is a turning point.
items.d: Joining iron atoms soaks up energy instead of giving it off, so the core collapses.

items.t: About 90 percent of stars are main sequence stars.
items.d: They are the most common kind of star in the universe.

items.t: A red giant would look more orange than red.
items.d: Its name says red, but the color we would see is closer to orange.

items.t: When core hydrogen runs out, fusion shifts into the outer layers.
items.d: Fusion means joining atoms. It moves outward, and the star swells into a red giant.

items.t: Neutron stars form from stars roughly 8 to 20 times as heavy as the Sun.
items.d: Stars in about this mass range can leave a neutron star behind.

items.t: Red dwarfs are the smallest main sequence stars.
items.d: These small stars make up about 75 percent of the stars in the Milky Way.

items.t: Some red dwarfs shine longer than the universe has existed.
items.d: Their life spans are longer than the age of the universe today.

items.t: A brown dwarf is not a true star.
items.d: It never gets heavy enough to join hydrogen into helium the way a real star does.

items.t: A magnetar is a neutron star with a hugely powerful magnetic field.
items.d: Its field can be about 10 trillion times stronger than a fridge magnet.

items.t: A star's mass sets its color, its heat, and its brightness.
items.d: A heavy new star turns out different from a light one.

items.t: Joining atoms in the core pushes outward and balances gravity.
items.d: Gravity pulls in. The push from the hot core matches it, so the star stays steady.

items.t: The heavier a star is, the shorter its main-sequence life.
items.d: More mass means a shorter time in that steady middle stage.

items.t: A star can swell to a few up to about 100 times its old size as a red giant.
items.d: Some grow only a few times bigger. Others grow about a hundred times bigger.

items.t: In a Sun-like red giant, helium in the core turns into carbon.
items.d: Deep inside, the star builds carbon while its outside grows huge.

items.t: Electrons pushing apart help a white dwarf hold itself up.
items.d: Their push balances gravity, so the white dwarf does not keep shrinking.

items.t: The core of a huge star can collapse in under one second.
items.d: In that brief moment, the whole core falls inward.

items.t: A neutron star can hold about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun.
items.d: That is more mass than our Sun, packed into a much smaller ball.

items.t: In a neutron star, electrons are squeezed into protons.
items.d: That leaves a star made mostly of tiny particles called neutrons.

items.t: A neutron star's magnetic field is about a trillion times Earth's.
items.d: A trillion means a million times a million, far beyond any magnet on Earth.

items.t: A star's mass decides which path its life will take.
items.d: Light stars and heavy stars do not change in the same way.

items.t: A supernova can light up the sky for weeks.
items.d: It can look like a new bright star in the night sky.

items.t: A supernova can reach a temperature of about a billion degrees Celsius.
items.d: A billion is written as 1,000,000,000, a one with nine zeros.

items.t: Chinese astronomers wrote down a supernova in the year 1054.
items.d: The cloud it left behind is the one we call the Crab Nebula.

items.t: A pulsar is a neutron star whose beams sweep past like a lighthouse.
items.d: We see a flash each time one of those beams swings past Earth.

items.t: Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first pulsar in 1967.
items.d: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star. She found the first as a Cambridge student.

items.t: At its peak, a supernova can shine about as bright as a whole galaxy.
items.d: For a short time, one star can match the light of a whole galaxy.

items.t: A neutron star spins faster because it shrinks as it forms.
items.d: A skater spins faster by pulling their arms in. The star does the same.

items.t: The first planets found outside our solar system orbit a pulsar.
items.d: Astronomers found those planets in 1992, around a spinning neutron star.

items.t: Spinning neutron stars called pulsars can help spacecraft find their way.
items.d: A NASA test on the International Space Station showed pulsar flashes can help work out a spacecraft's position.

items.t: The first pulsar signal was so steady it seemed too perfect.
items.d: A pulsar is a flashing neutron star. Bell Burnell jokingly called the signal little green men.

items.t: The hottest stars look blue, and the coolest stars look red.
items.d: It is the opposite of a stove knob, where red means hot!

items.t: Astronomers sort stars into types O, B, A, F, G, K and M, from hottest to coolest.
items.d: A memory trick: Oh, Be A Fine Girl or Guy, Kiss Me!

items.t: Class O stars are the hottest, with surfaces about 30,000 to 60,000 K. They shine blue.
items.d: That is many times hotter than the Sun's surface.

items.t: Class A stars look blue-white to white, with surfaces about 7,500 to 10,000 K.
items.d: Vega is a standard example of an A-type star.

items.t: Orange K stars have surfaces about 3,500 to 5,000 K. They are cooler than the Sun.
Red M stars are the coolest of the main star types, below about 3,500 K.
The Sun is a G-type star with a surface about 5,800 K.
items.d: Its full label is G2V, a main-sequence star.

items.t: The Sun is called a yellow star, but from Earth it actually looks white.
items.d: Never look straight at it, though. Sunglasses are not enough!

items.t: Very hot O stars give off most of their light as ultraviolet, which our eyes cannot see.
O-type stars are very rare. Only about 1 in 3,000,000 nearby main-sequence stars is one.
Red dwarfs make up roughly three out of four stars in the Milky Way.
Red dwarfs are the smallest and coolest main-sequence stars. They look more orange than red.
Proxima Centauri, the star nearest to the Sun, is a red dwarf.
Not one true red dwarf can be seen with the naked eye, because they are so dim.
items.d: You need a telescope to find them.

items.t: A small red dwarf could keep burning hydrogen for about 10 trillion years.
items.d: That is far longer than the Universe has existed so far.

items.t: Some red dwarfs are flare stars. Their light can double in brightness within minutes.
About 9 in 10 stars are main-sequence stars that turn hydrogen into helium in their cores.
A white dwarf is about as wide as Earth but hundreds of thousands of times heavier.
Brown dwarfs are not true stars. They give off almost no visible light.
items.d: Some can be seen with infrared light.

items.t: A red giant looks more orange than red.
Red giants are tens to hundreds of times wider than the Sun.
Red giants have cooler surfaces than the Sun but still outshine it, because they are so huge.
Arcturus is a K-type red giant about 36 light-years away.
items.d: It is a K-type star, so it looks orange.

items.t: Blue giants are hotter than about 10,000 K but only 5 to 10 times as wide as the Sun.
Betelgeuse is about 640 to 764 times as wide as the Sun.
Antares means rival of Ares, the Greek name for Mars. It is red like the planet.
If Antares sat where the Sun is, it would stretch out into the asteroid belt.
Rigel is a blue-white supergiant and the brightest star in Orion.
Supergiants shine from about 1,000 to over 1,000,000 times brighter than the Sun.
On the magnitude scale, a bigger number means a fainter star.
items.d: Sirius, the brightest night star, is about -1.4.

items.t: A difference of 5 magnitudes means a brightness factor of exactly 100.
items.d: A difference of 1 magnitude means a brightness factor of about 2.5.

items.t: Magnitude 6 is about the faintest star a person can see without a telescope.
Sirius, in Canis Major, is the brightest star in the night sky. It is nicknamed the Dog Star.
Sirius is about 8.6 light-years away, one of our nearest neighbours.
Sirius is really two stars. The small partner, Sirius B, is a white dwarf.
items.d: They circle each other about every 50 years.

items.t: More than half of all stars have one or more partner stars.
Alpha Centauri, our nearest star system, has three stars.
Some star systems have as many as seven stars.
A planet in a two-star system could have two suns in its sky.
Mizar and Alcor in the Big Dipper area look like a pair, but together they hold six stars.
Albireo looks like one star to the eye. A telescope splits it into an amber star and a blue-green one.
Algol dims from about magnitude 2.1 to 3.4 every 2.86 days.
items.d: The change happens during an eclipse in its star system.

items.t: Mira is a pulsating red giant. Its brightness cycle is about 332 days.
Cepheid variable stars pulse steadily, usually every 1 to 100 days.
Henrietta Swan Leavitt found that a Cepheid's pulse time is linked to how bright it really is.
Annie Jump Cannon sorted about 350,000 stars, more than anyone else.
items.d: She worked at the Harvard Observatory.

items.t: Hotter things glow with shorter wavelengths of light, so hotter stars look bluer.
Metal heated in a fire glows red first, then orange-red as it gets hotter.
items.d: Stars change color with heat in the same way.

items.t: Sirius is the brightest star in Earth's night sky.
Sirius is about 8.6 light-years from Earth.
Sirius looks almost twice as bright as Canopus, the next brightest star.
Sirius A gives off about 25 times as much light as the Sun.
Sirius has a faint white dwarf companion called Sirius B.
Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star in the constellation Orion.
Betelgeuse is about 400 to 600 light-years from the Sun.
Betelgeuse's radius is about 640 to 764 times the Sun's radius.
Betelgeuse slowly changes in brightness because it is a variable star.
In 1920, Betelgeuse became the first star beyond the Sun to have its apparent size measured.
Polaris lies less than 1 degree from the north celestial pole.
Polaris looks like one star, but it is really a system of three stars.
Polaris is a yellow supergiant in the constellation Ursa Minor.
Polaris is only about the 47th brightest star in the night sky.
Polaris pulses in brightness on a cycle of about four days.
Around 2750 BC, Thuban was closer to the north celestial pole than Polaris was.
Vega is about 25 light-years from the Sun.
Vega is the fifth-brightest star in the night sky.
Vega was the first star besides the Sun to be photographed.
Vega was the northern pole star around 12000 BCE.
Vega is one corner of the star pattern called the Summer Triangle.
Vega spins at about 236 kilometres per second at its equator, making it bulge.
Rigel is a blue supergiant about 850 light-years away.
Rigel is the brightest star in Orion and the seventh-brightest star in the night sky.
Rigel has about 18 to 24 times as much mass as the Sun.
Rigel has a radius more than 70 times the Sun's radius.
Rigel has used up the hydrogen fuel in its core.
Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to the Sun, about 4.25 light-years away.
Robert Innes discovered Proxima Centauri in 1915.
Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf with about one-eighth of the Sun's mass.
Proxima Centauri's diameter is about one-seventh of the Sun's diameter.
Proxima Centauri is too faint to see with unaided eyes.
Proxima Centauri is a flare star, so it can suddenly grow much brighter.
Proxima Centauri belongs to the Alpha Centauri star system.
Antares is about 550 light-years away.
If Antares replaced the Sun, its outer edge would reach into the asteroid belt.
Antares is the brightest star in the constellation Scorpius.
Antares gives off about 100,000 times as much light as the Sun.
Alpha Centauri A and B are the nearest pair of stars orbiting each other.
items.d: They are about 4.3 light-years from the Sun.

items.t: Alpha Centauri appears as the third-brightest star in the night sky.
Alpha Centauri A is a yellowish star similar to the Sun.
Alpha Centauri A and B orbit each other about once every 79 years.
Arcturus is about 36.7 light-years from the Sun.
Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern half of the celestial sky.
Arcturus has grown to about 25 times the Sun's size.
Aldebaran's name means the follower because it seems to follow the Pleiades across the sky.
Aldebaran is a red giant about 67 light-years away.
Aldebaran has a radius about 45 times the Sun's radius.
Canopus is the second-brightest star in the night sky, after Sirius.
Canopus is about 310 light-years from the Sun.
There are 88 official constellations.
items.d: Everyone shares this list, so each star picture keeps one name.

items.t: Stars in a constellation are not really connected.
items.d: They look close together from Earth, yet they are not linked in space.

items.t: People use constellations as landmarks because the patterns hold.
items.d: During a person's life the shapes stay put, so you can learn them.

items.t: For centuries, sailors used stars to find where they were at sea.
items.d: With no land in sight, familiar stars were their guide.

items.t: Robot spacecraft carry a star map to tell which way they point.
items.d: The map sits in the onboard computer and matches the stars it sees.

items.t: Meteor showers are named for the constellation they seem to leave.
items.d: The Orionids look as if they fly out from Orion.

items.t: The Orion Nebula sits below the three stars of Orion's Belt.
items.d: Find that short row, then look just underneath it.

items.t: The Big Dipper is shaped like a soup ladle.
items.d: A ladle is the deep spoon you use to dip soup from a pot.

items.t: The Big Dipper's seven stars sit inside the Great Bear.
items.d: Ursa Major is the whole constellation. The Dipper is the bright part.

items.t: Dubhe and Merak are the Pointers. They lead you to Polaris.
items.d: Draw a line through this pair and it aims at the North Star.

items.t: Mizar and faint Alcor are a famous pair in the Dipper's handle.
items.d: Try to see the tiny star tucked right beside Mizar.

items.t: Ursa Major is the third largest constellation of the 88.
items.d: Only two constellations spread across more of the sky.

items.t: Ptolemy listed Ursa Major among 48 constellations.
items.d: This Greek astronomer made his famous list in the 2nd century.

items.t: From mid-northern places, the Great Bear never sets.
items.d: It is circumpolar, so it stays above the horizon all night.

items.t: You can see the Andromeda Galaxy by eye on a dark night.
items.d: It is a giant galaxy far outside our own Milky Way.

items.t: Alioth is the brightest star in Ursa Major.
items.d: It shines brighter than any other star in the Great Bear.

items.t: A Haudenosaunee story sees three Dipper stars as hunters.
items.d: Alioth, Mizar, and Alkaid chase the Great Bear across the sky.

items.t: The Big Dipper has four stars in its bowl and three in its handle.
items.d: Together, those seven stars make the ladle.

items.t: In the UK and Ireland, the Big Dipper is called the Plough.
items.d: Same stars, new name: a plough is a farm tool for turning soil.

items.t: About five times the Pointers' gap brings you to Polaris.
items.d: Start with the two Pointer stars and extend that line outward.

items.t: Faint Alcor was long used as a test of sharp eyes.
items.d: If you can pick out this dim star in the Dipper, your eyes are sharp.

items.t: Arc along the Dipper's handle to Arcturus, then on to Spica.
items.d: Let the curve of the handle guide you to these two bright stars.

items.t: Five Big Dipper stars travel through space together.
items.d: They are the core of a family called the Ursa Major Moving Group.

items.t: Over a very long time, the Big Dipper's shape will change.
items.d: The stars drift, so the bowl opens up and the handle bends more.

items.t: Bootes can look like a kite or an ice cream cone.
items.d: Its name means herdsman, or plowman, in Ancient Greek.

items.t: Inuit sky stories see the Big Dipper as a caribou.
items.d: A caribou is a large deer that lives in the cold north.

items.t: Polaris lies less than one degree from the north pole of the sky.
items.d: Being so close to that pole makes Polaris our current North Star.

items.t: Polaris stays almost still as other stars circle it.
items.d: It sits almost on Earth's axis, the line through the North and South Poles.

items.t: How high Polaris sits is about equal to your latitude.
items.d: Travel north and the North Star climbs higher in the sky.

items.t: Polaris will not always be the North Star.
items.d: Earth wobbles. Polaris takes the job again after about 26,000 years.

items.t: About 6,000 years ago, Thuban in Draco became the North Star.
items.d: Long before Polaris, Thuban was the star nearest to north.

items.t: The Little Dipper is Ursa Minor: seven stars, four in the bowl.
items.d: The other three stars make the handle.

items.t: Kochab and Pherkad are called the Guardians of the Pole.
items.d: They circle near Polaris, keeping watch on the North Star.

items.t: Cassiopeia is easy to spot: five bright stars make a W.
items.d: Look for a wide zigzag, like the letter W, in the northern sky.

items.t: Cassiopeia is named for a queen, mother of Princess Andromeda.
items.d: In the old story she was the queen of Aethiopia.

items.t: Cassiopeia never sets from Canada, the northern US, or the British Isles.
items.d: It is circumpolar there, so it rides around the pole all night.

items.t: A rich band of the Milky Way runs through Cassiopeia.
items.d: That part of our galaxy looks cloudy because it is packed with stars.

items.t: In 1572 a brilliant supernova flared in Cassiopeia.
items.d: Tycho Brahe was the astronomer who watched this bright flare.

items.t: Orion's Belt is three bright stars: Alnitak, Alnilam, and Mintaka.
items.d: Look for this short, bright row. It is the easiest part of Orion.

items.t: Betelgeuse is a huge red supergiant in the constellation Orion.
items.d: Supergiant means it is an enormous star, and its color is red.

items.t: Rigel is a blue supergiant and the seventh brightest night star.
items.d: Only six stars in the night sky outshine Rigel. It lies in Orion.

items.t: Orion's Sword is a short line of three stars under the Belt.
items.d: It hangs downward from the belt like a little sword.

items.t: Extend Orion's Belt to the southeast and you find Sirius.
items.d: Sirius is the brightest star in the whole night sky.

items.t: Orion is a winter constellation in the north and a summer one in the south.
items.d: North and south have opposite seasons, so Orion's season flips too.

items.t: The Orion Nebula looks like a fuzzy patch, not a sharp star.
items.d: You can see that soft glow with just your eyes on a dark night.

items.t: The Orion Nebula is about 1,270 light-years from Earth.
items.d: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year.

items.t: The Orion Nebula is Earth's closest nursery of huge new stars.
items.d: Massive stars are being born in this bright cloud right now.

items.t: The Perseid meteors come from the comet Swift-Tuttle.
items.d: The shower is strongest from about 9 to 14 August.

items.t: Algol dims about every 2.9 days when one star passes in front of another.
items.d: Algol is in Perseus. The dip in light is an eclipse of one star by its partner.

items.t: The Summer Triangle is made of Vega, Deneb, and Altair.
items.d: Each star is the brightest one in its own constellation.

items.t: Crux, the Southern Cross, is the smallest of all 88 constellations.
items.d: It is tiny, but it is easy to spot in the southern sky.

items.t: Acrux is the brightest star in the Southern Cross. It is also the cross's southernmost star.
Mimosa, a star in the Southern Cross, is a blue giant.
Gacrux, a star in the Southern Cross, is a red giant.
The Coalsack is a dark nebula in Crux, the Southern Cross.
items.d: It is the most noticeable dark nebula in our sky.

items.t: The Jewel Box is a sparkling cluster of stars near the Southern Cross.
items.d: Its official name is NGC 4755.

items.t: Two bright stars in Centaurus, called the Southern Pointers, help you find the Southern Cross.
items.d: They are Alpha Centauri and Beta Centauri.

items.t: The Southern Cross is easy to see from the Southern Hemisphere.
The Southern Cross holds four Cepheid stars. A Cepheid is a star whose brightness pulses.
The Southern Cross is drawn on several national flags, including Australia and New Zealand.
In some Aboriginal Australian stories, the Southern Cross and the Coalsack are the head of the Emu in the Sky.
Alpha Centauri is the nearest star system to our Sun, about 4.4 light-years away.
Proxima Centauri is a faint red dwarf. It is the closest known star to our Sun.
Omega Centauri is the biggest and brightest globular cluster of stars in the Milky Way.
items.d: It is about 17,000 light-years away.

items.t: Centaurus A is a galaxy about 11 million light-years away. It is one of the closest active galaxies to us.
Beta Centauri is a blue giant star. Its other names are Hadar and Agena.
In Greek tales, Centaurus honors Chiron, a wise centaur who taught young heroes.
Centaurus is the ninth biggest of the 88 constellations by area.
Centaurus was one of 48 constellations listed by the astronomer Ptolemy long ago, in the 2nd century.
Centaurus has 281 stars visible in very dark skies, more than any other constellation.
Canopus, in the constellation Carina, is the second-brightest star in our night sky.
Canopus is about 313 light-years from Earth.
items.d: That means its light left it about 313 years ago.

items.t: Eta Carinae is a giant star system with a star about 100 times heavier than our Sun.
In 1843, Eta Carinae flared up and became as bright as some of the brightest stars in the sky.
Eta Carinae sits inside the Carina Nebula, a huge glowing cloud of gas about 8,000 light-years away.
In 1763, Lacaille split the huge old constellation Argo Navis into Carina, Puppis and Vela.
The False Cross is made of stars in Carina and Vela. People often mix it up with the real Southern Cross.
Antares, the red star of Scorpius, has a name that means 'rival of Mars' because it looks reddish like Mars.
Hawaiians see the shape of Scorpius as Maui's great fishhook, Ka Makau Nui o Maui.
In Tahiti, Scorpius is Matau a Maui, the fishhook. Its setting once marked the end of a tuna fishing ban.
Messier 6, a star cluster in Scorpius, is nicknamed the Butterfly Cluster.
NGC 6334 in Scorpius is called the Cat's Paw Nebula.
The Yolngu people of Arnhem Land see Orion as a canoe called Julpan.
The Seven Sisters (Pleiades) is one of the most widespread star stories in Aboriginal Australia.
The Wardaman people of Australia see the Coalsack dark cloud as the head of a lawman.
The Boorong people of Australia saw a possum in a tree in the stars of the Southern Cross.
The Kaurna people of Australia called the Milky Way 'wodliparri', which means 'house river'.
The Boorong people saw and remembered Eta Carinae's big brightening in the 1840s.
Many Aboriginal groups in northern Australia use a calendar with six seasons.
Pacific voyagers once steered by the rising and setting spots of named stars.
items.d: Some star compasses use as many as 150 stars.

items.t: Pacific navigators steered by a star low on the horizon, then switched to another as the first rose too high.
In 1980, Nainoa Thompson sailed Hawaii to Tahiti and back without instruments.
items.d: He navigated using Hawaiian wayfinding.

items.t: Navigators also read ocean swells. Swells are a steadier guide than waves, which are pushed by local winds.
Navigators watched birds, sailing against their morning flight and along it in the evening to find land.
Matariki is the Pleiades star cluster. In New Zealand, its June or July rising marks the Māori new year.
Many Māori traditions see nine stars in Matariki. Hiwa-i-te-rangi is known as the wishing star.
New Zealand first held a public holiday for Matariki on 24 June 2022.
The Chinese Twenty-Eight Mansions follow the Moon's path across the sky over one lunar month.
The Azure Dragon of the East is one of China's Four Symbols in the sky. It is linked to spring.
Constellation stars look grouped from Earth, but they are not really connected.
Astronomers officially recognize 88 constellations.
Meteor showers are named for the constellation they seem to come from.
items.d: The Orionids seem to spread outward from Orion.

items.t: The constellations you can see depend on the season and your place on Earth.
Stars appear slightly farther west each night because Earth travels around the Sun.
Sailors have long used familiar stars to find their way.
items.d: Using the sky to find your way is called celestial navigation.

items.t: People in Earth's Northern and Southern Hemispheres see different parts of the sky.
The ecliptic is the path the Sun seems to follow across the sky during a year.
items.d: It matches the flat plane of Earth's orbit.

items.t: The ecliptic, the Sun's yearly path, is named for eclipses.
items.d: Eclipses happen only when the Moon crosses this path.

items.t: The zodiac extends about 8 degrees north and south of the ecliptic.
items.d: So the belt is about 16 degrees wide.

items.t: The traditional zodiac divides a full circle into 12 equal signs.
items.d: Each sign covers 30 degrees, and 12 x 30 = 360 degrees.

items.t: The Sun's yearly path actually crosses 13 constellations, including Ophiuchus.
The celestial equator crosses the ecliptic at two points called the equinoxes.
Planets usually appear near the ecliptic because their orbits lie close to Earth's orbital plane.
The Moon stays near the ecliptic because its orbit is tilted only about 5.1 degrees from it.
Earth's axis slowly wobbles like the axis of a spinning top.
items.d: One complete wobble takes about 26,000 years.

items.t: Earth's slow wobble shifts the equinoxes by about 1 degree every 72 years.
Thuban was the north pole star around 3000 BC.
items.d: Earth's slow wobble changes which star points north over long periods.

items.t: Vega will become a pole star in about 12,000 years.
Babylonian astronomers divided the ecliptic into 12 equal signs over 2,000 years ago.
The word zodiac comes from a Greek word meaning "of little animals."
items.d: Many traditional zodiac signs are represented by animals.

items.t: The Sun appears inside Ophiuchus from about November 29 to December 18.
Ophiuchus is the 11th largest of the 88 constellations.
items.d: It covers about 948 square degrees of sky.

items.t: Barnard's Star in Ophiuchus is one of the nearest stars to our Sun.
items.d: Only stars in the Alpha Centauri system are closer.

items.t: The ancient Babylonian sky guide MUL.APIN listed 66 stars and constellations.
items.d: It sorted them into three paths called Enlil, Anu, and Ea.

items.t: MUL.APIN used an ideal year with 12 months of 30 days.
items.d: That ideal calendar contained 360 days.

items.t: Babylonian calendars sometimes added a thirteenth month to match the seasons.
items.d: The risings of stars such as the Pleiades and Sirius helped guide the choice.

items.t: The ancient Egyptian civil year had 365 days but no leap years.
items.d: Its New Year slowly moved through the seasons.

items.t: Ancient Egyptians linked Sirius returning to the dawn sky with the yearly Nile flood.
The Egyptian calendar had 12 months of 30 days, followed by 5 extra days.
items.d: It also divided the year into three seasons.

items.t: Ancient Egyptian astronomers divided part of the sky into 36 star groups called decans.
items.d: Each decan covered 10 degrees.

items.t: A different decan rose at dawn about every ten days.
items.d: The Greek name for these star groups meant "tenths."

items.t: Decans could work as a star clock during the night.
items.d: The rising of each new group marked another part of the night.

items.t: Stonehenge lines up with the summer solstice sunrise and winter solstice sunset.
The Nebra sky disc is about 3,600 to 3,800 years old.
items.d: It is among the oldest known pictures of the cosmos.

items.t: Seven dots on the Nebra sky disc are thought to show the Pleiades star cluster.
Two gold arcs on the Nebra sky disc span about 82 degrees.
items.d: That matches the angle between summer and winter solstice sunsets where it was found.

items.t: A heliacal rising is a star's first return to the eastern dawn sky after being hidden by sunlight.
Several ancient cultures used stars returning at dawn to help time farming activities.
Matariki is the Māori name for the Pleiades.
items.d: Its appearance in the dawn sky marks the start of the Māori new year.

items.t: The traditional Chinese calendar follows both the Moon and the Sun.
items.d: It adds an extra month when needed to stay matched with the seasons.

items.t: The Chinese calendar has 24 solar terms that track the Sun and the seasons.
A traditional Chinese system combines two name sets to form a 60-year cycle.
items.d: The sets contain 10 Heavenly Stems and 12 Earthly Branches.

items.t: Most years divisible by 4 are leap years, but century years must also divide by 400.
items.d: The year 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 was not.

items.t: One Earth spin measured against the stars takes about 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds.
items.d: This is called a sidereal day.

items.t: A star reaches the same sky position about four minutes earlier each night.
items.d: This timing shift helps different constellations appear in different seasons.

items.t: A tropical year runs from one March equinox to the next.
items.d: It lasts about 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes, and 45 seconds.

items.t: Earth's seasons come from its tilt of about 23.4 degrees, not its distance from the Sun.
Earth's Northern and Southern Hemispheres always have opposite seasons.
items.d: When one hemisphere has summer, the other has winter.

items.t: A galaxy is a huge collection of stars, gas, dust, and planets held by gravity.
items.d: Without gravity, those stars and clouds would not stay together.

items.t: There are three main galaxy shapes: spiral, elliptical, and irregular.
items.d: Irregular galaxies look less orderly than spirals and ellipticals.

items.t: Spiral galaxies look like giant pinwheels turning in space.
items.d: A disk of stars surrounds a thicker bulge in the center.

items.t: A spiral galaxy's youngest stars are born in its arms.
items.d: The arms hold plenty of gas, the stuff new stars are made from.

items.t: A spiral galaxy has a flat disk, a central bulge, and a round halo.
items.d: The bulge is mostly older stars. The halo has round star clusters.

items.t: About two-thirds of spiral galaxies are barred spirals.
items.d: The Milky Way and Andromeda both have a bar of stars across the center.

items.t: Elliptical galaxies can look completely round or oval.
items.d: Some are ball-shaped, and some are stretched like an egg.

items.t: Elliptical galaxies usually hold little gas or dust.
items.d: Their stars are generally older than the stars in a spiral galaxy.

items.t: Irregular galaxies come in odd shapes, not neat spirals or ovals.
items.d: Some look like rings, skinny sticks, or small clumps of stars.

items.t: Passing near another galaxy can give an irregular galaxy its odd shape.
items.d: Gravity between the galaxies tugs their stars and gas into a new form.

items.t: Irregular galaxies can hold a lot of gas and dust.
items.d: Gas and dust are the ingredients for making new stars.

items.t: The biggest galaxies contain trillions of stars.
items.d: Some are more than a million light-years from side to side.

items.t: The smallest galaxies have just a few thousand stars.
items.d: They are only a few hundred light-years wide.

items.t: Most galaxies are dwarfs, much smaller than the Milky Way.
items.d: They have a few billion stars and are about one hundredth the Milky Way's size.

items.t: Most large galaxies have a giant black hole in the center.
items.d: Astronomers call that kind a supermassive black hole.

items.t: Most galaxies are about 10 to 13.6 billion years old.
items.d: Ten billion is a 1 followed by 10 zeros. These galaxies are ancient.

items.t: A galaxy group usually holds about 100 galaxies or fewer.
items.d: The galaxies' gravity pulls them together as a group.

items.t: A galaxy cluster can hold thousands of galaxies at once.
items.d: That is a much bigger crowd than a galaxy group.

items.t: From Earth, the Milky Way looks like a faint band of light.
items.d: You are looking through the starry disk of our own galaxy.

items.t: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy more than 100,000 light-years across.
items.d: Its stars form a wide, flat disk.

items.t: We live on a spiral arm, about halfway from the Milky Way's center.
items.d: Earth is not in the galaxy's core, and not at its outer edge.

items.t: The Sun is about 27,000 light-years from the Milky Way's center.
items.d: Light from the center takes about 27,000 years to reach the Sun.

items.t: The Sun lies near a small arm called the Orion Spur.
items.d: It is also called the Orion Arm and sits between the Sagittarius and Perseus arms.

items.t: The Milky Way has two major spiral arms: Scutum-Centaurus and Perseus.
items.d: These arms wrap out from the ends of a bar of stars in the center.

items.t: Our solar system takes about 240 million years to circle the Milky Way.
items.d: One full circle around the galaxy is a very long trip.

items.t: Most stars in the Milky Way's disk orbit the center very fast.
items.d: Their speed is about 200 to 220 kilometers per second.

items.t: The Milky Way contains about 100 billion to 400 billion stars.
items.d: The count is a range because so many stars are too faint to tally.

items.t: A giant black hole named Sagittarius A* sits at the Milky Way's center.
items.d: Its mass is about 4 million times the Sun's mass.

items.t: The word galaxy comes from a Greek name meaning milky circle.
items.d: Milky Way is English for the Latin via lactea, a milky road.

items.t: The Local Group, our galaxy neighborhood, has more than 50 galaxies.
items.d: The Milky Way is one galaxy in that group.

items.t: Andromeda, the Milky Way, and Triangulum are the biggest Local Group galaxies.
items.d: The rest of the group is mostly smaller dwarf galaxies.

items.t: The Local Group belongs to the Laniakea supercluster.
items.d: Our galaxy group is one small piece of that much bigger structure.

items.t: Andromeda is the nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way.
items.d: Among big galaxies, none is nearer to us than Andromeda.

items.t: Andromeda is about 152,000 light-years across.
items.d: It contains roughly a trillion stars.

items.t: Andromeda moves toward the Milky Way at about 110 kilometers per second.
items.d: That is about 110 kilometers (about 68 miles) every second.

items.t: On a dark, moonless night, Andromeda can be seen with just your eyes.
items.d: It appears as a faint little cloud, not a single bright point.

items.t: Around 964, astronomer al-Sufi called Andromeda a little cloud.
items.d: This is the earliest known writing about a galaxy beyond our own.

items.t: The Large Magellanic Cloud is about 163,000 light-years from us.
items.d: It lies in the southern constellations Dorado and Mensa.

items.t: The Large Magellanic Cloud is a small satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
items.d: It has about 20 billion stars.

items.t: The Tarantula Nebula is inside the Large Magellanic Cloud.
items.d: It is the Local Group's busiest region for forming new stars.

items.t: The Magellanic Clouds are named for the explorer Ferdinand Magellan.
items.d: Magellan wrote about them on his voyage that began in 1519. That made them well known in Europe.

items.t: In 1987, astronomers saw a star explode in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
items.d: They named it SN 1987A. It was a nearby exploding star.

items.t: The Small Magellanic Cloud is about 200,000 light-years away.
items.d: Its home constellation is Tucana, in the southern sky.

items.t: The Small Magellanic Cloud is a dwarf irregular galaxy.
items.d: Across, it measures about 19,000 light-years.

items.t: The Small Magellanic Cloud is visible across the Southern Hemisphere.
items.d: People south of the equator can see it in the night sky.

items.t: The Triangulum Galaxy is a spiral about 2.9 million light-years away.
items.d: It has about 30 to 40 billion stars. Under a very dark sky, some people can see it with no telescope.

items.t: In 1845, Lord Rosse first saw spiral arms in the Whirlpool Galaxy.
items.d: His telescope in Ireland had a mirror about 1.8 meters (72 inches) across.

items.t: In the 1920s, Edwin Hubble proved that other galaxies exist.
items.d: He used stars called Cepheids, which brighten and dim, to measure distance.

items.t: A quasar is a galaxy center that shines with huge brightness.
items.d: Gas falling into a giant black hole powers that bright light.

items.t: A black hole does not suck up everything nearby. From far away it pulls like any object with the same mass.
If the Sun turned into a black hole with the same mass, the planets would keep orbiting just as before.
items.d: Gravity depends on mass, not on what the object is made of.

items.t: The black hole in the middle of our galaxy weighs about 4 million times as much as the Sun.
Some black holes form when a giant star runs out of fuel and explodes as a supernova.
The event horizon is like the surface of a black hole. It is the point of no return.
Inside the event horizon, you would need to go faster than light to escape. Even light is trapped.
The glow around a black hole comes from the accretion disk, a hot, swirling disk of gas.
items.d: The black hole itself is dark. The gas around it shines.

items.t: Thin, bright rings of light appear around a black hole's shadow, from every viewing angle.
Some light rings around a black hole come from light that circled the hole several times before reaching us.
At the center of a black hole is the singularity, where matter is thought to be squeezed to infinite density.
Scientists do not yet know if the singularity is a real thing or just a math idea.
items.d: Not knowing is how science finds new things to explore.

items.t: Supermassive black holes hold hundreds of thousands to billions of times the Sun's mass.
Intermediate-mass black holes would sit between small and huge ones. Scientists are still studying them.
Cygnus X-1 was the very first black hole candidate that astronomers found.
A simple black hole can be described with just three things: its mass, its electric charge and its spin.
Near a black hole, time runs slower. A far-away watcher sees a falling object seem to slow down.
Stephen Hawking showed that black holes should slowly give off a tiny bit of energy. Small ones do it faster.
The first pulsar was spotted by Jocelyn Bell in data recorded on August 6, 1967.
The first pulsar sent a pulse evenly every 1.337 seconds, like a very steady clock.
The first pulsar signal was jokingly nicknamed LGM-1, short for Little Green Men.
items.d: It was soon explained as a natural, fast-spinning star.

items.t: A pulsar works like a lighthouse. We only see its beam when it points toward Earth.
Pulsars pulse very regularly, from a few milliseconds to a few seconds between pulses.
The pulsar PSR B1937+21 spins once about every 1.6 milliseconds.
items.d: That is about 600 spins in one second.

items.t: Some fast-spinning pulsars keep time so steadily that they rival the best atomic clocks on Earth.
A neutron star is only about 10 kilometers in radius, about the size of a small city.
All of Earth's mass squeezed to neutron star density would fit in a ball about 300 meters across.
A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh more than 5 billion tonnes.
Gravity on a neutron star is about 200 billion times stronger than gravity on Earth.
Magnetars are neutron stars with extremely powerful magnetic fields.
A magnetar's magnetic field is at least 100,000 times stronger than the strongest magnet people have made.
Starquakes on a magnetar's surface can shake its magnetic field and set off giant flashes of gamma rays.
A giant flare from a magnetar 50,000 light-years away even affected Earth's atmosphere in 2004.
The Crab Pulsar is what is left of a star that exploded in a supernova seen from Earth in the year 1054.
The Crab Pulsar spins about 30 times every second.
The Crab Pulsar is only about 20 kilometers across, and it sits at the heart of the Crab Nebula.
Albert Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916.
Gravitational waves travel at the speed of light.
The strongest gravitational waves come from huge events, like two black holes crashing together.
In 1974, a pair of orbiting stars, one of them a pulsar, gave the first proof that gravitational waves exist.
On September 14, 2015, LIGO first detected gravitational waves, from black holes 1.3 billion light-years away.
The 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics honored the direct detection of gravitational waves.
The first gravitational waves detected came from black holes about 29 and 36 times the Sun's mass merging.
Sagittarius A*, the black hole at our galaxy's center, is about 27,000 light-years from Earth.
The first picture of Sagittarius A* was released in May 2022.
The first-ever picture of a black hole, in the galaxy M87, was released on April 10, 2019.
The black hole in galaxy M87 weighs about 6.5 billion times as much as the Sun.
The Event Horizon Telescope linked eight telescopes at six sites to work like one telescope as big as Earth.
The black hole picture data was too big to send online, so it was flown on hard drives by freight plane.
The Orion Nebula is about 1,500 light-years from Earth.
items.d: It is the closest large star-forming region to us.

items.t: You can spot the Orion Nebula without a telescope from a dark place.
The Orion Nebula is a stellar nursery where many new stars are forming.
Four bright young stars in the Orion Nebula are called the Trapezium.
items.d: Their positions make a shape like a trapezoid.

items.t: The Orion Nebula is an enormous cloud of gas and dust.
The Crab Nebula is about 6,500 light-years away in the constellation Taurus.
The Crab Nebula is about six light-years wide.
A fast-spinning neutron star called a pulsar sits at the heart of the Crab Nebula.
The pulsar inside the Crab Nebula appears to pulse about 30 times each second.
Bright wisps in the Crab Nebula move at about half the speed of light.
items.d: They travel outward from the pulsar at the nebula's center.

items.t: The Ring Nebula is about 2,000 light-years away in the constellation Lyra.
The Ring Nebula formed from glowing material released by a Sun-like star.
The Ring Nebula is more complex than a simple ring.
items.d: Its inner rim contains dark knots of dense gas.

items.t: The Pleiades cluster contains over 1,000 stars loosely held together by gravity.
The Pleiades star cluster is easy to see without a telescope from a dark place.
The Pleiades star cluster is also called the Seven Sisters.
Radiation from a Pleiades star is breaking apart a nearby reflection nebula.
The Eagle Nebula is about 7,000 light-years away in the constellation Serpens.
items.d: It is home to the Pillars of Creation.

items.t: The Pillars of Creation are about 4 to 5 light-years tall.
The Eagle Nebula spans about 70 by 55 light-years.
New stars are forming inside the dusty columns of the Pillars of Creation.
Light and winds from young stars slowly wear away the Pillars of Creation.
The globular star cluster M13 is about 25,000 light-years from Earth.
More than 100,000 stars fill the globular cluster M13.
Stars near the center of M13 are about 100 times more crowded than stars near our Sun.
The Dumbbell Nebula was the first planetary nebula ever discovered.
items.d: Charles Messier found it in 1764.

items.t: The Dumbbell Nebula looks like two bright lobes through a backyard telescope.
The Dumbbell Nebula is about 1,200 light-years away in the constellation Vulpecula.
Planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets.
items.d: The name arose because they can look round like planets in small telescopes.

items.t: The globular cluster M22 is about 10,000 light-years away in Sagittarius.
Globular clusters like M22 are about 12 to 13 billion years old.
Abraham Ihle found M22 in 1665 while looking toward Saturn.
items.d: It was among the first globular clusters discovered.

items.t: The globular cluster M3 is about 34,000 light-years away in Canes Venatici.
The globular cluster M3 contains more than 500,000 stars.
The Beehive Cluster is about 600 light-years away.
items.d: It is one of the closest open star clusters to Earth.

items.t: The Beehive Cluster has about 1,000 stars.
items.d: It is about 600 to 700 million years old.

items.t: Galileo showed that the Beehive Cluster was made of many stars.
items.d: He saw about 40 of its stars.

items.t: The Beehive Cluster looks like a blur in Cancer without a telescope.
items.d: Binoculars can reveal about 20 stars.

items.t: The Beehive Cluster is also known as Praesepe.
The Lagoon Nebula is about 5,200 light-years away in Sagittarius.
The Lagoon Nebula is faintly visible without a telescope under dark skies.
Hot young stars make the gas in the Lagoon Nebula glow.
items.d: That glowing gas makes it an emission nebula.

items.t: The Lagoon Nebula contains a young open star cluster called NGC 6530.
The Helix Nebula is about 650 light-years away in Aquarius.
items.d: It is one of the closest planetary nebulae to Earth.

items.t: The bright ring of the Helix Nebula is nearly three light-years across.
The Helix Nebula looks nearly half as wide as the full Moon in our sky.
Omega Centauri is about 17,000 light-years away toward the constellation Centaurus.
Omega Centauri holds about 10 million stars together with gravity.
The Cat's Eye Nebula is about 3,000 light-years away in the constellation Draco.
The Cat's Eye Nebula has at least eleven rings.
items.d: Each ring is the edge of a giant bubble of gas.

items.t: An exoplanet is any planet beyond our solar system.
items.d: Earth is a planet too, but it sits in our solar system, so it is not an exoplanet.

items.t: Scientists have confirmed more than 6,000 planets beyond our solar system.
items.d: Confirmed means the planet has been checked and agreed to be real.

items.t: Some planets beyond our solar system wander alone and circle no star.
items.d: Most planets we know of do orbit a star. These ones travel alone.

items.t: A planet can show up as a tiny dip in its star's light.
items.d: That dip is called a transit. It happens when the planet crosses the star.

items.t: The first planet found around a Sun-like star was spotted in October 1995.
items.d: The planet is named 51 Pegasi b.

items.t: Proxima Centauri b is about 4 light-years away from Earth.
items.d: It is still much too far away for people to visit.

items.t: Planets around other stars include gas giants, Neptune-like worlds, super-Earths, and rocky planets.
items.d: A rocky planet has a solid surface, a bit like Earth.

items.t: Some planets around other stars are lava worlds, with seas of melted rock.
items.d: Some others are so puffy that they are very light for their size.

items.t: The Kepler telescope watched about 150,000 stars for tiny dips in light.
items.d: NASA's TESS telescope uses that same transit method today.

items.t: A star wobbles slightly when a planet's gravity tugs on it.
items.d: As the star moves toward us and away, its light shifts a little.

items.t: A coronagraph blocks a star's glare so a planet next to it can be seen.
items.d: It is like covering a bright lamp with your hand to see a faint light nearby.

items.t: Planets we have photographed are mostly giant worlds still hot from forming.
items.d: These giant planets glow on their own, which makes them easier to see.

items.t: When a star's gravity magnifies a far star, a planet can add a smaller spike of light.
items.d: This search method is called gravitational microlensing.

items.t: The habitable zone is the distance from a star where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface.
items.d: Too close, and surface water would boil. Too far, and it would freeze.

items.t: The habitable zone is also called the Goldilocks zone.
items.d: Like the story, it is not too hot and not too cold.

items.t: A star's habitable zone depends on the star's size and brightness.
items.d: A big bright star and a small dim star do not have the zone in the same place.

items.t: A planet in the habitable zone still might not have life.
items.d: The zone only means liquid water is possible, not that life is there.

items.t: NASA's Kepler space telescope launched on March 6, 2009.
items.d: It was NASA's first mission sent to hunt for planets.

items.t: Kepler discovered more than 2,600 planets outside our solar system.
items.d: Those planets all orbit stars far beyond our own Sun.

items.t: NASA's TESS planet hunter launched on April 18, 2018.
items.d: TESS looks for planets that orbit stars beyond our solar system.

items.t: Scientists search for biosignature gases that could be signs of life.
items.d: These gases in a planet's air might offer a clue to life.

items.t: A super-Earth can have up to about ten times the mass of Earth.
items.d: It is heavier than Earth, but lighter than Neptune or Uranus.

items.t: Our solar system has no super-Earths, but they are common among exoplanets found so far.
items.d: Scientists have found many around other stars.

items.t: The super-Earth 55 Cancri e keeps one face pointed at its star.
items.d: It is tidally locked, just as our Moon always shows one side to Earth.

items.t: The TRAPPIST-1 planets are about 40 light-years from Earth.
items.d: That is about 378 trillion km (235 trillion miles).

items.t: TRAPPIST-1 was the first known star with seven Earth-size planets.
items.d: All seven of those worlds circle that one star.

items.t: Three of the seven TRAPPIST-1 planets sit in the habitable zone.
items.d: That is the region where liquid water could exist on the surface.

items.t: All seven TRAPPIST-1 planets orbit closer in than Mercury does to our Sun.
items.d: Mercury is our Sun's closest planet, and these seven are even nearer their star.

items.t: Proxima Centauri b orbits its star in about 11.2 Earth days.
items.d: It also orbits inside the habitable zone, where liquid water might be possible.

items.t: The star TRAPPIST-1 has only about 9 percent of the Sun's mass.
items.d: If the Sun were 100 equal parts, this star would be about 9 parts.

items.t: The TRAPPIST-1 planets orbit in a steady, repeating rhythm.
items.d: Their orbits line up in a regular pattern called an orbital resonance.

items.t: Hot Jupiters are gas giants that circle their star in under 10 days.
items.d: A year on a hot Jupiter is shorter than 10 days on Earth.

items.t: A hot Jupiter usually keeps one side facing its star all the time.
items.d: One half stays in endless daylight, and the other half stays dark.

items.t: Ultra-hot Jupiters have a dayside hotter than 2,200 kelvin.
items.d: Kelvin is a science temperature unit, and this dayside is extremely hot.

items.t: The planet 51 Pegasi b orbits its star in about four days.
items.d: Its year is only about four Earth days long.

items.t: 51 Pegasi b is about 50 light-years away, in the constellation Pegasus.
items.d: Pegasus is a constellation, a pattern of stars in the night sky.

items.t: 51 Pegasi b is nicknamed Dimidium, which is Latin for half.
items.d: The name fits because its mass is at least about half of Jupiter's.

items.t: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
items.d: They won it for discovering 51 Pegasi b, a planet around another star.

items.t: HD 209458 b was the first known planet outside our solar system seen crossing its star.
items.d: A transit is that crossing, and it makes the star's light dip a little.

items.t: HD 209458 b was the first planet outside our solar system to have its air measured.
items.d: Scientists measured the planet's atmosphere.

items.t: A year on HD 209458 b lasts only about 3.5 Earth days.
items.d: That is less than one week on Earth.

items.t: Kepler-16b was the first confirmed planet found orbiting two stars.
items.d: From that planet, two suns would shine in the sky.

items.t: Kepler-16b is about Saturn's size and takes 229 days to orbit its two stars.
items.d: Half an Earth year is about 183 days, so 229 days is longer.

items.t: The first confirmed planets beyond our solar system were found in 1992 around a pulsar.
items.d: A pulsar is the core left behind after a star explodes.

items.t: The Arecibo message was beamed into space on November 16, 1974.
items.d: It was sent from the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico.

items.t: The Arecibo message was aimed at the star cluster Messier 13.
items.d: Messier 13 is about 25,000 light-years from Earth.

items.t: The Arecibo message held 1,679 bits, set in 73 rows and 23 columns.
items.d: 73 times 23 is 1,679, so the picture grid uses every bit.

items.t: The Arecibo picture showed numbers, DNA parts, a person, our solar system, and the telescope.
items.d: DNA is a chemical in living things. The numbers shown were 1 to 10.

items.t: On August 15, 1977, a strong radio burst called the Wow! signal was detected.
items.d: Jerry Ehman wrote Wow! next to it. It lasted 72 seconds and was never detected again.

items.t: Frank Drake came up with the Drake equation in 1961.
items.d: It helps discuss possible civilizations beyond Earth, but does not give one exact answer.

items.t: The Big Bang is how astronomers explain the way our universe began.
items.d: It was not an explosion in one spot. Space itself grew and stretched.

items.t: The universe began as a tiny, hot point and then stretched out to become as huge as it is today.
items.d: Stretching space is why people joke that 'Everywhere Stretch' is a better name.

items.t: In 1927, astronomer Georges Lemaitre had the big idea that the universe is expanding.
items.d: He worked out that space could be stretching, long before many people agreed.

items.t: Edwin Hubble found that other galaxies are moving away from us.
items.d: Galaxies are like dots on a balloon that is being blown up.

items.t: The farthest galaxies move away faster than the ones close to us.
items.d: The more space between us, the more stretching happens, so the faster they seem to go.

items.t: Stars, planets, comets and asteroids were not there at the very beginning of the universe.
items.d: At first there were only hot, tiny particles mixed with light and energy.

items.t: As the universe expanded and took up more space, it cooled down.
items.d: Like a hot drink spreading out, things got cooler as everything got more spread out.

items.t: Over a very long time, atoms came together to form the first stars and galaxies.
items.d: Gravity slowly pulled the gas into clumps.

items.t: One second after the Big Bang, the universe was about 10 billion degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is far hotter than the middle of our Sun.

items.t: Within about five minutes of the Big Bang, most of the helium we see today had formed.
items.d: Helium is the gas that makes party balloons float.

items.t: About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the first atoms began to form.
items.d: Before that, the universe was too hot for atoms to stay together.

items.t: The cosmic microwave background is the oldest light we can see in the universe.
items.d: It is like a baby picture of the universe.

items.t: After the first atoms formed, the universe stayed dark for about 200 million years.
items.d: Then the first stars switched on and lit it up.

items.t: The first stars were 30 to 300 times heavier than our Sun and millions of times brighter.
items.d: They were giants compared to the Sun.

items.t: In 1998, astronomers found that the universe's expansion is speeding up.
items.d: They saw exploding stars that looked fainter than expected, so they were farther away.

items.t: Scientists suspect a mysterious thing called dark energy is making the expansion speed up.
items.d: Nobody knows yet what dark energy really is.

items.t: Dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe, far more than the ordinary matter that makes stars and us.
Dark matter does not give off, reflect or soak up light, so we cannot see it directly.
items.d: It is invisible to telescopes, but it has mass.

items.t: The gravity of dark matter can bend light from far-away galaxies.
items.d: That bending is one way astronomers can tell dark matter is there.

items.t: In the 1970s, Vera Rubin studied stars at the edges of spiral galaxies and found clues for dark matter.
items.d: The stars moved in a way that showed there was extra unseen mass.

items.t: Scientists have not yet found out what dark matter is made of.
items.d: That is one of the big open puzzles in astronomy.

items.t: Dark energy makes up about 68% of the universe.
items.d: It is the biggest slice, yet it is the most mysterious.

items.t: Dark matter and dark energy both have 'dark' in their names, but they are not the same thing.
items.d: Dark matter has gravity. Dark energy is the name for whatever makes expansion speed up.

items.t: The cosmic microwave background is leftover glow from the Big Bang that fills the whole universe.
The universe's stretching has cooled the cosmic microwave background to about 2.7 kelvin.
items.d: That is about minus 270 degrees Celsius, extremely cold.

items.t: There are roughly 400 particles of leftover Big Bang light in every cubic centimetre of space.
items.d: A cubic centimetre is about the size of a sugar cube.

items.t: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found the cosmic microwave background by accident in 1964.
items.d: They first thought the signal was just noise in their antenna.

items.t: Tiny bumps in the cosmic microwave background are like seeds for where galaxies later grew.
The observable universe is a sphere about 93 billion light-years across.
items.d: That is the part of space we can possibly see from Earth.

items.t: The observable universe may hold as many as 2 trillion galaxies.
items.d: That is 2,000,000,000,000 galaxies, each with billions of stars.

items.t: There may be more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches.
Every place in the universe has its own observable universe, and they can overlap.
items.d: Someone far away would see a slightly different patch of space.

items.t: In the far future, distant galaxies will fade from view as space keeps stretching.
items.d: Their light will not be able to reach us any more.

items.t: The straight-line link between how far a galaxy is and how fast it moves away is called Hubble's law.
items.d: Twice as far means about twice as fast.

items.t: In 1931, Georges Lemaitre said the universe began from a 'primeval atom'.
items.d: It was an early version of the Big Bang idea.

items.t: Astronomer Fred Hoyle is credited with first using the name 'Big Bang' on the radio in 1949.
items.d: The name did not become popular until the 1970s.

items.t: Big Bang models predict that about one quarter of ordinary matter in the universe is helium.
items.d: Measurements of old gas clouds match this idea.

items.t: In the first few minutes, protons and neutrons joined to form deuterium and helium nuclei.
Once neutral atoms formed, the foggy early universe became transparent to light.
items.d: Before that, light kept bumping into particles, like sunlight in thick fog.

items.t: Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman predicted the cosmic microwave background in 1948.
items.d: It was found about 16 years later.

items.t: The cosmic microwave background is almost the same in every direction, within about one part in 25,000.
items.d: Space looks very smooth on the big scale.

items.t: Redshift means light is stretched to longer waves, toward red, as a source moves away or space expands.
items.d: It is like a stretched slinky with longer waves.

items.t: Alan Guth proposed cosmic inflation in 1981, a super-fast stretch of space very early on.
items.d: It helps explain why the universe looks so smooth.

items.t: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
items.d: It measures distance, not time.

items.t: The nearest star to the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.24 light-years away.
items.d: Its light takes over four years to reach us.

items.t: Light travels at 299,792,458 metres per second, or about 300,000 km per second.
Type Ia supernovae help measure distance because astronomers can work out their true brightness.
items.d: If two have the same true brightness, the dimmer-looking one is farther away.

items.t: The name Milky Way comes from Latin words meaning "milky road."
From Earth, the Milky Way looks like a hazy band of light across the night sky.
Dark patches in the Milky Way are dust clouds blocking light from distant stars.
The Milky Way's glow combines the light of many stars too distant to see one by one.
More than one-third of people cannot see the Milky Way from home because of light pollution.
Near the North Pole, an aurora is called the northern lights, or aurora borealis.
Near the South Pole, an aurora is called the southern lights, or aurora australis.
The Sun sends tiny particles and energy toward Earth, along with light and heat.
Earth's magnetic field shields our planet from most particles sent by the Sun.
Earth's magnetic field guides particles from the Sun toward the poles, helping make auroras.
In auroras, oxygen can glow green or red, while nitrogen can glow blue or purple.
Green is the most common color seen in an aurora.
High above Earth, glowing oxygen atoms can make red auroras.
Auroras usually appear in a ring-shaped area around each magnetic pole.
Large aurora-making magnetic storms are most common near the peak of an 11-year Sun cycle.
Auroras happen very high up. Measurements found none below about 70 km.
Stars twinkle because their light passes through shifting layers of Earth's atmosphere.
Stars look like tiny points, so moving air can easily disturb their light.
Planets usually twinkle much less than stars do.
A star near the horizon usually twinkles more than a star high overhead.
Temperature differences can change air density and make starlight twinkle.
The International Space Station circles Earth about once every 90 minutes.
The International Space Station makes about 16 trips around Earth each day.
The International Space Station is about 109 meters long, nearly a football field.
You can sometimes see the International Space Station crossing the sky at dawn or dusk.
The International Space Station orbits about 400 km above Earth.
Zodiacal light is a faint glow made when sunlight scatters from dust in the Solar System.
Zodiacal light can look like a faint triangle rising from the horizon.
Most dust that makes zodiacal light is thought to come from a group of comets.
The Bortle scale rates night skies from Class 1, the darkest, to Class 9, inner-city skies.
About 83 percent of the world's people live under light-polluted skies.
Skyglow is the bright haze over cities caused by too much artificial light at night.
Skyglow hides faint stars and galaxies by making the sky around them brighter.
Skyglow is the spread-out brightness of the night sky, not light from one object.
Dark-sky preserves protect remote places from light pollution.
Most visible meteors come from space rocks about the size of a grain of sand.
Meteors usually become visible about 75 to 120 km above Earth.
Most meteors glow for only about one second.
Meteor colors reveal materials inside them. Magnesium can glow blue-green.
Astronomers call a meteor brighter than any planet a fireball.
About 25 million meteoroids and bits of space debris enter Earth's atmosphere each day.
A satellite flare happens when a satellite briefly reflects sunlight toward an observer.
Bright flashes from a tumbling satellite are nearly impossible to predict accurately.
You can see Mercury, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn as points of light without a telescope.
Venus is the most noticeable planet and can shine brightly near sunrise or sunset.
Stars range in color from blue to red, but most look white when you look with only your eyes.
Airglow is faint light from Earth's atmosphere, so the night sky is never completely dark.
A meteoroid is a space rock. It can be as tiny as dust or as big as a small asteroid.
items.d: Dust grains, pebbles, and bigger rocks in space can all be meteoroids.
