items.t: A shooting star is not a star. It is a space rock burning in the air.
items.d: In space it is a meteoroid. The glowing streak is the meteor.

items.t: A meteor brighter than the planet Venus is called a fireball.
items.d: Venus is very bright. A fireball shines even brighter than that planet.

items.t: A meteor shower happens when Earth flies through dust a comet left behind.
items.d: Lots of streaks can flash on the same night, all from one dusty trail.

items.t: A space rock that survives the fall and lands is called a meteorite.
items.d: Meteor is the sky streak. Meteorite is the rock you could pick up.

items.t: Most meteorites people find are about pebble-sized to fist-sized.
items.d: Think of a small stone that fits in your hand.

items.t: Meteoroids zoom into Earth's air at tens of thousands of kilometers per hour.
items.d: They move so fast that the air heats them until they glow.

items.t: Usually less than 5 percent of a falling space rock reaches the ground.
items.d: The rest burns away high in the sky and shows up as a meteor.

items.t: Meteorites often have a thin, shiny crust formed when the outside melts.
items.d: This melted outer layer is called a fusion crust.

items.t: Every Perseid meteor is a tiny piece of the comet Swift-Tuttle.
items.d: A whole shower can be made of crumbs from a single comet.

items.t: The Perseid meteor shower peaks in mid-August, around August 12 to 13.
items.d: Those busy nights are the best time to look for Perseid streaks.

items.t: Perseid meteors race at about 59 kilometers, or 37 miles, per second.
items.d: About 59 kilometers each second, for 3,600 seconds, is about 212,400 kilometers an hour.

items.t: Perseid meteors look like they fly out of the constellation Perseus.
items.d: The shower gets its name from Perseus, the spot the streaks point back toward.

items.t: Comet Swift-Tuttle, which makes the Perseids, takes 133 years to orbit the Sun.
items.d: The comet sheds dust along its path, and Earth meets that dust every August.

items.t: The Geminid meteor shower comes from the asteroid 3200 Phaethon.
items.d: Most meteor showers come from comet dust. This December shower comes from a rocky asteroid.

items.t: Under perfect conditions, about 120 Geminid meteors can be seen in one hour.
items.d: They peak around December 13 to 14, and they often look yellow.

items.t: The Leonid shower peaks in mid-November and comes from comet Tempel-Tuttle.
items.d: About every 33 years, at least 1,000 Leonids can streak by in one hour.

items.t: A comet is mostly ice, covered with dark material.
items.d: Far from the Sun, it stays frozen, like a dirty snowball in space.

items.t: Comets are icy leftovers from when the solar system formed, about 4.6 billion years ago.
items.d: They have kept their ice since the time the planets were forming.

items.t: A comet's nucleus is often only several kilometers, a few miles, across.
items.d: The bright tail can stretch far, but the solid icy center stays small.

items.t: A comet's nucleus mixes icy chunks, frozen gases, and dust.
items.d: The dust is stuck in the ice, a bit like a frozen, crumbly snowball.

items.t: Near the Sun, a comet warms up and grows a fuzzy cloud called a coma.
items.d: That cloud is a thin atmosphere around the comet's icy center.

items.t: A comet grows two tails near the Sun: one of dust and one of gas.
items.d: The gas tail is also called an ion tail. Both show up as the comet warms.

items.t: Past Neptune, the Kuiper Belt is a disc of icy bodies where many comets live.
items.d: Comets with shorter orbits often begin in this belt.

items.t: A short-period comet takes less than 200 years to orbit the Sun once.
items.d: If one orbit takes longer than 200 years, it is a long-period comet.

items.t: The Oort Cloud is about 100,000 times farther from the Sun than Earth is.
items.d: Many comets with very long orbits come from this far-off region.

items.t: Some comets from the Oort Cloud take about 30 million years to orbit the Sun.
items.d: One trip around the Sun can last about 30 million of our years.

items.t: Some comets, called sungrazers, get so close to the Sun that they break apart.
items.d: A few fall into the Sun. Others evaporate in the heat.

items.t: Most asteroids orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter, in the main belt.
items.d: Mars is the fourth planet and Jupiter is the fifth, with this rocky belt between them.

items.t: Some asteroids are less than 10 meters, about 33 feet, across.
items.d: Next to a town, these would look tiny, but each one is still a real rocky world.

items.t: Every asteroid added together still weighs less than Earth's Moon.
items.d: The belt has a huge number of rocks, but the Moon is heavier than all of them.

items.t: Asteroids are rocky leftovers from the solar system, about 4.6 billion years old.
items.d: They are spare pieces from the time the Sun and planets formed.

items.t: Most asteroids are lumpy and uneven. Only a few are close to round.
items.d: They look more like potatoes than like smooth balls.

items.t: More than 150 asteroids have a small moon traveling with them.
items.d: The little moon orbits the asteroid, just as our Moon orbits Earth.

items.t: An estimated 1.1 to 1.9 million main belt asteroids are over 1 kilometer wide.
items.d: That total leaves out the smaller rocks. It counts only the wide ones.

items.t: C-type asteroids, also called chondrites, are the most common asteroids.
items.d: In a big sorting of asteroids, the C-type pile would be the biggest.

items.t: M-type asteroids are metallic and contain nickel and iron.
items.d: They are one of the three main types of asteroids.

items.t: OSIRIS-REx was the first U.S. mission to bring asteroid samples to Earth.
items.d: Samples from asteroid Bennu were delivered to Earth on September 24, 2023.

items.t: On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART hit the moon Dimorphos on purpose.
items.d: DART was a kinetic impactor, a craft sent to bump an asteroid and nudge its path.

items.t: Dimorphos is only about 160 meters, or 530 feet, across.
items.d: It orbits Didymos, a larger asteroid about 780 meters, or 2,560 feet, wide.

items.t: Meteor Crater in Arizona is about 1.2 kilometers wide and about 170 meters deep.
items.d: About 50,000 years ago, a nickel-iron meteorite about 50 meters wide made the hole.

items.t: Namibia's Hoba meteorite weighs over 60 tonnes and is the largest intact one known.
items.d: It is about 84 percent iron and about 16 percent nickel. It did not leave a crater.

items.t: Halley's Comet orbits the Sun about once every 76 Earth years.
items.d: The wait is so long that seeing this comet twice is rare.

items.t: Halley's Comet will next return in 2061, still on its 76-year path.
items.d: Kids who watch the sky now may be adults when it comes back.

items.t: Halley's nucleus is about 15 by 8 kilometers and shaped like a lumpy potato.
items.d: It is longer than it is wide, about 9.3 miles by 5 miles.

items.t: Bits of Halley's Comet make the Eta Aquarid meteor shower each May.
items.d: Earth meets the comet's dusty trail, and those bits burn as meteors.

items.t: Halley's Comet also makes the Orionid meteor shower each October.
items.d: One comet, two showers: Eta Aquarids in May and Orionids in October.

items.t: In July 2020, people could see comet NEOWISE by eye from a dark sky.
items.d: Binoculars made the tail easier to see. Its nucleus is about 5 kilometers across.

items.t: Comet Hale-Bopp was bright enough to see by eye for about 18 months.
items.d: People watched it without a telescope in 1996 and 1997.

items.t: Hale-Bopp's nucleus is about 60 kilometers across, huge for a comet.
items.d: A center this wide is unusually large. Most comet nuclei are much smaller.

items.t: A solar eclipse happens at new moon. A lunar eclipse happens at full moon.
items.d: The Moon lines up with the Sun and Earth in both cases.

items.t: During a total solar eclipse, the Sun's faint outer atmosphere, called the corona, becomes visible.
Regular sunglasses are not safe for looking at the Sun, even during an eclipse.
items.d: Use safe eclipse glasses whenever any bright part of the Sun is visible.

items.t: There are four kinds of solar eclipse: total, partial, annular and hybrid.
There are three kinds of lunar eclipse: total, partial and penumbral.
Eclipses can only happen in eclipse seasons. Each season lasts about 35 days.
It is always safe to watch a lunar eclipse with your eyes alone.
items.d: The Moon is only reflecting sunlight, so it is not too bright to look at.

items.t: In a total solar eclipse, the Moon fully covers the Sun and the sky goes dark for people in its shadow.
In an annular eclipse, the Moon is far from Earth and looks too small to cover the Sun. A bright ring is left.
In a partial solar eclipse, the Moon covers only part of the Sun, which can look like a crescent.
A hybrid solar eclipse changes between total and annular along its path.
items.d: Earth's curved surface changes whether the Moon fully covers the Sun.

items.t: Every lunar eclipse can be seen from the half of Earth where it is night.
In a partial lunar eclipse, the Moon moves through only part of Earth's darkest shadow, the umbra.
A penumbral lunar eclipse is a faint dimming of the Moon. It can be hard to notice.
In a total lunar eclipse, the Moon turns orange or red.
items.d: Sunlight bends through Earth's air to reach it, and blue light is scattered away.

items.t: The more dust or clouds in Earth's air during a lunar eclipse, the redder the Moon looks.
The red light on a totally eclipsed Moon is like every sunrise and sunset shining onto it at once.
An eclipse happens when a planet or moon blocks sunlight or moves into another object's shadow.
A total solar eclipse happens somewhere on Earth about every year and a half.
Any one place on Earth sees a total solar eclipse only about once every 375 years, on average.
We do not get eclipses every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted compared with Earth's orbit.
items.d: The Moon usually passes just above or below the lined-up spot.

items.t: In a solar eclipse, the Sun looks darker. In a lunar eclipse, the Moon looks darker.
Safe solar viewers should meet an international standard called ISO 12312-2.
items.d: Look for that label on eclipse glasses.

items.t: If your eclipse glasses are torn, scratched or damaged, throw them away.
A pinhole projector lets you watch an eclipse safely by showing the Sun's image on a surface.
items.d: You stand with your back to the Sun. Never look at the Sun through the hole.

items.t: A supermoon is a full moon that happens when the Moon is near its closest point to Earth.
items.d: That is about 363,000 km away.

items.t: The Moon's distance from Earth changes. Its closest is about 363,000 km and its farthest is about 405,000 km.
A supermoon can look up to 14 percent bigger than the smallest full moon of the year.
items.d: That is hard to notice just by looking.

items.t: A supermoon can look about 30 percent brighter than the faintest full moon of the year.
The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and also about 400 times farther away.
items.d: That is why they look about the same size in our sky.

items.t: The corona is normally hidden because the Sun's bright surface shines much more strongly.
The diamond ring effect can appear as totality starts or ends, when bright sunlight vanishes or returns.
Baily's beads are bright dots of sunlight shining through valleys on the Moon's edge just before totality.
Under today's conditions, totality cannot last more than about 7 minutes 32 seconds in one place.
Long ago, Chinese observers called a solar eclipse an eating of the Sun.
items.d: Their eclipse records go back to around 720 BC.

items.t: Observations of the 1919 total solar eclipse helped confirm Einstein's theory of general relativity.
In 1868, scientists studied an eclipse with spectroscopes and learned more about what the Sun is made of.
A total lunar eclipse can last up to nearly 107 minutes.
The umbra is the dark middle of Earth's shadow. The penumbra is the lighter outer part.
A total lunar eclipse is sometimes called a blood moon.
A saros is a cycle of similar eclipses that repeats about every 18 years and 11 days.
Ancient Greeks saw Earth's round shadow on the Moon and used it as a clue that Earth is round.
Equinoxes happen twice a year, around 20 March and 23 September.
At an equinox, day and night are about the same length, though not exactly equal.
Around an equinox, the Sun rises almost exactly in the east and sets almost exactly in the west.
The word solstice comes from Latin words meaning sun and to stand still.
Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees, and that tilt causes the seasons.
Transits of Venus come in pairs eight years apart, with very long gaps between pairs.
items.d: The last pair was in 2004 and 2012.

items.t: During a transit of Mercury, the planet looks like a tiny black dot moving across the Sun.
An occultation is when one object hides another from view by passing in front of it.
The Moon is about 384,400 km from Earth on average.
The Moon is less than one-third as wide as Earth.
The Moon has a radius of about 1,740 km.
Moon gravity is only one-sixth as strong as Earth's gravity.
The Moon moves about 3.8 cm farther from Earth each year.
In sunlight, the Moon can reach about 127 C. In darkness, it can fall to about -173 C.
Ancient lava filled the Moon's giant dark plains billions of years ago.
Tycho Crater is more than 85 km wide.
The Moon has a very thin layer of gases called an exosphere.
About 30 Earth-sized planets could fit between Earth and the Moon.
If Earth were the size of a nickel, the Moon would be about as big as a coffee bean.
A spacecraft first photographed the Moon's far side in 1959.
Water ice rests in some permanently shadowed places near the Moon's poles.
More than 105 robotic spacecraft have been launched to explore the Moon.
The Moon's far-side crust can be about 60 km thick.
The Moon has eight main phases, from new Moon through waning crescent.
One Moon orbit takes about 27.3 days, but new Moon to new Moon takes about 29.5 days.
The Sun always lights half the Moon. Its phases show us different amounts of that half.
Moonlight is sunlight reflected from the Moon's surface.
A full Moon rises around sunset and sets around sunrise.
A new Moon rises and sets with the Sun, but we cannot see it in the daytime sky.
A first quarter Moon rises around midday and sets around the middle of the night.
The Moon spins once during each orbit, so the same side always faces Earth.
Earthshine is sunlight that bounces from Earth and faintly lights the Moon's dark part.
The Moon seems to rock slightly. This motion is called libration.
The Moon does not change shape during the month. Only its sunlit view changes.
Most coastlines have two high tides and two low tides each day.
The Moon's gravity pulls hardest on the part of Earth closest to it, helping make tides.
The biggest tides happen near new and full Moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up.
Smaller neap tides happen around the first and last quarter Moon.
The Sun also helps make tides, but its tide-making force is a little less than half the Moon's.
Earth's gravity raises rock tides about 10 to 15 cm high on the Moon.
Earth has about 80 times as much mass as the Moon.
The leading idea says the Moon formed after a huge impact about 4.5 billion years ago.
The young Moon was once covered by a deep ocean of melted rock called magma.
Moon rocks and Earth rocks have almost matching kinds of oxygen atoms.
The South Pole-Aitken basin is more than 2,500 km wide.
The South Pole-Aitken basin lies on the far side and averages about 10 km deep.
The Moon's maria are dark plains made of hardened lava called basalt.
Mare means sea in Latin. Early astronomers mistook the Moon's dark patches for water.
The dark plains called maria cover about 16% of the Moon, mostly on the side facing Earth.
The Moon's dark basalt plains reflect less light than its brighter highlands.
The Moon's far side is not always dark. It receives sunlight just like the near side.
Almost all craters on the Moon were made by space rocks hitting its surface.
Moon craters wear away very slowly because the Moon has no wind or rain.
Over time, a slight wobble lets people on Earth see about 59% of the Moon.
A waxing crescent appears in the western evening sky.
Light takes about 1.3 seconds to travel from the Moon to Earth.
The Sun is a yellow dwarf star about 4.5 billion years old.
items.d: It has been shining for a very, very long time.

items.t: The Sun is about 150 million kilometers from Earth.
items.d: That is about 93 million miles away.

items.t: The Sun is about 100 times wider than Earth.
items.d: A row of about 100 Earths would match the Sun from side to side.

items.t: The Sun is the only star in our solar system.
items.d: Every planet here travels around this one star.

items.t: At its equator, the Sun spins once about every 25 Earth days.
items.d: Earth spins once a day. The Sun's middle spins much more slowly.

items.t: The Sun has no solid surface. It is a giant ball of plasma.
items.d: With no hard ground, there is nowhere to stand or land.

items.t: The Sun has no moons, but eight planets orbit it.
items.d: Earth is one of those planets, traveling around the Sun.

items.t: The Sun's corona is about 500,000 degrees Celsius or hotter.
items.d: It can reach a few million degrees, much hotter than the bright surface.

items.t: The Sun is about 1.4 million kilometers across.
items.d: From side to side, that is about 865,000 miles.

items.t: About 1.3 million Earths would fit inside the Sun.
items.d: That is how many Earths it would take to fill the Sun.

items.t: The Sun holds about 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass.
items.d: If the solar system weighed 1,000 grams, the Sun would be about 998 grams.

items.t: Sunspots look dark because they are cooler than the gas around them.
items.d: They are still extremely hot. They look dark only next to hotter gas.

items.t: Solar flares are the most powerful bursts in the solar system.
items.d: A flare is a sudden, huge release of energy from the Sun.

items.t: The Sun sends huge clouds of magnetized particles into space.
items.d: These giant clouds are called coronal mass ejections.

items.t: Spicules are grass-like jets of plasma rising from the Sun.
items.d: They can shoot up at about 97 kilometers per second (60 miles per second).

items.t: About every 11 years, the Sun's magnetic poles flip.
items.d: Its magnetic north and south swap their polarity.

items.t: The word corona means crown in Latin and in Spanish.
items.d: It names the crown-like glow around the Sun.

items.t: The Sun takes about 230 million years to orbit the Milky Way once.
items.d: One trip around our galaxy takes that long.

items.t: The Sun is what gives Earth its light and its warmth.
items.d: Living things on Earth rely on that light and heat.

items.t: It would take almost 1,000 Jupiters to fill up the Sun.
items.d: Our star is so big that even Jupiter is small beside it.

items.t: The Sun's core reaches about 15 million degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is about 27 million degrees Fahrenheit, hot enough to fuse atoms.

items.t: In the Sun's core, hydrogen atoms crash together and become helium.
items.d: They hit so hard that they join and form a new element.

items.t: The Sun is just one star among billions and billions of stars.
items.d: Clear nights show many stars, but space holds far more.

items.t: Solar wind from the Sun pushes against interstellar space.
items.d: Its charged particles travel billions of kilometers before reaching that boundary.

items.t: Solar flares are ranked A, B, C, M, and X.
items.d: Each higher rank has 10 times the energy of the rank below.

items.t: Light from a solar flare takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
items.d: We see the flare only after its light finishes the trip.

items.t: Earth's air and magnetic field shield people from flare rays.
items.d: On the ground, those rays do not physically affect us.

items.t: A strong solar flare can disturb radio messages.
items.d: For a while, some radios may not send or receive clearly.

items.t: The Sun is a giant ball of hydrogen and helium gas.
items.d: Those two gases are what our star is made of.

items.t: Auroras can glow green and red in the night sky.
items.d: They usually shine near the poles, but sometimes much farther away.

items.t: The fastest coronal mass ejections exceed 1.6 million kilometers per hour.
items.d: That is faster than 1 million miles per hour.

items.t: One coronal mass ejection can throw out billions of tonnes of material.
items.d: One cloud can carry that much material away from the Sun.

items.t: A fast Sun cloud aimed at Earth can arrive in as little as 15 hours.
items.d: Slower clouds can take several days to get here.

items.t: A Sun cloud that reaches Earth can light up auroras.
items.d: Those lights are the northern lights and the southern lights.

items.t: The dark heart of a sunspot is the umbra, and the rim is the penumbra.
items.d: The umbra is the darkest center. The penumbra is lighter around it.

items.t: Strong magnetic fields make sunspots less dense than nearby gas.
items.d: Less dense means the gas in the spot is thinner than the gas beside it.

items.t: Some groups of sunspots are many times the size of Earth.
items.d: A big group can dwarf our whole planet.

items.t: Sunspots can last from a few hours to several days.
items.d: A strong group of spots can last for months.

items.t: The number of sunspots rises and falls about every 11 years.
items.d: That pattern is called the solar cycle.

items.t: Solar maximum is the sunspot peak. Solar minimum is the quiet lull.
items.d: More spots appear at the peak. Very few appear in the lull.

items.t: You can make a simple sundial with a stick on flat ground.
items.d: The stick's shadow moves through the day and helps tell the time.

items.t: Active regions with fast-changing magnetism often produce flares.
items.d: They are also the most likely source of big plasma clouds.

items.t: The photosphere is the deepest layer of the Sun we can see directly.
items.d: Deeper layers stay hidden. This is the layer that shines out.

items.t: The photosphere is only about 400 kilometers thick.
items.d: It cools from about 6,200 degrees Celsius at the bottom to about 3,700 at the top.

items.t: In the chromosphere, the Sun gets hotter as you move farther out.
items.d: The heat rises from about 3,700 to about 7,700 degrees Celsius.

items.t: The Sun's transition region is a layer only about 100 kilometers thick.
items.d: Heat jumps from about 7,700 to about 500,000 degrees Celsius there.

items.t: The corona can be seen unaided only while the Sun is fully eclipsed.
items.d: Otherwise, astronomers use a coronagraph to view that outer glow.

items.t: Early telescopes used curved, clear pieces of glass called lenses to focus light.
items.d: Lenses bend light so faraway things look closer.

items.t: Most telescopes today use curved mirrors to gather light from the night sky.
The bigger a telescope's mirror or lens is, the more light it can gather.
items.d: More light means fainter stars become easier to see.

items.t: Telescope mirrors and lenses must have no spots, scratches, or other flaws.
Big glass lenses are heavy and hard to make. They are also hard to hold in the right place.
A mirror can be very thin, so big telescope mirrors can be lighter than big lenses.
A curved telescope mirror can form an upside-down image.
items.d: Look at your face in a spoon and you will see it upside down.

items.t: Thin mirrors can be lighter than thick lenses, so they are easier to launch into space.
items.d: That is one reason space telescopes use mirrors.

items.t: The first practical telescopes were invented in the Netherlands in the early 1600s. They used lenses.
The word "telescope" was coined in 1611.
The oldest known record of a telescope is a patent request from the Netherlands in 1608.
In 1668, Isaac Newton built the first practical telescope that used a mirror to focus light.
Refracting telescopes can't practically be made much wider than about 1 metre across.
items.d: Their big lenses would be too heavy and hard to hold.

items.t: The largest mirror telescopes have mirrors more than 10 metres across.
Earth's air blocks X-rays and gamma rays, so those telescopes must be high up or in space.
X-rays are very hard to focus. X-ray telescopes use ring-shaped mirrors that skim the rays at a shallow angle.
Linking several radio dishes together makes them work like one bigger telescope.
items.d: This is called an interferometer.

items.t: Radio waves can pass through Earth's air and through clouds of gas and dust in space.
The first telescope built just to catch radio waves started working in 1937.
Dutch spectacle maker Hans Lippershey tried to patent a telescope around 1608, but did not succeed.
In 1609, Galileo heard about the Dutch telescope and built his own version.
Galileo's best telescope made things look about 30 times bigger.
Galileo's telescope showed things the right way up. Kepler's design from 1611 showed them upside down.
Johannes Kepler designed a better telescope in 1611. It gave a much wider view of the sky.
An achromatic lens brings two colours of light, such as red and blue, into focus together.
items.d: This makes images sharper, with fewer coloured fringes.

items.t: Newton's telescope used a small flat mirror to bounce light out to the side of the tube for viewing.
A Cassegrain telescope bounces light off two mirrors. This gives a long focal length in a short tube.
A big mirror can be held up along its whole back. That is why mirrors can be made much bigger than lenses.
Early metal telescope mirrors reflected only about two-thirds of the light, and they tarnished easily.
Modern telescope mirrors get a very thin coat of aluminium, added in a vacuum.
Air wobbles can blur and shift a telescope's image. Adaptive optics helps fix this.
Adaptive optics uses a bendy mirror to cancel out the blur that Earth's air adds to starlight.
Some telescopes shine a laser into the sky to make an artificial star. It helps them measure air blur.
Adaptive optics checks the air's blurring again and again, every few thousandths of a second.
Karl Jansky first detected radio waves from space in 1932. They came from our Milky Way galaxy.
Grote Reber, an amateur, built the first dish-shaped radio telescope. It was 9 metres wide.
China's FAST radio dish is 500 metres wide. Its area is as big as about 30 football fields.
The Very Large Array in New Mexico links 27 dish telescopes together into one.
Radio telescopes can observe many space objects during the day as well as at night.
A curved radio dish bounces incoming radio waves to one spot above it, called the focus.
Radio waves from space are very weak. A cell phone signal is a billion billion times stronger.
In 7x50 binoculars, the 7 is how much they magnify. The 50 is the front lens width in millimetres.
Binoculars use prisms to turn the image the right way up.
A telescope's magnification is the main lens or mirror's focal length divided by the eyepiece's focal length.
Binoculars show a wider view of the sky than most telescopes, and they are easier to carry.
Bright city lights make faint stars hard to see, so stargazers often travel to dark places.
William Herschel discovered infrared light in 1800.
Space dust soaks up visible light and glows in infrared. Infrared telescopes can see that glow.
Water vapour in the air absorbs infrared, so infrared telescopes are built high up in very dry places.
The space shuttle Discovery placed Hubble in orbit in 1990.
Hubble orbits about 483 km above Earth, beyond the air that blurs telescope views.
Hubble travels around Earth about once every 95 minutes.
Hubble is about 13.2 m long and had a launch mass of about 10,800 kg.
Hubble's main mirror measures 2.4 m across.
Space shuttle astronauts visited Hubble five times to repair and improve it.
Hubble helped show that the expansion of the universe is not slowing down.
Hubble was the first telescope to directly measure an exoplanet's atmosphere.
items.d: An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star beyond our solar system.

items.t: Light from galaxy GN-z11 traveled about 13.4 billion years before Hubble observed it.
The Hubble Space Telescope is named after astronomer Edwin Hubble.
Hubble's main mirror was shaped incorrectly, so its first pictures looked blurry.
Astronauts corrected Hubble's blurry vision during a shuttle mission in 1993.
Hubble's Pillars of Creation image shows stars forming in the Eagle Nebula.
Astronomers used Hubble to discover Styx, a tiny moon of Pluto, in 2012.
Hubble made 342 exposures over ten days to create the Hubble Deep Field.
The Hubble Deep Field covered a tiny patch of sky.
items.d: It looked as small as a tennis ball viewed from 100 m away.

items.t: Almost all of the roughly 3,000 objects in the Hubble Deep Field are galaxies.
The Hubble Deep Field studied a small area in the constellation Ursa Major.
The James Webb Space Telescope launched on December 25, 2021.
Webb circles the Sun near a place called L2, about 1.5 million km from Earth.
Webb has a five-layer sunshield that blocks infrared heat from the Sun, Earth, and Moon.
Webb's main mirror is about 6.5 m across.
Webb's giant mirror is built from 18 lightweight beryllium pieces.
Webb's mirrors have a thin gold coating that helps them observe infrared light.
items.d: All that gold together has about the mass of a golf ball.

items.t: Webb's sunshield is about the size of a tennis court.
Webb operates at less than 50 degrees above absolute zero.
An Ariane 5 rocket carried Webb into space.
Webb's main mirror is about 2.75 times wider than Hubble's main mirror.
Webb is named after James E. Webb, who led NASA from 1961 to 1968.
Webb studies the era when the universe's first stars and galaxies formed.
items.d: This era began roughly 50 million years after the big bang.

items.t: Webb's infrared vision can reveal baby stars hidden inside clouds of dust.
The Chandra X-ray Observatory launched on July 23, 1999.
Chandra observes from space because Earth's atmosphere absorbs X-rays.
Chandra's long orbit carries it as far as about 139,000 km from Earth.
Chandra sees X-rays from very hot places in space.
items.d: It studies galaxy clusters and hot matter around black holes.

items.t: Chandra is named after astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar.
Chandra can see details eight times sharper than earlier X-ray telescopes could.
Chandra's telescope collects X-rays with four pairs of mirrors nested together.
Chandra's mirrors were polished until their surfaces were smooth to within a few atoms.
Chandra's X-ray mirrors look more like glass barrels than round dishes.
Kepler discovered more than 2,600 planets beyond our solar system.
Kepler found planets by watching for tiny dips in a star's brightness.
items.d: A dip can happen when a planet passes in front of its star.

items.t: Kepler watched about 150,000 stars in a patch of the constellation Cygnus.
NASA retired Kepler in 2018 after the spacecraft ran out of fuel.
Kepler was NASA's first mission able to find Earth-size planets in habitable zones.
items.d: A habitable zone is the region around a star where liquid water might exist.

items.t: Kepler used a photometer, an instrument that measured the brightness of stars.
Spitzer observed the universe in infrared light for more than 16 years.
Gaia observed about two billion stars and other objects in space.
items.d: That is only about 1 percent of the Milky Way's stars.

items.t: MUL.APIN is a Babylonian star guide written on two clay tablets.
items.d: A star guide is a list that helps you find stars in the night sky.

items.t: Babylonian astronomers found that lunar eclipses repeat in a cycle of about 18 years.
items.d: This repeating pattern is now called the Saros cycle.

items.t: The Babylonians gave 12 zodiac signs to stars along the Sun's path.
items.d: The Sun's path is called the ecliptic. It passes through those 12 signs.

items.t: The Babylonians divided the sky into 360 degrees. We still use that today.
items.d: A full circle has 360 degrees. They also used slices of 30 degrees.

items.t: Babylonian astronomers counted by 60s, not only by 10s.
items.d: In this number system, groups of 60 were especially useful.

items.t: A Babylonian clay tablet recorded Halley's Comet in 164 BC.
items.d: They pressed the note into clay, so the comet visit was not forgotten.

items.t: The Babylonians are the first known people with a working theory of the planets.
items.d: They studied how the planets move and wrote rules that matched the sky.

items.t: Theon of Alexandria wrote a detailed astrolabe guide about 1,600 years ago.
items.d: His book showed readers how to use the astrolabe, piece by piece.

items.t: The rete is the turning part of an astrolabe that carries pointers for stars.
items.d: As the rete turns, its pointers show where bright stars appear on the astrolabe.

items.t: Sailors used a simplified mariner's astrolabe, built for rough seas.
items.d: Waves rock a ship. This kind was made so sailors could still measure the sky.

items.t: Aryabhata said Earth is round and turns on its axis once each day.
items.d: Because Earth turns, the Sun seems to rise in the morning and set at night.

items.t: Aryabhata explained solar and lunar eclipses in a scientific way.
items.d: He explained how the Moon can hide the Sun and how Earth's shadow can darken the Moon.

items.t: The Almagest is the only complete ancient astronomy treatise that still survives.
items.d: Ptolemy gathered many ancient ideas about the sky into this large work.

items.t: In Ptolemy's model, Earth sat at the center and planets circled around it.
items.d: Geo means Earth. A geocentric model puts Earth in the middle of the sky.

items.t: The Almagest names 48 constellations, the roots of many we use now.
items.d: A constellation is a picture people draw by linking stars in the sky.

items.t: In 964, al-Sufi's Book of Fixed Stars described 48 constellations.
items.d: He wrote about each star group and the stars that sit inside it.

items.t: In 964, al-Sufi made the earliest known recorded observation of the Andromeda Galaxy.
items.d: He described the faint object that we now know is a galaxy.

items.t: In 1901, the Antikythera mechanism was found in the sea near Greece.
items.d: It was named for the island of Antikythera, where the ship was found.

items.t: People built the Antikythera mechanism in the 2nd century BC.
items.d: That is more than 2,000 years ago, yet its bronze gears were still there.

items.t: Its largest gear is about 13 cm wide and originally had 223 teeth.
items.d: 13 cm is about the width of a small plate, covered in tiny teeth.

items.t: It could predict where sky objects would be, and eclipses, many years ahead.
items.d: Turning its dials showed the places of the Sun and Moon years later.

items.t: Eratosthenes is the first known person to measure around the whole Earth.
items.d: Around the whole Earth means the circumference, one full loop of the planet.

items.t: On the summer solstice, noon sunlight shone straight down a well in Syene.
items.d: The Sun was exactly overhead, so its rays reached the bottom of the well.

items.t: At Alexandria the shadow angle was about 7.2 degrees, or 1/50 of a circle.
items.d: A circle is 360 degrees. 360 divided by 50 is 7.2, so the angle is 1/50.

items.t: Alexandria and Syene were said to be about 5,000 stadia apart.
items.d: A stadion is an old length unit. He used that distance to size the Earth.

items.t: Aristarchus was the first known person to place the Sun at the center.
items.d: In his idea, Earth and the other planets travel around the Sun.

items.t: Aristarchus estimated the sizes of the Sun and Moon compared with Earth.
items.d: He tried to find how many Earths would fit across the Sun and the Moon.

items.t: Stonehenge is lined up with the sunrise on the summer solstice.
items.d: Stand there on that morning, and you are looking toward the rising Sun.

items.t: Building at Stonehenge started about 3100 BC and lasted until about 1600 BC.
items.d: People kept working on the stone circle for about 1,500 years.

items.t: Stonehenge's bluestones were brought from Wales, about 240 km away.
items.d: They came from the Preseli Hills, about 240 km (150 miles) from the circle.

items.t: Chinese astronomers recorded about 1,600 eclipses, starting in 750 BCE.
items.d: BCE means before year 1. They noted solar eclipses and lunar eclipses.

items.t: Chinese sky records tell of guest stars, new lights among the fixed stars.
items.d: A guest star was usually a comet, or a star that suddenly looked much brighter.

items.t: Chinese astronomers saw a supernova in 1054. It left behind the Crab Nebula.
items.d: They recorded a new bright light. Its expanding remains form the Crab Nebula.

items.t: Su Song finished a large sky clock tower in 1092, with an armillary sphere.
items.d: An armillary sphere is a set of rings that shows how the sky turns.

items.t: China's 28 lunar mansions appear on Shang oracle bones found at Anyang.
items.d: Each mansion is a part of the sky that the Moon visits during the month.

items.t: Maya astronomers carefully followed the repeating cycles of Venus.
items.d: They watched when Venus appeared and wrote the pattern down.

items.t: The Dresden Codex is a Maya book used as an astronomy almanac.
items.d: An almanac is a lookup book. This one listed sky events to watch for.

items.t: A table in the Dresden Codex marked dates when solar and lunar eclipses were possible.
items.d: It warned readers about days when an eclipse might happen.

items.t: Egyptians used the rising of Sirius to mark the start of the Nile flood.
items.d: That star's return was a key date for setting their yearly calendar.

items.t: A 365-day calendar was already in use at the start of Egyptian history.
items.d: They counted 365 days in a year so they could plan the seasons ahead.

items.t: Hipparchus is famous for finding the precession of the equinoxes.
items.d: The equinox point slowly shifts against the stars, a tiny bit each year.

items.t: Hipparchus made the first known full star list from the Western world.
items.d: His catalogue gave each star a place, so others could find it again.

items.t: Hipparchus is believed to have ranked stars from 1, brightest, to 6, faintest.
items.d: A 1 marked a bright star. A 6 marked a star that was just visible.

items.t: In 1420, Prince Ulugh Beg, an astronomer, founded a large observatory in Samarkand.
items.d: He studied the sky himself. The observatory was his place for measuring it.

items.t: The stars Aldebaran, Altair, and Deneb still use their Arabic names.
items.d: Astronomers long ago named them, and sky maps kept those old names.

items.t: Al-Khwarizmi's 830 sky tables tracked the Sun, the Moon, and the planets.
items.d: The book is called the Zij al-Sindhind. A zij is a set of sky tables.

items.t: The Nebra sky disc is bronze inlaid with gold, from about 1800 to 1600 BC.
items.d: Gold shapes set into the bronze show things people saw in the sky.

items.t: A group of seven stars on the Nebra disc is read as the Pleiades.
items.d: The Pleiades are a tight cluster of stars that people have watched for ages.

items.t: The Vedanga Jyotisha is the oldest known Indian astronomy text.
items.d: It is dated to about 1400 to 1200 BCE, more than 3,000 years ago.

items.t: Copernicus said the Sun, not Earth, sits at the center of the universe.
items.d: His idea changed how people pictured the sky.

items.t: Nicolaus Copernicus was born in 1473 in the city now called Toruń.
items.d: At the time, the city was called Thorn.

items.t: Copernicus's big book on the heavens came out in 1543, just before he died.
items.d: It was called De revolutionibus orbium coelestium.

items.t: Copernicus started the Copernican Revolution, a huge change in how people understood the universe.
An ancient Greek named Aristarchus suggested a Sun-centered universe about 1,800 years before Copernicus.
items.d: Good ideas can wait a very long time.

items.t: Copernicus began university in Kraków together with his brother Andrew.
Tycho Brahe was born in Denmark in 1546.
items.d: He grew up to be a famous star watcher.

items.t: In 1572, Tycho saw a bright star appear where none had been seen before.
items.d: It became brighter than every other star and planet in the sky.

items.t: Tycho is often called the greatest astronomer before the telescope.
items.d: He measured the sky with his eyes and special tools, without a telescope.

items.t: The king of Denmark offered Tycho the island of Hven so he could build an observatory.
Tycho named his castle observatory Uraniborg, after Urania, the muse of astronomy.
Tycho imagined the Sun going around Earth while the other planets go around the Sun.
items.d: It was a mix of the old and new ideas.

items.t: Johannes Kepler was born in 1571 in Weil der Stadt, in what is now Germany.
Kepler is best known for his three laws of planetary motion.
items.d: They describe how planets travel around the Sun.

items.t: Kepler worked out his laws by studying Tycho Brahe's careful observations of Mars.
Kepler made the Rudolphine Tables, lists of where stars and planets would be.
items.d: They were made to replace older, less accurate tables.

items.t: In October 1604 Kepler watched a bright new star appear in the evening sky.
Kepler wrote Somnium, a story about a fantastic trip to the Moon.
items.d: It is an early example of science fiction.

items.t: Kepler's book Harmonice Mundi was published in 1619.
Galileo was born in Pisa in 1564.
items.d: He grew up to use the telescope in a brand new way.

items.t: Galileo built an improved telescope and found Jupiter's four biggest moons.
Galileo saw that Venus has phases, just like our Moon.
items.d: He saw it change shape through his telescope.

items.t: Through his telescope, Galileo saw mountains and craters on the Moon.
Galileo studied sunspots, the dark spots on the Sun.
items.d: Never look at the Sun without proper eye protection.

items.t: Galileo noticed that a pendulum keeps the same beat even when it swings a little wider or narrower.
Galileo saw that the Milky Way is made of a huge number of stars packed close together.
items.d: From far away, they look like a glowing cloud.

items.t: The Galilean moons were the first moons found anywhere beyond Earth.
Ganymede, one of Galileo's moons, is the biggest moon in the solar system.
items.d: It is even bigger than the planet Mercury.

items.t: Io, another moon Galileo found, is the most volcanically active world in the solar system.
Isaac Newton was born at Woolsthorpe Manor, a small hamlet in Lincolnshire, England.
Newton's famous book, the Principia, was first published in 1687.
Newton figured out the laws of motion and the law of universal gravity.
Newton used gravity math to explain Kepler's laws of planet motion.
Newton built the first reflecting telescope, which uses a mirror instead of a lens.
Newton showed that a prism splits white light into the colors of a rainbow.
Newton helped invent calculus, a kind of math for studying things that change.
Newton ran the Royal Mint and made British coins more accurate and safer.
Newton was president of the Royal Society from 1703 to 1727.
Edmond Halley mapped the stars of the southern sky.
Halley helped pay to print Newton's great book, the Principia.
Halley saw that watching Venus cross the Sun could help measure distances in space.
Halley once dived 18 meters deep in the River Thames using a diving bell.
Halley's Comet takes about 76 years to go around the Sun.
Halley's Comet will come back in 2061.
Edmond Halley correctly predicted that a comet would return in 1758.
items.d: That comet is now named after him.

items.t: Halley's Comet was last seen from Earth in 1986.
Dust from Halley's Comet makes two meteor showers each year, in May and October.
items.d: They are the Eta Aquarids and the Orionids.

items.t: William Herschel found the planet Uranus on 13 March 1781.
items.d: It was the first planet discovered since ancient times.

items.t: The Hubble Space Telescope was deployed by the space shuttle Discovery in 1990.
Hubble orbits about 483 km above Earth.
items.d: That is about 300 miles above Earth.

items.t: Hubble's main mirror is 2.4 metres across.
items.d: That is 94.5 inches across.

items.t: Hubble travels around Earth at about 27,000 km per hour.
Hubble discovered moons around Pluto and watched a comet hit Jupiter.
Hubble's first pictures were blurry. Astronauts added corrective optics in 1993.
items.d: The new optics helped Hubble make sharp pictures.

items.t: Astronauts flew five missions to service Hubble from 1993 to 2009.
Cecilia Payne showed that stars are made mainly of hydrogen and helium.
In 1925, Cecilia Payne earned Radcliffe College's first astronomy PhD.
An astronomer first doubted Payne's hydrogen result, then later reached the same answer.
In 1956, Payne-Gaposchkin was the first woman promoted to full professor within Harvard Arts and Sciences.
A talk about a 1919 eclipse expedition inspired Cecilia Payne to study astronomy.
Henrietta Leavitt identified 1,777 variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds.
items.d: Variable stars change in brightness over time.

items.t: Leavitt found that brighter Cepheid stars pulse more slowly than dimmer ones.
Leavitt's discovery made Cepheid stars useful for measuring distances to other galaxies.
items.d: Their pulse rate helps astronomers work out their true brightness.

items.t: Henrietta Leavitt was deaf and worked as a human computer at Harvard Observatory.
items.d: A human computer studied information and performed calculations.

items.t: Vera Rubin found that stars near a spiral galaxy's edge orbit about as fast as stars nearer its centre.
Rubin's galaxy studies gave strong evidence for dark matter, mass that cannot be seen directly.
Astronomer Vera Rubin worked for years with instrument maker Kent Ford.
items.d: Their tools helped them measure how fast stars orbit in galaxies.

items.t: In 2019, a telescope was renamed the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.
In 1967, student Jocelyn Bell spotted an odd mark on chart paper. It was the first known pulsar.
The first pulsar signal was nicknamed LGM-1. It actually came from a spinning neutron star.
In 2018, Jocelyn Bell Burnell gave her entire $3 million prize to help more students study physics.
At age 19, Chandrasekhar calculated a white dwarf's mass limit during a voyage to England.
items.d: The limit is about 1.4 times the Sun's mass.

items.t: Chandrasekhar shared the 1983 Nobel Prize for studying how stars are built and change.
NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory is named after astronomer Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar.
Carl Sagan helped create the 13-part TV series Cosmos in 1980.
items.d: It introduced astronomy to hundreds of millions of viewers.

items.t: Carl Sagan urged NASA to take the Pale Blue Dot photo of Earth from about 6 billion km away.
items.d: In the picture, our whole planet looks like a tiny speck.

items.t: Carl Sagan helped choose the sounds and images placed on the Voyager Golden Record in 1977.
Sagan's research helped show why Venus is extremely hot.
items.d: A runaway greenhouse effect traps a great deal of heat there.

items.t: Katherine Johnson graduated from college at age 18 with degrees in mathematics and French.
Katherine Johnson calculated the path for Alan Shepard's 1961 spaceflight.
items.d: Shepard became the first American to travel into space.

items.t: John Glenn asked Katherine Johnson to check a computer's calculations before his orbital flight.
Katherine Johnson's backup charts helped guide Apollo 13 safely home in 1970.
In 1924, Edwin Hubble found Cepheid stars in Andromeda and showed it lies beyond the Milky Way.
In 1929, Hubble showed that farther galaxies move away faster.
items.d: This relationship is evidence that the universe is expanding.

items.t: Edwin Hubble created a system for classifying galaxies that astronomers still use.
In 1927, Georges Lemaitre argued that galaxies moving apart show the universe is expanding.
Lemaitre's 1931 primeval atom idea became the first form of the Big Bang theory.
Webb studies infrared light and has a five-layer sunshield.
items.d: The shield protects the telescope from heat and infrared radiation.

items.t: Annie Jump Cannon arranged star types as O, B, A, F, G, K, M. Astronomers still use this order.
Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930 at age 24 using a blink comparator.
items.d: The device helped him compare pictures of the night sky.

items.t: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background in 1964.
Cosmic microwave background light was released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
items.d: It comes from when the young universe first became transparent.

items.t: LIGO first detected gravitational waves in 2015 from two merging black holes.
items.d: The waves had travelled about 1.3 billion light-years.

items.t: In 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced a planet orbiting a Sun-like star.
items.d: 51 Pegasi b circles its star in about 4.2 days.

items.t: Astronomers published the first picture of a black hole, called M87*, in 2019.
A light-year is how far light travels in one Earth year.
items.d: It measures distance, even though the name sounds like a time.

items.t: One light-year is about 9 trillion kilometres.
items.d: That is about 6 trillion miles, a huge distance even for light.

items.t: Sunlight takes about 8.3 minutes to reach us.
items.d: We see the Sun as it was 8.3 minutes ago.

items.t: The nearest large galaxy, Andromeda, is about 2.5 million light-years away.
items.d: Light from Andromeda takes about 2.5 million years to arrive.

items.t: Violet light waves are the shortest we can see. Red are the longest.
items.d: Violet is about 380 nanometres, a tiny length. Red is about 700.

items.t: Each colour in a rainbow is a different wavelength of light.
items.d: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet are different waves.

items.t: Hotter objects shine in shorter waves, so their colour changes.
items.d: As something heats up, the light it gives off shifts colour.

items.t: Light's spectrum runs from long radio waves to short gamma rays.
items.d: Our eyes see only a small part of this huge range of light.

items.t: One parsec is about 3.26 light-years.
items.d: Ten parsecs is about 32.6 light-years, because 10 times 3.26 is 32.6.

items.t: The Moon drifts about 3.8 centimetres farther from Earth each year.
items.d: Scientists time laser pulses that bounce off mirrors on the Moon.

items.t: Light moving away from us gets stretched. That is called redshift.
items.d: Stretching makes the light waves longer than they started.

items.t: Light moving toward us gets squeezed. That is called blueshift.
items.d: Squeezing makes the light waves shorter than they started.

items.t: As space expands, light from far galaxies is stretched redder.
items.d: Astronomers call this stretch cosmological redshift.

items.t: A bigger redshift means the light has travelled farther.
items.d: More redshift means a longer trip for that galaxy's light.

items.t: On the largest scales, farther galaxies move away faster.
items.d: That overall pattern is called Hubble's law.

items.t: Hubble's law was the first clear sign the universe is expanding.
items.d: Edwin Hubble published the key galaxy observations in 1929.

items.t: Parallax looks biggest in views taken about six months apart.
items.d: Earth is then on opposite sides of its orbit around the Sun.

items.t: The farther a star is, the smaller its parallax shift.
items.d: A nearby star seems to jump more as Earth moves around the Sun.

items.t: In 1838, Friedrich Bessel measured the parallax of 61 Cygni.
items.d: He used that tiny sky shift to work out the star's distance.

items.t: Parallax is a nearby thing seeming to shift against far ones.
items.d: Hold a thumb out and switch eyes. It hops. Stars do that too.

items.t: Right ascension and declination are sky longitude and latitude.
items.d: Together they give every sky point a steady map address.

items.t: One hour of right ascension equals 15 degrees.
items.d: Two hours equal 30 degrees, because 2 times 15 is 30.

items.t: An astronomical unit is about the average Earth-Sun distance.
items.d: It is defined as exactly 149,597,870,700 metres.

items.t: In empty space, light moves at exactly 299,792,458 metres a second.
items.d: That rounds to about 300,000 kilometres per second.

items.t: No signal or energy can travel faster than light in empty space.
items.d: Light speed is the limit for carrying news across space.

items.t: In 1676, Ole Romer showed that light takes time to travel.
items.d: He learned this by watching Jupiter's moon Io.

items.t: The Milky Way galaxy is about 100,000 light-years across.
items.d: Even light would take about 100,000 years to cross it.

items.t: Astronomers use a ladder of methods to measure space distances.
items.d: Each step is checked against the method from the step before.

items.t: A standard candle is an object whose true brightness is known.
items.d: Compare that with how bright it looks, and you get distance.

items.t: Henrietta Leavitt linked a Cepheid's pulse rate to brightness.
items.d: Time the pulses, and you learn how bright the star truly is.

items.t: A galaxy cluster can bend passing light, like a giant lens.
items.d: Astronomers call this effect a gravitational lens.

items.t: A perfect gravity lens can make a distant light look like a ring.
items.d: That bright circle is called an Einstein ring.

items.t: Eratosthenes measured Earth's size using shadows in two cities.
items.d: On his measuring day, Syene had no shadow. In Alexandria the shadow angle was about 7.2 degrees.

items.t: In 1919, eclipse teams tested whether gravity bends starlight.
items.d: Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson led those observations.

items.t: A moving clock is measured to tick slower than a resting clock.
items.d: To a resting watcher, the moving clock runs slow.

items.t: In 1971, atomic clocks flew around Earth to test relativity.
items.d: Hafele and Keating carried them east and west on airliners.

items.t: In empty space, everyone measures the same speed of light.
items.d: Move fast or sit still, and light still passes at that speed.

items.t: Gravity is mass bending space and time.
items.d: The bigger the mass, the more it bends space and time.

items.t: GPS has to include special relativity to help us navigate.
items.d: Special relativity is part of how those satellites guide us.

items.t: Helium was first seen in 1868 as a yellow line in sunlight.
items.d: Jules Janssen saw it during a total solar eclipse in India.

items.t: Helium was first trapped on Earth in 1895 by William Ramsay.
items.d: That was about 27 years after the yellow line was seen in the Sun.

items.t: A star's spectrum can reveal its ingredients and temperature.
items.d: Splitting the starlight shows which elements are in the star.

items.t: Dark lines in the Sun's rainbow come from absorbing elements.
items.d: Kirchhoff and Bunsen matched those lines to lab elements.

items.t: On the magnitude scale, brighter stars have smaller numbers.
items.d: Magnitude 1 is exactly 100 times brighter than magnitude 6.

items.t: A fist held at arm's length covers about 10 degrees of sky.
items.d: You can use that fist to roughly measure spaces between stars.

items.t: The Sun and the Moon look about the same size in our sky.
items.d: Their angular size, the patch of sky they cover, is about equal.

items.t: The Sun is a star.
items.d: It looks much bigger than other stars because it is much closer to Earth.

items.t: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
items.d: In empty space, light travels about 300,000 kilometers in one second.

items.t: Earth takes about a year to go around the Sun.
items.d: Earth spins as it travels, so different places get daylight at different times.

items.t: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight.
items.d: As the Moon goes around Earth, we see different amounts of its sunny side.

items.t: The Moon spins once in about the same time it takes to go around Earth.
items.d: That is why we see nearly the same side of the Moon from Earth all the time.

items.t: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks some of the Sun's light from reaching Earth.
items.d: People in the Moon's shadow can see the Sun partly or fully covered.

items.t: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.
items.d: It takes about 88 Earth days to go around the Sun once.

items.t: Venus takes longer to spin once than it takes to go around the Sun.
items.d: One spin takes about 243 Earth days. One trip around the Sun takes about 225.

items.t: Mars owes much of its red color to rusty dust.
items.d: Some of the iron in its rocks and dust has reacted with oxygen, like rust on an old bike.

items.t: Mars has two small moons.
items.d: Their names are Phobos and Deimos.

items.t: Jupiter is the biggest planet in our solar system.
items.d: The Great Red Spot you can see in pictures of Jupiter is a huge storm.

items.t: Saturn's rings are made mostly of pieces of ice.
items.d: The pieces stay in motion, circling Saturn.

items.t: Uranus spins almost on its side.
items.d: Picture a spinning top that keeps spinning while tipped almost all the way over.

items.t: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to circle the Sun.
items.d: It is the farthest of the eight planets from the Sun.

items.t: We live in a galaxy called the Milky Way.
items.d: A galaxy is a huge group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.

items.t: The eight planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
items.d: Earth is the third planet in that line.

items.t: Our solar system is the Sun and everything that travels around it.
items.d: That includes eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and icy objects.

items.t: The Sun and the planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
items.d: They grew inside a spinning cloud of gas and dust.

items.t: Earth's average distance from the Sun is about 150 million kilometers.
items.d: Nonstop at 100 kilometers per hour, the drive would take more than 170 years.

items.t: If the Sun were a basketball, Earth would be a tiny seed about 25 meters away.
items.d: On this model, the Moon is a speck about 7 centimeters from Earth.

items.t: The four planets closest to the Sun are rocky worlds.
items.d: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars all have solid ground.

items.t: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are giant planets.
items.d: They are much bigger than Earth and have no solid ground to stand on.

items.t: Jupiter and Saturn are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
items.d: These light gases are the main ingredients of those two giant planets.

items.t: The Sun holds more than 99 percent of the solar system's material.
items.d: All the planets and moons together are only a small share.

items.t: So far, Earth is the only place we know that has life.
items.d: Spacecraft look for water and chemical clues, but they have not found living things elsewhere.

items.t: About 109 Earths could fit side by side across the Sun.
items.d: The Sun is about 1.4 million kilometers across.

items.t: The Sun has about 1.3 million times Earth's volume.
items.d: Volume tells how much space something takes up.

items.t: Deep in the Sun, hydrogen nuclei join to form helium and release energy.
items.d: That energy eventually reaches us as light and heat.

items.t: The Sun's surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius.
items.d: The core is far hotter, about 15 million degrees Celsius.

items.t: Sunspots are darker patches on the Sun.
items.d: They are cooler patches linked to the Sun's magnetism, but they are still very hot.

items.t: The Sun blows a stream of particles called the solar wind.
items.d: These particles stream far past the planets. Some help create auroras on Earth.

items.t: Earth's seasons happen because the planet is tilted.
items.d: The tilt is about 23.5 degrees. The half leaning toward the Sun has summer.

items.t: Earth is closest to the Sun in January.
items.d: It is farthest in July. The difference is small and does not cause the seasons.

items.t: Earth has a magnetic field that reaches far into space.
items.d: Compass needles line up with it. It also guides many particles from the Sun.

items.t: Auroras are colorful lights in the sky near Earth's poles.
items.d: They appear when particles from space hit gases high in the air. Green is the most common color.

items.t: From space, Earth looks mostly blue, with white clouds.
items.d: Oceans cover most of the surface, and clouds swirl above green and brown land.

items.t: Some Mars rovers were lowered by a rocket platform.
items.d: After a parachute slowed them, the platform hovered and set the rover down on cables.

items.t: Mercury is the smallest of the eight planets.
items.d: It is about 40 percent wider than Earth's Moon.

items.t: From sunrise to sunrise on Mercury takes about 176 Earth days.
items.d: Daylight lasts about 88 Earth days, then night lasts about 88 more.

items.t: Mercury has almost no air to hold in heat.
items.d: Daytime can reach about 430 degrees Celsius. Night can drop to about minus 180.

items.t: Some deep craters at Mercury's poles hold water ice.
items.d: Their floors never get sunlight, so the ice can stay frozen.

items.t: Venus is almost the same size as Earth.
items.d: It is only a little smaller, but a thick blanket of air makes it very different.

items.t: Venus is the hottest planet, hotter even than Mercury.
items.d: Thick carbon dioxide air traps heat. The surface is about 460 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Air pressure on Venus is about 90 times the pressure on Earth.
items.d: The air is so heavy that a spacecraft needs to be very strong to work there.

items.t: Venus spins in the opposite direction from Earth.
items.d: Because of that backward spin, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.

items.t: Venus is the brightest planet in our sky.
items.d: People call it the Morning Star or the Evening Star, but it is a planet, not a star.

items.t: Thick clouds hide the rocky surface of Venus.
items.d: Spacecraft used radar, which can see through clouds, to map the ground.

items.t: Mars takes about 687 Earth days to go around the Sun.
items.d: One Earth year is about 365 days, so Mars takes almost two Earth years.

items.t: A day on Mars is only a little longer than a day on Earth.
items.d: It lasts about 24 hours and 37 minutes.

items.t: Mars has a thin atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide.
items.d: Its pressure is under one hundredth of Earth's, far too thin to breathe.

items.t: Mars is usually very cold.
items.d: A typical temperature is about minus 60 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Gravity on Mars is about 38 percent as strong as on Earth.
items.d: An object would feel about 38 percent as heavy on Mars as it does on Earth.

items.t: Mars has ice caps at both poles.
items.d: They contain frozen water and frozen carbon dioxide, also called dry ice.

items.t: Mars has dry riverbeds and old lake bottoms.
items.d: They show that liquid water flowed there a long time ago.

items.t: Dust storms on Mars can grow huge.
items.d: Some spread across much of the planet and hide the surface for weeks.

items.t: Sunsets on Mars can look blue.
items.d: Fine dust scatters light so the glow around the setting Sun looks blue.

items.t: The biggest volcano in the solar system is on Mars.
items.d: Olympus Mons is more than twice as tall as Mount Everest and hundreds of kilometers wide.

items.t: Mars has a canyon system thousands of kilometers long.
items.d: Valles Marineris is about 4,000 kilometers long, far longer than the Grand Canyon.

items.t: Phobos races around Mars in about 8 hours.
items.d: It moves so fast that, from Mars, it rises in the west and sets in the east.

items.t: Jupiter spins so fast that its day lasts about 10 hours.
items.d: The quick spin makes Jupiter a little wider around the middle than from top to bottom.

items.t: Jupiter's stripes are bands of clouds.
items.d: Neighboring bands blow in opposite directions in very strong winds.

items.t: At Jupiter's cloud tops, gravity is about 2.5 times Earth's.
items.d: An object there would feel about 2.5 times as heavy as it does on Earth.

items.t: Jupiter's four biggest moons were discovered in 1610.
items.d: Galileo Galilei found Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto with a telescope.

items.t: Ganymede is the biggest moon in the solar system.
items.d: This moon of Jupiter is wider than the planet Mercury.

items.t: Two Voyager spacecraft left Earth in 1977 to visit the giant planets.
items.d: Each one carries a disk of sounds and pictures, a greeting from Earth.

items.t: Io, a moon of Jupiter, has many active volcanoes.
items.d: Jupiter's gravity squeezes Io as it orbits, heating the inside until rock melts.

items.t: Europa's surface is a cracked shell of ice.
items.d: The cracks and magnetic clues are strong signs of a salty ocean under the ice.

items.t: Saturn's average density is less than the density of water.
items.d: Its average density is about 70 percent of water's.

items.t: Saturn's rings are very wide but amazingly thin.
items.d: They stretch tens of thousands of kilometers, yet many parts are only about 10 meters thick.

items.t: A giant six-sided cloud pattern surrounds Saturn's north pole.
items.d: Strong winds around the pole help form this unusual shape.

items.t: Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere.
items.d: Its air is mostly nitrogen. It is so cold that methane, a gas on Earth, forms lakes.

items.t: Enceladus shoots jets of water ice into space.
items.d: A spacecraft flew through the spray and found water vapor and ice grains.

items.t: A probe named Huygens landed on Titan in 2005.
items.d: It touched down on Saturn's largest moon and sent photos back from the surface.

items.t: Uranus takes about 84 Earth years to orbit the Sun.
items.d: One year on Uranus lasts about as long as 84 years on Earth.

items.t: Methane gas makes Uranus and Neptune look blue.
items.d: Methane soaks up red light, so the light that bounces back looks blue or blue-green.

items.t: Neptune has some of the fastest winds in the solar system.
items.d: Those winds can blow at more than 1,000 kilometers per hour.

items.t: Triton orbits Neptune backward.
items.d: It circles opposite Neptune's spin. Its surface is colder than minus 200 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Pluto is a dwarf planet, smaller than Earth's Moon.
items.d: It usually orbits beyond Neptune. It shares that icy region with many other objects.

items.t: Pluto takes about 248 Earth years to go around the Sun.
items.d: Earth goes around the Sun 248 times while Pluto goes around once.

items.t: Pluto has five known moons.
items.d: The biggest, Charon, is so large that they both orbit a point in the space between them.

items.t: A spacecraft flew past Pluto in 2015.
items.d: New Horizons saw icy mountains, a bright heart-shaped region and a plain of nitrogen ice.

items.t: Ceres is a dwarf planet in the asteroid belt.
items.d: It orbits between Mars and Jupiter and is the largest object there.

items.t: The asteroid belt is mostly empty space.
items.d: The rocks are far apart. Together they hold much less material than the Moon.

items.t: Some asteroids share Jupiter's path around the Sun.
items.d: Called Trojans, they travel in groups ahead of Jupiter and behind it.

items.t: Spacecraft have brought pieces of asteroids back to Earth.
items.d: Scientists study those old rocks to learn what the planets formed from.

items.t: The Moon is about 384,000 kilometers from Earth.
items.d: At 100 kilometers per hour, nonstop, the trip would take about 160 days.

items.t: The Moon is about one quarter as wide as Earth.
items.d: Earth is about 13,000 kilometers across, and the Moon is about 3,500.

items.t: Gravity on the Moon is about one sixth as strong as on Earth.
items.d: An object would feel about one sixth as heavy on the Moon as it does on Earth.

items.t: The Moon has almost no air.
items.d: Without air, there is nothing to breathe, so astronauts carry oxygen in their suits.

items.t: Daylight on the Moon lasts about two weeks.
items.d: Night lasts about two weeks too. A full day there is about as long as a month on Earth.

items.t: The far side of the Moon is not always dark.
items.d: It gets two weeks of sunshine, just like the side that faces Earth. We just cannot see it from here.

items.t: The dark patches on the Moon are plains of old lava.
items.d: Long ago people thought they were seas. They are really dry rock.

items.t: Footprints on the Moon can last a very long time.
items.d: There is no wind or rain to erase them.

items.t: Water ice sits in shadowed craters near the Moon's poles.
items.d: The Sun never shines on those floors, so the ice stays frozen.

items.t: The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth.
items.d: It drifts about 4 centimeters farther each year. Mirrors left on the Moon help measure this.

items.t: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth blocks sunlight from the Moon.
items.d: The Moon can look reddish because Earth's air bends some red light into the shadow.

items.t: From the Moon's near side, Earth looks big and bright.
items.d: Earth is wider than the Moon, and its clouds reflect a lot of sunlight.

items.t: Yuri Gagarin was the first person to orbit Earth.
items.d: He flew on April 12, 1961. His trip around the planet took about 108 minutes.

items.t: Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman in space.
items.d: She orbited Earth in 1963, flying for almost three days.

items.t: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon.
items.d: The Apollo 11 landing was in July 1969. Buzz Aldrin stepped out soon after Armstrong.

items.t: Twelve Apollo astronauts walked on the Moon.
items.d: Six landings between 1969 and 1972 each had two people walk on the surface.

items.t: Apollo crews brought about 380 kilograms of Moon rocks to Earth.
items.d: Labs on Earth still study those rocks to learn what the Moon is made of.

items.t: Apollo crews took about three days to reach the Moon.
items.d: Then a small lander flew down while the main ship stayed in orbit around the Moon.

items.t: The International Space Station orbits about 400 kilometers up.
items.d: It goes around Earth about once every 90 minutes.

items.t: The space station travels at about 28,000 kilometers per hour.
items.d: Crews see about 16 sunrises during a single day on Earth.

items.t: Astronauts float because they are falling around Earth.
items.d: Gravity still pulls. They fall together with the station, so their feet do not press down.

items.t: Astronauts exercise for about two hours each day in orbit.
items.d: Their bodies do less work against gravity, so exercise keeps muscles and bones strong.

items.t: In orbit, water forms round floating blobs.
items.d: Because it is falling with the station, it is not pulled flat. It clings together as a ball.

items.t: The sky looks black in space even when the Sun is out.
items.d: There is no air to scatter sunlight. On Earth, that scattering makes the sky blue.

items.t: A rocket moves forward by pushing gas out the back.
items.d: The gas pushes back on the rocket just as hard, and that push lifts it.

items.t: Most of a rocket at liftoff is propellant.
items.d: Propellant includes fuel and an oxidizer. Empty tanks and used stages drop away during flight.

items.t: Many rockets head east to get a boost from Earth's spin.
items.d: The ground itself is moving east, fastest near the equator.

items.t: A returning crew capsule uses a heat shield, then parachutes.
items.d: The shield takes the heat of rushing into the air. Parachutes slow the final fall.

items.t: A small helicopter named Ingenuity flew on Mars.
items.d: In 2021 it made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. Its blades spun fast in the thin air.

items.t: The Sun is about 1.4 million kilometers wide.
items.d: That is about 100 times wider than Earth.

items.t: The Sun holds about 99.8 percent of all the mass in our solar system.
items.d: All the planets, moons, and other objects share the remaining 0.2 percent.

items.t: It would take more than 330,000 Earths to match the Sun's mass.
items.d: The Sun is incredibly heavy compared with our planet.

items.t: The Sun is about 1,000 times as massive as Jupiter, our biggest planet.
items.d: Jupiter is giant, but the Sun is much, much bigger.

items.t: Almost 1,000 Jupiters could fit inside the Sun.
items.d: Jupiter is the biggest planet, and the Sun still dwarfs it.

items.t: Our Sun is an average-sized star. Some stars are smaller, and some are up to 1,000 times wider.
Many stars have a partner star, but our Sun travels alone.
items.d: More than half of all stars live in groups of two or more.

items.t: The Sun is a giant ball of hydrogen and helium.
items.d: Its own gravity holds it together in a round shape.

items.t: The Sun is a yellow dwarf star, a common kind of star in our galaxy.
items.d: Dwarf here just means medium-sized, not tiny.

items.t: The Sun is really white, even though it can look yellow from Earth.
items.d: Earth's air scatters some of its light, so it looks yellow or orange to us.

items.t: Gravity at the Sun's surface is about 28 times stronger than gravity on Earth.
items.d: A child who weighs 30 kg here would feel as heavy as 840 kg there.

items.t: The Sun's average density is only a little greater than water's.
items.d: It is much denser inside and much thinner near the outside.

items.t: The center of the Sun is about 15 million degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is hotter than anything we can make on Earth for everyday use.

items.t: The Sun's visible surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That sounds hot, but it is cool compared with the Sun's core.

items.t: The Sun's outer atmosphere is much hotter than its surface, reaching about 2 million degrees Celsius.
items.d: Scientists are still studying why this happens.

items.t: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old.
items.d: It formed from a giant spinning cloud of gas and dust.

items.t: The cloud that made the Sun squeezed together, spun faster, and flattened into a disk.
items.d: Our planets later formed in that disk.

items.t: The Sun is a little less than halfway through its life.
items.d: It will keep shining for about another 5 billion years.

items.t: The Sun will spend about 10 to 11 billion years as a main-sequence star.
items.d: Our Sun is a calm, long-lasting star.

items.t: The Sun is slowly getting brighter, by about 1 percent every 100 million years.
items.d: That change is far too slow for anyone to notice.

items.t: The Sun will eventually become a small, hot star called a white dwarf.
items.d: That change will happen about 5 billion years from now.

items.t: The Sun has already used up nearly half of the hydrogen in its core.
items.d: It still has plenty left for billions of years.

items.t: The Sun shines because of nuclear fusion in its core.
items.d: In fusion, hydrogen is squeezed together to make helium.

items.t: The Sun's huge mass creates strong gravity and enormous pressure inside it.
items.d: That pressure, plus the heat, lets fusion happen in the core.

items.t: Every second, the Sun's core turns about 600 billion kilograms of hydrogen into helium.
items.d: That is a lot of hydrogen, but the Sun is so big it can keep going.

items.t: Every second, the Sun turns about 4 billion kilograms of matter into energy.
items.d: That energy is what shines out as sunlight.

items.t: In the Sun's main fusion chain, about 0.7 percent of the starting mass turns into energy.
items.d: A tiny bit of mass makes a huge amount of energy.

items.t: In 1.5 millionths of a second, the Sun gives off more energy than people use in a whole year.
items.d: The Sun is an amazing power plant.

items.t: The Sun's fusion makes tiny ghostly particles called neutrinos.
items.d: About 65 billion pass through every square centimeter facing the Sun each second.

items.t: The Sun's core is about 150 grams per cubic centimeter, around 8 times denser than gold.
items.d: Yet it is still a hot gas, not a solid.

items.t: The core holds roughly half of the Sun's mass.
items.d: It is only the innermost quarter of the Sun by distance.

items.t: Most of the Sun's energy is made in a small region around its center.
items.d: About 91 percent is made within the inner fifth of the Sun's radius.

items.t: The Sun has layers, with the core in the middle.
items.d: Outside the core are the radiative zone and then the convection zone.

items.t: In the radiative zone, energy travels outward as radiation.
items.d: This layer is just outside the core.

items.t: Energy can take about 170,000 years to travel from the core to the top of the convection zone.
items.d: It bounces around like a pinball.

items.t: After leaving the Sun's surface, sunlight needs only about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
items.d: The slow part of the trip is inside the Sun.

items.t: In the convection zone, large bubbles of hot plasma rise toward the Sun's surface.
items.d: Big bubbles of hot gas rise toward the surface, like boiling soup.

items.t: The Sun's surface has bubbling cells called granules.
items.d: Each granule is about 1,000 kilometers across.

items.t: A granule on the Sun lasts only about 20 minutes.
items.d: Then a new one bubbles up in its place.

items.t: The photosphere is the Sun's visible surface, the part that gives off the light we see.
items.d: It is only about 400 kilometers thick.

items.t: The chromosphere's name comes from Greek words meaning sphere of color.
items.d: The name comes from Greek.

items.t: The chromosphere looks red because its hydrogen glows at a red wavelength.
items.d: Glowing hydrogen gas makes the red color.

items.t: The word corona is Latin for crown.
items.d: It is usually hidden by the Sun's bright surface.

items.t: The Sun spins once about every 25 days at its equator and every 36 days near its poles.
items.d: It is a ball of gas, so different parts spin at different speeds.

items.t: The Sun takes about 230 million years to travel once around the Milky Way.
items.d: It moves together with the whole solar system.

items.t: The Sun's gravity holds the whole solar system together.
items.d: It keeps every planet moving in its path.

items.t: The closest star to the Sun is Proxima Centauri.
items.d: It is a small red dwarf star.

items.t: Activity on the Sun creates space weather that can travel about 150 million km to Earth.
Space weather can damage satellites and cause electrical blackouts on Earth.
Solar wind comes from the Sun's hot outer atmosphere, called the corona.
Earth's atmosphere and magnetic field shield us from most of the solar wind.
Earth's magnetic field stretches into a long tail on the side facing away from the Sun.
Energy from a solar flare travels through space at the speed of light.
A huge solar eruption that often comes with a flare is called a coronal mass ejection.
Northern lights near the North Pole are also called aurora borealis.
Southern lights near the South Pole are also called aurora australis.
Oxygen can make auroras glow green or red. Nitrogen can make them blue or purple.
Solar particles follow Earth's magnetic field lines toward the poles, where they make auroras.
Auroras are not only on Earth. They have also been seen on Jupiter and Saturn.
Sunspots are cooler areas on the Sun where magnetic fields are tightly packed.
A sunspot can remain on the Sun for a few days or for several months.
Sunspots are usually about 1,600 to 161,000 km across.
The number of sunspots rises and falls during the Sun's roughly 11-year cycle.
