items.t: Elephants roll in mud or dust to protect their skin from the sun and biting insects.
items.d: Mud works like a sunscreen and bug spray in one.

items.t: An elephant's big ears work like a radiator to let heat out of its body.
items.d: Flapping them cools the blood in the ears.

items.t: Elephants sleep only about 3 to 4 hours a day.
items.d: They spend most of the rest of the day eating and walking.

items.t: An elephant can eat about 136 kilograms of food in one day.
items.d: Elephants spend much of the day eating.

items.t: An elephant's closest living relatives are manatees, dugongs and hyraxes.
items.d: The hyrax is a small furry animal about the size of a rabbit.

items.t: There are three living kinds of elephants: African bush, African forest and Asian.
items.d: Each kind looks a little different from the others.

items.t: The African bush elephant is the largest animal that lives on land.
items.d: No other land animal today is bigger.

items.t: African forest elephants are the smallest elephants and have straight tusks that point down.
items.d: They live in thick forests in Africa.

items.t: Forest elephants can carry large seeds more than 5 km, earning the name gardeners of the forest.
items.d: This helps spread seeds through the forest.

items.t: An African elephant family is led by an older female called the matriarch.
items.d: She guides the family to food and water.

items.t: Asian elephants have no matriarch the way African elephants do.
items.d: Their herds are related females, their daughters and young males.

items.t: Asian elephants can walk up to about 80 km a day looking for food.
items.d: They eat roots, grasses, fruit and bark.

items.t: A baby elephant often sucks its trunk for comfort, like a child sucking a thumb.
items.d: The trunk is a very useful thing to cuddle.

items.t: Hippos spend most of their time in the water.
items.d: They come out mostly at night to eat grass.

items.t: A hippo's eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on its head.
items.d: It can breathe, see and hear while the rest of its body stays underwater.

items.t: A hippo's nose and ears close by themselves to keep water out.
items.d: This happens automatically when it dips under.

items.t: A hippo's closest living relatives are whales, dolphins and porpoises.
items.d: Long ago they shared the same ancestors.

items.t: Hippos are dense enough to sink and move along the bottom of a river.
items.d: They do not swim. They stroll along the river bed.

items.t: A hippo has to come up for air at least every six minutes.
items.d: Hippos spend most of their day in the water.

items.t: Hippos make a red, oily skin liquid that works like sunscreen and keeps their skin moist.
items.d: It may look like blood, but it is not blood.

items.t: A hippo's canine and incisor teeth keep growing throughout its life.
items.d: Its canine teeth can reach about 50 cm long.

items.t: Rival male hippos show off by opening their mouths up to about 150 degrees wide.
items.d: It is how rival hippos say, look how big I am.

items.t: A baby hippo is about ten times bigger than a human baby at birth.
items.d: Mother hippos can nurse their calves even underwater.

items.t: Hippos eat only about 40 kilograms of food a night, which is not much for such a big animal.
items.d: They walk out of the water after dark to graze.

items.t: A group of hippos is called a school.
items.d: Some groups, called pods, can have over 100 hippos.

items.t: There are two kinds of hippos: the common hippo and the much smaller pygmy hippo.
items.d: The pygmy hippo is shy and lives in West Africa.

items.t: A rhino's horn is made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails and hair.
items.d: It is not bone.

items.t: If a rhino's horn breaks off, it can slowly grow back.
items.d: Just like your nails, the horn keeps growing.

items.t: Five kinds of rhinos are alive today: two in Africa and three in Asia.
items.d: Black and white rhinos live in Africa.

items.t: Rhinos have three toes on each foot.
items.d: Rhinos are big animals that stand on just three toes per foot.

items.t: The white rhino is the heaviest kind of rhino and the Sumatran rhino is the lightest.
items.d: A white rhino can weigh about 2,300 kg.

items.t: Rhino skin is like thick armour, made of a tight net of tough fibres called collagen.
items.d: Your own skin has collagen too.

items.t: A newborn rhino can stand up and start drinking milk just two to three hours after birth.
items.d: Baby rhinos get going fast.

items.t: Oxpecker birds ride on rhinos and eat the ticks off their skin.
items.d: The rhino gets cleaned and the bird gets lunch.

items.t: A black rhino can run about 64 km/h.
items.d: That is as fast as a car in town.

items.t: A tapir has a short, bendy snout like a mini elephant trunk, and it can use it as a snorkel.
items.d: Tapirs are most closely related to horses and rhinos.

items.t: Baby tapirs are striped and spotted like little watermelons on legs.
items.d: The markings fade after a few months.

items.t: Chimpanzees and bonobos are humans' closest living relatives.
items.d: They are our closest relatives that are alive today.

items.t: Nearly every studied chimpanzee population uses tools.
items.d: Different chimp communities may use different kinds of tools.

items.t: Chimpanzees trim twigs to pull termites from their mounds.
items.d: The changed twig becomes a handy food tool.

items.t: West African chimpanzees crack hard nuts with stones or branches.
items.d: The stone or branch works like a hammer.

items.t: A chimpanzee community can have more than 200 members.
items.d: That is a very large ape community.

items.t: Chimpanzees often travel in small groups of six or fewer.
items.d: These small groups can change from day to day.

items.t: Fruit is the main food in a chimpanzee's diet.
items.d: Chimpanzees eat other foods too, but fruit comes first.

items.t: Chimpanzees communicate with sounds, faces and touch.
items.d: A look, call or gentle touch can carry a message.

items.t: Chimp groups often split apart and later join again.
items.d: Scientists call this a fission-fusion society.

items.t: Gorillas are the largest primates alive today.
items.d: They are bigger than any other primate alive today.

items.t: Adult male gorillas can weigh about 136 to 227 kg.
items.d: Their size makes them much heavier than most primates.

items.t: The leader of a gorilla group is called a silverback.
items.d: This is the name for the leader of the group.

items.t: Gorillas are herbivores, so they eat mostly plants.
items.d: Plant foods make up most of a gorilla's meals.

items.t: Gorillas build nests where they can sleep.
items.d: Their sleeping shelter is made for resting.

items.t: There are two gorilla species, eastern and western.
items.d: Gorillas are split into these two species.

items.t: A gorilla troop usually has about 8 to 11 members.
items.d: The troop travels and lives as a social group.

items.t: A wild gorilla used a stick to test how deep water was.
items.d: The stick helped the gorilla check before wading in.

items.t: Gorillas usually walk on all fours using their knuckles.
items.d: This way of moving is called knuckle-walking.

items.t: Every gorilla has its own fingerprints, just like every person.
items.d: The ridge patterns are different for each gorilla.

items.t: The name orangutan comes from Malay words meaning person and forest.
items.d: Orang means person, and hutan means forest.

items.t: An adult male orangutan's arm span is about 2 metres.
items.d: Arm span is the reach from one hand to the other.

items.t: Orangutans are the most solitary great apes.
items.d: They spend more time alone than other great apes do.

items.t: Orangutans make different nests for daytime and nighttime use.
items.d: Each nest is built for a particular time of day.

items.t: Fruit is the most important part of an orangutan's diet.
items.d: It is the main part of what orangutans eat.

items.t: There are three orangutan species.
items.d: One is the Tapanuli orangutan.

items.t: An orangutan mother may nurse her young for up to eight years.
items.d: That is longer than any other mammal nurses its young.

items.t: Wild orangutans live only in parts of Borneo and Sumatra.
items.d: Both are large islands in Southeast Asia.

items.t: Orangutans spend most of their time in trees.
items.d: Much of an orangutan's life happens above the ground.

items.t: Gibbons travel by swinging from branch to branch.
items.d: This arm-swinging movement is called brachiation.

items.t: Gibbon pairs sing duets, and their young may join in.
items.d: A gibbon family can make music together.

items.t: Gibbons have no tails.
items.d: Like every other ape, a gibbon is tailless.

items.t: Gibbons can leap as far as 8 metres between branches.
items.d: That is about the length of a small bus.

items.t: A gibbon's wrist works a little like a ball-and-socket joint.
items.d: This flexible wrist helps during branch-to-branch swinging.

items.t: There are six species of baboon.
items.d: All six belong to the same group of monkeys.

items.t: A baboon troop usually has about 50 animals.
items.d: Baboons commonly live together in large social groups.

items.t: Baboons have special sitting pads with no nerves.
items.d: These tough pads help make sitting more comfortable.

items.t: Lemurs are found naturally only on Madagascar.
items.d: Madagascar is a large island off Africa's east coast.

items.t: Madame Berthe's mouse lemur is the world's smallest primate.
items.d: It weighs only about 30 grams.

items.t: Females lead the social order in many lemur species.
items.d: This is called female social dominance.

items.t: An aye-aye has a thin, flexible middle finger.
items.d: It uses this unusual finger to pull food from tiny holes.

items.t: Dwarf and mouse lemurs can slow their bodies down to save energy.
items.d: They do this in certain seasons.

items.t: A tarsier's eyes can be as large as its whole brain.
items.d: Some tarsiers have eyes that are even larger than their brains.

items.t: Tarsiers can turn their heads 180 degrees in either direction.
items.d: They can look directly behind themselves.

items.t: Every tarsier species is nocturnal.
items.d: Nocturnal animals are active mainly at night.

items.t: Tarsiers are the only living primates that eat only animals.
items.d: Other living primates include plants in their diets.

items.t: A tarsier's head and body are only about 10 to 15 cm long.
items.d: That does not include the tail.

items.t: Capuchin monkeys use rocks as hammers and anvils.
items.d: They strike nuts and fruits against rocks to open them.

items.t: Bonobo groups have a female-led social structure.
items.d: This is unusual among apes.

items.t: Bonobos sometimes share food with unrelated strangers.
items.d: They do not share only with close family members.

items.t: Japanese macaques warm themselves in hot springs during winter.
items.d: These snow monkeys soak in naturally heated water.

items.t: A giraffe calf grows about 1.2 meters in its first year.
items.d: That is about 4 feet. The calf gets much taller while it is still very young.

items.t: A newborn giraffe is about 1.9 meters tall.
items.d: That is about 6 feet, as tall as many grown-ups.

items.t: A newborn giraffe weighs about 68 kilograms.
items.d: That is about 150 pounds. A newborn giraffe is already very heavy.

items.t: A giraffe's tongue can be up to about 53 centimeters long.
items.d: That is about 21 inches, longer than a school ruler.

items.t: A baby giraffe can run within a few hours of being born.
items.d: Only a few hours old, it can already run around.

items.t: In a giraffe herd, at least one giraffe is often on the lookout.
items.d: Someone in the herd is often watching the land for danger.

items.t: No two zebras have the same stripes.
items.d: Each zebra has its own pattern. The stripes are like a name you can see.

items.t: A group of zebras is called a herd or a zeal.
items.d: Zeal is a fun extra name for a zebra group.

items.t: A baby zebra can stand about 20 minutes after it is born.
items.d: Just 20 minutes old, a baby zebra can already stand by itself.

items.t: Zebras in hotter places tend to have more stripes.
items.d: A zebra from a hot home often has more stripes than one from a cooler home.

items.t: A zebra's teeth keep growing for its whole life.
items.d: Grazing wears the teeth down, so they grow to keep up.

items.t: Zebras sometimes migrate in herds of thousands.
items.d: They travel together to find better places to eat.

items.t: Grevy's zebra is endangered.
items.d: Grevy's zebra is one kind of zebra, and very few are left in the wild.

items.t: The moose is the largest member of the deer family.
items.d: No other kind of deer grows as large as a moose.

items.t: A big moose can weigh about 900 kilograms.
items.d: That is nearly 2,000 pounds. A moose is a very heavy animal.

items.t: A moose's wide hooves work like snowshoes.
items.d: The broad hooves help a moose walk on top of deep snow.

items.t: A moose can swim about 16 kilometers or more without a stop.
items.d: That is about 10 miles or more, a long swim for such a big animal.

items.t: A moose can run up to about 56 kilometers an hour for a short way.
items.d: That is up to about 35 miles an hour, and only for a short time.

items.t: A full-grown moose can eat up to about 32 kilograms a day.
items.d: That is up to about 70 pounds of food in one day.

items.t: The flap of skin under a moose's chin is called a bell.
items.d: It hangs under the chin and is easy to spot on a moose.

items.t: Bison are the heaviest land animals in North America.
items.d: They weigh more than any other animal that lives on land there.

items.t: Bison can run up to about 56 kilometers an hour.
items.d: That is up to about 35 miles an hour.

items.t: Bison horns can grow about 60 centimeters long.
items.d: That is about 2 feet. The horns are curved and pointed.

items.t: A Bactrian camel has two humps that store fat.
items.d: The humps hold fat. They do not hold water.

items.t: A Bactrian camel can close its nostrils to block sand.
items.d: Shut nostrils help keep blowing sand out of its nose.

items.t: Bactrian camels have bushy eyebrows and two rows of long eyelashes.
items.d: The brows and extra lashes help keep sand out of their eyes.

items.t: An adult Bactrian camel stands over 2 meters tall at the hump.
items.d: That is over 7 feet, taller than most grown-up people.

items.t: A Bactrian camel paces, moving both legs on one side together.
items.d: Both legs on the left move forward, then both legs on the right.

items.t: A baby Bactrian camel can run when it is only a few hours old.
items.d: Only a few hours after birth, it can already run.

items.t: Wild Bactrian camels are critically endangered.
items.d: Critically endangered means they are very rare in the wild.

items.t: A llama is a South American relative of the camel, with no hump.
items.d: It belongs to the camel family, but its back is smooth.

items.t: Llamas are domestic animals of the Andes Mountains.
items.d: People of the Andes keep llamas and use them to help with work.

items.t: A llama often carries about 23 to 34 kilograms.
items.d: That is a load of about 50 to 75 pounds.

items.t: A loaded llama can walk up to about 32 kilometers in a day.
items.d: That is about 20 miles while it carries a pack.

items.t: If the load is too heavy, a llama will refuse to move.
items.d: It simply stands still until the pack is light enough.

items.t: Mountain goats are not true goats, but they are close relatives.
items.d: Their name says goat, but they are only close cousins of true goats.

items.t: Rough pads on a mountain goat's toes grip like climbing shoes.
items.d: Each toe has a rough pad underneath that helps the goat grip.

items.t: A mountain goat can jump nearly 3.7 meters in one bound.
items.d: That is nearly 12 feet in a single leap.

items.t: A mountain goat's white coat blends in on snowy peaks.
items.d: Against the snow, the white fur is hard to see.

items.t: A baby mountain goat is on its feet within minutes of birth.
items.d: In its mountain home, it must stand within minutes.

items.t: A white-tailed deer's coat changes with the seasons.
items.d: It is reddish-brown in summer and grayish-brown in winter.

items.t: Only male white-tailed deer grow antlers.
items.d: Males are called bucks. The points on their antlers are called tines.

items.t: White-tailed deer feed mostly at dawn and dusk.
items.d: Dawn is sunrise and dusk is sunset. That is when they eat the most.

items.t: A white-tailed deer can sprint up to about 48 kilometers an hour.
items.d: That is up to about 30 miles an hour.

items.t: A white-tailed deer can leap up to about 3 meters high.
items.d: That is a jump of up to about 10 feet.

items.t: Reindeer and caribou are the same kind of deer.
items.d: People use both names. The scientific name is Rangifer tarandus.

items.t: Both male and female reindeer grow antlers.
items.d: You can see antlers on reindeer moms and dads.

items.t: Hair on a reindeer's feet helps it grip ice and snow.
items.d: That hair also helps on frozen ground and mud.

items.t: Reindeer are the only deer with a fully hairy nose.
items.d: No other deer has hair that covers the nose completely.

items.t: In spring, reindeer can form herds of 50,000 to 500,000.
items.d: A group that big is called a super-herd.

items.t: Beavers are the largest rodents in North America.
items.d: Only the South American capybara is bigger among rodents in the whole world.

items.t: A beaver can swim underwater for up to about 15 minutes.
items.d: Its nose and ears shut tight to keep the water out.

items.t: Beavers have see-through inner eyelids.
items.d: They work a bit like built-in swim goggles to help the beaver see underwater.

items.t: A beaver's chisel-like front teeth never stop growing.
items.d: They keep growing to replace the parts that wear away.

items.t: Apart from humans, beavers change their surroundings more than almost any other animal.
items.d: Few other animals change the places where they live as much.

items.t: Beavers build dams and lodges from branches, rocks, plants and mud.
items.d: A lodge is the beaver family's cozy home.

items.t: A beaver's flat tail works like a rudder when it swims.
items.d: A rudder is the part of a boat that steers it.

items.t: Beaver front teeth look orange or reddish-brown.
items.d: Iron in the teeth gives them that color.

items.t: A single porcupine can have more than 30,000 quills.
items.d: That is a huge number of quills on one animal.

items.t: Porcupines cannot shoot or throw their quills.
items.d: Quills can come loose when another animal touches them.

items.t: A porcupine warns others by stomping its feet, hissing and shaking its quills.
items.d: These actions are warning signals.

items.t: A baby porcupine is called a porcupette.
items.d: Say it out loud: por-cu-PET.

items.t: Porcupine quills are modified hairs coated with keratin.
items.d: Thick plates of keratin cover each quill.

items.t: Hedgehogs have spines everywhere except on their face, legs and belly.
items.d: Their soft belly is why they curl up into a ball.

items.t: A hedgehog curls into a tight ball, tucking in its head, tail and legs.
items.d: The spines then point out in every direction.

items.t: Baby hedgehogs are born with soft, short spines.
items.d: The spines harden as the babies grow.

items.t: Hedgehogs eat mostly insects.
items.d: They also swim quite well and can even climb trees.

items.t: Hedgehog spines are hollow hairs made stiff by keratin.
items.d: Keratin is the same stuff in your hair and fingernails.

items.t: Hedgehogs are mostly active at night.
items.d: Animals that come out at night are called nocturnal.

items.t: No hedgehogs are native to Australia or the Americas.
items.d: They live naturally in parts of Europe, Asia and Africa.

items.t: Capybaras are the largest rodents in the world.
items.d: No other living rodent is larger.

items.t: A capybara can stay underwater for up to five minutes.
items.d: It dives to hide from animals that might hunt it.

items.t: A capybara's eyes, ears and nostrils sit high on its head.
items.d: That lets it watch while most of its body stays underwater.

items.t: Capybaras chew from side to side, like a camel, not up and down.
items.d: An adult can eat about 2.7 to 3.6 kg of grass a day.

items.t: Adult capybaras usually weigh between 35 and 66 kg.
items.d: That is about 77 to 146 pounds.

items.t: Capybaras have slightly webbed feet and just a tiny tail.
items.d: Webbed feet help them paddle through water.

items.t: Capybaras live in every South American country except Chile.
items.d: They are native across most of the continent.

items.t: Some birds perch on a capybara's back and watch for prey.
items.d: They swoop down when they spot something to catch.

items.t: Hares can run up to about 80 km/h over short distances.
items.d: That is about as fast as a car on a country road.

items.t: Baby hares are born with fur and open eyes.
items.d: Baby rabbits are born blind and hairless.

items.t: People have domesticated rabbits, but no hare species has been domesticated.
items.d: Hares remain wild animals.

items.t: European rabbits live in burrow systems called warrens.
items.d: A warren can house one to five bucks and one to eight does.

items.t: A European rabbit is pregnant for about 30 days.
items.d: A litter usually has three to seven babies, called kittens.

items.t: Rabbits and hares have four front teeth in the top jaw. Rodents have only two.
items.d: That is one way scientists tell the two groups apart.

items.t: About 4 in every 10 kinds of mammal are rodents.
items.d: Mice, squirrels, beavers and capybaras are all rodents.

items.t: Rodents have one pair of front teeth in each jaw that never stop growing.
items.d: They gnaw often to wear the teeth down.

items.t: A squirrel uses its bushy tail for balance when it jumps through trees.
items.d: The tail works like a tightrope walker's pole.

items.t: Tree squirrels can climb down headfirst.
items.d: They rotate their ankles by 180 degrees so their claws can grip the bark.

items.t: The squirrel family includes tree squirrels, ground squirrels and flying squirrels.
items.d: There are about 285 kinds in all.

items.t: Flying squirrels glide instead of truly flying.
items.d: A furry flap of skin stretches from wrist to ankle like a little parachute.

items.t: Hamsters carry food in their cheek pouches to storage rooms underground.
items.d: Full cheeks can make a hamster's head look two or three times bigger.

items.t: The golden hamster, also called the Syrian hamster, is the most common pet hamster.
items.d: Pet hamsters are mostly active at night.

items.t: Moles have velvety fur and very small eyes and ears.
items.d: They spend their lives digging tunnels underground.

items.t: Moles mostly eat earthworms.
items.d: Some mole food stores have held over a thousand earthworms.

items.t: Each mole front paw has an extra thumb-like digit that helps it dig.
items.d: Moles are great diggers.

items.t: The star-nosed mole has a nose with 22 fleshy, finger-like feelers.
items.d: The star-shaped nose is packed with over 25,000 tiny touch sensors.

items.t: Shrews look like mice, but they are not rodents.
items.d: Shrews hunt insects and worms.

items.t: Some kinds of shrew use echolocation to sense their surroundings.
items.d: Echolocation means listening to echoes of their own sounds.

items.t: An Etruscan shrew weighs only about 1.8 grams on average.
items.d: It weighs only about 1.8 grams, less than a paperclip or two.

items.t: An Etruscan shrew's heart can beat about 1,500 times a minute.
items.d: That is up to about 25 beats each second.

items.t: There are more than 1,300 species of bats.
items.d: That is a huge variety of shapes, sizes and diets.

items.t: Bats are the second largest mammal group by number of species.
items.d: Only rodents have more species.

items.t: Some bats weigh less than a penny.
items.d: Other bats are much larger.

items.t: The largest bats have a wingspan of about 1.8 metres.
items.d: That is wider than many adults are tall.

items.t: The scientific name Chiroptera means "hand wing" in Greek.
items.d: The name describes how a bat's wing is built.

items.t: A bat's wing has four long fingers and a thumb joined by thin skin.
items.d: Its wing is built a little like a human hand.

items.t: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly.
items.d: No other mammal can fly.

items.t: Flexible wing skin lets a bat turn quickly in the air.
items.d: This helps insect-eating bats catch bugs while flying.

items.t: Bats are grouped into two main types, microbats and megabats.
items.d: Most bat species belong to the microbat group.

items.t: Many microbats eat flying insects such as moths.
items.d: They often catch their food at night.

items.t: Microbats use echoes to judge an object's size and distance.
items.d: They listen for sounds that bounce back from nearby objects.

items.t: Megabats live in tropical parts of the world.
items.d: Warm tropical habitats provide plenty of plant food.

items.t: Megabats eat fruit, nectar and pollen.
items.d: Their meals can also help plants grow and reproduce.

items.t: Bats live almost everywhere on Earth.
items.d: They avoid polar regions, extreme deserts and a few isolated islands.

items.t: Bats rest in places called roosts.
items.d: Roosts can be caves, tree hollows, old buildings or narrow cracks.

items.t: Some bats hibernate during winter.
items.d: Hibernation helps them spend the cold season resting.

items.t: Some bats move to different roosts as the seasons change.
items.d: A summer roost and a winter roost may meet different needs.

items.t: Some bat colonies contain millions of bats.
items.d: A colony is a group of bats living or resting together.

items.t: Insect-eating bats consume millions of bugs each night.
items.d: This may help farmers use fewer pesticides.

items.t: More than 500 plant species depend on bats for pollination.
items.d: These plants include mangoes and bananas.

items.t: Fruit-eating bats spread seeds to new places.
items.d: The scattered seeds help rainforests grow back.

items.t: About one fifth of mammal species are bats.
items.d: Bats make up a surprisingly large part of the mammal family.

items.t: Bats are not blind. They have good eyesight and strong hearing.
items.d: The saying "blind as a bat" is incorrect.

items.t: A bat's heart can beat about 1,000 times a minute during flight.
items.d: Flying requires lots of energy.

items.t: A flying squirrel can turn halfway around while gliding.
items.d: It can make a 180-degree turn in midair.

items.t: A flying squirrel raises its tail to brake before landing.
items.d: Its tail helps slow the glide near a tree.

items.t: There are about 50 species of flying squirrels.
items.d: Despite their name, all of them are gliders.

items.t: Flying squirrels live in North America, Central America and Asia.
items.d: Different species live in different forests.

items.t: Flying squirrels make nests inside sheltered tree spaces.
items.d: They use tree cavities, woodpecker holes and abandoned bird nests.

items.t: Flying squirrels are nocturnal, meaning they are active at night.
items.d: They rest during much of the day.

items.t: A flying squirrel's large eyes help it move around in the dark.
items.d: Large eyes are useful for this nighttime mammal.

items.t: Flying squirrels sometimes share a winter nest with family.
items.d: Resting together helps them stay warm.

items.t: Northern flying squirrels eat insects, seeds, nuts and fungi.
items.d: Insects are animals, while seeds, nuts and fungi are not.

items.t: Colugos belong to a mammal order called Dermoptera.
items.d: This order is separate from bats, squirrels and primates.

items.t: Colugos are the closest living relatives of primates.
items.d: Humans, apes and monkeys are primates.

items.t: A colugo's gliding skin stretches from its neck to its fingers and tail.
items.d: The wide membrane acts like a living glider.

items.t: Colugos have been recorded gliding as far as 150 metres.
items.d: They can travel a long way between trees without touching the ground.

items.t: Some colugo teeth are shaped like tiny combs.
items.d: The comb-like teeth help groom the animal's gliding membrane.

items.t: Colugos live only in trees.
items.d: The word for an animal that lives in trees is arboreal.

items.t: Gliding is more like a controlled fall than true flight.
items.d: A glider makes only a small amount of lift.

items.t: A colugo has gliding skin between its fingers.
items.d: This web helps the colugo control its path through the air.

items.t: Colugos are sometimes called flying lemurs, but they are not lemurs.
items.d: They cannot truly fly.

items.t: Colugos live in the tropical rainforests of Southeast Asia.
items.d: They live in warm, dense forests.

items.t: There are two living colugo species.
items.d: They are the Sunda colugo and the Philippine colugo.

items.t: A colugo's eyes cannot move independently.
items.d: It turns its head when it wants to look around.

items.t: Colugos are herbivores that eat leaves, buds, flowers and fruit.
items.d: Herbivores eat plant foods.

items.t: A sugar glider uses its tail like a rudder while gliding.
items.d: The tail helps it stay steady and steer between trees.

items.t: Kangaroos are the only large mammals that hop on two legs to get around.
items.d: Hopping is their main way of moving from place to place.

items.t: A newborn kangaroo joey is about the size of a lima bean.
items.d: A lima bean is a small bean you might see in soup.

items.t: A mother kangaroo carries her joey in a pouch called a marsupium.
items.d: The joey stays in the pouch while it grows and develops.

items.t: A kangaroo's tail works like a third leg when it moves slowly.
items.d: The tail also helps the kangaroo balance.

items.t: A red kangaroo hops comfortably at about 20 to 25 kilometres per hour.
items.d: That is about 12 to 16 miles per hour.

items.t: A joey usually stays in the pouch for about nine months.
items.d: Nine months is a long stay for a baby in a pouch.

items.t: A group of kangaroos is called a mob.
items.d: A kangaroo group can also be called a court or a troupe.

items.t: A koala is a marsupial, not a bear.
items.d: Some people say koala bear, but that name is wrong.

items.t: Eucalyptus leaves make up most of a koala's food.
items.d: Koalas live in trees and eat the leaves there.

items.t: Koalas can sleep for up to twenty hours a day.
items.d: If a koala sleeps twenty hours, four hours are left in the day.

items.t: Koalas get enough water from leaves that they rarely drink.
items.d: They do not need to visit water very often.

items.t: A baby koala lives in the pouch for about six to seven months.
items.d: The pouch is where the baby keeps growing after birth.

items.t: A newborn koala weighs no more than half a gram.
items.d: Half a gram is tiny, far less than a teaspoon of sugar.

items.t: Wombats leave droppings shaped like little cubes.
items.d: A cube has six flat square faces, a little like a die.

items.t: A wombat's pouch faces backward.
items.d: Its opening points toward the back of the mother's body.

items.t: Wombats dig big burrows with strong claws and front teeth.
items.d: Their front teeth are rodent-like, and they dig long tunnel homes.

items.t: The Tasmanian devil is the largest living meat-eating marsupial.
items.d: No larger meat-eating marsupial is alive today.

items.t: Wild Tasmanian devils live only on the island of Tasmania.
items.d: Tasmania is an island state just south of mainland Australia.

items.t: A Tasmanian devil has 42 teeth, the same number as a dog.
items.d: Dogs have 42 teeth too, so the numbers match.

items.t: A platypus has more webbing on its front feet than its back feet.
items.d: Webbing is the skin between the toes that helps it swim.

items.t: A platypus hunts underwater with its eyes, ears, and nostrils closed.
items.d: Its bill can sense prey while those parts stay shut.

items.t: A platypus does not have a working stomach.
items.d: People have a working stomach. A platypus does not.

items.t: A platypus mother has no teats. Milk comes out through her skin.
items.d: Milk comes through tiny skin pores, and the baby drinks it there.

items.t: A platypus tail stores fat and can steer like a rudder.
items.d: A rudder is a flat part that helps turn while swimming.

items.t: Early scientists thought a preserved platypus might be a fake.
items.d: It looked so strange they wondered if animals were sewn together.

items.t: Echidnas and the platypus are the only living mammals that lay eggs.
items.d: Every other mammal alive today is born live, not hatched from an egg.

items.t: An echidna's spines are special hairs made of keratin.
items.d: Keratin is also what your hair and fingernails are made of.

items.t: A baby echidna is called a puggle.
items.d: Puggle is one name used for a young echidna.

items.t: A mother echidna lays an egg and puts it straight into her pouch.
items.d: She places the egg in the pouch as soon as she lays it.

items.t: An echidna's snout can sense electricity to find food.
items.d: That sense helps it locate worms, termites, and ants.

items.t: The Virginia opossum is the world's northernmost marsupial.
items.d: No other marsupial lives farther north than this opossum.

items.t: An opossum's tail can grab branches and carry small things.
items.d: It uses the tail to hold a branch or a small object.

items.t: A Virginia opossum has 50 teeth.
items.d: That is more teeth than any other land mammal in North America.

items.t: A newborn opossum is about the size of a honeybee.
items.d: A honeybee is tiny, and so is a brand-new opossum.

items.t: Most marsupial babies are born tiny and continue growing in a pouch.
items.d: The pouch is on the mother's belly.

items.t: Marsupials naturally live in Australasia and the Americas.
items.d: Their homes include Australia, New Guinea, nearby islands, and the Americas.

items.t: About 70 percent of the world's marsupial species live in Australia.
items.d: One count found roughly 334 marsupial species alive today.

items.t: The red kangaroo is the largest living marsupial.
items.d: It can grow up to 1.8 metres tall, about 5 feet 11 inches.

items.t: Marsupial babies are usually born after about 12 to 33 days.
items.d: That is a short pregnancy. The baby then grows in the pouch.

items.t: Only five kinds of monotreme live today: the platypus and four echidnas.
items.d: That means one platypus species and four echidna species.

items.t: Monotreme means single opening in Greek.
items.d: The Greek name refers to one body opening.

items.t: Monotreme mothers feed their babies milk, just like other mammals.
items.d: The baby gets milk from its mother, as other mammal babies do.

items.t: All living monotremes come from Australia and New Guinea.
items.d: The platypus and the echidnas have their wild homes there.

items.t: Numbats eat almost nothing but termites.
items.d: Termites are tiny insects, and they are nearly all a numbat eats.

items.t: A numbat catches termites with a long, sticky tongue.
items.d: The tongue is narrow and coated in sticky saliva.

items.t: The numbat is the only marsupial fully active in the daytime.
items.d: It looks for termites while the sun is up.

items.t: Sugar gliders glide on flaps of skin between their front and back legs.
items.d: These skin flaps are called patagia. They spread out for the glide.

items.t: A sugar glider can glide 50 metres or more.
items.d: Fifty metres is about 55 yards, a long trip for a small animal.

items.t: A quokka is about the size of a pet cat.
items.d: It can also climb small trees and shrubs.

items.t: The striped thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, is now extinct.
items.d: It had 15 to 20 dark stripes across its back, rump, and the base of its tail.

items.t: Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal.
items.d: It keeps them warm in cold ocean water.

items.t: Sea otters use rocks to crack open shellfish. Few mammals use tools!
items.d: A rock on the belly works like a little table.

items.t: Sea otters may wrap themselves in kelp so they do not drift away.
items.d: Kelp is a long seaweed that grows in the sea.

items.t: Sea otters mostly eat animals without backbones, like sea urchins.
Sea otters have no blubber. Their thick fur keeps them warm instead.
An adult sea otter weighs about 14 to 45 kg.
items.d: That is roughly as heavy as a big dog.

items.t: Honey badgers have very loose skin, so they can twist around inside it.
Honey badgers eat lots of things, like insects, frogs, lizards, rodents, birds and eggs.
Honey badgers raid beehives to eat bee larvae and honey.
Honey badgers live across most of Africa south of the Sahara desert.
The wolverine is the largest land member of the weasel family.
Wolverines live mostly in remote forests in the far north.
Mother wolverines dig dens in the snow to raise their babies.
Wolverines hide extra food to eat later when food is hard to find.
A wolverine is small but very strong for its size.
items.d: It has powerful jaws, sharp claws and a thick hide.

items.t: Spotted hyenas live in big groups called clans, with up to 80 members.
In a spotted hyena clan, the females are in charge.
The spotted hyena's whooping call is one of the most famous sounds in Africa.
Spotted hyena cubs are born with their eyes open.
Spotted hyenas can run up to about 60 km per hour.
The spotted hyena is the most common large meat-eater in Africa.
Meerkats take turns standing guard while the others look for food.
A meerkat group can have anywhere from 2 to 30 members.
Adult meerkats teach pups to eat scorpions safely.
items.d: They remove the stinger first.

items.t: Meerkats live in underground tunnels with two to three levels.
Meerkats live in southern Africa, in places like Botswana, Namibia and South Africa.
Meerkats mostly eat insects, especially beetles.
A skunk can spray its smelly musk several meters away.
Striped skunks eat both plants and animals.
Raccoons have a black patch of fur around their eyes, like a mask.
Raccoons are usually active at night and eat both plants and animals.
Raccoons are common all over North America, from Canada to Panama.
The giant otter is the longest member of the weasel family, up to 1.8 m.
Giant otters live in family groups of about three to eight.
Giant otters eat almost only fish.
Giant otters live mostly in and along the Amazon River in South America.
The least weasel is the smallest living mammal in the carnivore group.
A male least weasel weighs only about 36 to 250 g.
Badgers live in burrows called setts, with many rooms and entrances.
Earthworms are the most important food for European badgers.
A group of badgers is often called a clan.
The binturong smells like hot buttered popcorn.
The fossa lives only on the island of Madagascar.
The fossa is the biggest meat-eating mammal on Madagascar.
The fossa has very bendy ankles, so it can climb down trees head-first.
The aardwolf mainly eats termites.
The aardwolf is part of the hyena family.
An aardwolf can lap up as many as 300,000 termites in one night.
In far northern winters, a stoat's fur turns white. Only its tail tip stays black.
The orca is the largest member of the dolphin family.
items.d: Orcas are dolphins, even though they are often called whales.

items.t: Orcas live in close family groups called pods.
items.d: A pod may have a few to about 20 related orcas.

items.t: Each orca family has its own learned calls.
items.d: The special calls work like sound badges for the family.

items.t: Orcas have the most varied diet of all whales and dolphins.
items.d: Each orca population usually specializes in certain foods.

items.t: Female orcas usually live about 50 years in the wild.
items.d: Some female orcas have reached at least 90 years old.

items.t: A humpback whale can grow about 18 meters long.
items.d: A large humpback can weigh about 36 metric tons.

items.t: A humpback whale's tail flukes can span about 5.5 meters.
items.d: Flukes are the two broad halves of a whale's tail.

items.t: A newborn humpback is about 4 to 4.9 meters long.
items.d: That is about as long as a family car.

items.t: Some humpbacks migrate about 8,000 kilometers.
items.d: They travel between warm breeding areas and cold feeding waters.

items.t: Some humpbacks swim about 4,800 kilometers from Alaska to Hawaii.
items.d: They can complete this journey in as few as 28 days.

items.t: Humpbacks sometimes make curtains of bubbles around fish.
items.d: This teamwork is called bubble-net feeding.

items.t: Humpbacks are famous for leaping out of the water.
items.d: This kind of jump is called a breach.

items.t: Humpbacks strain krill and small fish from water using baleen.
items.d: The baleen plates work like a giant sieve.

items.t: A male humpback's song can last about 30 minutes.
items.d: The whale may repeat the whole song for hours.

items.t: Humpback whale songs slowly change over time.
items.d: Their shared tune does not stay exactly the same forever.

items.t: Humpbacks in the same ocean region sing nearly identical songs.
items.d: Whales sharing an area can share a tune.

items.t: Bottlenose dolphins can locate prey with echolocation.
items.d: They send out high-pitched sounds and listen for echoes.

items.t: Bottlenose dolphins swallow fish whole, head first.
items.d: They do not chew the fish into little pieces.

items.t: Bottlenose dolphins can live for 40 to 60 years.
items.d: Their lives can last many decades.

items.t: Resting bottlenose dolphins often swim slowly in tight groups.
items.d: They surface to breathe at steady, careful intervals.

items.t: The sperm whale is the largest toothed whale.
items.d: Unlike baleen whales, toothed whales have teeth.

items.t: Sperm whales routinely dive about 610 meters deep.
items.d: A dive can last about 45 minutes.

items.t: A sperm whale has 20 to 26 large teeth on each side of its lower jaw.
items.d: Most of its large teeth are in the bottom jaw.

items.t: Blue whales can grow about 34 meters long.
items.d: The largest can weigh about 150,000 kilograms.

items.t: Blue whales feed almost entirely on tiny krill.
items.d: Krill are small animals that look a little like shrimp.

items.t: A very large blue whale may eat about 5,400 kilograms of krill in a day.
items.d: An enormous whale can gather food that is very small.

items.t: Blue whales may live about 80 to 90 years.
items.d: A blue whale's life can span many human generations.

items.t: Blue whales are among the loudest animals on Earth.
items.d: Another whale may hear a blue whale from about 1,600 kilometers away.

items.t: Gray whales migrate about 16,000 kilometers round trip each year.
items.d: This is one of the longest yearly journeys made by any mammal.

items.t: Gray whales find food by rolling sideways near the sea floor.
items.d: They suck up sediment and food from the bottom.

items.t: A newborn gray whale is about 4.3 to 4.9 meters long.
items.d: It weighs about 900 kilograms at birth.

items.t: Gray whales have calves in warm waters near Baja California, Mexico.
items.d: They spend the winter in the area's lagoons and bays.

items.t: Bowhead whales have the longest baleen plates of any whale.
items.d: Baleen helps them strain food from seawater.

items.t: A bowhead whale can push through sea ice about 20 centimeters thick.
items.d: Its thick skull helps it open a breathing place in the ice.

items.t: Beluga calves are dark gray, not white.
items.d: Their bodies turn white as they grow up.

items.t: A beluga has a flexible, round forehead called a melon.
items.d: The melon helps focus and shape the beluga's sounds.

items.t: Belugas make whistles, squeals, moos, chirps and clicks.
items.d: Their many different sounds make a lively underwater chorus.

items.t: Belugas can nod and turn their heads from side to side.
items.d: They can do this because their neck bones are not fused together.

items.t: Harbor porpoises are shy and usually do not bow-ride boats.
items.d: Bow-riding means swimming in the wave at the front of a moving boat.

items.t: Harbor porpoises mainly eat fish that swim in schools.
items.d: Their foods include herring and mackerel.

items.t: The vaquita lives only in the northern Gulf of California, Mexico.
items.d: This small porpoise has a very limited natural home.

items.t: Vaquitas have black patches around their eyes and lips.
items.d: These dark markings stand out on their pale faces.

items.t: The vaquita is only about 1.5 meters long.
items.d: It is one of the smallest whales, dolphins or porpoises.

items.t: Each North Atlantic right whale has a unique pattern of head bumps.
items.d: The pale bumps are called callosities.

items.t: Right whales strain tiny animals called copepods from seawater.
items.d: Their baleen plates filter these tiny crustaceans from the water.

items.t: A spinner dolphin can turn up to four times during one leap.
items.d: It spins its body while flying through the air.

items.t: Spinner dolphins hunt at night and rest during the day.
items.d: Their daily rest lasts about four to five hours.

items.t: Spinner dolphins may gather in schools of hundreds at night.
items.d: During the day, they split into much smaller groups.

items.t: The fin whale is the second-largest whale species.
items.d: Only the blue whale is larger.

items.t: A fin whale's lower jaw has different colors on each side.
items.d: The left side is dark, while the right side is white.

items.t: Male and female walruses both grow tusks.
items.d: A tusk is a tooth that grows out of the mouth.

items.t: A walrus tusk can grow about 1 metre long.
items.d: That is about as long as a guitar.

items.t: A big male Pacific walrus can weigh over 2,000 kilograms.
items.d: That is heavier than a small car.

items.t: Walruses mostly eat clams and other shellfish.
items.d: They find this food down on the sea floor.

items.t: A walrus sucks the meat out of shellfish with its lips.
items.d: It presses its lips around the shell and slurps the meat out.

items.t: A thick layer of blubber keeps a walrus warm.
items.d: Blubber is fat under the skin, like a built-in winter coat.

items.t: A walrus has a throat sac that helps it float.
items.d: The sac fills with air and works like a bubble.

items.t: A newborn walrus weighs about 33 to 85 kilograms.
items.d: That is as heavy as a child up to a grown-up.

items.t: Sea otters use rocks as tools to open shellfish.
items.d: They are one of the few mammals that use tools.

items.t: Sleeping sea otters sometimes hold paws.
items.d: They float side by side with their paws together.

items.t: Resting sea otters gather in groups called rafts.
items.d: A raft is usually all males or all females.

items.t: A sea otter stores food in a loose skin pouch.
items.d: The pouch lies under the arm and across the chest.

items.t: A sea otter may wrap itself in kelp to rest.
items.d: The kelp holds it so it does not drift away.

items.t: A sea otter can hold its breath for about five minutes.
items.d: That is much longer than a person usually can.

items.t: Sea otters help kelp forests by eating sea urchins.
items.d: Eating urchins keeps their numbers down, which protects the kelp.

items.t: A manatee can grow up to about 4 metres long.
items.d: Some weigh as much as about 590 kilograms.

items.t: Manatees eat more than 60 kinds of plants.
items.d: These plants grow in fresh water and in the sea.

items.t: A manatee can swim about 30 kilometres an hour.
items.d: It only goes that fast in a short burst.

items.t: Old stories link manatees with mermaids.
items.d: Mermaids are make-believe. Manatees are real.

items.t: Manatees' closest relatives are elephants and hyraxes.
items.d: A hyrax is a small mammal. The family link is a real surprise.

items.t: Manatees are often called sea cows.
items.d: The name fits their slow, peaceful, plant-eating life.

items.t: A manatee's tail is shaped like a paddle.
items.d: It is broad and flat, like the blade of a boat paddle.

items.t: A manatee comes up to breathe before 20 minutes pass.
items.d: It has lungs, so it must reach the air.

items.t: Dugongs eat mostly seagrass.
items.d: Seagrass is a plant that grows underwater in the sea.

items.t: A newborn dugong is about 1.2 metres long.
items.d: It already weighs about 30 kilograms.

items.t: Sea lions and fur seals are called eared seals.
items.d: A small ear flap shows on each side of the head.

items.t: True seals are also called earless seals.
items.d: They have no ear flaps, but they can still hear.

items.t: Eared seals swim mostly with their front flippers.
items.d: They pull forward by stroking with those flippers.

items.t: True seals and walruses mostly swim with back flippers.
items.d: They move the back flippers and lower body from side to side.

items.t: Blubber can be as much as half of a seal's weight.
items.d: In a 100 kilogram seal, up to 50 kilograms can be blubber.

items.t: The southern elephant seal is the biggest seal.
items.d: It can be about 5 metres long and weigh over 3,000 kilograms.

items.t: Elephant seals are named for the male's big nose.
items.d: That nose looks a bit like a short elephant trunk.

items.t: An elephant seal can hold its breath over 100 minutes.
items.d: That is longer than 1 hour and 40 minutes.

items.t: Weddell seals keep breathing holes open in the ice.
items.d: A hole lets them breathe while the sea is frozen over.

items.t: Weddell seals can dive about 600 metres deep.
items.d: On a deep dive they can stay down for up to an hour.

items.t: Weddell seals live all around Antarctica.
items.d: They are at home in the cold seas around that continent.

items.t: A California sea lion's usual call is a bark.
items.d: Barking is the sound they use most.

items.t: California sea lions use whiskers to feel underwater vibrations.
items.d: The whiskers notice tiny vibrations moving through the water.

items.t: California sea lions live along North America's west coast.
items.d: They rest on islands along that same coast.

items.t: California sea lions are clever and can be trained.
items.d: Trainers can teach them to perform different tasks.

items.t: Every harbor seal has its own pattern of spots.
items.d: Spots can be dark on light fur, or light on dark fur.

items.t: A harbor seal pup can swim within hours of birth.
items.d: Within hours, the pup can dive too.

items.t: The Hawaiian monk seal is the only seal native to Hawaii.
items.d: No other seal species has Hawaii as its natural home.

items.t: A harp seal pup is born with a white coat.
items.d: That coat lasts about 2 to 3 weeks, then the pup sheds it.

items.t: Adult harp seals have a dark harp shape on the back.
items.d: The mark can also look like a wishbone.

items.t: The Steller sea lion is the biggest seal with ear flaps.
items.d: Big males can weigh up to about 1,120 kilograms.

items.t: A ringed seal mother builds a birth lair in the ice.
items.d: Her pup is born inside this hollow in the thick ice.

items.t: The monk seal's Hawaiian name means a dog that runs in rough water.
items.d: The words picture a dog running through choppy waves.

items.t: A great white shark has about 300 triangular teeth with jagged edges.
items.d: That is a lot of teeth for one mouth!

items.t: Great white teeth sit in rows like a conveyor belt. Back teeth move forward to replace lost ones.
items.d: So a shark always has fresh teeth ready.

items.t: Great whites can sense the tiny electric fields that animals make using special pits.
items.d: The pits are called ampullae of Lorenzini.

items.t: Great white sharks are thought to live for more than 70 years.
items.d: That is about as long as a very long human life.

items.t: Great whites are partly warm-blooded, so they can stay active even in cooler water.
items.d: Most fish are fully cold-blooded.

items.t: Great whites can swim up to about 24 km/h using their strong tails.
items.d: That is about as fast as a speedy bike ride.

items.t: A baby great white is already about 1.5 metres long when it is born.
items.d: It swims away from its mother right away.

items.t: A great white can smell a single drop of blood from about half a kilometre away.
Sharks do not chew. They tear off chunks of food and swallow them whole.
A great white can go a month or two without a big meal.
Shark skin is so rough that people have sometimes used it like sandpaper.
The whale shark is the biggest fish in the whole world.
items.d: It is a shark, not a whale.

items.t: The whale shark is one of only three kinds of sharks that filter tiny food out of the water.
A whale shark has sieve-like pads in its mouth that strain small food from the water.
items.d: They are thought to be changed gill rakers.

items.t: A whale shark has hundreds of rows of tiny teeth, but it does not use them to eat.
Every whale shark has its own pattern of spots and stripes, like a fingerprint.
Whale sharks may live for 80 to 130 years.
A whale shark's eggs hatch inside its mother, and she then gives birth to live young.
Whale sharks eat mostly tiny plankton, krill, fish eggs and small fish that swim in schools.
A whale shark's skin can be up to 15 cm thick.
items.d: That is about as thick as a ruler is long.

items.t: A whale shark swims with its mouth open and filters whatever floats into it.
A hammerhead shark has a wide head with pores that sense the electric fields of other animals.
A hammerhead can see above and below at the same time, because its eyes are far apart on its wide head.
The great hammerhead is the biggest hammerhead and is about 4 metres long on average.
Scientists think a hammerhead's odd head shape helps it sense, turn and handle food.
items.d: That head shape is called a cephalofoil.

items.t: The giant oceanic manta ray can be about 7 metres wide.
items.d: That is wider than a big truck is long.

items.t: Manta rays have one of the biggest brains compared with body size of any fish.
Manta rays are filter feeders. They strain tiny plankton out of the water.
Mantas have horn-shaped fins on each side of their mouths.
Mantas sometimes leap right out of the water, and scientists are not sure why.
Mantas visit cleaning stations on coral reefs to have parasites removed.
Stingrays are cartilage fish. Their skeletons are made of bendy cartilage, not bone.
items.d: Your ears and nose have cartilage too.

items.t: A stingray breathes through openings called spiracles, just behind its eyes.
A stingray's eyes are on top of its body, but its mouth is underneath.
Stingrays have flat teeth that crush hard shells.
Stingrays hide by stirring up sand and settling down beneath it.
A shark's skeleton is made of light, bendy cartilage instead of bone.
Shark skin is covered in tiny tooth-like scales called dermal denticles.
Sharks keep growing new teeth all their lives. Some lose 30,000 or more.
There are more than 500 kinds of shark in the world.
The dwarf lanternshark is only about 17 cm long.
Sharks have a lateral line that feels water moving and pressure changing nearby.
Sharks have no gas-filled swim bladder like bony fish. A big oil-filled liver helps them float.
The Greenland shark may be the longest-living animal with a backbone, possibly living for centuries.
The shortfin mako is the fastest known shark, reaching about 74 km/h in short bursts.
The cookiecutter shark is small, only about 42 to 56 cm long.
The cookiecutter shark glows green, the strongest glow known in any shark.
The cookiecutter shark swims up and down as much as 3 km each day.
The Greenland shark swims very slowly, at about 0.3 metres per second.
items.d: That is slower than most people walk.

items.t: Megalodon was a giant shark that lived about 23 to 3.6 million years ago. It is extinct now.
Piranhas have one row of sharp teeth in each jaw.
items.d: The upper jaw and the lower jaw each have one row.

items.t: Piranhas eat many kinds of food, including plant material.
items.d: They are not animals that eat only meat.

items.t: Most piranhas are about 12 to 35 cm long.
items.d: Their size varies among species.

items.t: Piranhas are native to the Amazon basin in South America.
items.d: A river basin is the land drained by a river and its smaller waterways.

items.t: Despite their name, electric eels are not true eels.
items.d: They are not closely related to true eels.

items.t: Electric eels get most of their oxygen by breathing air.
items.d: They rise to the surface and gulp air.

items.t: An electric eel can grow to about 2 m long and weigh about 20 kg.
items.d: That is longer than many adults are tall.

items.t: Electric eels live on muddy river bottoms and sometimes in swamps.
items.d: They are native to South America.

items.t: An electric eel's electric organs contain cells called electrocytes.
items.d: Electrocytes are modified muscle cells.

items.t: Some electric eels in human care have lived for more than 20 years.
items.d: These were eels that people kept and cared for.

items.t: Electric eels keep growing throughout their lives.
items.d: An older electric eel may be larger than a younger one.

items.t: An arapaima can grow to about 3 m long.
items.d: It is among the largest freshwater fish.

items.t: Arapaima must rise to the water's surface to breathe air.
items.d: Unlike most fish, they depend on air from above the water.

items.t: An arapaima has a modified swim bladder that works much like a lung.
items.d: Its lung-like tissue takes oxygen from the air.

items.t: Arapaima scales have a hard outer layer that acts like armour.
items.d: The outer layer is hardened with minerals.

items.t: Arapaima are native to the Amazon and Essequibo basins.
items.d: Both river basins are in South America.

items.t: Arapaima can live in lakes with very little oxygen in the water.
items.d: Breathing air at the surface helps them live there.

items.t: Some sturgeon live for well over 100 years.
items.d: Some do not become adults until they are at least 20 years old.

items.t: Sturgeon appeared about 174 to 201 million years ago in the fossil record.
items.d: Their group has existed since the time of dinosaurs.

items.t: Sturgeon have five rows of bony plates called scutes.
items.d: The scutes form armour along their bodies.

items.t: A sturgeon has four whisker-like barbels near its toothless mouth.
items.d: The barbels are sense organs that help it explore.

items.t: The sturgeon family contains 27 species.
items.d: All belong to the fish family called Acipenseridae.

items.t: Catfish are named for barbels that look like a cat's whiskers.
items.d: Barbels are feeler-like sense organs near the mouth.

items.t: Taste is an important sense that catfish use to find food.
items.d: Their sense of taste helps guide them toward a meal.

items.t: Catfish generally have no scales.
items.d: Their bodies often have bare skin instead.

items.t: Catfish come in an unusually wide range of sizes.
items.d: The catfish group includes both tiny fish and very large ones.

items.t: Catfish are one of the most varied groups of vertebrate animals.
items.d: Vertebrates are animals with backbones, and this group has many kinds.

items.t: Salmon usually begin life in fresh water, live at sea, then return to fresh water.
items.d: This type of life cycle is called anadromous.

items.t: Adult salmon return to the fresh water where they were born to reproduce.
items.d: Their journey can lead back to the same home stream.

items.t: Salmon use memories of smells to find their home stream.
items.d: Their sense of smell helps guide the journey.

items.t: Some salmon travel more than 1,400 km upstream.
items.d: That is a very long swim against the river's flow.

items.t: Female salmon dig shallow nests called redds in river gravel.
items.d: A redd is a hollow where salmon lay their eggs.

items.t: Salmon carry nutrients from the ocean into rivers and nearby land.
items.d: These nutrients include nitrogen and phosphorus.

items.t: Depending on the species, salmon spend about one to five years at sea.
items.d: They later return to fresh water to reproduce.

items.t: Koi are colourful ornamental carp first developed in Japan in the 1820s.
items.d: They originated in Japan's Niigata region.

items.t: Common carp can grow up to 120 cm long and weigh more than 40 kg.
items.d: That is a very large carp.

items.t: Common carp are omnivores.
items.d: Omnivores eat both plant and animal material.

items.t: Common carp have two pairs of barbels around their mouths.
items.d: One pair sits at the corners of the upper lip.

items.t: People have introduced common carp to most continents and about 59 countries.
items.d: They now live far beyond their original range.

items.t: Common carp do not have a stomach.
items.d: Food moves through their digestive system without entering a stomach.

items.t: Trout are close relatives of salmon.
items.d: Some trout also have life cycles that include journeys between rivers and the sea.

items.t: Trout usually prefer clear, cool water at about 10 to 16°C.
items.d: They can live in streams, wetlands, and lakes.

items.t: Steelhead are a coastal sea-going form of rainbow trout.
items.d: They spend time at sea and return to fresh water.

items.t: Some sea-going trout spend up to three years at sea.
items.d: They later return to freshwater streams to reproduce.

items.t: Trout mostly eat other fish and soft-bodied water animals.
items.d: Their food can include aquatic invertebrates, animals without backbones.

items.t: Goldfish are native to China.
items.d: China is their original home.

items.t: Goldfish belong to the carp family.
items.d: The scientific name of this fish family is Cyprinidae.

items.t: Goldfish in human care can live for more than 10 years.
items.d: They can be long-term animal companions.

items.t: Goldfish can remember things for at least three months.
items.d: The popular claim that they remember for only three seconds is a myth.

items.t: Some ocean animals make their own light. This is called bioluminescence.
items.d: It is light made by a living creature, not by the Sun or a lamp.

items.t: Glowing sea animals make light with a chemical reaction inside the body.
items.d: Energy from the reaction leaves as light, a bit like a glow stick.

items.t: Glowing animals live from the sunny sea surface all the way to the seafloor.
items.d: Some glow near the waves. Others glow in the deep, where it is always dark.

items.t: Ocean animals glow to find food, signal friends, or slip away safely.
items.d: A flash can send a signal, draw food closer, or help the animal slip away.

items.t: Most living light in the ocean is blue or green.
items.d: In the deep sea, the glows you would see are mostly blue-green.

items.t: Some deep-sea animals glow on their bellies to hide their shadow.
items.d: From below, their light matches the daylight above, so they blend in.

items.t: In the deep eastern Pacific, about 76% of the main animal groups can glow.
items.d: That means making light is very common for animals in that deep water.

items.t: The ocean sunfish is the world's largest bony fish.
items.d: It is a giant of the sea, and its round body looks like a big plate.

items.t: The ocean sunfish is called Mola mola, Latin for a round millstone.
items.d: A millstone is a round stone used to grind grain, and the fish is round too.

items.t: Ocean sunfish eat mostly jellyfish.
items.d: They also eat small fish, tiny drifting animals, and algae.

items.t: A sunfish can jump about 3 metres out of the water.
items.d: That is about 10 feet, higher than the top of a normal door.

items.t: A mother ocean sunfish can release up to 300 million eggs at one time.
items.d: That is more eggs than any other known animal with a backbone.

items.t: A sunfish's teeth are joined into one beak.
items.d: The teeth grow together, so the mouth works like a beak.

items.t: One young sunfish grew from 26 kg to 399 kg in 15 months.
items.d: It gained 373 kg. That is a huge jump in a little over a year.

items.t: The father seahorse carries the eggs in a pouch on his body.
items.d: The mother can place up to 1,500 eggs in that pouch.

items.t: Seahorses have no stomach, so they must eat very often.
items.d: Without a stomach, food cannot stay stored for a big meal later.

items.t: A seahorse can move each eye on its own, at the same time.
items.d: The two eyes can look in different directions, like a chameleon's eyes.

items.t: The dwarf seahorse is one of the slowest fish, at about 1.5 metres per hour.
items.d: In one hour it swims only about 1.5 metres, a few of your steps.

items.t: Seahorses swim upright, and they do not have a tail fin.
items.d: Most fish push with a tail fin. A seahorse stays standing in the water.

items.t: Clownfish live among sea anemones, which shelter them and their nests.
items.d: The anemone's stinging tentacles make a safe home for the clownfish.

items.t: A coat of slime keeps a clownfish from being stung by an anemone.
items.d: The slime covers the fish, so the stinging tentacles do not hurt it.

items.t: Clownfish are all born male. The biggest one becomes female.
items.d: Every clownfish starts as a male. Only the largest in the group changes.

items.t: A father clownfish guards the eggs and fans them with his fins.
items.d: The eggs hatch in about six to eight days.

items.t: An anglerfish lure is the tip of a fin ray on its back.
items.d: It grows from the front part of the back fin, and the tip is the bait.

items.t: A deep-sea anglerfish lure glows because glowing bacteria live in it.
items.d: The bacteria make the light that shines in the dark.

items.t: In some deep-sea anglerfish, a tiny male attaches to a much bigger female.
items.d: He can stay stuck to her, and sometimes their bodies join.

items.t: The vampire squid does not eat blood. It eats drifting bits of food.
items.d: Those drifting bits are called marine snow, like a slow shower of leftovers.

items.t: The vampire squid lives about 600 to 900 metres down, with little oxygen.
items.d: It is always dark there, and the water holds very little oxygen.

items.t: Tiny light organs called photophores cover almost all of a vampire squid.
items.d: These spots can shine, so the squid can glow in the deep dark.

items.t: The Mariana snailfish lives about 6,200 to 8,100 metres deep.
items.d: It is one of the deepest fish known in the ocean.

items.t: The Mariana snailfish is pale and tadpole-shaped, up to about 29 cm long.
items.d: That is only about as long as a school ruler, even in the deepest sea.

items.t: A pelican eel's mouth is huge, and its jaw is about a quarter of its length.
items.d: The mouth is much bigger than the slim body behind it.

items.t: The tip of a pelican eel's tail glows pink and can flash red.
items.d: A small organ at the tail tip makes that pink glow and those red flashes.

items.t: The barreleye has a clear dome head and tube-shaped eyes that point up.
items.d: The eyes look like barrels and can see upward through the clear head.

items.t: The giant oarfish is the longest bony fish alive, up to about 8 metres.
items.d: Eight metres is about as long as two cars parked end to end.

items.t: Oarfish mostly eat tiny drifting animals, such as krill and shrimp.
items.d: Krill and shrimp are small, so even a giant oarfish eats tiny meals.

items.t: People thought coelacanths had died out about 66 million years ago.
items.d: In 1938, a living coelacanth was found off the coast of South Africa.

items.t: Coelacanth fossils are more than 410 million years old.
items.d: Fossils show that coelacanths have a history going back that far.

items.t: Living coelacanths give birth to live babies, which is rare in fish.
items.d: Most fish lay eggs. Coelacanth young grow inside and are born live.

items.t: Many lanternfish rise toward the surface at dusk and sink back before dawn.
items.d: They spend the bright day deeper down, and the night closer to the top.

items.t: Atlantic bluefin tuna are warm-blooded, which is unusual for a fish.
items.d: They can manage their body heat instead of always matching the sea.

items.t: Flying fish usually glide about 50 metres, and up to 400 metres.
items.d: Rising air under them can stretch a short glide into a much longer one.

items.t: Flying fish can travel faster than 70 kilometres per hour.
items.d: They speed up in the water, then burst into the air and glide.

items.t: Flying fish use wide side fins like wings to lift them in the air.
items.d: Those fins act like little wings and make lift, the force that holds them up.

items.t: The opah is the only fish known to keep its whole body warm.
items.d: Most fish stay the same temperature as the water. An opah does not.

items.t: An opah stays warm with heat from its flapping side fins.
items.d: A heat swap in its gills keeps that warmth in the blood.

items.t: A swordfish can warm its eyes 10 to 15 degrees Celsius above the water.
items.d: Warmer eyes help it see while it hunts in cold, deep water.

items.t: A yellowfin tuna can swim at up to about 21 metres per second.
items.d: That is about 75 kilometres per hour (about 47 miles per hour).

items.t: A sailfish has a huge back fin that can stretch the whole length of its back.
items.d: The fin is called a sail because it is so big along the fish's back.

items.t: Corals are animals, not plants or rocks. Each tiny one is called a polyp.
items.d: Most polyps are only a few millimetres across.

items.t: Tiny algae live inside most reef-building corals and share their food with them.
items.d: The coral gives the algae a safe home in return.

items.t: The algae inside coral can give it up to 90 percent of the food they make.
items.d: The coral and algae are partners, so both gain.

items.t: The bright colours of many stony corals come from the tiny algae living inside them.
When a stressed coral lets its algae go, it turns bright white. This is called bleaching.
items.d: The coral loses its colour and its main food helper.

items.t: Warmer sea water is linked to widespread coral bleaching.
Some corals can take in a different kind of algae, which may help them handle heat better.
Reef-building corals need clear water so sunlight can reach the algae inside them.
items.d: Algae use sunlight to make food, like plants do.

items.t: Coral reefs can thrive in tropical water with very few nutrients.
items.d: Coral and algae pass nutrients back and forth.

items.t: A coral colony is made of many polyps that are genetically identical.
items.d: It is like a city of copies living together.

items.t: Stony corals build a hard skeleton out of calcium carbonate.
items.d: Over many years these skeletons build up into reefs.

items.t: Soft corals have no hard skeleton like stony corals do.
Many corals tuck in their tentacles by day and spread them out at night to catch plankton.
Coral tentacles have stinging cells that help catch tiny food floating by.
Corals of one kind often release eggs and sperm all together at night, often near a full moon.
items.d: It is a huge underwater show.

items.t: Animals much like today's reef-building corals first appeared about 535 million years ago.
About 25 percent of all marine species live in, on or around coral reefs.
items.d: That is from a tiny part of the ocean.

items.t: Coral reefs are as full of different life as tropical rainforests.
Healthy coral reefs can soak up up to 97 percent of a wave's energy.
items.d: This helps protect the coast from big waves.

items.t: About one billion people benefit from coral reefs, directly or indirectly.
Coral reefs cover less than 0.1 percent of the world's ocean area.
Most coral reefs like water that is about 26 to 27 degrees Celsius.
Reef-building tropical corals do not grow deeper than about 50 metres.
items.d: Deeper down, there is too little sunlight.

items.t: Healthy tropical reefs grow outward only about 1 to 3 centimetres a year.
An atoll is a ring-shaped reef that circles a lagoon.
A barrier reef is separated from the shore by a deep channel or lagoon.
Charles Darwin explained that a reef around a sinking volcanic island can turn into an atoll.
items.d: First a fringing reef, then a barrier reef, then a ring.

items.t: Some coral reefs are older than old-growth redwood forests.
items.d: Reefs are called living museums of history.

items.t: The Great Barrier Reef stretches over 2,300 kilometres along Australia's coast.
The Great Barrier Reef is made of over 2,900 separate reefs.
items.d: It also includes about 900 islands.

items.t: More than 1,500 kinds of fish live on the Great Barrier Reef.
Sea stars are not fish. They have no gills, scales or fins.
There are about 2,000 kinds of sea stars.
items.d: They live only in salt water.

items.t: Sea stars have no blood. They pump sea water through their bodies instead.
Sea stars walk on tiny tube feet under their arms.
items.d: An adult sunflower sea star has about 15,000 of them.

items.t: Sea stars, sand dollars, sea urchins and sea cucumbers are all echinoderms.
items.d: They share a five-point body pattern.

items.t: Some sea stars have 10, 20 or even 40 arms.
A sea star can grow back an arm it has lost.
items.d: A few can even grow a whole new body from one arm.

items.t: Sea stars have eyespots at the tips of their arms that sense light.
A jellyfish is about 95 percent water.
Jellyfish have no brain, no blood and no heart.
items.d: A simple net of nerves lets them sense light and smell.

items.t: A jellyfish has just one opening that works as its mouth and its exit.
A jellyfish's middle layer is a thick, bouncy jelly called mesoglea.
A box jellyfish has 24 eyes, and some of them have lenses.
items.d: Its bell is shaped like a box.

items.t: A moon jelly is almost see-through. You can see four horseshoe shapes inside.
A sea urchin chews with an organ called Aristotle's lantern.
A sea urchin walks using lots of bendy tube feet and its spines.
Some sea urchins can live for more than 100 years.
Sponges are animals with no true organs, and their bodies are full of tiny pores.
items.d: Water flows through the pores, and the sponge filters food from it.

items.t: Clownfish live safely among sea anemone tentacles that sting other fish.
items.d: A mucus coating on the clownfish helps it avoid the stings.

items.t: Octopuses have rounded bodies, bulging eyes and eight long arms.
The common octopus has the scientific name Octopus vulgaris.
items.d: Scientific names help people identify the same species worldwide.

items.t: An octopus can swim backward by blasting water through a tube called a siphon.
items.d: The water pushes the octopus in the opposite direction.

items.t: Octopuses explore small openings with their arms while searching for food.
Octopuses can change colour to blend in or communicate with other octopuses.
Octopuses usually live alone in dens made from rocks.
Some octopuses arrange rocks to make a door for their den.
items.d: They can close the rock door behind them after going inside.

items.t: An octopus has three hearts, one main heart and two hearts for its gills.
Octopus blood looks blue because it contains a copper-rich protein.
About two-thirds of an octopus's nerve cells are in the nerve cords of its arms.
items.d: Its arms can perform complex movements and explore nearby objects.

items.t: Octopus arms contain no bones. Their muscles help support and move them.
An octopus has a hard, sharp beak around its mouth.
A giant Pacific octopus can have an arm span of up to about 4.8 metres.
The mimic octopus can copy the appearance of animals such as lionfish and sea snakes.
The veined octopus collects coconut shells and uses them to build a shelter.
Even a large octopus can squeeze through a gap only a little wider than 2.5 cm.
items.d: Its boneless body can fit through surprisingly narrow spaces.

items.t: A squid has eight arms and two longer tentacles around its mouth.
Squid travel by squirting water through a funnel, a method called jet propulsion.
Like octopuses, squid have three hearts.
Squid have colour-changing skin cells called chromatophores.
items.d: They control these cells to help match the colours around them.

items.t: A squid can release a cloud of ink to distract a nearby predator.
A squid's mouth contains a sharp beak made mainly from a material called chitin.
Most squid are no more than about 60 cm long.
Some squid make light and use it as camouflage.
items.d: Light underneath them can help hide their dark outline in the water.

items.t: Squid have giant nerve fibres that can be up to about 1 mm wide.
items.d: These wide fibres carry nerve signals very quickly.

items.t: Squid have advanced eyes that are similar in some ways to vertebrate eyes.
items.d: Vertebrates are animals with backbones, including fish and people.

items.t: A cuttlefish has an internal shell-like part called a cuttlebone.
Cuttlefish have unusual pupils shaped like the letter W.
Cuttlefish can rapidly change their skin colour to match their surroundings.
A cuttlefish has three separate hearts.
Cuttlefish blood has an unusual green-blue colour.
Cuttlefish are typically about 15 to 25 cm long.
Cuttlefish cannot see colour, but they can detect polarized light.
items.d: Polarized light has waves lined up in particular directions.

items.t: Cuttlefish skin has yellow-orange, red and brown-black colour cells.
A nautilus shell is divided into chambers on the inside.
A tube called the siphuncle runs through the chambers of a nautilus shell.
A nautilus can have from 50 to more than 90 tentacles.
Nautiluses have remained relatively unchanged for hundreds of millions of years.
A nautilus may live for more than 20 years.
items.d: That is a long life compared with many octopuses and squid.

items.t: Depending on the species, a nautilus shell is about 10 to 25 cm across.
A nautilus has a simple pinhole eye with no lens.
items.d: Light enters through a small opening instead of passing through a lens.

items.t: Molluscs are the second-largest animal group after arthropods.
items.d: Arthropods include insects, spiders and crabs. Snails, clams, squid and octopuses are all molluscs.

items.t: Molluscs make up about 23% of all named marine organisms.
items.d: They are the largest animal group in the sea by number of named species.

items.t: About 80% of known mollusc species are gastropods, the group containing snails and slugs.
The radula is a tooth-covered feeding ribbon found only in molluscs.
items.d: Many snails use it to scrape and move bits of food.

items.t: A mollusc's basic body plan includes a muscular foot.
items.d: In different molluscs, the foot can help with crawling, digging or gripping.

items.t: Molluscs have a body covering called a mantle, with a cavity used for breathing.
Fossils of snails, clams and squid relatives date back more than 500 million years.
Some molluscs produce pearls and the shiny material called mother of pearl.
Giant clams can grow to about 120 cm across and weigh more than 200 kg.
A peacock mantis shrimp can snap its club at about 83 km/h.
items.d: It reaches that speed from a standstill, with no running start.

items.t: Mantis shrimp eyes have 12 to 16 kinds of light-sensing cells.
items.d: Most humans have only four visual pigments.

items.t: One mantis shrimp eye can judge distance by itself.
items.d: Each eye has trinocular vision, which means it can see depth on its own.

items.t: Some mantis shrimp pairs stay together for up to 20 years.
items.d: Only some species do this, and those pairs can last a very long time.

items.t: Most mantis shrimp grow to about 10 cm long.
items.d: The zebra mantis shrimp is much bigger and can reach 38 cm.

items.t: Shrimp paddle forward, but they zip backward to get away.
items.d: Little paddles called swimmerets push them ahead. A tail flick sends them back.
