Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system.
Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system. It is even bigger than Mercury.
Evidence shows that Jupiter's moon Europa has a vast ocean beneath its icy crust.
Jupiter has faint rings. The Voyager 1 spacecraft discovered them in 1979.
Saturn is about nine times wider than Earth.
If Earth were a nickel, Saturn would be about as big as a volleyball.
Saturn is less dense than water, so it could float in an enormous bathtub.
A day on Saturn lasts only about 10.7 hours.
Saturn's rings contain billions of small chunks of ice and rock coated with dust.
Saturn has seasons because its axis is tilted, much like Earth's.
Uranus is tilted so far that it appears to spin sideways.
Uranus was the first planet discovered with the help of a telescope.
The moons of Uranus are named for characters created by Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.
Uranus has the most extreme seasons in the solar system because of its unusual tilt.
Methane gas in Uranus's atmosphere helps give the planet its blue-green color.
Winds on Uranus can reach about 900 km per hour.
Within about five minutes of the Big Bang, most of today's helium had formed.
items.d: Then the universe cooled, and this early element-making stopped.

items.t: The universe is expanding, and the expansion is speeding up.
items.d: Space keeps stretching, and that stretch is getting quicker.

items.t: The oldest light we can see is the cosmic microwave background.
items.d: It is the earliest light astronomers can observe in the universe.

items.t: Whole atoms formed about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
items.d: It was finally cool enough for electrons to stick to atomic nuclei.

items.t: Stars are born inside huge clouds of gas and dust.
items.d: Astronomers call these giant birthplaces molecular clouds.

items.t: Gravity pulls clumps of gas together until they collapse and begin forming stars.
items.d: This happens inside huge clouds of gas and dust.

items.t: Stars make their energy by nuclear fusion deep in their cores.
items.d: Fusion releases energy, and that energy heats the star so it shines.

items.t: Some stars last a few million years. Others last trillions.
items.d: Each star has its own lifetime, and those lifetimes differ a lot.

items.t: Red dwarfs burn hydrogen so slowly they can shine for trillions of years.
items.d: They use their hydrogen little by little, so the glow lasts and lasts.

items.t: When a Sun-like star runs out of core hydrogen, it swells into a red giant.
items.d: The star expands and cools as it changes into a red giant.

items.t: A white dwarf is about Earth-sized, but far more massive than Earth.
items.d: It can be hundreds of thousands of times more massive than our planet.

items.t: Betelgeuse is an orange-red supergiant about 700 light-years away.
items.d: This huge star glows with a clear orange-red colour.

items.t: Betelgeuse is about 700 times the size of the Sun.
items.d: It is also about 15 times more massive than the Sun.

items.t: A supernova is the biggest explosion humans have ever seen.
items.d: Nothing else people have seen in space is a bigger blast.

items.t: A galaxy like the Milky Way has about two or three supernovas each century.
items.d: In our galaxy, these giant star explosions are rare.

items.t: Supernovas spread elements made inside stars out into space.
items.d: The blast carries both stored elements and newly made ones through space.

items.t: Word of the day: nebula.
items.d: A nebula is a giant cloud of dust and gas, mostly hydrogen and helium.

items.t: The Hubble Space Telescope launched on April 24, 1990.
items.d: It orbits Earth in low Earth orbit and is still working.

items.t: Some nebulae are called star nurseries because new stars form in them.
items.d: They earn that name because stars are born inside these clouds.

items.t: Webb orbits the Sun about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth.
items.d: It stays about 1 million miles away while both orbit the Sun.

items.t: The closest known nebula to Earth is the Helix Nebula.
items.d: No other known cloud of gas and dust in space sits closer to us.

items.t: Most galaxies are spirals, ellipticals, or irregulars.
items.d: Spirals swirl, ellipticals look rounder, and irregulars look messy.

items.t: The biggest galaxies hold trillions of stars.
items.d: They can stretch more than a million light-years from side to side.

items.t: The smallest galaxies have only a few thousand stars.
items.d: Some are only a few hundred light-years from side to side.

items.t: Earth sits on a Milky Way spiral arm, about halfway from the centre.
items.d: We are not in the middle of the galaxy, and not at the outer edge.

items.t: The Milky Way is a barred spiral with about 100 billion stars.
items.d: A barred spiral has a bar of stars across its bright centre.

items.t: The Sun takes about 250 million years to circle the Milky Way once.
items.d: Earth and the planets ride along with the Sun on that huge loop.

items.t: Andromeda is the closest large galaxy to the Milky Way.
items.d: It is the nearest big galactic neighbour to our own galaxy.

items.t: You can see Andromeda with your own eyes from a dark sky.
items.d: City lights hide it, so you need a night that is truly dark.

items.t: To find Andromeda, start with Cassiopeia, a W-shaped constellation.
items.d: Cassiopeia can also look like an M, depending on its tilt in the sky.

items.t: Word of the day: light-year.
items.d: A light-year is not a time. It is how far light travels in one year.

items.t: One light-year is about 9 trillion kilometres (6 trillion miles).
items.d: Light travels that whole distance in a single Earth year.

items.t: When we look at faraway objects, we are looking back in time.
items.d: Their light takes so long to arrive that we see the past, not now.

items.t: The nearest star beyond the Sun is about 4.3 light-years away.
items.d: Light from that star takes about 4.3 years to reach our planet.

items.t: A black hole is not a hole. It is matter packed into a tiny space.
items.d: A huge amount of stuff is squeezed into a very small spot.

items.t: Inside a black hole's event horizon, not even light can escape.
items.d: Gravity just inside that boundary is strong enough to hold light in.

items.t: Black holes do not suck things in like giant vacuum cleaners.
items.d: Their pull does not vacuum up everything else in space.

items.t: Our galaxy's central black hole has about 4 million times the Sun's mass.
items.d: Scientists call it Sagittarius A*.

items.t: The black hole in galaxy M87 has about 6.5 billion times the Sun's mass.
items.d: It was the first black hole astronomers ever captured in a picture.

items.t: So much data came from the first black hole photo that hard drives were shipped.
items.d: The files were so large that sending them online was not practical.

items.t: Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,000 planets around other stars.
items.d: Planets that orbit a star other than the Sun are called exoplanets.

items.t: One way to find a far planet is to watch its star's light dip.
items.d: The dip happens when the planet crosses the star. This is a transit.

items.t: The Gaia spacecraft has measured about 1.7 billion stars.
items.d: An older mission, Hipparcos, surveyed only about 118,000 stars.

items.t: The first planet found around a Sun-like star was discovered in 1995.
items.d: Its name is 51 Pegasi b, and its star is similar to our Sun.

items.t: TRAPPIST-1 is the first known system with seven Earth-sized planets.
items.d: Seven planets, each about Earth's size, circle a single star.

items.t: All seven TRAPPIST-1 planets orbit closer to their star than Mercury does to the Sun.
items.d: None of them orbits as far out as Mercury orbits our Sun.

items.t: The fastest pulsars spin hundreds of times every second.
items.d: They turn hundreds of times in about the time of one heartbeat.

items.t: The International Space Station zooms around Earth at about 8 kilometres every second.
items.d: That is about 28,000 km every hour, so fast it circles Earth in about 90 minutes.

items.t: Astronauts on the space station see 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every single day.
items.d: The station circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so day and night keep flipping.

items.t: A crew of seven people from different countries can live on the International Space Station.
items.d: They live and work together high above Earth.

items.t: The International Space Station is bigger inside than a six-bedroom house.
items.d: It is about 109 metres long from end to end.

items.t: People have lived on the International Space Station without a break since November 2000.
items.d: Crews take turns, so someone has always been on board.

items.t: Astronauts exercise at least two hours every day in space.
items.d: Without exercise, their muscles and bones would get weak.

items.t: The space station has a robotic arm called Canadarm2 that is about 17 metres long.
items.d: It helps move big pieces of the station, like a giant crane.

items.t: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 were both launched in 1977.
items.d: They have been travelling through space for decades.

items.t: Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012. Voyager 2 followed in 2018.
items.d: Interstellar space is the space between the stars.

items.t: Each Voyager carries a golden record with sounds and pictures of Earth.
items.d: A team led by scientist Carl Sagan chose what went on each record.

items.t: Voyager 1 was the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth.
items.d: That is as far as light travels in one whole day.

items.t: Apollo 11's lunar module landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
items.d: It was named Eagle, after the eagle on the mission badge.

items.t: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins were the crew of Apollo 11.
items.d: Collins stayed in orbit while the other two landed on the Moon.

items.t: Apollo 11 astronauts brought home about 21.5 kg of Moon rocks and dust.
items.d: Scientists studied them to learn about the Moon's history.

items.t: About 600 million people watched the first Moon walk live on TV.
The Apollo 11 crew splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on July 24, 1969.
items.d: Their capsule landed in the sea with parachutes.

items.t: Sputnik 1, launched on 4 October 1957, was the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth.
Sputnik 1 was a shiny metal ball about 58 cm across.
items.d: It was about as wide as a big beach ball.

items.t: Sputnik 1 sent out radio beeps that people on Earth could hear with radio receivers.
items.d: It circled Earth about once every 96 minutes.

items.t: Yuri Gagarin was the first person to travel into space, on 12 April 1961.
items.d: He flew in a spacecraft called Vostok 1.

items.t: Yuri Gagarin's space flight lasted 108 minutes and went once around Earth.
Valentina Tereshkova orbited Earth 48 times in nearly three days.
items.d: She is the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.

items.t: Sally Ride became the first American woman in space in 1983, on the shuttle Challenger.
Sally Ride used the shuttle's robotic arm to release a satellite and then catch it again.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched into orbit in 1990 on the space shuttle Discovery.
items.d: It is named after the astronomer Edwin Hubble.

items.t: Hubble was built so astronauts could fix it in space.
items.d: Five shuttle missions repaired and upgraded it.

items.t: Webb's main mirror is 6.5 metres wide and made of 18 gold-coated hexagons.
items.d: The gold helps it reflect infrared light very well.

items.t: Webb travels around the Sun about 1.5 million km from Earth.
Webb's sunshield is about the size of a tennis court and keeps the telescope cold.
items.d: It has five thin layers.

items.t: NASA's space shuttles flew 135 missions between 1981 and 2011.
The five shuttles that flew in space were Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, Atlantis and Endeavour.
Ingenuity was the first helicopter to fly on another planet, on Mars in April 2021.
items.d: It weighed only about 1.8 kg.

items.t: Ingenuity carried a tiny piece of cloth from the Wright brothers' 1903 airplane to Mars.
Curiosity, a Mars rover about the size of a car, landed on Mars on August 6, 2012.
Curiosity was lowered to Mars by a rocket-powered sky crane on ropes.
The Curiosity rover zaps rocks with a laser to find out what they are made of.
The Perseverance rover landed in Jezero Crater on Mars on February 18, 2021.
Perseverance has microphones, and it recorded the sound of wind on Mars.
Perseverance collects rock samples that a future mission might bring back to Earth.
Philae made the first soft landing on a comet on 12 November 2014.
items.d: It was carried there by the European spacecraft Rosetta.

items.t: Parker Solar Probe was launched in 2018 to study the Sun. Its heat shield is made of carbon.
In 2021, Parker Solar Probe became the first spacecraft to enter the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona.
Skylab, launched in 1973, was the first space station of the United States.
Mir was the first space station built in pieces while in orbit.
items.d: It was put together from 1986 to 1996.

items.t: Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk on March 18, 1965. It lasted about 12 minutes.
In space there is no air, so a spacesuit gives an astronaut everything needed to breathe.
Twelve people walked on the Moon during six Apollo landings.
items.d: The last landing was Apollo 17 in December 1972.

items.t: Apollo 8 was the first crewed mission to orbit the Moon.
items.d: Astronaut William Anders took the famous Earthrise photo.

items.t: A volcano is an opening where lava, small rocks, and steam reach Earth's surface.
Melted rock is magma underground. After it erupts, it is called lava.
Magma can hold trapped gas, a bit like the fizz inside a sealed soda bottle.
Cinder cones are the simplest type of volcano.
Shield volcanoes grow from runny lava flows and have wide, gently sloping sides.
items.d: From far away, their shape looks like a warrior's shield.

items.t: Volcanoes can be active, dormant, or extinct.
items.d: Dormant means sleeping.

items.t: Some eruptions blast material high into the sky. Others produce slow lava flows.
Hot spots are very hot areas deep inside Earth where lighter magma rises.
Underwater volcanoes can form where tectonic plates pull apart and magma rises.
Io, one of Jupiter's moons, has volcanic plumes erupting from its surface.
Magma rises because it is lighter than nearby solid rock.
items.d: It can gather underground in spaces called magma chambers.

items.t: What magma is made of helps decide how explosive an eruption will be.
Thin, runny magma lets gas escape easily, making eruptions gentler.
Thick magma traps gas more easily, so pressure can build inside it.
Volcanic mudflows form when hot volcanic material mixes with water, snow, or ice.
Earth's crust is about 30 km thick on average beneath land.
Earth's crust is only about 5 km thick beneath the ocean.
The mantle is Earth's biggest layer. It is about 2,900 km thick.
items.d: This rocky layer is mostly solid, but it moves very slowly.

items.t: Earth's outer core is made of liquid iron and nickel.
Earth's inner core is a solid ball made of iron and nickel.
An earthquake happens when two blocks of Earth suddenly slip past each other.
Earth has four main layers: crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core.
Earth's outer shell is split into moving plates, like pieces of a giant puzzle.
Most earthquakes happen along faults near the edges of tectonic plates.
items.d: A fault is a break between blocks of rock.

items.t: Rough plate edges can stick while the rest of each plate keeps moving.
items.d: This stores energy until the edges finally slip.

items.t: When a fault slips, seismic waves carry energy away in every direction.
items.d: These waves make the ground shake.

items.t: A small quake can be called a foreshock only after a larger quake follows it.
A main earthquake is followed by smaller earthquakes called aftershocks.
Scientists need readings from at least three seismograph stations to locate an earthquake.
One whole step up in earthquake magnitude means 10 times greater wave height on a seismogram.
One whole step up in earthquake magnitude means about 32 times more energy is released.
Most fossils begin when a plant or animal is quickly buried by sediment.
Soft body parts usually decay before fossilizing, while hard bones or shells may remain.
Many fossils form when minerals fill tiny spaces in buried remains.
items.d: This can preserve teeth, bones, shells, and wood.

items.t: A trace fossil records what an animal did instead of preserving its body.
items.d: A fossil footprint is one example.

items.t: Fossils of land animals are much scarcer than fossils of animals that lived in water.
The fossil record is incomplete, so it shows only part of life's long history.
Soft tissues rarely become fossils, but rare examples can reveal lots about ancient life.
Earth's rigid outer shell has seven or eight major plates and many smaller ones.
Tectonic plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Plate boundaries come in three main types: convergent, divergent, and transform.
items.d: Plates can move together, apart, or slide past each other.

items.t: Earth's continents were once joined in one huge land mass called Pangaea.
The Ring of Fire around the Pacific Plate is Earth's most active volcanic zone.
The Ring of Fire stretches for about 40,000 km around the Pacific Ocean.
About two-thirds of the world's active or dormant volcanoes are in the Ring of Fire.
About 90% of the world's earthquakes happen within the Ring of Fire.
The Mohs scale ranks how well minerals resist scratches, from 1 to 10.
Diamond is the hardest mineral on the Mohs scale, with a ranking of 10.
Khufu's Great Pyramid is the largest of the three main pyramids at Giza.
items.d: It is the biggest one in the famous pyramid group.

items.t: Each year the Nile flooded and left rich soil that farmers used for crops.
items.d: When the water went down, the soil it left was good for planting food.

items.t: The Nile River flows from south to north.
items.d: Face north, and the water is moving the same way you are looking.

items.t: Hatshepsut was a woman pharaoh who ruled Egypt for 21 years.
items.d: She was the ruler of Egypt for 21 years, a long time to lead a country.

items.t: Ramesses II built more monuments to himself than any other pharaoh.
items.d: A monument is something big, like a statue or temple, made so people remember you.

items.t: The Great Pyramid was the tomb of the pharaoh Khufu.
items.d: A pharaoh was the king of ancient Egypt, and this pyramid was made for him.

items.t: The Great Pyramid was built around 2600 BC and took about 26 years.
items.d: If builders started when a baby was born, that child would be 26 at the end.

items.t: The Great Pyramid once stood about 147 metres tall (about 481 feet).
items.d: About 49 floors of 3 metres each would reach that height, because 49 times 3 is 147.

items.t: The Great Pyramid was built from about 2.3 million stone blocks.
items.d: Together, those blocks weighed about 6 million tonnes.

items.t: For more than 3,700 years, the Great Pyramid was the tallest thing people had built.
items.d: Year after year, nothing built by people stood taller than this pyramid.

items.t: Thousands of workers called up for the job built the Great Pyramid.
items.d: Conscript means people who were called up by the ruler to do a job.

items.t: When it was new, the whole Great Pyramid was covered in smooth white limestone.
items.d: Casing stones made every side smooth and white.

items.t: More than one million animal mummies have been found in Egypt, and many are cats.
items.d: A great number of those animal mummies are cats.

items.t: Tutankhamun became pharaoh when he was only about 8 or 9 years old.
items.d: That is about the same age as you.

items.t: A team led by Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922.
items.d: Excavators are diggers who uncover old things. Carter led them.

items.t: Tutankhamun's tomb held more than 5,000 objects.
items.d: That is a huge number of objects to find in one tomb.

items.t: The Rosetta Stone was found in July 1799 near Rosetta, in the Nile Delta.
items.d: A French army officer found the stone in the Nile Delta.

items.t: The Rosetta Stone repeats one message in hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Greek.
items.d: Hieroglyphs and Demotic are two Egyptian scripts. The bottom text is Greek.

items.t: The Rosetta Stone's message is a decree from 196 BC praising King Ptolemy V.
items.d: A decree is an official message. This one was written to honor the king.

items.t: In 1822, Jean-Francois Champollion announced in Paris how to read hieroglyphs.
items.d: He shared the key that let people read ancient Egyptian writing again.

items.t: The Rosetta Stone has been on show at the British Museum almost nonstop since 1802.
items.d: It has been there for more than 200 years, with only a few short breaks.

items.t: The Nile is about 7,000 kilometres long, one of the longest rivers on Earth.
items.d: At 30 kilometres a day, walking along it would take more than 200 days.

items.t: Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt were joined into one land around 3150 BC.
items.d: The two lands became one country more than 5,000 years ago.

items.t: Hatshepsut is the second woman confirmed to have ruled Egypt as pharaoh.
items.d: She ruled in her own right, with the full power of a pharaoh.

items.t: Hatshepsut built a famous temple at Deir el-Bahari, across from Luxor.
items.d: It stands opposite the city of Luxor.

items.t: Hatshepsut's trading trip to Punt brought back 31 living myrrh trees.
items.d: Punt was a land they visited for trade, and the trees were still alive.

items.t: Hatshepsut was often shown wearing a false beard, a sign of pharaoh power.
items.d: The beard was not her own hair. It was a symbol that she held royal power.

items.t: Ramesses II ruled for 66 years, one of the longest reigns of any pharaoh.
items.d: A reign is the time a ruler is in charge. His lasted 66 years.

items.t: Howard Carter began working in Egypt when he was only 17.
items.d: He was a teenager, already helping to copy pictures painted in tombs.

items.t: The Great Sphinx has a human head and the body of a lion.
items.d: It is one giant statue with a person's face and a lion's body.

items.t: The Great Sphinx is about 73 metres long and about 20 metres high.
items.d: From paw to tail, the body is about 73 metres long.

items.t: The Great Sphinx was carved from the solid rock of the Giza plateau.
items.d: Workers cut it from one mass of stone that was already in the ground.

items.t: The Sphinx's nose was not shot off by cannon fire. That story is a myth.
items.d: It is a popular tale, but cannon fire did not destroy the nose.

items.t: The Great Sphinx was carved between about 2600 BC and 2500 BC.
items.d: That makes it more than 4,500 years old.

items.t: The Valley of the Kings holds at least 63 tombs, across the Nile from Luxor.
items.d: The tombs sit on the west bank of the river, opposite modern Luxor.

items.t: The Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara rises in six giant steps.
items.d: Each step is smaller than the one below it, like a stone staircase.

items.t: Imhotep, Djoser's vizier, is credited with designing the Step Pyramid.
items.d: A vizier was the pharaoh's top official, like the lead planner.

items.t: The Step Pyramid is the earliest colossal stone building in Egypt.
items.d: Colossal means giant. It was Egypt's first truly huge building of stone.

items.t: Word of the day: papyrus
items.d: Papyrus is a plant. People made writing sheets from its stem. The word paper comes from it. A letter could be written on papyrus.

items.t: Papyrus sheets were first made in Egypt as far back as the third millennium BC.
items.d: The third millennium BC means the years from about 3000 BC to 2000 BC.

items.t: Egyptians also used papyrus reeds to build boats.
items.d: The plant was useful for more than paper. People built reed boats from it.

items.t: Senet was an Egyptian board game with 30 squares in three rows of 10.
items.d: Three rows of 10 squares make 30 squares, because 3 times 10 is 30.

items.t: A senet game was found in Tutankhamun's tomb.
items.d: Finding the game in his tomb shows it was packed among his things.

items.t: Listing everything in Tutankhamun's tomb took Howard Carter nearly 10 years.
items.d: He wrote careful notes on each object, and the job lasted almost 10 years.

items.t: In 1968, Abu Simbel's temples were moved to higher ground to save them.
items.d: The whole temples were shifted to higher ground so Lake Nasser would not cover them.

items.t: Abu Simbel's Great Temple has four giant statues of Ramesses II.
items.d: Each statue is about 20 metres tall (66 feet), carved in the 13th century BC.

items.t: Cleopatra is the only ruler of her dynasty known to have learned the Egyptian language.
items.d: A dynasty is a ruling family. She was born in Alexandria and ruled from 51 BC to 30 BC.

items.t: Queen Nefertiti's famous painted bust is at the Neues Museum in Berlin.
items.d: She was the queen of Akhenaten. A bust shows the head and shoulders, and hers is painted.

items.t: The ancient Olympic Games are traditionally dated to 776 BC.
items.d: They were held at Olympia in Greece.

items.t: Ancient Olympic winners got a crown of olive leaves, not a gold medal.
items.d: A wreath of leaves was the prize for being the best.

items.t: The ancient Greeks held the Olympics every four years. That gap was called an Olympiad.
items.d: An Olympiad also became a way to count time.

items.t: Ancient Olympic athletes ran, wrestled, boxed and raced chariots.
items.d: Pankration was another event.

items.t: The word stadium comes from the stadion, a short sprint that was the first Olympic event.
items.d: So every stadium is named after a footrace.

items.t: Cynisca of Sparta was the first woman to win at the ancient Olympics, with a chariot team she owned.
A Roman legion had about 5,000 soldiers on foot. It was split into ten smaller groups called cohorts.
A Roman legionary usually signed up for 25 years of service.
items.d: That is a very long time to be a soldier.

items.t: Roman soldiers were builders too. They made roads, bridges, ports and even whole new cities.
The Romans built more than 400,000 km of roads. That is about ten times around Earth.
items.d: Earth is about 40,000 km around, so 400,000 km wraps around 10 times.

items.t: The Appian Way is one of the oldest and most important Roman roads.
items.d: Milestones along it showed travelers the numbered miles.

items.t: Ancient Greece had about 1,500 city-states, each called a polis.
items.d: City-states used different systems of rule, including democracy and aristocracy.

items.t: Greek city-states founded colonies. This spread Greek language, religion and art.
Spartan boys began their training at age seven, in a school system called the agoge.
The word democracy comes from Greek and means people power.
Cleisthenes grouped Athenians into ten groups by where they lived, not by how rich they were.
Socrates was a Greek thinker from Athens who taught by asking short questions.
items.d: He never wrote books. We know him from what his students wrote.

items.t: Plato founded the Academy, a school of ideas in Athens.
items.d: Many of his writings are conversations, called dialogues.

items.t: Aristotle tutored a boy named Alexander, who grew up to be Alexander the Great.
Aristotle was the first person to study biology in an organized way.
Archimedes was born in the seaport city of Syracuse, Sicily.
items.d: He was a Greek thinker who loved math and machines.

items.t: Archimedes explained buoyancy: fluid pushes up with the weight of the fluid an object moves aside.
items.d: That is why a boat floats.

items.t: The Colosseum is the largest ancient amphitheatre ever built, and the largest still standing.
The Colosseum could hold about 50,000 to 80,000 people.
The Colosseum had a retractable awning, the velarium, to keep sun and rain off the crowd.
Augustus was the first Roman emperor. He ruled from 27 BC to AD 14.
items.d: The month of August is named after him.

items.t: Augustus began the Pax Romana, a long period of relative peace in the Roman world.
Roman aqueducts sloped only a tiny bit, about 1 part in 4,800, so water flowed without pumps.
items.d: Gravity did all the work.

items.t: The aqueducts of Rome added up to over 415 km. Some still bring water to Rome today.
Pompeii had at least 31 bakeries, each with a wood-burning oven.
items.d: The town was buried by ash when Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79.

items.t: Julius Caesar created the Julian calendar, which the Romans used.
Julius Caesar wrote Commentaries about events in Gaul.
Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon river with his army, openly defying the Roman Senate.
Romans called breakfast ientaculum, lunch prandium and dinner cena.
Most Roman citizens visited a public bath at least once a day.
Many Romans lived in apartment blocks called insulae.
The Romans spoke Latin.
items.d: Many words in English, French, Spanish and Italian come from Latin.

items.t: The Parthenon was a temple of Athena on the Acropolis in Athens.
After Alexander's conquests, Greek culture spread into North Africa and Western Asia.
Hadrian's Wall in Britain stretches about 117 km. Work began in AD 122.
Hadrian's Wall became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
items.d: Three Roman legions built most of it in about six years.

items.t: Roman legionaries carried a big rectangular shield called a scutum.
Many Roman bridges were built so well that people still use them today.
Sparta had two kings ruling at the same time.
The Greek alphabet developed in the Archaic period of ancient Greece.
Roman soldiers spent most of their time on training and daily jobs, not on fighting.
Aristotle taught at a building in Athens called the Lyceum.
Vikings were the first Europeans known to reach North America.
Vikings began settling Iceland in the 9th century.
Vikings used an alphabet of angular letters called runes.
Many everyday English words came from the Vikings' Old Norse language.
Horned Viking helmets are a myth. There is no evidence that Vikings wore them.
Viking longships were fast and agile, using both sails and oars.
Longship builders overlapped the wooden planks that formed the hull.
items.d: This building method is called clinker-building.

items.t: Some longships had dragon-shaped carvings on their bows.
items.d: These decorated vessels were sometimes called dragonships.

items.t: The Gokstad Viking ship is nearly 24 metres long.
Longships used oars near coasts and on rivers to speed up quickly.
A Viking longship could reach about 28 kilometres per hour.
items.d: That is about 15 knots in good conditions.

items.t: Oak was a favourite wood for longships because it was strong and resisted rot.
A boy training to become a knight could become a page at about age seven.
A page training to be a knight could become a squire at about age 14.
Knights were expected to be brave, skilled and courteous.
The joust was the most popular contest at many knights' tournaments.
A motte was a flat-topped mound of earth used as the base of some castles.
A bailey was a protected yard inside a castle where the household lived.
A moat was a ditch around a castle that made tunnelling and moving towers harder.
The keep was a castle's main living place, often a great tower.
Curtain walls were tall, thick walls surrounding a castle's bailey.
A portcullis was a gridded wooden gate strengthened with metal.
items.d: It could be lowered to block a castle entrance.

items.t: Norman builders put up many castles in England after 1066.
Complete suits of plate armour appeared in Europe by about 1420.
A full suit of plate armour weighed about 15 to 25 kilograms.
A person wearing plate armour could still run, jump and move freely.
Chain mail was made from many tiny linked rings of iron or steel.
Warriors usually wore a shirt of chain mail beneath their plate armour.
Jousting was very popular with Norman-English knights.
A tilt barrier kept jousting horses apart so they would not collide.
Jousting is the official state sport of Maryland in the United States.
L'Anse aux Meadows is a Viking site at the northern tip of Newfoundland, Canada.
L'Anse aux Meadows became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978.
The Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows dates to about the year 1000.
Tree rings show that Vikings cut wood at L'Anse aux Meadows in 1021.
Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad found the Viking site at L'Anse aux Meadows.
items.d: They were Norwegian. Helge was an explorer and Anne Stine was an archaeologist.

items.t: More than 800 Norse objects have been uncovered at L'Anse aux Meadows.
The Bayeux Tapestry is nearly 70 metres long but only about 50 centimetres tall.
The Bayeux Tapestry shows events from England and Normandy in the 11th century.
The Bayeux Tapestry is really an embroidery because its pictures were stitched.
The Bayeux Tapestry contains the first known picture of Halley's Comet.
The final scenes of the Bayeux Tapestry are missing.
Traditional English longbows were made from yew wood.
Some luxury medieval books used vellum made from stretched calf skin.
A manuscript is truly illuminated only if its decoration includes gold or silver.
The Book of Kells is the best-known illuminated manuscript in the English-speaking world.
Medieval craft workers trained as apprentices, then journeymen, then masters.
Guilds controlled who was allowed to trade in many medieval towns.
Guilds kept shared funds to help members who were ill or elderly.
Indus Valley cities had some of the world's first known city sanitation systems.
items.d: These systems carried dirty water away from homes and streets.

items.t: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were very large Indus cities.
items.d: Each city likely held about 30,000 to 60,000 people.

items.t: Indus people carved stone seals with pictures of animals.
items.d: A common stone for these seals was called steatite.

items.t: No one has learned to read Indus Valley writing yet.
items.d: We can see the signs, but we still do not know what they mean.

items.t: The Indus Valley civilization lasted about 2,000 years.
items.d: That is about 3300 BCE to 1300 BCE. BCE means before the year 1.

items.t: Mohenjo-daro had a huge, well-built bath called the Great Bath.
items.d: Enormous means truly huge. Well-built means the makers were very careful.

items.t: Aryabhata, in Gupta India, studied place value and pi.
items.d: He studied how a digit's place changes its value, and he got pi, a circle number, to four decimal places.

items.t: The base-10 place value number system began in Gupta India.
items.d: In 10, the 1 means one ten. In 100, that 1 means one hundred.

items.t: Farmers found the Terracotta Army while digging a well.
items.d: They made the surprise find on 29 March 1974.

items.t: The clay army was made for Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor.
items.d: An emperor is the ruler of an empire.

items.t: Three pits hold more than 8,000 clay soldiers.
items.d: That is a huge crowd of statues, all made to look like soldiers.

items.t: The clay soldiers' faces do not all look the same.
items.d: Stand them in a row, and you would see a new face each time.

items.t: Long ago, the clay soldiers were painted in color.
items.d: The colors came from precious stones that had been ground up.

items.t: All Great Wall sections together run about 21,196 km.
items.d: That is about 13,170 miles. It is not one single wall, but many parts.

items.t: The best-known parts of the Great Wall were built by the Ming.
items.d: The Ming dynasty was a family line of rulers that built those famous sections.

items.t: The earliest Great Wall parts date to the 7th century BC.
items.d: BC means before the year 1, so these walls are very old.

items.t: The Great Wall had watchtowers along its length.
items.d: Barracks were buildings where the wall's guards could stay.

items.t: Early Chinese compasses used a magnetic rock called lodestone.
items.d: People called one kind a south-governor because it showed south.

items.t: People traditionally credit Cai Lun with the invention of paper.
items.d: Cai Lun was an official at the Han dynasty court in China.

items.t: Word of the day: Mesopotamia
items.d: It means land between rivers. The Tigris and Euphrates run through it.

items.t: Ancient Mesopotamia is credited with inventing the wheel.
items.d: A wheel lets people roll heavy loads instead of dragging them.

items.t: Polynesian sailors steered by stars low in the night sky.
items.d: They aimed at a star near the horizon, then picked a new star as it rose.

items.t: Birds helped Polynesian sailors find land in the open ocean.
items.d: Sailors went against the birds' morning path and followed them at night.

items.t: Historic Polynesian sailors are not known to have used navigation tools on board.
items.d: Ocean swells travel in a straight direction, helping sailors check their course.

items.t: Polynesian voyaging canoes had two hulls side by side.
items.d: The hulls were equal in length and tied firmly side by side.

items.t: Polynesian sailors settled Hawaii, Easter Island, and New Zealand.
items.d: Those places are far apart, and the sailors reached them by canoe.

items.t: Marshall Islanders made stick charts of islands and waves.
items.d: The charts showed islands and the pattern of waves around them.

items.t: Maya writing was the most developed writing system in the pre-Columbian Americas.
items.d: It was more highly developed than any other known writing system there at that time.

items.t: The Maya used one of the earliest known written zeros.
items.d: Their zero could mark an empty place in a number.

items.t: The Maya kept time with several calendars that fit together.
items.d: Using more than one calendar helped them track the days carefully.

items.t: The Maya grew cacao for members of the elite.
items.d: Cacao is the tree whose seeds people use to make chocolate.

items.t: More than 6 million Maya people are living today.
items.d: Together they speak more than 28 Mayan languages.

items.t: The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, stood on an island in a lake.
items.d: The island was in Lake Texcoco.

items.t: Bridges and causeways linked Tenochtitlan to the mainland.
items.d: A causeway is a raised road that crosses a lake or wet ground.

items.t: Canals criss-crossed the island city of Tenochtitlan.
items.d: The canals worked like watery streets between the buildings.

items.t: Word of the day: chinampa
items.d: A chinampa is a man-made garden plot. Aztec farmers used chinampas to grow food.

items.t: An aqueduct carried fresh spring water to Tenochtitlan.
items.d: An aqueduct is a water channel. This one started at Chapultepec springs.

items.t: Mexico City was built where Tenochtitlan once stood.
items.d: The newer city rose on the ruins of the older Aztec capital.

items.t: Many Aztec people spoke a language called Nahuatl.
items.d: Nahuatl was widely spoken in the Aztec world.

items.t: Cusco was the capital at the heart of the Inca Empire.
items.d: It was the center for running the empire's land and people.

items.t: The official language of the Inca Empire was Quechua.
items.d: An official language is the one used for the empire's main business.

items.t: Word of the day: quipu
items.d: A quipu is a set of knotted strings used to keep records and send messages.

items.t: Inca roads, called the Qhapaq Nan, reached the whole empire.
items.d: This road network reached every corner of the Inca lands.

items.t: The Inca built their empire without wheeled transport or iron tools.
items.d: They had no wheeled carts or iron tools, but their empire still grew huge.

items.t: Word of the day: chuno
items.d: Chuno is potato dried at freezing temperatures.

items.t: Machu Picchu stands on a mountain ridge high above the sea.
items.d: It is about 2,430 meters above sea level (about 7,970 feet).

items.t: Machu Picchu was built around the year 1450.
items.d: It may have been an estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti.

items.t: Machu Picchu has finely crafted dry-stone walls.
items.d: Dry-stone means the builders used no mortar between the stones.

items.t: Machu Picchu's terraces held up the slopes and grew corn.
items.d: These garden steps are called andenes, and corn grew on them.

items.t: In 1911, Hiram Bingham III told the world about Machu Picchu.
items.d: He was an American historian, and his news made the city famous.

items.t: Roald Amundsen and his team of five were the first people to reach the South Pole, on 14 December 1911.
items.d: They had 16 sled dogs with them.

items.t: Amundsen led the first expedition to sail through Canada's Northwest Passage.
items.d: It is an icy sea route through the far north of Canada.

items.t: Roald Amundsen learned to use sled dogs to carry goods across the ice.
items.d: Strong dogs can pull heavy loads over snow, which helped him in the race to the Pole.

items.t: Robert Scott's team reached the South Pole on 17 January 1912 and found the Norwegians had been there first.
items.d: They found Amundsen's tent nearby.

items.t: Three men walked through the Antarctic winter to collect emperor penguin eggs at Cape Crozier.
items.d: Scientists wanted the eggs to learn how penguins grow.

items.t: Apsley Cherry-Garrard called the winter egg trek 'the worst journey in the world'.
items.d: He used those words as the title of his book about the expedition.

items.t: Apsley Cherry-Garrard joined Scott's expedition as an assistant zoologist with no science training.
items.d: A zoologist studies animals.

items.t: Ernest Shackleton named his ship Endurance after his family motto.
items.d: The ship's first name was Polaris.

items.t: Endurance sank in the Weddell Sea on 21 November 1915.
items.d: The Weddell Sea is off the coast of Antarctica.

items.t: Sea ice covers the Weddell Sea all year round.
items.d: It lies off the coast of Antarctica.

items.t: The wreck of the Endurance was found on 5 March 2022.
items.d: It had been lost for more than 100 years.

items.t: The wreck of the Endurance lies about 3,000 metres deep, and it was still in very good shape.
items.d: That is about 3 km down on the seabed.

items.t: Shackleton's crew reached Elephant Island, a remote island where nobody lived and ships rarely came.
items.d: It is near Antarctica.

items.t: Shackleton and five men sailed the small lifeboat James Caird about 1,300 km to South Georgia.
items.d: That is about 800 miles across the Southern Ocean.

items.t: Ernest Shackleton chose Frank Wild as his second-in-command.
items.d: The second-in-command is the person who helps the leader.

items.t: Shackleton brought all the men stranded on Elephant Island home safely.
items.d: The group was rescued without loss of life.

items.t: Marco Polo was born around 1254 in Venice.
items.d: Venice is famous for its canals.

items.t: Marco Polo set off for Asia in 1271 when he was 17, with his father and uncle.
items.d: The trip took them across lands far from home.

items.t: Kublai Khan made Marco Polo a foreign emissary.
items.d: An emissary is someone sent to carry out jobs for a ruler.

items.t: Marco Polo returned to Venice in 1295 after 24 years away.
items.d: He had left when he was a teenager.

items.t: Marco Polo told his travel stories to Rustichello da Pisa, who wrote them down in a book.
items.d: The book is called The Travels of Marco Polo.

items.t: Ferdinand Magellan's fleet had five ships and about 270 men.
items.d: Their goal was to sail across the seas to reach Asia.

items.t: Ferdinand Magellan gave the Pacific Ocean its name.
items.d: Pacific means calm or peaceful.

items.t: Magellan's ship Victoria, led by Juan Sebastian Elcano, finished the trip around the world in 1522.
items.d: Only about 18 or 19 of the first crew got back to Spain.

items.t: Christopher Columbus was born in the Republic of Genoa.
items.d: He later sailed for Spain.

items.t: Columbus left Spain in August 1492 with three ships, the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria.
items.d: Each ship was small compared with ships today.

items.t: Columbus landed on an island in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492.
items.d: It was his first landing in the Americas.

items.t: On 29 May 1953, Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary were the first confirmed to reach the top of Everest.
items.d: Tenzing was a Sherpa mountaineer.

items.t: Expedition leader John Hunt said Hillary and Tenzing reached Everest's top together, as a team.
items.d: He described their achievement as teamwork.

items.t: A 2020 survey by Nepal and China measured Mount Everest at about 8,849 metres tall.
items.d: That is almost 9 km above sea level.

items.t: Mount Everest is named after Sir George Everest, a British surveyor in India.
items.d: A surveyor measures land and mountains.

items.t: The Nepali name for Mount Everest, Sagarmatha, means roughly 'head in the sky'.
items.d: The mountain's peak is very high.

items.t: Challenger Deep is named after HMS Challenger, a British Royal Navy survey ship.
items.d: The ship's crews explored the oceans.

items.t: In January 1960 the submarine Trieste made the first trip down to Challenger Deep.
items.d: Trieste was a deep-diving vessel called a bathyscaphe.

items.t: Challenger Deep is at the southern end of the Mariana Trench and is about 10,935 metres deep.
items.d: That is about 11 km below sea level.

items.t: President Thomas Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark on an expedition soon after the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.
items.d: The purchase gave the US a huge new area of land.

items.t: The Corps of Discovery was a group of soldiers and volunteers led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark.
items.d: They set out in May 1804.

items.t: Lewis's Newfoundland dog, Seaman, was the only animal to finish the whole Lewis and Clark trip.
items.d: Seaman was a big, strong dog.

items.t: The Lewis and Clark team first saw the Pacific Ocean on 7 November 1805.
items.d: They had travelled for about a year and a half to get there.

items.t: Between 1405 and 1433, Zheng He led seven treasure voyages across Asia.
items.d: His fleets sailed from China.

items.t: A giraffe brought to China from Malindi was seen as a qilin, a lucky mythical creature.
items.d: Zheng He's ships carried it home.

items.t: Ibn Battuta set off from Tangier at age 21 and travelled for about 30 years.
items.d: He was born there in 1304 and travelled from 1325 to 1354.

items.t: Ibn Battuta travelled about 117,000 km over about 30 years.
items.d: Earth's distance around is about 40,000 km.

items.t: Hiram Bingham led the 1911 Yale expedition that made Machu Picchu famous around the world.
items.d: A local man, Melchor Arteaga, led him to the site.

items.t: Fridtjof Nansen made the first crossing of Greenland's interior on skis in 1888.
items.d: Greenland is covered by a huge sheet of ice.

items.t: Nansen's ship Fram was frozen into Arctic ice and drifted along with it.
items.d: The plan was to let the moving ice carry the ship.

items.t: Fridtjof Nansen won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922 for helping people made homeless by World War I.
items.d: He was an explorer, and he also helped others.

items.t: Charles Darwin was 22 when he joined HMS Beagle for a voyage that began in December 1831.
items.d: The voyage ended in October 1836.

items.t: The Beagle voyage was planned for about two years, but it lasted almost five.
items.d: It sailed around the world.

items.t: Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
Marie Curie is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
items.d: She won in physics and chemistry.

items.t: In 1903, Marie Curie shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for work on radioactivity.
Marie Curie won a 1911 Nobel Prize for discovering radium and polonium.
Marie Curie named polonium after her homeland, Poland.
The name radium comes from the Latin word for ray.
As a schoolboy, Isaac Newton built sundials and models of windmills.
Newton's book Principia explained laws of motion and gravity in one system.
Newton built the first known working telescope that used a mirror.
items.d: This type is called a reflecting telescope.

items.t: Newton showed that a prism splits white light into visible colors.
Newton helped make British coins more accurate and harder to copy.
Isaac Newton was born on Christmas Day in 1642.
Charles Darwin sailed around the world on HMS Beagle for almost five years.
Young Charles Darwin loved collecting beetles.
Darwin spent years studying barnacles and won the Royal Medal in 1853.
Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.
items.d: The book presented his theory of evolution with evidence.

items.t: Birds Darwin collected in the Galapagos were later identified as 12 finch species.
In 1609, Galileo made a telescope that enlarged objects about three times.
Galileo discovered Jupiter's four largest moons.
Jupiter's four big moons are called Galilean satellites in Galileo's honor.
Galileo saw that Venus has phases like the Moon.
Galileo found that pendulums of the same length keep time together.
Galileo saw mountains and craters on the Moon through his telescope.
Galileo first mistook Saturn's rings for planets.
Jane Goodall began studying wild chimpanzees in Tanzania in 1960.
A chimpanzee called David Greybeard was the first to warm up to Jane Goodall.
Goodall saw chimpanzees make tools from grass stalks to fish for termites.
Goodall gave the chimpanzees names instead of numbers.
Jane Goodall wrote 32 books, including 15 books for children.
Nikola Tesla helped design the modern alternating current electricity system.
items.d: Alternating current is also called AC.

items.t: A Tesla coil makes high-voltage, high-frequency alternating current.
The unit called the tesla measures magnetic flux density.
items.d: It was named in honor of Nikola Tesla.

items.t: Nikola Tesla could do integral calculus in his head.
Tesla showed a radio-controlled boat in 1898.
Einstein won the 1921 Nobel Prize for explaining the photoelectric effect.
Einstein's equation E = mc2 connects mass and energy.
When Einstein was five, his father gave him a compass.
Einstein found his own proof of the Pythagorean theorem before he turned 13.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming saw that mould on a culture plate had cleared nearby bacteria.
items.d: This observation led to penicillin.

items.t: Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine for penicillin.
Fleming discovered lysozyme, a substance that can dissolve some bacteria.
Pasteurization was named after Louis Pasteur.
items.d: It heats food and drink to stop bacterial contamination.

items.t: Louis Pasteur was born in Dole, France, in 1822.
Mary Anning found the first complete Plesiosaurus skeleton in 1823.
Mary Anning found the first pterosaur skeleton discovered outside Germany.
Anning helped show that some mysterious stones were fossilized animal dung.
items.d: Fossilized dung is called a coprolite.

items.t: Michael Faraday first showed electrical energy being changed into motion in 1821.
Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction using wire coils around an iron ring.
Copernicus proposed a model with the Sun, rather than Earth, at the center.
Ada Lovelace's Note G is often called the first published computer program.
In 2014 Malala Yousafzai won the Nobel Peace Prize at age 17.
items.d: She was the youngest person ever to win a Nobel Prize.

items.t: The United Nations called 12 July 2013 Malala Day, her 16th birthday.
items.d: On that day she gave a speech about education for children.

items.t: Malala Yousafzai campaigns for education, especially for girls.
items.d: She also speaks up for children's rights, including the right to learn.

items.t: At 15, Greta Thunberg began a school strike for the climate in Sweden.
items.d: In 2018 she began alone outside parliament, where Sweden's leaders meet.

items.t: Greta Thunberg's strike grew into the worldwide Fridays for Future movement.
items.d: It spread from one solo strike to people in countries around the world.

items.t: In August 2019 Greta Thunberg sailed across the Atlantic to New York.
items.d: She left from Plymouth, England, and the trip ended in New York City.

items.t: In 1930 Gandhi led the Dandi Salt March, a walk of about 400 km.
items.d: About 400 km is about 250 miles. The march protested a British tax on salt.

items.t: Gandhi led India's freedom movement through nonviolent resistance.
items.d: Nonviolent resistance means standing up for change without hurting people.

items.t: Gandhi was first called Mahatma, meaning great-souled, in 1914.
items.d: The title was first used for him in South Africa.

items.t: Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison, starting on Robben Island.
items.d: Robben Island is where his long prison time began.

items.t: Nelson Mandela was set free from prison in 1990.
items.d: President F. W. de Klerk released him that year.

items.t: In 1994 Nelson Mandela became South Africa's first Black head of state.
items.d: A head of state is a country's top leader. He won the first election open to every adult.

items.t: Nelson Mandela received more than 250 honours, including the Nobel Peace Prize.
items.d: A honour is a special award for doing great things. He won more than 250 of them.

items.t: In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery.
items.d: This happened in Montgomery, Alabama. She stayed seated when told to move.

items.t: The Montgomery bus boycott that followed Rosa Parks lasted 381 days.
items.d: A boycott means people join together and stop using something. This one lasted more than a year.

items.t: In 1963 Martin Luther King Jr. gave the 'I Have a Dream' speech.
items.d: He was a leader of the March on Washington, where he gave that speech.

items.t: Martin Luther King Jr. won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.
items.d: He was honoured for fighting racial inequality with nonviolent resistance.

items.t: The US holiday for Martin Luther King Jr. was first observed in 1986.
items.d: The holiday honours his nonviolent work against racial inequality.

items.t: Kailash Satyarthi shared the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize with Malala Yousafzai.
items.d: Sharing a prize means both people were honoured together that year.

items.t: Kailash Satyarthi started Bachpan Bachao Andolan to protect children.
items.d: The name means Save Childhood Movement. It works to keep children safe.

items.t: Kailash Satyarthi's team freed over 138,000 children in India from child labour.
items.d: Child labour means children are forced to work. His team helps them become free.

items.t: In 1980 India gave Mother Teresa the Bharat Ratna, its highest civilian award.
items.d: A civilian award is for people who are not in the military. This is India's top one.

items.t: Mother Teresa won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.
items.d: She was honoured for her work to overcome poverty and distress.

items.t: In 1977 Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement to plant trees.
items.d: It is a group that cares for nature. Its main work is planting trees.

items.t: In 2004 Wangari Maathai became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
items.d: No African woman had received the Nobel Peace Prize before her.

items.t: Wangari Maathai was the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a PhD.
items.d: A PhD, or Doctor of Philosophy, is one of the highest university degrees.

items.t: In 1913 Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
items.d: He was the first non-European, and the first Indian, to win any Nobel Prize.

items.t: Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
items.d: He wrote the words and composed the music for both countries' special songs.

items.t: Rabindranath Tagore founded Visva-Bharati University.
items.d: A university is a school for older students. He created this one.

items.t: Mary Kom won an Olympic bronze medal in boxing at London 2012.
items.d: Flyweight is a boxing group based on weight. Her medal came in that event.

items.t: Mary Kom has won the World Amateur Boxing Championship six times.
items.d: She grew up in rural Manipur, India, then became a world champion boxer.

items.t: At Tokyo 2020, Neeraj Chopra's javelin throw of 87.58 m won gold.
items.d: A javelin is a long spear. Athletes try to throw it as far as they can.

items.t: Neeraj Chopra was the first Indian to win Olympic gold in athletics.
items.d: Athletics means track and field events, like running, jumping, and throwing.

items.t: Sachin Tendulkar played his first Test cricket match in 1989, at age 16.
items.d: A Test is a long cricket match between countries. His was against Pakistan on 15 November 1989.

items.t: Sachin Tendulkar scored 100 centuries in international cricket.
items.d: A century means 100 runs in one innings. He did that 100 times for India.

items.t: Sachin Tendulkar was part of India's 2011 Cricket World Cup winning team.
items.d: Across six World Cups for India, this was his first win.

items.t: P. V. Sindhu is the first Indian woman to win two Olympic medals.
items.d: She won badminton silver at Rio 2016 and bronze at Tokyo 2020.

items.t: In 2019 Sindhu was the first Indian to win gold at the badminton World Championships.
items.d: She won gold at the World Championships, the big world badminton contest.

items.t: B. R. Ambedkar led the committee that wrote India's Constitution.
items.d: A constitution is the basic set of rules for a country.

items.t: Savitribai Phule is widely regarded as India's first woman teacher.
items.d: Widely regarded means many people agree she was the first.

items.t: In 1848 Savitribai Phule helped found a school for girls at Bhide Wada, Pune.
items.d: Bhide Wada is the place in Pune where that girls' school began.

items.t: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery on 17 September 1849.
items.d: Slavery means people were owned and forced to work. She got herself free.

items.t: Harriet Tubman made about 13 trips and rescued about 70 enslaved people.
items.d: She went back again and again so others could reach freedom too.

items.t: Helen Keller lost her sight and hearing from illness at 19 months old.
items.d: She was younger than two. The illness left her unable to see or hear.

items.t: Anne Sullivan was Helen Keller's teacher and lifelong companion.
items.d: A companion is someone who stays with you. Anne taught Helen and stayed.

items.t: In 1904 Helen Keller earned a college degree at Radcliffe.
items.d: She was the first person who was deaf and blind to earn a Bachelor of Arts.

items.t: Jesse Owens won four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics.
items.d: He won the 100 m, the 200 m, the long jump, and the 4x100 m relay.

items.t: Most of Frida Kahlo's paintings are small pictures of herself.
items.d: These are called self-portraits. She painted them at a small size.

items.t: Frida Kahlo's family home, La Casa Azul, is now a museum.
items.d: La Casa Azul means the Blue House. It is the Frida Kahlo Museum.

items.t: In 1960 Ruby Bridges, age six, was the first African American child at William Frantz Elementary.
items.d: The school is in New Orleans. U.S. marshals walked with her to school each day.

items.t: Atoms are incredibly tiny, about 100 picometers across.
items.d: That is far too small to see, even with a normal microscope.

items.t: Every atom has a nucleus in the middle, made of protons and usually neutrons.
items.d: Tiny electrons form a swarm around it.

items.t: Almost all of an atom's mass is packed into its tiny nucleus.
items.d: The swarm of electrons around it weighs very little.

items.t: Protons have a positive charge, and neutrons have no charge at all.
items.d: Electrons are negative.

items.t: Hydrogen atoms have one proton. Oganesson atoms have 118 protons.
items.d: The number of protons tells you which element it is.

items.t: Mendeleev used his periodic table to predict properties of elements not yet found.
items.d: He left gaps for them and guessed their properties.

items.t: There are 118 known elements. The first 94 occur naturally on Earth.
items.d: The rest are made by scientists.

items.t: The noble gases sit in group 18. They were not found yet when Mendeleev made his table.
items.d: Helium and neon are noble gases.

items.t: An element's atomic number is the number of protons in its nucleus.
items.d: Carbon has 6 protons, so its atomic number is 6.

items.t: Elements in the same group of the periodic table tend to behave in similar ways.
items.d: That is why the table is so useful to chemists.

items.t: In a solid, particles cannot move around freely. They only jiggle in place.
items.d: That is why a rock keeps its shape.

items.t: A liquid takes the shape of its container, and it is almost impossible to squash.
items.d: Juice fills a cup, then fills a bottle the same way.

items.t: Liquids are very hard to squash, but gases can be squashed. Gas molecules are far apart.
items.d: A bike pump squeezes air into a smaller space.

items.t: Plasma forms when it is so hot that electrons break away from their atoms.
items.d: It is a fourth state of matter, after solid, liquid and gas.

items.t: About 99% of ordinary matter in the universe is plasma.
items.d: Here on Earth, solids, liquids and gases are far more common.

items.t: Stars are almost pure balls of plasma.
items.d: Our Sun is one of them.

items.t: Lightning and glowing neon signs both contain plasma.
Pure water is neutral. It has a pH of 7 at 25 degrees Celsius.
items.d: Acids are below 7 and bases are above 7.

items.t: Lemon juice tastes sour because it has citric acid. Its pH is about 2.2.
items.d: Its low pH means the juice is acidic.

items.t: Each step on the pH scale is a tenfold change in hydrogen ions.
items.d: A liquid at pH 3 has ten times more hydrogen ions than one at pH 4.

items.t: Red cabbage and hibiscus flowers contain pigments that work as natural pH indicators.
items.d: They change color depending on how acidic a liquid is.

items.t: When an acid reacts with a base, it is called neutralization. The products are a salt and water.
Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate. It is not the same thing as baking powder.
items.d: They are different kitchen ingredients.

items.t: Quartz sand, also called silica, is the main raw material for making glass.
items.d: Beach sand and glass are close relatives.

items.t: Glass is an amorphous solid. Its atoms are not in a neat repeating pattern.
items.d: A salt crystal is neat. Glass is more jumbled.

items.t: Borosilicate glass resists cracking when its temperature changes suddenly.
items.d: Handy for glass dishes that go in a hot oven.

items.t: Obsidian is natural glass from volcanoes. It breaks into very sharp edges.
items.d: People long ago used it to make cutting tools.

items.t: Lightning striking sand can melt it into glass shaped like branching roots.
items.d: These are called fulgurites.

items.t: Plastics are materials made mainly of polymers.
The first fully synthetic plastic was invented in New York in 1907.
Thermoplastics can be heated and reshaped again and again without changing chemically.
The word plastic comes from a Greek word meaning able to be shaped or molded.
A mixture has two or more substances that can be separated by physical methods.
items.d: You can pick raisins out of a trail mix.

items.t: Mixtures can be separated by filtering, freezing, or distilling.
items.d: A coffee filter separates grounds from liquid.

items.t: In a chemical reaction, the amount of each element stays the same. Atoms just rearrange.
items.d: Nothing is lost. Atoms are not created or destroyed.

items.t: Reactions that release heat are exothermic. Reactions that absorb heat are endothermic.
items.d: Burning a candle gives out heat.

items.t: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up, so it can work again.
Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. These are called isotopes.
items.d: Carbon always has 6 protons, but not always the same neutrons.

items.t: Only two elements are liquid at 0 degrees Celsius: bromine and mercury.
Hydrogen and helium, the lightest elements, were made in the Big Bang.
Gold's chemical symbol, Au, comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold.
Gold is the most malleable metal. One gram can be beaten into a sheet of one square meter.
items.d: That sheet would be thinner than a hair.

items.t: Helium is the second most common element in the observable universe, after hydrogen.
Oxygen gas makes up about 21% of Earth's atmosphere.
items.d: Most of the rest is nitrogen.

items.t: The oxygen in Earth's air is made by photosynthesis.
items.d: Plants, algae and some bacteria release it.

items.t: Diamond is a form of the element carbon, with atoms in a crystal pattern.
items.d: Pencil graphite is also made of carbon.

items.t: Volcanic eruptions carried diamonds up to the surface, inside rocks called kimberlites.
Light travels about 300,000 km every second through empty space.
items.d: In one second, light could travel around Earth more than seven times.

items.t: Sunlight takes a little over 8 minutes to reach Earth.
items.d: The sunlight you see began its trip more than 8 minutes ago.

items.t: Light moves more slowly through water or glass than through empty space.
Water droplets split, bend, and reflect sunlight to make a rainbow.
In a main rainbow, red is outside and violet is inside.
A double rainbow has a faint second arc with its colours reversed.
Every rainbow is really a full circle.
items.d: From the ground, you usually see only the upper part of the circle.

items.t: To see a rainbow, look for water ahead with the low Sun behind you.
A glass prism can split white light into a spectrum of colours.
A prism bends blue light more than red light.
The daytime sky looks blue because air scatters blue light more than red light.
Sunsets look red because much of the blue light has scattered away.
items.d: Light from a low Sun travels through a longer path of air.

items.t: William Herschel discovered invisible infrared light in 1800.
People give off infrared light that thermal cameras can detect.
Remote controls commonly use infrared light to command appliances.
Infrared is often called heat radiation.
Sound travels through air at about 343 metres per second at 20°C.
Sound travels faster in water than in air.
items.d: In fresh water at 20°C, it travels about 1,481 metres per second.

items.t: Sound travels faster through warm air than through cold air.
An echo is a sound that bounces off a surface and returns a moment later.
A clear echo needs a reflecting surface more than about 17 metres from the sound source.
Bats, dolphins, and whales use echoes to navigate.
items.d: This way of locating things is called echolocation.

items.t: Sonar technology finds things by using echoes.
A passing siren sounds higher as it approaches and lower as it moves away.
items.d: This change in pitch is called the Doppler effect.

items.t: People typically hear sounds from about 20 to 20,000 hertz.
items.d: Hertz measures how many sound vibrations happen each second.

items.t: Dogs can hear pitches up to about 45,000 hertz, much higher than people can.
Some bats can hear pitches as high as 200,000 hertz.
A freely falling object speeds up by about 9.8 metres per second each second.
items.d: This is what happens when air resistance is ignored.

items.t: You would weigh about 0.5% more at the poles than at the equator.
items.d: Earth's gravity is slightly stronger near the poles.

items.t: Gravity near the space station is almost 90% as strong as it is on the ground.
items.d: Astronauts float because they and the station are falling around Earth together.

items.t: Friction is a force that resists surfaces sliding against each other.
Friction can change movement energy into heat.
items.d: Rubbing two surfaces together can make them warmer.

items.t: Oil and other lubricants reduce friction between surfaces.
Break a bar magnet in two, and each piece has a north and south pole.
Opposite magnetic poles attract each other.
items.d: A north pole and a south pole pull together.

items.t: A compass needle is a magnet that lines up with Earth's magnetic field.
Iron, nickel, and cobalt are strongly attracted to magnets.
The six simple machines include the lever, pulley, wedge, screw, wheel and axle, and inclined plane.
Simple machines change the size or direction of a force to make jobs easier.
An object stays still or moves in a straight line at a steady speed unless a force acts on it.
items.d: This idea is Newton's first law of motion.

items.t: Force equals mass times acceleration.
items.d: This rule is Newton's second law of motion, often written as F = ma.

items.t: When two things push on each other, their forces are equal and opposite.
items.d: This idea is Newton's third law of motion.

items.t: Water pushes up on an object with a force equal to the weight of water it displaces.
items.d: This is called Archimedes' principle.

items.t: Steel ships float because their air-filled shape makes them less dense overall than water.
Heat naturally flows from a hotter object to a colder object.
Metals such as copper and gold conduct heat well.
Air conducts heat poorly, so trapped air can act as insulation.
Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving.
If the same object doubles its speed, it has four times as much kinetic energy.
Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two numbers before it.
items.d: It starts 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Next comes 8 + 13 = 21.

items.t: Fibonacci used the sequence to count an imaginary family of growing rabbits.
items.d: In the story, a new pair grows up in one month, then has a new pair every month.

items.t: Fibonacci introduced this sequence to Western Europe in his 1202 book, Liber Abaci.
items.d: Western European mathematicians learned the pattern from that book.

items.t: Ratios of Fibonacci numbers get closer and closer to about 1.618.
items.d: 13 divided by 8 is 1.625. 21 divided by 13 is about 1.615.

items.t: Sunflower seed spirals often use counts that sit next to each other in Fibonacci's list.
items.d: The clockwise count and the counterclockwise count are usually a neighboring pair.

items.t: Zero is an even number because it is a multiple of 2.
items.d: 2 x 0 = 0. Zero is neither prime nor composite.

items.t: You cannot divide by zero. Ordinary arithmetic gives no answer.
items.d: If 12 divided by 0 had an answer, 0 times that answer would be 12. But 0 times any number is 0.

items.t: The place-value zero we use was developed in India. Its name, shunya, means void.
items.d: In 205 the 0 holds an empty tens place: two hundreds, no tens, and five ones.

items.t: The Maya used zero in their numbers and calendar, on their own.
items.d: They developed it separately from the Old World.

items.t: In ancient Babylon a mark showed an empty place, but it was not treated as a number.
items.d: Their numbers were grouped by 60s. The mark held a column open.

items.t: 2 is the only even prime. Every other even number can be divided by 2.
items.d: 6 = 2 x 3, so 6 is not prime. The only factors of 2 are 1 and 2.

items.t: Around 300 BC, Euclid proved that the prime numbers go on forever.
items.d: No list of primes can be the full list. There is always another one.

items.t: Every whole number above 1 is prime, or primes multiplied in only one way.
items.d: 30 = 2 x 3 x 5. You may swap the order, but the primes stay the same.

items.t: The sieve of Eratosthenes finds primes by crossing out multiples.
items.d: Up to 30, the primes left are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 and 29.

items.t: The golden ratio is about 1.618. Its digits never end and never repeat.
items.d: A closer start is 1.618033988, and the digits keep going with no repeating block.

items.t: In a regular pentagon, the diagonal divided by a side is the golden ratio.
items.d: A side of 10 cm gives a diagonal of about 16.18 cm, since 10 x 1.618 = 16.18.

items.t: Many popular claims about the golden ratio in art are exaggerated.
items.d: A study of 565 paintings found artists usually did not use it to pick canvas sizes.

items.t: At age 19, Gauss proved a regular 17-sided shape can be drawn with compass and straightedge.
items.d: It was the first discovery of this kind in over 2,000 years.

items.t: A famous story says young Gauss added 1 through 100 quickly and got 5,050.
items.d: Pair 1 with 100 up to 50 with 51. Each pair is 101, and 50 x 101 = 5,050.

items.t: Ramanujan taught himself much of his advanced maths with only a few books.
items.d: He was born in Erode, India, in 1887.

items.t: In 1913 Ramanujan wrote to G. H. Hardy, who invited him to England.
items.d: Hardy, a Cambridge mathematician, saw original ideas in the letter.

items.t: 1,729 is the smallest number that is the sum of two positive cubes in two different ways.
items.d: 1 cubed plus 12 cubed is 1,729. So is 9 cubed plus 10 cubed.

items.t: A hexagon has six sides, and honeycomb cells are hexagons.
items.d: Regular hexagons can cover a flat surface with no gaps.

items.t: In a regular hexagon, each side equals the radius of the circle around it.
items.d: If that radius is 4 cm, every side is 4 cm too.

items.t: Each inside angle of a regular hexagon is 120 degrees.
items.d: Its inside angles total 720 degrees. Since all six are equal, 720 divided by 6 is 120.

items.t: Saturn has a giant hexagon-shaped cloud pattern around its north pole.
items.d: A six-sided shape from geometry also shows up in those clouds.

items.t: In a group of just 23 people, two share a birthday about half the time.
items.d: The chance is about 50.7 percent. Those 23 people make 253 pairs.

items.t: With 70 people, the chance that two share a birthday is about 99.9 percent.
items.d: The chance grows from about half at 23 people to nearly sure at 70.

items.t: Pi is about 3.14159. It is a circle's distance around, divided by its diameter.
items.d: The digits never end or repeat. Using 3.14, diameter 10 cm gives 10 x 3.14 = 31.4 cm.

items.t: William Jones first used the letter pi for this number in 1706.
items.d: Leonhard Euler helped make the symbol popular in 1736 and in 1748.

items.t: Old estimates for pi include 25/8 in Babylon and about 3.16 in Egypt.
items.d: 25 divided by 8 equals 3.125. Pi is about 3.1416, so both estimates were close.

items.t: There are exactly five Platonic solids, with 4, 6, 8, 12 and 20 faces.
items.d: Euclid showed these are the only regular convex solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron.

items.t: NASA's JPL uses 15 decimal places of pi for its most accurate space maths.
items.d: That value is 3.141592653589793, used for travel between planets.

items.t: 38 digits of pi measure a universe-wide circle to about a hydrogen atom's width.
items.d: That is 37 places after the point, plus the 3 in front.

items.t: With 96-sided polygons, Archimedes placed pi between 3 plus 10/71 and 3 plus 1/7.
items.d: 3 plus 10/71 is about 3.1408. 3 plus 1/7 is about 3.1429. Pi lies between them.

items.t: A sphere's volume is two thirds of the tight cylinder around it.
items.d: Archimedes proved this. The sphere's surface area is two thirds of that cylinder's too.

items.t: On a lever, weights balance when weight times distance matches on both sides.
items.d: A 2 kg weight 3 m from the pivot balances 6 kg at 1 m, because 2 x 3 = 6 x 1.

items.t: In a right triangle, the two short sides squared add up to the long side squared.
5, 12 and 13 fit a right triangle too. They are a Pythagorean triple.
Babylonians knew the right-triangle rule about 1800 BC, long before Pythagoras.
items.d: The clay tablet Plimpton 322 lists many whole-number triples that fit the rule.

items.t: There are hundreds of different proofs of the Pythagorean theorem.
items.d: One book, The Pythagorean Proposition, gathers 370 proofs.

items.t: A Mobius strip has only one side and only one edge.
items.d: A finger can trace the whole surface and return without crossing an edge.

items.t: Make a Mobius strip by giving paper a half twist, then joining the ends.
items.d: A half twist turns one end by 180 degrees before you tape the ends.

items.t: Cut a Mobius strip along its middle and you get one longer loop, not two pieces.
items.d: That new loop has four half twists.

items.t: A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros.
items.d: It is 10 to the power of 100: one hundred 10s multiplied together.

items.t: Nine-year-old Milton Sirotta invented the word googol in 1920.
items.d: He was the nephew of the mathematician Edward Kasner.

items.t: In a magic square, every row, column and both main diagonals add to the same number.
items.d: The Lo Shu, from a Chinese turtle legend, is a 3 by 3 square whose lines each sum to 15.

items.t: In Pascal's triangle, each number is the sum of the two numbers just above it.
items.d: Each row adds to a power of 2: 1, then 2, then 4, then 8, doubling each time.

items.t: Four colors are enough for any flat map so regions sharing a side differ.
items.d: People noticed this in 1852. Appel and Haken proved it in 1976 with a computer.

items.t: The first four perfect numbers are 6, 28, 496 and 8128.
items.d: 6 = 1 + 2 + 3. And 28 = 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14. The ancient Greeks knew these four.

items.t: Ada Lovelace wrote steps for a machine to calculate special numbers. Many call it the first published program.
items.d: Her notes were published in 1843.

items.t: Ada Lovelace imagined that a machine might one day make music, not just do sums.
items.d: She wrote this in the 1840s, long before any modern computer existed.

items.t: Ada Lovelace added notes to an article about a machine. Her notes were three times longer than the article.
ENIAC, finished in 1945, was a giant computer that weighed about 27 tonnes.
items.d: That is heavier than about five elephants.

items.t: ENIAC used about 18,000 glass parts called vacuum tubes to do its sums.
items.d: Today a tiny chip does far more with no glowing tubes at all.

items.t: Six women programmed ENIAC.
items.d: They included Kay McNulty, Betty Jean Jennings and Betty Holberton.

items.t: Computers use binary, a number system with only two digits: 0 and 1.
items.d: Counting in binary goes 0, 1, 10, 11, 100.

items.t: A single binary digit is called a bit. The word is short for binary digit.
In binary, 101 means 4 + 0 + 1, which is 5.
items.d: Each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on.

items.t: Computers use binary because two states, like on and off, are easy to build with electric circuits.
items.d: A switch is either on (1) or off (0).

items.t: A byte is usually a group of eight bits.
items.d: Computer memory is often counted in bytes.

items.t: One byte can hold 256 different values, from 0 to 255.
items.d: That is because 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 256.

items.t: In 1947, a real moth was found stuck in a computer relay and taped into the team's log book.
items.d: The team jokingly called it the first actual bug they had found.

items.t: Grace Hopper is often credited with creating the first compiler, a tool that translates computer code.
Grace Hopper helped create COBOL, a programming language that reads a bit like English.
items.d: She was nicknamed Grandma COBOL.

items.t: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 while he worked at a science lab called CERN.
The very first website went online in December 1990. It explained the web project itself.
The World Wide Web was given away free. It had no patent and no fees, so anyone could use it.
The web and the Internet are not the same. The web is a system of linked pages built on the Internet.
items.d: The Internet is the network of wires and computers underneath.

items.t: The first message sent over ARPANET in 1969 was just 'lo'. The computer crashed after two letters of 'login'.
